lessons.title: 73. Ch 2 · Grammar B: honorifics
lessons.subtitle: 연세 · 성함 · 님 · 계시다 · 드시다 · -(으)시-

explanations.title: Four ways to express honorifics
explanations.body:
In Korean, when you talk about a person who is superior in status, you use honorifics to show the superiority of the subject. Honorifics can be expressed in four ways:

1. A few special nouns in place of regular nouns, for example 연세 instead of 나이 for “age” and 성함 instead of 이름 for “name”.
2. The honorific suffix 님 attached to a noun or title, for example 선생님, 병장님.
3. A few special verbs in place of regular verbs, for example 계시다 instead of 있다 and 드시다 instead of 먹다 for “to eat”.
4. The honorific infix –(으)시 attached to a verb, for example 이시다, 되시다, 안녕하시다.

The special nouns and special verbs are all listed in the dictionary, because they are completely different from their regular counterparts; the book’s glossary marks them with the upward arrow ↑.

rows: not to exist; not to possess
tables.title: Special nouns, the suffix 님 and special verbs

explanations.title: The honorific infix –(으)시
explanations.body: The infix –(으)시 goes between the verb stem and the verb ending: verb stem + (으)시 + verb ending. After a stem that ends in a consonant it is 으시; after a stem that ends in a vowel it is 시. With the formal ending ㅂ니다 the ㅂ attaches to 시, so 일하 + 시 + ㅂ니다 is said 일하십니다.

rows: The stem ends in a consonant
읽다 → 읽 + 으시 + ㅂ니다; 많다 → 많 + 으시 + ㅂ니다
The stem ends in a vowel
이다 → 이 + 시 + ㅂ니다; 일하다 → 일하 + 시 + ㅂ니다

lessons.title: 75. Ch 2 · Grammar C: the informal speech style -아요 / -어요
lessons.subtitle: 좋아요 · 있어요 · 가요 · 와요 · 해요 · 이에요 / 예요 · -(으)세요

explanations.title: The informal polite style
explanations.body: The informal speech style, marked by the verb ending –아/어요, is the most widely used in spoken Korean. It is used when the speaker (or writer) is in a casual yet polite relationship with the person addressed, so it is also called informal polite speech or informal-high speech. Unlike the formal ending –ㅂ/습니다 from Chapter 1, you can use –아/어요 for a statement, a question, a command or request, and even a suggestion without changing its form. Intonation and context tell you which one is meant.

rows: The last syllable of the stem has the vowel ㅏ or ㅗ
The last syllable of the stem has any other vowel

explanations.title: When the stem ends in a vowel: deletion and contraction
explanations.body:
When 아/어요 is added to a stem that ends in a vowel (가 in 가다), a deletion or contraction occurs:

• stem ends in ㅏ or ㅓ: the 아 or 어 is deleted (가 + 아요 → 가요; 서 + 어요 → 서요).
• stem ends in ㅡ and is one syllable: the ㅡ is deleted and –어요 is attached (크 + 어요 → 커요).
• stem ends in ㅡ and has more than one syllable: the ㅡ is deleted and –아요 or –어요 is attached, depending on the vowel before ㅡ (바쁘 + 아요 → 바빠요; 슬프 + 어요 → 슬퍼요).
• contraction: 오 + 아요 → 와요 (ㅗ + ㅏ = ㅘ); 다니 + 어요 → 다녀요 (ㅣ + ㅓ = ㅕ).
• 하다 is the only verb with a stem in ㅏ that behaves differently: 하 + 아요 → 해요; 공부하 + 아요 → 공부해요; 일하다 → 일해요.

explanations.title: ~이다 and the honorific infix
explanations.body:
~이다 is the only verb that behaves this way: after a noun that ends in a consonant it is 이에요; after a noun that ends in a vowel 이에요 can contract to 예요 (학생이다 → 학생이에요; 의사이다 → 의사예요).

When you add the honorific infix –(으)시 (page “Honorifics”), 어요 has to follow, and (으)시어요 contracts to (으)세요: 계시 + 어요 → 계세요; 하시 + 어요 → 하세요.

lessons.title: 76. Ch 2 · Grammar D: connecting clauses with -고
lessons.subtitle: 저는 군인이고 친구는 학생입니다 · stem + 고

explanations.title: The conjunctive ending -고
explanations.body:
In English, when we connect two or more clauses we use connecting words (conjunctions) such as and, or, because, when, before. In Korean, we use verb endings attached to the stem of a verb, called conjunctive or connective endings. Throughout the course you will learn quite a few of them, and the very first is –고, which means “and”.

In 저는 군인이고 친구는 학생입니다, 고 is attached to the stem of the verb 이다 in the first clause, so the whole sentence is “I am a serviceman and my friend is a student.”

explanations.body:
Recall the objectives of the chapter and ask yourself whether you have achieved them (the book asks you to tick Yes or No). If you tick “No” for any item, the book suggests: review that section on your own; find a study partner and review it as a pair or group; and tell your academic advisor or team leader which areas you need more help with so they can offer other activities tailored to your learning style and needs.

Now I am able to: talk about family members using Korean kinship terms; ask for and give biographical information such as age, jobs and marital status.

Now I have a clear understanding of: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary section; native Korean numerals and counters; the verbs expressing possession, 있다 (to have) and 없다 (not to have); honorifics; the informal speech style verb ending 아요/어요; the conjunctive ending –고; and the Sino-Korean syllables 남 (男) and 여 (女).

lessons.title: 79. Ch 3 · Topic A: Rooms and houses
lessons.subtitle: 영수 씨 집에는 방이 몇 개 있어요? · 방 · 거실 · 부엌 · 층 · ~하다

explanations.title: What Chapter 3 teaches (우리 집)
explanations.body:
Chapter 3, “My House”, has three topic presentations, four grammar points (the book’s Topic C has its own two: the object marker and ~에서), activities, a self-evaluation and the core vocabulary.

When you finish the chapter you will be able to: talk about the layout of a house; talk about the location of objects in relation to each other; describe objects using size and colors; and talk about typical daily activities in specific locations.

You will become familiar with: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; the verbs that express existence, ~에 있다 and ~에 없다; the demonstratives 이, 그 and 저; the object marker ~을/를; the location marker that works with action verbs, ~에서; and the Sino-Korean syllables 색 (色), 식 (食) and 실 (室).

explanations.title: Vocabulary strategy: understand the “verb maker” ~하다
explanations.body:
Korean has borrowed a large number of Chinese words as well as words from other languages, and many have become an integral part of the vocabulary. Most of these borrowed words are nouns and cannot be used as verbs as they are. To use them as verbs we add 하다. 하다, literally “to do”, readily turns borrowed words into verbs. For example, 식사 (食事) is a Sino-Korean word meaning “meal” or “eating”; adding 하다 gives the verb 식사하다, “to eat” or “to dine”. Another example is the borrowed English word 골프 (golf): adding 하다 turns it into a verb phrase meaning “to play golf”.

The book gives six Sino-Korean nouns and nine English loan words and asks you to make them into verbs and guess the meanings; the verbs and meanings below are my key.

rows: to eat a meal; to dine
tables.title: Sino-Korean nouns

explanations.title: 하다 with pure Korean words, and the object marker
explanations.body: The “verb maker” 하다 also works well with many pure Korean words (설거지하다, 일하다, 밥하다). When 하다 turns a noun into an action verb, as in 공부하다 (to study) and 이메일하다 (to email), the object marker ~을/를 can be inserted between the noun and 하다. In spoken language, however, the object marker is usually left out. Both of these are correct:

explanations.body: In the dialog the counter 개 counts things (방이 네 개, 화장실은 두 개) and 층 means “floor”. lessons.title: 81. Ch 3 · Grammar A: ~에 있다 and ~에 없다 (existence at a place)
lessons.subtitle: 제 동생이 뉴욕에 있어요 · 계세요 · 학교가 몬트레이에 있어요

explanations.title: Verbs that express existence
explanations.body:
In Chapter 2 you learned that Koreans use 있다 and 없다 to express possession, as in 나는 아이파드가 있어요 (I have an iPod). The literal meanings are “As for me, an iPod exists” and “doesn’t exist”, because the verbs literally mean “to exist” and “not to exist”. So Koreans also use these verbs to say that an object or a person is or is not at a certain place. The location marker ~에 (in 기숙사에, 뉴욕에) can be translated “at”, “on” or “in”.

When you speak of the location of a person of higher status, such as your teacher, commander, parents or grandparents, use 계시다 ↑ and 안 계시다 ↑ instead of 있다 and 없다.

explanations.title: Word order and nuance
explanations.body:
In Korean it is easy to tell how nouns are used because they are followed by markers (subject, object, topic, location). In 우리 학교가 몬트레이에 있어요 you can tell the functions of 우리 학교 and 몬트레이 from the subject marker 가 and the location marker 에, so you can re-position the two nouns without changing the meaning: 우리 학교가 몬트레이에 있어요 / 몬트레이에 우리 학교가 있어요 (My school is in Monterey).

Occasionally, re-positioning the subject and the location changes the nuance: 학교가 몬트레이에 있어요 means “The school is in Monterey”, but 몬트레이에 학교가 있어요 means “There is a school in Monterey”. When an unspecified noun such as 학교 (school), 사람 (people) or 초콜렛 (chocolate) is the subject in the first configuration, it is read as “the ~”; when it comes after the location, as in the second, it is read as “a ~”.

lessons.title: 82. Ch 3 · Grammar B: the demonstratives 이, 그 and 저
lessons.subtitle: 이 책상 · 그 책상 · 저 책상 · 이것 · 그것 · 저것 · 이건 · 이게

explanations.title: Three demonstratives
explanations.body:
Demonstratives are the words used to point to an object or a person in sight, as in “this book/man” or “that book/man over there”. Korean has three: 이, 그 and 저.

이 refers to an object or person near the speaker; 그 refers to an object or person near the listener but away from the speaker; 저 refers to an object or person away from both the speaker and the listener. 그 can also refer to something or someone out of sight which both the speaker and the listener know about, or which has been mentioned before.

rows: Near the listener, away from the speaker
Away from both the speaker and the listener

explanations.title: How they are used
explanations.body: English demonstratives can be pronouns (“I bought these”), adjectives (“I wore that dress”) or even adverbs (“The fish was this big”). Korean demonstratives are used mainly as adjectives that modify nouns, so 이, 그 and 저 are usually followed by the noun being modified (이 책, 저 선생님, 그 컴퓨터). Used alone as “this thing”, the forms are 이것 (이거), 그것 (그거) and 저것 (저거). 것 is often shortened to 거 in informal speech; there is no space between the demonstrative and 것/거.

explanations.title: Contracted forms
explanations.body: With the markers 은 and 이, 이것 / 그것 / 저것 have contracted forms.

explanations.title: Object markers 을 / 를
explanations.body: The object marker 을 or 를 is placed after a noun to mark it as the object of a verb (in “He drove a truck”, “a truck” is the object of “drove”). 을 goes after a noun that ends in a consonant; 를 goes after a noun that ends in a vowel.

lessons.title: 85. Ch 3 · Grammar D: the location marker ~에서 with action verbs
lessons.subtitle: 도서관에 있어요 · 도서관에서 공부해요 · 방에서 음악을 들어요

explanations.title: ~에 or ~에서?
explanations.body:
Recall that the location marker 에 is used with 있다 or 없다 and is translated “at”, “on” or “in”. There is one more location marker with the same meaning: 에서. While ~에 is used with 있다, 없다 and 계시다 (the honorific form of 있다), ~에서 is for action verbs.

In 저는 도서관에 있어요 (I am in the library) 에 goes with 있어요; in 저는 도서관에서 공부해요 (I study in the library) 에서 goes with 공부해요, which is an action verb.

units.title: Semester 1 · Unit 1 · Chapter 4: My Life at DLI (DLI 생활)

lessons.title: 88. Ch 4 · Topic A: Facilities, countries and languages
lessons.subtitle: 저희 학교를 소개하겠습니다 · 도서관 · 우체국 · 기숙사 · 한국어 · 관 · 장 · 국 · 어 · 인

explanations.title: What Chapter 4 teaches (DLI 생활)
explanations.body:
Chapter 4, “My Life at DLI”, has three topic presentations, four grammar points, activities, a self-evaluation and the core vocabulary.

When you finish the chapter you will be able to: describe the locations of the DLI facilities using spatial terms; comprehend and respond to simple classroom instructions; and ask for and give directions.

You will become familiar with: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; the polite request/command forms -(으)세요 and -지 마세요; ㄹ irregular verbs; the direction/destination marker (으)로 (toward; to); the attributive form of a stative verb -(으)ㄴ; and the Sino-Korean syllables 관 (館), 장 (場), 국 (國), 어 (語) and 인 (人).

explanations.title: Vocabulary strategy: use the words you already know
explanations.body:
In the past three chapters you have acquired quite a few words and a few strategies. Use the words you already know as a point of reference instead of rote memorization. The book gives three examples:

1. 식당 “a restaurant; a cafeteria”. You learned the Sino-Korean 식 (食), eating, meal, food, in Chapter 3, and words that contain it, such as 식사하다 (to have a meal) and 음식 (food). Since 식당 is a place for having a meal, you can figure out the meaning of 당 and easily recall 식당.
2. 교실 “a classroom”. Recall 실 (室), a room, as in 침실 and 거실. You have not learned the Sino-Korean 교 yet, but you have seen it in 학교 (a school). So it is easier to construct and remember the meaning of 교실.
3. 사거리 “an intersection; a crossroads”. 사 (four) is one of the numbers you learned in Chapter 2. An intersection is a point where two streets cross, forming a four-way junction, so you can guess that 거리 is a way, street or road. Since you know what 사 and 거리 mean, you can tell what 삼거리 and 오거리 mean.

Language is a system in which the same patterns occur repeatedly.

explanations.title: 어 (語) and 말
explanations.body:
1. Both 어 (語) and 말 refer to a language or a word. 어 is a Sino-Korean word and must be used as part of another word, as in 한국어 and 중국어. In contrast, the pure Korean word 말 can stand alone. 어 is usually “language” or “word”; 말 can be language, word, speech, utterance or talk, depending on the context.
2. ~말 can be interchangeable with ~어, as in 일본어 / 일본말, 중국어 / 중국말, 한국어 / 한국말.
3. When 어 is preceded by a Sino-Korean country name such as 일본어, 중국어, 불란서어 and 러시아어, often the rest of the syllables of the country name (except the first syllable) are dropped: 독(일)어 → 독어, 일(본)어 → 일어, 불(란서)어 → 불어. Note that ~말 is not interchangeable with ~어 in shortened forms.

explanations.title: Pronunciation guide: a final consonant before a vowel
explanations.body:
In English, “stop it” and “bull’s eye” are pronounced /staa pit/ and /bul zai/, as if they were spelled “sto pit” and “bull seye”. We can observe this phenomenon in Korean as well.

1. When a syllable-final consonant is followed by a vowel, the sound of the final consonant is carried over to the next syllable.
2. When a consonant cluster is followed by a vowel, only the second consonant is carried over to the next vowel.

explanations.title: Making polite requests and commands
explanations.body: In English, when we make a polite request, we use “please”, as in “Please go home” or “Please don’t go home”. In Korean we make a polite request by adding -(으)세요 or -지 마세요 to the verb stem of an action verb.

The verb stem ends in a vowel

explanations.title: -(으)세요 is also a statement and a question
explanations.body: Keep in mind that -(으)세요 is a combination of the honorific marker 시 and the informal speech style ending 어요. Like -어요, -(으)세요 can be a statement, a question or a polite request depending on the context and intonation. (The book writes “TV”; here it is written 티브이 so that it can be spoken.)

lessons.title: 91. Ch 4 · Grammar B: ㄹ irregular verbs
lessons.subtitle: 열다 → 엽니다 · 살다 → 삽니다 · 알다 → 아세요 · 졸다 · 돌다 · 멀다 · 떠들다

explanations.title: Verbs whose stems end in ㄹ
explanations.body:
The Korean language has quite a few verbs whose stems end in ㄹ: 열다 (to open), 살다 (to live), 알다 (to know), 졸다 (to doze) and others. These are known as ㄹ irregular verbs because they drop the ㄹ when their stems are followed by ㄴ, ㅂ or ㅅ. (It is easy to remember these consonants as NPS: N for ㄴ, P for ㅂ, S for ㅅ.)

There are four common situations when the stems are followed by ㄴ, ㅂ or ㅅ:
1. -ㅂ니다 (formal polite ending): 엽니다, 삽니다, 압니다, 좁니다.
2. -십니다 (the honorific 시 + ㅂ니다): 여십니다, 사십니다, 아십니다, 조십니다.
3. -세요 (the honorific 시 + 어요): 여세요, 사세요, 아세요, 조세요.
4. -는 (the attributive form of the verb): 문을 여는 학생 (a student who opens the door), 뉴욕에 사는 학생 (a student who lives in New York). The book deals with this fourth situation later.

rows: The verb stem ends in ㄹ and is followed by ㄴ, ㅂ or ㅅ
열다: 여 + ㅂ니다 → 엽니다; 여 + 십니다 → 여십니다
살다: 사 + ㅂ니다 → 삽니다; 사 + 십니다 → 사십니다

lessons.subtitle: 왼쪽으로 · 체육관으로 · 본부로 · 교실로 · 가다 · 오다

explanations.title: Direction / destination marker: noun + (으)로
explanations.body: The marker (으)로 is used to express directions or a destination. When it is attached to a noun indicating direction or location, it can be translated “toward”, “in the direction of” or “to”. It is combined with verbs denoting movement, such as 가다, 오다 and their compound verbs.

lessons.title: 94. Ch 4 · Grammar D: the attributive form of stative verbs -(으)ㄴ
lessons.subtitle: 큰 집 · 좋은 집 · 빨간 사과 · 하얀 건물 · 먼 나라 · 넓은 주차장

explanations.title: Stative verbs before a noun
explanations.body:
Recall the Korean “adjectives” you learned in Chapter 2: 넓다 (to be wide), 많다 (to be many/much), 아름답다 (to be beautiful) and others. In English they are adjectives, but in Korean they are verbs. Their dictionary forms all end in -다 (크다, 예쁘다, 넓다) and they can be conjugated (많습니다, 많아요, 많고, 많아서). Because of these verb-like characteristics they are called stative verbs or descriptive verbs.

Unlike English adjectives, which can modify a noun freely as in “a beautiful house” or “a large boat”, Korean stative verbs cannot modify a noun unless they go through some “cosmetic” changes and are turned into the attributive form: stative verb stem + (으)ㄴ + noun.

rows: The verb stem ends in a vowel
The verb stem ends in a consonant

explanations.title: Color verbs
explanations.body: For stative verbs for colors, drop ㅎ and add ㄴ to the stem, as if the stem ended in a vowel: 빨갛다 → 빨갛 → (drop ㅎ) 빨가 + ㄴ → 빨간 (red). (The English is the book’s.)

explanations.title: A note on 멀다 → 먼 (my remark)
explanations.body: In the advertisement “먼 나라 이웃 나라” the stem of 멀다 (to be far) loses its ㄹ before ㄴ, exactly as the ㄹ irregular verbs do (Grammar B): 멀 + ㄴ → 먼. The book does not state this rule for the attributive form; the remark is mine. 가깝다 (near) turns into 가까운 (a ㅂ-changing verb that the book has not explained yet); the form is given for reference.

explanations.title: Activity 1 (classroom): the commands left out in part; Simon Says
explanations.body: The listening part (matching five classroom conversations to pictures) and the picture part (writing the proper command under each of five pictures) depend on audio and pictures. In Activity 2 you write three commands in Korean on cards and play “Simon Says”, which in Korean is 대장님 가라사대 (literally, “the chief says”). Simon reads a command with or without 대장님 가라사대 in front of it; the class obeys only a command preceded by it. For example, if Simon says 대장님 가라사대, “앉으세요”, everyone must sit down; if Simon simply says “앉으세요”, no one should move.

explanations.body: The book’s Core Vocabulary lists the core words of the chapter with an example sentence for each (the sentences are the book’s; the book gives no English for them). Where the book prints two forms together (건너편/맞은편, 불어/프랑스어, 조금/좀, 곧장/쭉, 첫 번째/첫째) each is shown on its own row, and where it writes 우회전(하다) the verb is shown. explanations.title: What Chapter 5 teaches (하루 일과)
explanations.body:
Chapter 5, “Daily Activities”, has three topic presentations, four grammar points, activities, a self-evaluation and the core vocabulary.

When you finish the chapter you will be able to: ask and answer questions about time; talk about daily routines; and ask and answer questions about days of the week, dates, months and years.

You will become familiar with: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; the direction markers 에서 (from) and 에 (to); the conjunctive ending for sequential actions -아서/-어서 (and then); ~ 전에 / -기 전에 (before); ~ 후에 / -(으)ㄴ 후에 (after); the informal blunt speech style verb ending 아/어; and the Sino-Korean syllables 매 (每), 일 (日), 전 (前), 주 (週) and 후 (後).

explanations.title: Vocabulary strategy: group synonyms and antonyms
explanations.body: While learning Korean you will meet words with similar or identical meanings (synonyms) or opposite meanings (antonyms). Grouping synonyms or antonyms helps you remember them more easily. The book gives these groups of similar meaning: 우회전하다 = 오른쪽으로 돌다 and 세탁하다 = 빨래하다; and these of opposite meaning: 오전 (a.m.) ↔ 오후 (p.m.), 남 ↔ 여, 일찍 (early) ↔ 늦게 (late), 낮 (day) ↔ 밤 (night). (↔ denotes antonyms.)

explanations.title: Vocabulary Builder: match the antonyms
explanations.body: The book gives four pairs to match: 시작 (beginning), 자주 (often), 자다, 끝 (end), 열다, 가끔 (occasionally), 일어나다, 닫다. The first one is done for you (자다 ↔ 일어나다 is not it; the pairing is mine). The key is mine.

explanations.title: How to read the time in Korean
explanations.body: The hour is a pure Korean number + 시; the minutes are a Sino-Korean number + 분: 1시 45분 = 한 시 사십오 분, or 두 시 십오 분 전 (“fifteen minutes before 2”). 4시 30분 = 네 시 삼십 분, or 네 시 반 (반 = half).

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 매 (每) and 일 (日)
explanations.body: The first syllable of 매일 is 매 (每), meaning every or each, as in 매달 (every month; each month) and 매년 (every year; each year). The second syllable 일 (日) depicts the sun and so means the sun or a day, as in 일요일 (Sunday) and 평일 (weekday; “regular day”). The book warns you not to confuse this 日 (the sun; a day) with 一 (one), because they sound the same.

lessons.title: 99. Ch 5 · Grammar A: the direction markers ~에서 and ~에
lessons.subtitle: 산호세에서 와요 · 산호세에 가요 · from and to

explanations.title: 에서 and 에 with movement verbs
explanations.body:
Recall the location markers 에서 and 에 from Chapter 3. They are interpreted as “at”, “on” or “in”, as in 저는 몬트레이에서 공부해요 (I study in Monterey) and 저는 몬트레이에 있어요 (I am in Monterey).

However, when these markers are used with movement verbs such as 가다 (to go) and 오다 (to come), they are direction markers: 에서 is interpreted as “from” and 에 as “to”: 저는 산호세에서 와요 (I am coming from San Jose), 저는 산호세에 가요 (I am going to San Jose).

So ~에서 and ~에 have dual meanings that are determined strictly by the verbs that accompany them. Because Korean verbs are usually placed at the end of a sentence, listeners cannot determine the specific meaning of ~에서 and ~에 until they hear the verb.

lessons.title: 100. Ch 5 · Grammar B: the sequence ending -아서/-어서
lessons.subtitle: 가서 · 와서 · 일어나서 · 일어서서 · and then

explanations.title: -고 and -아서/-어서
explanations.body:
Recall that the first conjunctive ending -고 from Chapter 2 is translated “and”. In the second sentence below, -고 implies that the two actions, eating and taking a shower, occur in sequence: “In the morning I eat and then take a shower.”

Likewise, the conjunctive ending -아서/-어서 can connect two actions or events in sequence. However, -아서/-어서 is used when the first verb shows motion, such as 가다 (to go), 오다 (to come) or 일어나다 (to get up). Other Korean verbs that show motion are 서다 (to stand up), 앉다 (to sit down), 나가다 (to go out), 나오다 (to come out) and so on.

-아서/-어서 can also connect clauses in a cause-and-effect relationship; the book discusses that in Chapter 7.

explanations.title: The rule: verb stem + -아서/어서
explanations.body: When the last syllable of the verb stem contains the vowel ㅏ or ㅗ, add 아서: 가 + 아서 → 가서; 오 + 아서 → 와서. When the last syllable contains a vowel other than ㅏ or ㅗ, add 어서: 일어서 + 어서 → 일어서서. (The forms below are mine; the examples are the book’s.)

explanations.title: 1. The meanings of the days of the week
explanations.body: Hanja characters depicting each day of the week represent the basic elements and “stars” of the universe.

explanations.title: 2. Expressing dates in Korean
explanations.body: Dates are usually written in Arabic numerals, but they have to be read in Sino-Korean. Go from the general to the specific: 년 (year) comes before 월 (month) and 일 (day). June and October have to be read as 유월 and 시월, not as 육월 and 십월.

explanations.body: This Sino-Korean word means “before and after”: 전 (前) means before and 후 (後) means after. The book asks you to guess 식전, 식후, 오전 and 오후; the meanings are mine.

lessons.title: 102. Ch 5 · Grammar C: expressing “before” and “after”
lessons.subtitle: 수업 전에 · 먹기 전에 · 수업 후에 · 먹은 후에 · 한 후에

explanations.title: “Before”: ~ 전에 and -기 전에
explanations.body: In English “before” and “after” show that an event, date or time precedes or follows another. Koreans use ~ 전에 or -기 전에 for “before” and ~ 후에 or -(으)ㄴ 후에 for “after”. ~ 전에 and ~ 후에 follow a noun denoting an event, date or time, as in 수업 전에 (before class); -기 전에 and -(으)ㄴ 후에 follow the stem of a verb denoting an activity, as in 학교 가기 전에 (before going to school) or 먹은 후에 (after eating).

rows: 식사 → 식사 전에; 수업 → 수업 전에
먹다 → 먹기 전에; 식사하다 → 식사하기 전에

explanations.title: “After”: ~ 후에 and -(으)ㄴ 후에
explanations.body: After a noun add 후에 (수업 → 수업 후에). When a verb stem ends in a consonant add 은 후에 (먹다 → 먹은 후에); when it ends in a vowel add ㄴ 후에 (공부하다 → 공부한 후에). The book’s footnote adds that you can also say “after -ing” with (으)ㄴ 다음에, as in 공부한 다음에 비디오 게임을 합니다.

lessons.subtitle: 많아 · 있어 · 먹어 · 이야 · 야 · 아니야 · 먹지 마

explanations.title: Informal polite → informal blunt
explanations.body: Recall the informal speech style -아요/어요 from Chapter 2. It is used in casual yet polite settings where social distance needs to be maintained. Removing 요 from -아요/어요 gives the informal blunt speech style, which is typically used where social distance does not need to be maintained (between friends or siblings). Older people also use it with younger people they are close to. (It is also known as the informal plain form, the informal non-polite form and the intimate form; in Korean, 반말.)

explanations.title: How to use this list
explanations.body: The book’s Core Vocabulary lists the core words of the chapter with an example sentence for each (the sentences are the book’s; the book gives no English for them). The book writes ~까지, ~부터, ~분, ~시, ~번, ~년, ~월, ~일, ~주, ~쯤, ~정도, ~에게 with a leading ~, and -아서/어서, ~ 전에/-기 전에 and ~ 후에/-(으)ㄴ 후에 with their verb forms; here the bare words are listed and the verb forms are in the grammar lessons. Where the book lists a noun with (~하다) the verb is shown on its own row. Numerals in the examples are written in Hangul (100 → 백, 2000년 → 이천년, 24시간 → 스물네 시간, 2월 14일 → 이월 십사일, 3천 명 → 삼천 명) so that they can be spoken, and the two English labels in the Monday and Wednesday sentences (“Class A”, “PT”) are left out. I have written 너 with the book’s ↓ mark as a gloss: it is for someone close or younger.

explanations.title: Self-evaluation
explanations.body:
Recall the objectives of the chapter and ask yourself whether you have achieved them (the book asks you to tick Yes or No). If you tick “No” for any item, the book suggests: review that section on your own; find a study partner and review it as a pair or group; and tell your academic advisor or team leader which areas you need more help with so they can offer other activities tailored to your learning style and needs.

Now I am able to: ask and answer questions about time; talk about daily routines; ask and answer questions about days of the week, dates, months and years.

Now I have a clear understanding of: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; the direction markers 에서 (from) and 에 (to); the conjunctive ending for sequential actions -아서/-어서 (and then); ~ 전에 / -기 전에 (before); ~ 후에 / -(으)ㄴ 후에 (after); the informal blunt speech style verb ending 아/어; and the Sino-Korean syllables 매 (每), 일 (日), 전 (前), 주 (週) and 후 (後).

explanations.title: What Chapter 6 teaches (날씨와 취미)
explanations.body:
Chapter 6, “Weather and Hobbies”, has three topic presentations, four grammar points, activities, a self-evaluation and the core vocabulary.

When you finish the chapter you will be able to: talk about the four seasons and the weather; and talk about hobbies and weekend activities in a simple phrase or sentence.

You will become familiar with: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; -고 싶다 / 싶어하다 (want to; wish to); -(으)러 가다 / 오다 (go/come to do something); ㅂ irregular verbs; and the Sino-Korean syllable 구 (球). (The book’s “Let’s …” section, -(으)ㅂ시다, is in the chapter too.)

explanations.title: A note on 끼었습니다 (past tense for the present weather)
explanations.body: You will hear native speakers say 오늘은 안개가 끼었습니다, “it is foggy today”, or 오늘은 구름이 끼었습니다, “it is cloudy today”. Because 끼었습니다 is the past tense of 끼다, you may wonder why a Korean speaker would use the past tense to describe the present weather. 끼다 literally means “to form”. When you say 구름이 낍니다 (present tense) you are saying that clouds are forming now. When you say 구름이 끼었습니다 the sentence implies that clouds have already formed and, as a result, it is cloudy.

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 구 (球)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means a ball or sphere, as in 지구 (the earth; “sphere of earth”) and 전구 (light bulb; “electric ball”). It is also used to mean “-ball”, as in baseball, basketball, volleyball, kickball and so on. The book asks you to guess 농구, 축구 and 야구 (its notes: 농 籠 a basket, 축 蹴 kick, 야 野 a field); the meanings are mine.

lessons.title: 108. Ch 6 · Grammar A: ㅂ irregular verbs
lessons.subtitle: 춥다 → 추워요 · 덥다 → 더워요 · 쉽다 → 쉬워요 · 어렵다 → 어려워요 · 가깝다 · 고맙다 · 반갑다

explanations.title: Stative verbs whose stems end in ㅂ
explanations.body: So far you have learned quite a few stative verbs whose stems end in ㅂ: 쉽다 (to be easy), 어렵다 (to be difficult), 춥다 (to be cold), 덥다 (to be hot), 가깝다 (to be close; to be near), 반갑다 (to be glad) and 고맙다 (to be thankful). These are commonly known as ㅂ irregular verbs, because when the verb stem is followed by a vowel in conjugation, the ㅂ is dropped from the stem and 우 is added.

rows: The stem ends in ㅂ and is followed by a vowel
덥 + 어요 → 더우어요 → 더워요; 쉽 + 어요 → 쉬우어요 → 쉬워요

lessons.title: 109. Ch 6 · Grammar B: expressing wishes with -고 싶다 and -고 싶어하다
lessons.subtitle: 먹고 싶어요 · 가고 싶어요 · 먹고 싶어해요 · 배우고 싶어해요

explanations.title: Want to, wish to, would like to
explanations.body: In English we use “want to”, “wish to” and “would like to”. In Korean we use -고 싶다 or -고 싶어하다. If the subject is the first person (I, we) or the second person (you), -고 싶다 is used; if the subject is the third person (he, she, John, they and so on), -고 싶어하다 is used. They attach to the stem of an action verb.

rows: The subject is 1st or 2nd person (I, we, you)
add 고 싶다 to the verb stem
먹다 → 먹고 싶다; 공부하다 → 공부하고 싶다
The subject is 3rd person (he, she, they, etc.)
add 고 싶어하다 to the verb stem
먹다 → 먹고 싶어하다; 공부하다 → 공부하고 싶어하다

explanations.title: Dialog: what do you usually do on the weekend?
explanations.body: Mike, a DLI student, and his conversation partner Soyeon, a graduate student, are talking about their weekend activities and hobbies. The book’s footnote says the -기 in 달리기 (running) is a “gerund maker” attached to a verb stem; you will learn it in a later chapter. (The English is mine.)

examples.text: 마이크: 소연 씨는 주말에 보통 뭐 해요?
examples.translation: maikeu: soyeon ssineun jumare botong mwo haeyo? — Soyeon, what do you usually do on the weekend?

examples.text: 강소연: 공원에서 산책해요. 그리고 집에서 음악도 들어요. 마이크 씨는 주말에 뭐 해요?
examples.translation: gangsoyeon: gongwoneseo sanchaekaeyo. geurigo jibeseo eumakdo deureoyo. maikeu ssineun jumare mwo haeyo? — I take a walk in the park. And I listen to music at home too. What do you do on weekends, Mike?

lessons.title: 112. Ch 6 · Grammar D: the purpose of coming and going, -(으)러 가다/오다

explanations.title: To go to do something
explanations.body: When we go to a restaurant to eat we say “I am going (to the restaurant) to eat.” “To eat” following the verb “is going” shows the purpose of going. Koreans express the purpose of coming and going with -(으)러 가다 or -(으)러 오다, as in 점심을 먹으러 (식당에) 갑니다 or 점심을 먹으러 (식당에) 옵니다.

explanations.title: What Chapter 7 teaches (몬트레이 시내에서)
explanations.body:
Chapter 7, “Downtown Monterey”, has three topic presentations, four grammar points, activities, a self-evaluation and the core vocabulary.

When you finish the chapter you will be able to: list and discuss businesses around town; order food and drink at a restaurant; and ask for services at a hair salon or barber shop.

You will become familiar with: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; the negating adverbs 안 and 못; the conjunctive ending -아/어서 for cause and effect (and thus; because); the auxiliary verb -아/어 주다 used to express “the sense of providing service”; -(으)ㄹ까요? (Shall we …?); and the Sino-Korean syllables 소 (所), 음 (飮) and 점 (店).

explanations.title: Strategy: construct a phrase or sentence from related words
explanations.body: If you learn words in context, you are more likely to retain them longer and recognize them better. When you work on a set of new words, first group related words and then construct a phrase or sentence that uses them. For example, with the four new words 돈 (money), 기름 (gasoline), 찾다 (to withdraw) and 넣다 (to put in), group 돈 with 찾다 and 기름 with 넣다, and then build a phrase with each pair.

explanations.title: Dialog: what would you like to eat?
explanations.body: At a Korean restaurant, PFC Thomas and his Korean friend Jinyeong are about to place an order. The book’s footnote: 뭐 드시겠어요? is a common expression used at a restaurant and means “What would you like to have?”; 뭐 is a contracted form of 무엇. (The English is mine.)

examples.text: 종업원: 뭐 드시겠어요?
examples.translation: jongeobwon: mwo deusigesseoyo? — What would you like to have?

examples.text: 진영: 토마스 씨, 매운 음식 괜찮아요?
examples.translation: jinyeong: tomaseu ssi, maeun eumsik gwaenchanayo? — Thomas, is spicy food okay for you?

examples.text: 토마스: 저는 매운 음식은 못 먹어요. 김치도 매워서 못 먹어요.
examples.translation: tomaseu: jeoneun maeun eumsigeun mon meogeoyo. gimchido maewoseo mon meogeoyo. — I can’t eat spicy food. I can’t eat kimchi either because it is spicy.

examples.text: 진영: 그래요? 그럼, 불고기하고 비빔밥 어때요?
examples.translation: jinyeong: geuraeyo? geureom, bulgogihago bibimbap eottaeyo? — Is that so? Then how about bulgogi and bibimbap?

examples.text: 토마스: 네, 좋아요. 우리 만두도 시킵시다. 오늘은 아주 배가 고파요.
examples.translation: tomaseu: ne, joayo. uri mandudo sikipsida. oneureun aju baega gopayo. — Yes, good. Let’s order dumplings too. I am very hungry today.

examples.text: 진영: 그래요. 여기 불고기 일 인분, 만두 일 인분, 비빔밥 하나 주세요.
examples.translation: jinyeong: geuraeyo. yeogi bulgogi il inbun, mandu il inbun, bibimbap hana juseyo. — Okay. Please give us one serving of bulgogi, one serving of dumplings and one bibimbap.

examples.text: 종업원: 네, 알겠습니다. 음료수는 뭐 드시겠어요?
examples.translation: jongeobwon: ne, algetseumnida. eumnyosuneun mwo deusigesseoyo? — Yes, understood. What would you like to drink?

examples.text: 진영: 저는 콜라 한 잔 주세요.
examples.translation: jinyeong: jeoneun kolla han jan juseyo. — I would like a glass of cola, please.

examples.text: 토마스: 저는 맥주 한 병 주세요. 그리고 물도 좀 갖다 주세요.
examples.translation: tomaseu: jeoneun maekju han byeong juseyo. geurigo muldo jom gatda juseyo. — I would like a bottle of beer, please. And please bring some water too.

examples.text: 진영: 여기 계산서 좀 주세요. 신용카드 받습니까?
examples.translation: jinyeong: yeogi gyesanseo jom juseyo. sinyongkadeu batseumnikka? — (After finishing the meal) Please give us the bill. Do you accept credit cards?

examples.text: 종업원: 네, 받습니다. 계산서 여기 있습니다.
examples.translation: jongeobwon: ne, batseumnida. gyesanseo yeogi itseumnida. — Yes, we do. Here is your bill.

explanations.title: Naming the food of a country
explanations.body: When referring to food from different countries or regions, add 음식 after a country or regional name, as in 한국음식, 미국음식, 서양음식 (Western food) and 일본음식. 한국음식 is usually abbreviated as 한식, 서양음식 as 양식, and 일본음식 as 일식.

explanations.title: Cultural note: kimchi
explanations.body: Kimchi is a traditional Korean fermented dish made of vegetables with a variety of seasonings. It is the most common side dish served with Korean meals. Although Koreans make kimchi from many vegetables, the Napa cabbage kimchi (배추 김치) is the most common type. Koreans make dishes like kimchi stew (김치찌개), kimchi fried rice (김치볶음밥) and even kimchi pizza (김치피자). Despite its spicy flavor, many foreigners in Korea develop a taste for kimchi and find themselves missing it after returning home. The dish is so essential to Koreans that “space kimchi” was developed by the Korea Aerospace Research Institute for the first Korean astronaut.

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 음 (飮)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means drink or swallow.

explanations.title: Counting drinks and dishes
explanations.body: In the dialog the customers order with the counters 병 (bottles), 잔 (glasses and cups) and 인분 (servings). The native numbers 한, 두, 세, 네 go before 병 and 잔; the Sino-Korean numbers 일, 이, 삼, 사 go before 인분 (the book’s examples are 불고기 일 인분, 맥주 한 병, 콜라 한 잔, 맥주 두 병, 불고기 사 인분하고 맥주 세 병).

explanations.title: Cultural notes: 방, 이발소 and 미용실
explanations.body:
머리방, whose literal meaning is “hair room”, is a popular term for 미용실 or 미장원 (a hair salon). Since the late 1990s many small businesses have dropped 실 (室), 원 (院) or 점 (店) and used the pure Korean 방 as part of their business names. Some of the popular 방’s in Korea are 노래방 (a karaoke bar), 빨래방 (a laundromat), 게임방, PC방, 꾸밈방 (a home interior shop) and 책방 (a bookstore).

이발소 or 이용원 (a barbershop) is a place where men get a haircut and a shave, and 미용실, 미장원 or 머리방 (a beauty parlor or hair salon) is its counterpart for women. However, it is also common for a man to get a haircut at 미용실.

lessons.title: 119. Ch 7 · Grammar A: the negating adverbs 안 and 못
lessons.subtitle: 안 먹어요 · 못 먹어요 · 공부 안 해요 · 잘 못 해요

explanations.title: Negating with 안 and 못
explanations.body: In English we use “not” to negate a verb, as in “He is not learning Japanese.” In Korean we negate a verb by placing 안 or 못 in front of it. 안 is translated as “not” and 못 as “cannot” or “unable to”.

examples.text: 김 선생님은 김치를 안 먹어요.
examples.translation: gim seonsaengnimeun gimchireul an meogeoyo. — Mr. Kim does not eat kimchi. (He chooses not to.)

examples.text: 김 선생님은 김치를 못 먹어요.
examples.translation: gim seonsaengnimeun gimchireul mon meogeoyo. — Mr. Kim cannot eat kimchi. (He is unable to.)

explanations.title: The difference
explanations.body: The first sentence (안) implies that Mr. Kim chooses not to eat kimchi (although he could eat it), and the second (못) means that he is unable to eat kimchi. 안 can negate action verbs as well as stative verbs, but 못 usually negates only action verbs.

rows: 가다 → 안 가다; 넓다 → 안 넓다
place 못 before an action verb
가다 → 못 가다; 마시다 → 못 마시다

explanations.title: Examples
explanations.body: The sentences are the book’s; the English is the book’s except where I added the clarifications in brackets.

examples.text: 밤에는 커피를 안 마셔요.
examples.translation: bameneun keopireul an masyeoyo. — I do not drink coffee at night.

examples.text: 제 기숙사 방은 안 넓어요.
examples.translation: je gisuksa bangeun an neolbeoyo. — My dormitory room is not spacious.

examples.text: 아파서 오늘 파티에 못 가요.
examples.translation: apaseo oneul patie mot gayo. — Because I am ill, I cannot go to the party today.

examples.text: 저는 피아노를 안 배워서 못 쳐요.
examples.translation: jeoneun pianoreul an baewoseo mot cheoyo. — Since I have not learned the piano, I cannot play it.

explanations.title: Note 1: verbs made of a noun + 하다
explanations.body: To negate a verb constructed from “noun + 하다”, such as 공부하다 or 청소하다, place 안/못 between the noun and 하다. The book marks the wrong order with an asterisk: *저는 주말에 안 청소합니다 and *저는 주말에 못 청소합니다 are ungrammatical.

examples.text: 저는 주말에 청소 안 합니다.
examples.translation: jeoneun jumare cheongso an hamnida. — I do not clean my house on the weekend.

examples.text: 저는 주말에 청소 못 합니다.
examples.translation: jeoneun jumare cheongso mo tamnida. — I cannot clean my house on the weekend.

explanations.title: Note 2: when there is an adverb
explanations.body: When there is an adverb in a sentence, 안 and 못 negate the adverb, not the verb.

examples.text: 저는 수영을 잘 못 합니다.
examples.translation: jeoneun suyeongeul jal mo tamnida. — I do not swim well. (I swim, but not well.)

examples.text: 저는 수영을 빨리 못 합니다.
examples.translation: jeoneun suyeongeul ppalli mo tamnida. — I do not swim quickly. (I swim, but not quickly.)

explanations.title: Follow-up 2: 안 or 못?
explanations.body: The book asks you to circle the fitting word in parentheses and translate; the book says both may work for some sentences. The answers and the English are my key.

lessons.title: 120. Ch 7 · Grammar B: giving reasons with -아서/어서 (and thus; because)
lessons.subtitle: 비가 와서 · 작아서 · 맛있어서 · 안 먹어서 · 생일이어서

explanations.title: -아서/어서 for cause and effect
explanations.body: The conjunctive ending -아서/어서 can be interpreted as (1) “and then” (sequential events) and (2) “and thus” (cause and effect). The first meaning was covered in Chapter 5; here you meet the second. “It is raining and thus I can’t go hiking” is virtually the same as “Because it is raining, I can’t go hiking” or “Since it is raining, I can’t go hiking.” So -아서/어서 can be translated as “and therefore”, “so”, “because” or “since”. The first clause (비가 와서, it is raining, and thus …) is the cause and the second clause (등산 못 가요, I can’t go hiking) is the effect.

rows: The last syllable of the verb stem contains ㅏ or ㅗ
옷이 작다 → 옷이 작아서; 날씨가 좋다 → 날씨가 좋아서
The last syllable contains a vowel other than ㅏ or ㅗ
한식이 맛있다 → 한식이 맛있어서; 아침을 안 먹다 → 아침을 안 먹어서
tables.title: verb stem + 아서/어서

examples.text: 날씨가 좋아서 공원에 사람이 많아요.

examples.translation: achimeul an meogeoseo baega gopayo. — Since I did not eat breakfast, I am hungry.

explanations.title: Some forms
explanations.body: The forms are mine (ㅂ irregular verbs: 덥다 → 더워서, 춥다 → 추워서; 이다 → 이어서 after a consonant, as in 친구 생일이어서).

explanations.title: Follow-up 3: causes and effects
explanations.body: The book prints six causes in Column A and six effects in Column B and asks you to match them and join the pairs with -아서/어서. Only the first match (밥을 안 먹다 → 너무 배가 고파요) is given in the book; the other matches and the joined sentences are my key (the English is mine; 시원한 and 너무 are not in the core list).

lessons.title: 121. Ch 7 · Grammar C: asking for a service with -아/어 주세요
lessons.subtitle: 열어 주세요 · 닫아 주세요 · 가르쳐 주세요 · 도와 주세요 · 해 주세요

explanations.title: The auxiliary verb for providing service
explanations.body: Earlier you learned that the verbs 주다 and 드리다 (the honorific of 주다) mean “to give”. However, when 주다 or 드리다 is used as part of the auxiliary verb -아/어 주다 or -아/어 드리다, it implies that the subject provides or offers a service, or does something for someone else’s benefit. 친구가 책을 읽어 줍니다/드립니다 implies that my friend is (providing the service of) reading a book to someone else. So if you want someone to do something for you, ask with -아/어 주세요. Stative verbs do not work with -아/어 주다 and -아/어 드리다.

rows: The last syllable of an action verb stem contains ㅏ or ㅗ
문을 닫다 → 문을 닫아 주다 / 닫아 드리다
The last syllable contains a vowel other than ㅏ or ㅗ
문을 열다 → 문을 열어 주다 / 열어 드리다

explanations.title: -(으)ㄹ까요?
explanations.body: -(으)ㄹ까요? can be used when making an invitation or suggestion, when asking for thoughts or input, and when offering a service or favor. The subject of the sentence can be omitted when using -(으)ㄹ까요?.

rows: A verb stem ends in a consonant
A verb stem ends in a vowel
tables.title: verb stem + (으)ㄹ까요?

explanations.title: Three uses
explanations.body: 1. Making an invitation or suggestion. 2. Asking for thoughts or offering a favor. In a situation where the speaker offers a favor or service to the listener, we often combine -아/어 주다/드리다 with the expression, as in -아/어 줄까요 / 드릴까요? (The English is the book’s except for the rows I added.)

explanations.title: Activity 2: a question and an answer on a Korean-American website
explanations.body: Jungmin wants to get her hair done this weekend. On the “Koreans in America” website she finds this question and answer. The book glosses 추천하다 as “to recommend”. The English is mine; the book’s three comprehension questions have my answers below the text.

rows: Park Minchul Hair (박민철 헤어), in San Jose.
Why is that salon a good choice?
The hairdressers do hair well, so you will like it (and it is usually busy).
What is Jungmin advised to do before going, and why?
Make a reservation, because there are usually many people.

explanations.title: Self-evaluation
explanations.body:
Recall the objectives of the chapter and ask yourself whether you have achieved them (the book asks you to tick Yes or No). If you tick “No” for any item, the book suggests: review that section on your own; find a study partner and review it as a pair or group; and tell your academic advisor or team leader which areas you need more help with so they can offer other activities tailored to your learning style and needs.

Now I am able to: list and discuss businesses around town; order food and drink at a restaurant; ask for services at a hair salon or barber shop.

Now I have a clear understanding of: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; the negating adverbs 안 and 못; the conjunctive ending -아/어서 for cause and effect (and thus; because); the auxiliary verb -아/어 주다 used to express “the sense of providing service”; and the Sino-Korean syllables 소 (所), 음 (飮) and 점 (店).

explanations.title: Activities left out
explanations.body: Activity 1 (listening to three dialogs between a male hairstylist and a female customer and matching hairstyle pictures), Activity 2c (two voice mails), the hairstyle pictures and celebrity photos of Activity 3, and the role-play cards are audio, picture or class activities.

lessons.title: 125. Ch 8 · Topic A: Traveling last weekend
lessons.subtitle: 지난 주말에 샌프란시스코에 갔습니다 · 출발 · 도착 · 돌아다니다 · 품 (品) · 복 (服)

explanations.title: What Chapter 8 teaches (지난 주말)
explanations.body:
Chapter 8, “Last Weekend”, has three topic presentations, four grammar points, activities, a self-evaluation and the core vocabulary.

When you finish the chapter you will be able to: comprehend and respond to simple information regarding weekend activities; narrate past weekend activities in a simple paragraph; and recognize and respond to different military ranks.

You will become familiar with: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; the past tense “marker” -았/었; the auxiliary verb -아/어야 하다 or -아/어야 되다 (must; have to); the markers ~은/는, 만 and 도; the auxiliary verb -아/어 보다 (try; try -ing); and the Sino-Korean syllables 대 (大), 복 (服), 소 (小), 소 (少), 중 (中) and 품 (品).

explanations.title: Strategy: compound verbs that end in -가다, -오다 or -다니다
explanations.body: Previewing the Core Vocabulary you may have met verbs that end in -가다, -오다 or -다니다 (to go to and from; to attend), such as 돌아가다, 돌아오다 and 돌아다니다. They are compound verbs, made from two verbs: for example 돌아오다 consists of 돌다 and 오다. The stem of the first verb is followed by 아/어, which works as “glue”, and then comes the second verb. Koreans almost always express movement with -가다, -오다 or -다니다. To say “walk to school” they say 학교에 걸어가다 (“walk and go to school”) or 학교에 걸어오다 (“walk and come to school”); for “come in” they say 들어오다 (“be in and come”); for “return home” 집에 돌아가다 (“turn and go home”) or 집에 돌아오다 (“turn and come home”).

explanations.title: Core words and phrases of Topic B
explanations.body: The meanings are the book’s. The book lists 진급(하다), 처음(으로), 축하(하다) with (하다) or (으로) in parentheses; they are split here, and 아/어 보다 is explained in a grammar lesson. 파티 and 파티하다 are from the book’s Loan Words.

explanations.title: Officer ranks (장교 계급)
explanations.body: The book shows the officer ranks with their insignia (the insignia are pictures and are not reproduced). The Korean names and their English equivalents are from the book’s chart. 준위 is a warrant officer; in the chart there is no rank next to 준위 in the middle column (N/A).

explanations.title: The ladder
explanations.body: From the lowest of these ranks to the highest (the order follows the book’s chart and its example sentences: 준위 is just below 소위; 소령 is just above 대위; 중령 is just below 대령; 소장 is just above 준장; 중장 is just above 소장). The same three-way pattern 소 · 중 · 대 (young, middle, big) repeats in each group: 소위, 중위, 대위; 소령, 중령, 대령; and 소장, 중장, 대장, with 준장 (“deputy commander”) below 소장.

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 大, 中, 小 and 少
explanations.body: Three of these four Chinese characters are used in ranks for officers. 大 (대), which means great, big or large, is used in 대위, 대령 and 대장. 中 (중), which means middle or medium, is used in 중위, 중령 and 중장. 小 (소), which means small or little, is used in 소형, “small style”. 少 (소), which means young or a few, is used in 소년 (young boy) and 소녀 (young girl). Which one is used for 소위, 소령 and 소장, 小 or 少? The book’s hint: which sounds better, “small officer” or “young officer”? (The answer, in the Core Vocabulary, is 少: “young officer”.)

lessons.title: 127. Ch 8 · Grammar A: the past tense marker -았/었
lessons.subtitle: 먹었습니다 · 갔어요 · 했어 · 봤어요 · 마셨어요 · 썼어요

explanations.title: Making the past tense
explanations.body: Recall the three speech styles indicated by verb endings attached to the stem of a verb: (1) formal polite -ㅂ니다/습니다, as in 먹습니다; (2) informal polite -아요/어요, as in 먹어요; and (3) informal blunt -아/어, as in 먹어. We use the three forms for the present tense: 나는 매일 김치를 먹습니다/먹어요/먹어 (“I eat kimchi every day”). To make the past tense of a verb, simply add the past tense “marker” 았/었 to the verb stem and then end it with the appropriate verb ending. The past tense “marker” is also known as the past tense suffix or infix.

rows: The last syllable of the verb stem contains ㅏ or ㅗ
add 았 and one of the endings (습니다/어요/어)
많다: 많 + 았 + 습니다 → 많았습니다; 많았어요; 많았어
The last syllable contains a vowel other than ㅏ or ㅗ
add 었 and one of the endings
먹다: 먹 + 었 + 습니다 → 먹었습니다; 먹었어요; 먹었어

explanations.title: The conjugation rules are the same as for -아요/어요
explanations.body: Because the past tense marker 았/었 consists of 아/어 and ㅆ, it follows the same conjugation rules as the informal -아요/어요. When 았/었 is attached to a stem that ends in a vowel, the same deletion or contraction applies (see Chapter 2). The book’s table, with my forms:

rows: ㅏ → 았: last syllable 많 has ㅏ
ㅓ → 었: last syllable 먹 has ㅓ
deletion: 가 + 았 → 갔 (the same vowel is dropped)
ㅡ is dropped and 었 added: 쓰 → ㅆ + 었 → 썼
하 + 았 → 했: the only ㅏ-ending verb that behaves this way

explanations.title: Forms of more verbs
explanations.body: The forms below are mine; ㅂ irregular verbs behave as in Chapter 6 (즐겁다 → 즐거웠다). 이다 becomes 이었다 after a consonant and 였다 after a vowel.

explanations.title: Follow-up 1: Jinsoo’s daily routine and what he did yesterday
explanations.body: The book prints Jinsoo’s daily routine on the left and the incomplete narration of what he did yesterday on the right, and asks you to supply the past-tense verbs. The left column is the book’s (spelled out: 7시 → 일곱 시, 11시쯤 → 열한 시쯤, 5시 → 다섯 시, 8시쯤 → 여덟 시쯤); the completed right column is my key (the English is mine).

lessons.title: 128. Ch 8 · Grammar B: trying and experience with -아/어 보다
lessons.subtitle: 먹어 봤어요 · 가 봤어요 · 살아 봤어요 · 먹어 보세요

explanations.title: Try; try -ing
explanations.body: In English, to express experimentation or experience we use the verb “try” or “try -ing”, as in “I tried kimchi for the first time” or “I tried opening the door.” In Korean we use the auxiliary verb -아/어 보다. This auxiliary verb is used with action verbs only.

rows: The last syllable of the stem contains ㅏ or ㅗ
살다 → 살아 보다; 가다 → 가아 보다 → 가 보다
The last syllable contains a vowel other than ㅏ or ㅗ
먹다 → 먹어 보다; 읽다 → 읽어 보다
tables.title: action verb stem + 아/어 보다

explanations.title: Forms
explanations.body: The forms below are mine: the past form 봤어요 asks or says whether you have tried it; the request 보세요 asks someone to try it.

explanations.title: Follow-up 3: asking about experiences
explanations.body: In the book partners take turns asking each other questions with -아/어 봤어요 from List A or List B; if the answer is negative, the asker suggests what to try with -아/어 보세요. explanations.title: Activity 1: how Koreans spend holidays and weekends
explanations.body: The book prints a short article and asks you to identify the activities and places in English. The article: 한국 사람들은 주말과 휴일에 TV나 영화를 많이 봅니다. 최근 한 조사에서는 TV나 영화 보기가 35%, 인터넷•컴퓨터가 28%, 운동 25%, 여행은 12%이었습니다. 여행 장소는 산 38%, 바닷가 25%, 호수•강 22%, 박물관 15%로 나타났습니다. The book glosses 조사 as “research; poll” and 장소 as “a place; site”. My reading of the figures:

examples.text: 한국 사람들은 주말과 휴일에 티브이나 영화를 많이 봅니다.
examples.translation: hanguk saramdeureun jumalgwa hyuire tibeuina yeonghwareul mani bomnida. — Koreans watch a lot of TV or movies on weekends and holidays.

explanations.title: Activity 1 (second set): General Ann Dunwoody and her family
explanations.body: The text is about General Ann Dunwoody, America’s first female four-star general, and her family. The book asks you to circle the rank words and the past-tense verbs and to name four facts about her family. The book glosses 되다 “to become”, 조종사 “a pilot” and 태어나다 “to be born”. The English is mine; the book’s first sentence reads 앤 던우디는 장군은, which is a typo for 앤 던우디 장군은; the date is spelled out.

rows: the third female Army helicopter pilot

examples.text: 앤 던우디 장군은 이천팔년 십일월 십사일에 대장으로 진급했습니다.
examples.translation: aen deonudi jangguneun icheonpallyeon sibirwol sipsaire daejangeuro jingeupaetseumnida. — General Ann Dunwoody was promoted to four-star general on November 14, 2008.

examples.text: 앤의 가족은 모두 군인입니다.
examples.translation: aenui gajogeun modu guninimnida. — Ann’s family are all soldiers.

examples.text: 앤의 할아버지 헨리 던우디는 육군 준장이었습니다.
examples.translation: aenui harabeoji helli deonudineun yukgun junjangieotseumnida. — Ann’s grandfather Henry Dunwoody was an Army brigadier general.

examples.text: 그리고 앤의 아버지도 육군 준장이었습니다.
examples.translation: geurigo aenui abeojido yukgun junjangieotseumnida. — And Ann’s father was also an Army brigadier general.

examples.text: 앤의 언니는 세번째 육군 여자 헬리콥터 조종사가 되었습니다.
examples.translation: aenui eonnineun sebeonjjae yukgun yeoja hellikopteo jojongsaga doeeotseumnida. — Ann’s older sister became the third female Army helicopter pilot.

examples.text: 그리고 앤의 남편은 공군 대령이었습니다.
examples.translation: geurigo aenui nampyeoneun gonggun daeryeongieotseumnida. — And Ann’s husband was an Air Force colonel.

explanations.title: Activity 3: an alibi e-mail from PFC Ha Inyoung
explanations.body: At a military base in Seoul two laptop computers were stolen last Saturday; all servicemen in the barracks must report where they were from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. KATUSA soldier PFC Ha Inyoung sends this e-mail to his mother (the book’s header is 어머님, 안녕하세요? …; the e-mail addresses and the date line are left out, and the book glosses 오늘 as “today”). The English is mine.

rows: left the barracks for the supermarket
met ten friends from the barracks
had a bulgogi barbecue party and lunch

examples.text: 어머님, 안녕하세요? 별 일 없으세요?
examples.translation: eomeonim, annyeonghaseyo? byeol il eopseuseyo? — Mother, hello. Is everything all right?

examples.text: 저는 잘 지내요.
examples.translation: jeoneun jal jinaeyo. — I am doing well.

examples.translation: je chingu piteo asijo? — You know my friend Peter, right?

examples.translation: piteoga jinan jue sangbyeongeuro jingeupaesseoyo. — Peter was promoted to corporal last week.

examples.text: 그래서 오늘 오후에 진급파티를 했어요.
examples.translation: geuraeseo oneul ohue jingeuppatireul haesseoyo. — So we had a promotion party this afternoon.

examples.text: 열 시쯤 슈퍼마켓에 가서 한국 음식을 샀어요.

examples.translation: yeoldu sijjeum gongwoneseo gisuksa chingu yeol myeongeul mannasseoyo. — Around twelve I met ten friends from the dormitory at the park.

examples.translation: geogieseo bulgogi babekyu patireul haesseoyo. — We had a bulgogi barbecue party there.

examples.text: 점심을 먹은 후 세 시쯤 공원 배구장에서 배구를 했어요.
examples.translation: jeomsimeul meogeun hu se sijjeum gongwon baegujangeseo baegureul haesseoyo. — After lunch, around three, we played volleyball at the park’s volleyball court.

examples.text: 그리고 일곱 시에 기숙사에 돌아왔어요.

examples.translation: gisuksa chingu se myeongi patie mot wasseoyo. — Three friends from the dormitory could not come to the party.

explanations.title: Dialog: my younger brother came to Monterey
explanations.body: Two Korean friends going to college in Monterey are talking about their last long weekend. They are friends, so they use the informal blunt style. (The English is mine; the book glosses 잘 지냈어 nowhere: 잘 지내다 is “to get along well”.)

examples.text: 최민영: 상훈아, 연휴 동안 잘 지냈어?
examples.translation: choeminyeong: sanghuna, yeonhyu dongan jal jinaesseo? — Sanghoon, did you have a good long weekend?

examples.text: 이상훈: 어, 동생이 몬트레이에 놀러 와서 좀 바빴어.
examples.translation: isanghun: eo, dongsaengi monteureie nolleo waseo jom bappasseo. — Yeah, my younger brother came to Monterey to visit, so I was a bit busy.

examples.text: 최민영: 그럼, 수족관에도 갔어?

examples.text: 이상훈: 응. 동생이 수족관을 아주 좋아했어. 그래서, 동생한테 기념품도 사 줬어. 너는 연휴에 뭐 했어?
examples.translation: isanghun: eung. dongsaengi sujokgwaneul aju joahaesseo. geuraeseo, dongsaenghante ginyeompumdo sa jwosseo. neoneun yeonhyue mwo haesseo? — Yes. My brother liked the aquarium very much. So I bought him a souvenir too. What did you do over the long weekend?

examples.translation: choeminyeong: eo, jibanireul jom haeya haeseo… tto, daeum jue siheomi isseoseo gongbudo jom haeya haesseo. — Well, I had to do some housework… and also, I have a test next week, so I had to study a bit too.

lessons.title: 131. Ch 8 · Grammar C: the markers ~은/는, 만 and 도
lessons.subtitle: 오후에는 · 오후에만 · 오후에도 · 제 친구는 · 제 친구만 · 제 친구도

explanations.title: Three more markers
explanations.body: So far you have learned markers attached to nouns to show their grammatical function: the time marker 에, the subject marker 이/가, the location marker 에서, the object marker 을/를, the source marker 에서 and the direction marker (으)로. You now learn three more, including the topic marker ~은/는 that you met in Chapter 1. They differ from the earlier markers in that they can be attached not only to nouns but also to phrases (any of the underlined words and phrases of a sentence).

rows: as for; speaking of; when it comes to

explanations.title: Attaching them to different parts of a sentence
explanations.body: Adding the markers to the phrase 오후에 (in the afternoon) of 오후에 제 친구가 도서관에서 한국어를 공부합니다 (“My friend studies Korean in the library in the afternoon”) gives the first three sentences below. When the markers are attached to the subject or the object, the subject marker and the object marker are dropped. (The English is the book’s.)

explanations.title: The two functions of the topic marker
explanations.body:
The topic marker has two major functions: to indicate the topic and provide emphasis, and to provide contrast.

1. Topic and emphasis: the emphasized phrase generally moves to the front of the sentence, and the topic marker is usually translated as “as for”, “speaking of” or “when it comes to”.

2. Contrast: the topic marker puts the noun or phrase in contrast with other nouns or phrases.

lessons.title: 132. Ch 8 · Grammar D: obligation and urgency with -아/어야 하다/되다
lessons.subtitle: 해야 해요 · 해야 돼요 · 일어나야 해요 · 가야 했어요

explanations.title: Must; have to; should
explanations.body: In English we often use modals like “must”, “have (got) to” and “should” to express different degrees of obligation or urgency, as in “I must report it by six”, “You have to finish it” or “You should go with me.” When Koreans express obligation or urgency, they often use the auxiliary verb -아/어야 하다 or -아/어야 되다. Depending on the context it can be interpreted as “must”, “have to” or “should”.

rows: The final syllable of the verb stem contains ㅏ or ㅗ
닫다 → 닫아야 하다/되다; 오다 → 와야 하다/되다
The final syllable contains a vowel other than ㅏ or ㅗ
먹다 → 먹어야 하다/되다; 다니다 → 다녀야 하다/되다
tables.title: verb stem + 아/어야 하다 or 아/어야 되다

explanations.title: In the past and with the markers
explanations.body: Past tense: 해야 했어요 / 해야 됐어요 (“had to”). The markers of the previous lesson can be attached: 지난 주말에는 … (as for last weekend), 지난 주말에도 … (last weekend, too) and 지난 주말에만 … (only last weekend). The English is mine except for the first three examples above.

explanations.title: Activity 2: a short biography of John Steinbeck
explanations.body: The passage gives brief biographical data about John Steinbeck, the famous writer who was born in Salinas. The book asks you to circle the past-tense verbs and to write in English what happened to him in each year. The text is the book’s (the English and the table are mine). In the book’s passage the sentence about his books names two works in English: “1939년에 The Grapes of Wrath, 1962년에는 The Winter of Our Discontent를 썼습니다”, which is left out of the examples below because the titles are in English; the other sentences are given with the years spelled out.

rows: wrote The Grapes of Wrath; received the Pulitzer Prize
wrote The Winter of Our Discontent; received the Nobel Prize

explanations.title: Self-evaluation
explanations.body:
Recall the objectives of the chapter and ask yourself whether you have achieved them (the book asks you to tick Yes or No). If you tick “No” for any item, the book suggests: review that section on your own; find a study partner and review it as a pair or group; and tell your academic advisor or team leader which areas you need more help with so they can offer other activities tailored to your learning style and needs.

Now I am able to: comprehend and respond to simple information regarding weekend activities; narrate past weekend activities in a simple paragraph; recognize and respond to different military ranks.

Now I have a clear understanding of: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; the past tense “marker” -았/었; the auxiliary verb -아/어야 하다 or -아/어야 되다 (must; have to); the markers ~은/는, 만 and 도; the auxiliary verb -아/어 보다 (try; try -ing); and the Sino-Korean syllables 대 (大), 복 (服), 소 (小), 소 (少), 중 (中) and 품 (品).

explanations.title: What Chapter 9 teaches (여행 계획)
explanations.body:
Chapter 9, “Travel Plans”, opens Unit 3 of the Semester 1 Student’s Edition. It has three topic presentations, grammar in focus, activities, a self-evaluation and the core vocabulary.

When you finish the chapter you will be able to: have a simple telephone conversation; respond appropriately to telephone messages; narrate future events or actions in a simple paragraph; offer, accept, or reject an informal invitation; and talk about travel plans.

You will become familiar with: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; the auxiliary verb -(으)ㄹ 거다 (to be going to); the auxiliary verbs -(으)ㄹ 수 있다 (can) and -(으)ㄹ 수 없다 (cannot); the conjunctive ending -(으)면 (if); the dual functions of ~와/과, ~하고 and ~(이)랑; and the Sino-Korean syllables 기 (機) and 화 (話).

explanations.title: Strategy: use a mind map
explanations.body:
A mind map is “a diagram used to represent words, ideas, tasks, or other items linked to and arranged radially around a central key word or idea” (“Mind Map”, Wikipedia). Mind maps can be used to generate, classify and learn target vocabulary in a language.

How to use one: first choose a theme, an idea or a concept from the glossary and put it in a circle in the middle of the paper. The book’s example is 여행 계획 (a travel plan). Then add other important concepts and related words around the circle. Continue working outward, free your mind and quickly add other key words and ideas; you may use arrows, icons or other visual aids to show links between related elements. Choose a theme for the chapter and develop your own mind map on a blank sheet of paper.

The words around 여행 계획 in the book’s mind map are below (the English is mine; the book’s picture shows them as labels around the circle).

explanations.title: Pronunciation guide: 의 sounds like 에
explanations.body: Have you noticed that 의 sounds like /에/? The possessive marker 의, as in 선생님의 책상 (the teacher’s desk), is pronounced as /에/ in natural conversation. Therefore 386(국)의 2937 is read as 삼팔육국에 이구삼칠. The book’s further examples are 친구의 방, 아버지의 사무실 and the numbers 393의 2098 and 795국의 8223.

explanations.title: Ways to read a telephone number
explanations.body:
The book lists these ways, using 242-4928 and 498-5812 as examples:
1. Digit by digit: 이사이(의) 사구이팔.
2. In units or “chunks”: 이백사십이(국)의 사천구백이십팔 번. 국 comes after the first three digits and can be omitted; historically 국 stands for 전화 교환국 (the central office of a phone company).
3. As a combination of 1 and 2: 이사이(국)의 사천구백이십팔.
4. Using native and Sino-Korean numbers (particularly when a number contains the numbers one and two): 사구팔의 오팔하나둘. This is a common practice because Koreans want to distinguish 1 and 2 as clearly as possible (the Sino-Korean numbers 1 and 2, 일 and 이, sound similar). A zero (0) can be read as 공 or 영.

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 화 (話)

explanations.title: Dialog: What will you do during the coming school break?
explanations.body: PFC Jones and PFC Baek are talking in the hallway about their “exodus” holiday plans. (The English is mine. The book writes 3박 4일, which is spelled out as 삼박사일; its footnote says that 기 (-ing) attached to the verb stem turns the verb into a noun, a gerund, as in 사기 in 비행기 표 사기가 힘들어.)

examples.text: 존스 일병: 좋아. 언제 갈 거야?
examples.translation: jonseu ilbyeong: joa. eonje gal geoya? — Good. When are we going?

examples.text: 백 일병: 금요일 밤에.
examples.translation: baek ilbyeong: geumyoil bame. — Friday night.

examples.translation: jonseu ilbyeong: geurae? nan geu ttaeneun gal su eopseo. — Is that so? I can’t go at that time.

examples.translation: baek ilbyeong: geureom toyoireun eottae? — Then how about Saturday?

examples.text: 백 일병: 차가 편해. 그리고 방학 때는 비행기 표 사기가 힘들어.

explanations.title: Core words and phrases of Topic B
explanations.body: The meanings are the book’s (from the Core Vocabulary). The book also lists -(으)ㄹ 거다 and -(으)ㄹ 수 있다/없다 here; they have their own grammar lessons. The Korean forms ~때, ~(으)로, ~박 ~일 and 한 ~ are written here without the book’s ~ and ( ) marks; 메시지 appears in the dialog.

to be difficult; to be challenging

explanations.title: Two ways to count days
explanations.body: There are two different ways to count days in Korean: using Sino-Korean numbers, as in 일일, 이일, 삼일, 사일, 오일 and so on, and using native Korean numbers, as in 하루, 이틀, 사흘, 나흘, 닷새 and so on. The book’s table is below.

explanations.title: Verb stem + 기: a noun
explanations.body: In the dialog, 사기 (buying) is the verb 사다 with 기 attached to the stem. 기 (-ing) turns a verb into a noun form (a gerund). 비행기 표 사기가 힘들어 = “buying plane tickets is hard”.

examples.text: 비행기 표 사기가 힘들어.

lessons.title: 139. Ch 9 · Grammar A: a planned future with -(으)ㄹ 거다
lessons.subtitle: 갈 거예요 · 갈 겁니다 · 갈 거야 · 먹을 거예요 · 놀 거예요

explanations.title: Expressing a (planned) future event
explanations.body: Koreans use the auxiliary verb -(으)ㄹ 거다 to express a future event, particularly one that has been planned. It is normally translated as “to be going to”. We use -ㄹ 거다 if the verb stem ends in a vowel and -을 거다 if the stem ends in a consonant. 거다 in -(으)ㄹ 거다 is a short form of 것이다, so it has to be rendered in one of these ways: -(으)ㄹ 겁니다 (formal speech), -(으)ㄹ 거예요 (informal speech) or -(으)ㄹ 거야 (informal blunt speech).

The verb stem ends in a consonant
먹다 → 먹을 겁니다 / 먹을 거예요 / 먹을 거야

explanations.title: Expressing ability and inability: “can” and “cannot”
explanations.body: In English we often use “can” or “able to” to express ability or capability (“He can hold his breath for two minutes”; “He can play golf next weekend”), and we negate them with “cannot” or “unable to”. In Korean we use -(으)ㄹ 수 있다 for “can” and -(으)ㄹ 수 없다 for “cannot”. We add ㄹ 수 있다/없다 if the verb stem ends in a vowel and 을 수 있다/없다 if it ends in a consonant. As with -(으)ㄹ 거다, a stem that ends in ㄹ (놀다, 만들다) takes 수 directly: 놀 수 있어요, 만들 수 있어요 (mine).

The verb stem ends in a consonant

explanations.title: Expressing a conditional
explanations.body: In English the conjunction “if” signals that a clause is conditional. In Korean we use the conjunctive ending -(으)면 to signal a conditional clause, as in 날씨가 좋으면 등산 갈 거예요 (If the weather is good, I will go hiking). The book’s translations for -(으)면 are “if; in case; when”. Add 면 if the verb stem ends in a vowel or ㄹ, and 으면 if it ends in a consonant other than ㄹ.

rows: The verb stem ends in a vowel or ㄹ
The verb stem ends in a consonant other than ㄹ

lessons.title: 142. Ch 9 · Grammar D: “and” and “with” — ~과/와, ~하고, ~(이)랑
lessons.subtitle: 남동생과 여동생 · 커피와 아이스크림 · 책이랑 가방 · 친구와 함께 · 엄마가 아기랑

explanations.title: Noun connectors: “and”
explanations.body: In English we use “and” to connect nouns, as in “I like coffee and ice cream.” In Korean we use ~과/와, ~(이)랑 and ~하고 to connect nouns. ~(이)랑 and ~하고 are used in colloquial or informal settings; ~과/와 is for written or formal settings. ~하고 stays the same. After a noun that ends in a consonant add 과 or 이랑; after a noun that ends in a vowel add 와 or 랑.

explanations.title: A list of several nouns
explanations.body: When enumerating a series of nouns, Koreans tend to use a connector between all the nouns. In informal speech Koreans tend to add ~하고 or ~(이)랑 even after the final noun.

explanations.title: Noun markers: “(along) with”
explanations.body: We can also use ~와/과, ~하고 and ~(이)랑 as noun markers, translated as “(along) with” or “(together) with”. We can add 같이 or 함께 (together) to any of the markers to stress “along” or “together”.

examples.text: 엄마가 아기랑 함께 놀아요.

explanations.title: Travel agency ads (Activity 2, Reading)
explanations.body: You and a classmate are planning a trip for the Thanksgiving holiday. The book shows three ads from local travel agencies and asks you to fill in a table in English (destination, duration, cost, other features) using your dictionary for unknown words. The ads’ Korean is the book’s; the book writes 4박 5일, 3박 4일, 11/28일-11/30일 and 15%, which are spelled out here. The prices, telephone numbers and street addresses in the ads are not shown; the table below gives the prices. The English is mine.

explanations.title: Activity 1 (Reading and writing): PFC Robb’s essay
explanations.body: PFC Robb wrote an essay about his recent trip to San Francisco and a plan for his next trip to L.A.; he asked you to review it and correct the underlined errors (the answers may vary). The text below is the book’s, with MWR, 1박 2일 and Golden Gate Bridge spelled out in Hangul or dropped. The underlining is not visible in the text, so the errors I found are listed in the next card. The English is mine; the glosses in parentheses translate what the sentence says as written.

examples.text: 지난주에 제 여자친구과 같이 샌프란시스코에 갔다 올 거예요.
examples.translation: jinanjue je yeojachingugwa gachi saenpeuransiseukoe gatda ol geoyeyo. — (Last week I am going to go and come back from San Francisco with my girlfriend.)

examples.text: 국방 외국어대학의 엠더블유알에서 일박이일 버스관광 패키지가 있었어요.
examples.translation: gukbang oegugeodaehagui emdeobeuryuareseo ilbagiil beoseugwangwang paekijiga isseosseoyo. — There was a one-night, two-day bus tour package at the Defense Language Institute’s MWR.

examples.text: 샌프란시스코의 금문교가 아주 멋있었어요.
examples.translation: saenpeuransiseukoui geummungyoga aju meosisseosseoyo. — The Golden Gate Bridge in San Francisco was very impressive.

examples.text: 차이나타운에 가서 중국 음식도 먹고, 여자친구이랑 사진도 많이 찍을 거예요.
examples.translation: chainataune gaseo jungguk eumsikdo meokgo, yeojachinguirang sajindo mani jjigeul geoyeyo. — (I will go to Chinatown, eat Chinese food, and take a lot of photos with my girlfriend.)

examples.text: 다음 달에는 사흘 동안 연휴가 있어서 엘에이 제 친구 집에 놀러 갈 거예요.
examples.translation: daeum dareneun saheul dongan yeonhyuga isseoseo erei je chingu jibe nolleo gal geoyeyo. — Next month there is a three-day long weekend, so I am going to visit my friend’s home in L.A.

examples.text: 엘에이에 가면 친구하고 함께 할리우드 거리에 갔어요.

explanations.title: How to use this list
explanations.body:
The book’s Core Vocabulary lists the core words of the chapter with an example sentence for each (the sentences are the book’s; the book gives no English for them). The book writes pairs together (부탁(하다)/부탁드리다, 잠시만/잠깐만, 핸드폰/휴대폰, 초대(하다), 환갑/회갑, 머무르다/머물다, 노래(하다/부르다), 메시지/메세지); they are split here. The book’s Additional Vocabulary section is a blank list for words you add yourself.

The example sentences with digits are respelled in Hangul (257국의 1348번 → 이오칠국의 일삼사팔 번, 560국의 2050번 → 오육공국의 이공오공 번, 100명 → 백 명, 3개월 → 삼 개월, 3박 4일 → 삼박사일, 2시간 → 두 시간); the possessive 의 in a phone number and in 부모님의 is said 에. 휴대폰, 회갑, 메세지 and 노래하다 reuse the book’s sentence of the matching word with the variant substituted.

explanations.title: What Chapter 10 teaches (로스앤젤레스 가는 길에)
explanations.body:
Chapter 10, “On the Way to Los Angeles”, has three topic presentations, grammar in focus, activities, a self-evaluation and the core vocabulary.

When you finish the chapter you will be able to: talk about trip planning, including the means of transportation; compare two things or people; give and understand directions; and use the proper kinship terms for an extended family.

You will become familiar with: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; the comparative 보다 (더) (more … than; …er than); the conjunctive ending -기 때문에 (because); ~때문에 (because of); the attributive forms of action verbs -는, -(으)ㄴ and -(으)ㄹ; and the Sino-Korean syllables 부 (父), 모 (母), 출 (出), 입 (入) and 구 (口).

explanations.title: Strategy: organize a word map card
explanations.body:
Earlier you were introduced to flash cards. They work because the words are easy to access and you can review them readily and repeatedly. As you become more proficient in Korean you may want more than an example sentence on a card: your own Korean definition, antonyms, synonyms, and a drawing that illustrates the new word. One possible layout has five elements: 1. a new vocabulary word; 2. a simple picture or clip art you can describe with the new word; 3. a description of the picture; 4. your own Korean definition of the new word; 5. an antonym or a synonym.

The book’s model card is for 비싸다: the picture shows something expensive (the book suggests an Apple computer or a BMW), the description is 옷이 너무 비싸요 plus the price of the clothes ($700), the definition is 가격이 높아요, and the antonym is 싸다. Choose one of the words of the chapter and make a card with all five elements; for other words use a larger index card (at least 4 by 6 inches).

explanations.body: The book leaves the itinerary to you. Two of the possible routes that use three different means of transportation and reach Jeju the same day are shown here; the times are from the timetables above. lessons.title: 148. Ch 10 · Grammar A: comparing with ~보다 (더)
lessons.subtitle: 일본말보다 더 쉬워요 · 더 · 보다 · 가장 · 비행기가 기차보다 더 빨라요

explanations.title: Expressing comparison
explanations.body:
Look at 한국말이 쉬워요 (Korean is easy), 한국말이 더 쉬워요 (Korean is easier) and 한국말이 일본말보다 더 쉬워요 (Korean is easier than Japanese). 더 is the counterpart of the English -er or “more”, but it comes before the adjective or adverb (더 쉬워요, 더 아름다워요). 보다 is the counterpart of “than”, and it comes after the second noun being compared.

Markers attached to nouns show the grammatical function of the nouns, so swapping the two nouns does not change the meaning: 한국말이 일본말보다 더 쉬워요 = 일본말보다 한국말이 더 쉬워요. As long as the noun with ~보다 is in the sentence, 더 can be left out.

examples.text: 한국말이 쉬워요.
examples.translation: hangungmari swiwoyo. — Korean is easy.

examples.text: 한국말이 더 쉬워요.
examples.translation: hangungmari deo swiwoyo. — Korean is easier.

examples.text: 한국말이 일본말보다 더 쉬워요.
examples.translation: hangungmari ilbonmalboda deo swiwoyo. — Korean is easier than Japanese.

examples.text: 한국말이 일본말보다 (더) 쉬워요.
examples.translation: hangungmari ilbonmalboda (deo) swiwoyo. — Korean is easier than Japanese. (더 can be left out when 보다 is there.)

examples.text: 일본말보다 한국말이 더 쉬워요.
examples.translation: ilbonmalboda hangungmari deo swiwoyo. — Korean is easier than Japanese. (the nouns swapped; the meaning is the same)

examples.text: 미국이 멕시코보다 (더) 커요.
examples.translation: migugi meksikoboda (deo) keoyo. — The U.S. is larger than Mexico.

examples.text: 이 옷이 더 아름다워요.
examples.translation: i osi deo areumdawoyo. — This dress is more beautiful. (mine; the book writes 더 아름다워요 as an example)

examples.text: 비행기가 기차보다 더 빨라요.
examples.translation: bihaenggiga gichaboda deo ppallayo. — A plane is faster than a train. (mine)

explanations.title: Forms
explanations.body: The informal polite forms below are mine (ㅂ and 르 stems change: 춥다 → 추워요, 빠르다 → 빨라요). The superlative 가장 (“the most; the -est”) is in the book’s Core Vocabulary, with the example 미국에서 알래스카 주가 가장 큽니다.

explanations.title: Follow-up 2: make comparison statements
explanations.body: In the book partners take turns making a comparison aloud from two nouns and a stative verb; the book’s model is 알래스카 주가 메인 주보다 더 추워요 or 메인 주보다 알래스카 주가 더 추워요. The nouns and verbs are the book’s (it adds “market” for 시장). Which noun comes out ahead is a matter of fact or opinion; the sentences below are my sample key, and the other order of the nouns, with the opposite meaning, is also grammatical.

미시시피 강이 카멜 강보다 더 길어요.
