explanations.title: Dialog: asking for directions
explanations.body: PFC Jones is calling PFC Baek, who has already arrived in L.A., to ask for directions to his home. (The English is mine. The book writes L.A., 68번, 101번 and Vermont; they are spelled out here, and the Latin spelling of Vermont is dropped.)

examples.text: 존스 일병: 백 일병, 지금 어디야?
examples.translation: jonseu ilbyeong: baek ilbyeong, jigeum eodiya? — PFC Baek, where are you now?

examples.text: 백 일병: 응. 엘에이 우리 집이야. 오늘 오후에 도착했어. 넌 언제 올 거야?
examples.translation: baek ilbyeong: eung. erei uri jibiya. oneul ohue dochakaesseo. neon eonje ol geoya? — Yes. I’m at our house in L.A. I arrived this afternoon. When will you come?

examples.text: 존스 일병: 난 김 이병하고 내일 아침에 출발할 거야. 오늘 차에 기름도 넣었어. 백 일병, 너희 집에 어떻게 가?
examples.translation: jonseu ilbyeong: nan gim ibyeonghago naeil achime chulbalhal geoya. oneul chae gireumdo neoeosseo. baek ilbyeong, neohui jibe eotteoke ga? — I’m leaving tomorrow morning with PV2 Kim. I put gas in the car today too. PFC Baek, how do we get to your house?

examples.text: 백 일병: 먼저 육십팔 번 길로 살리나스로 가. 첫 번째 사거리에서 우회전해. 계속 곧장 가면 백일 번 고속도로 입구가 나와.
examples.translation: baek ilbyeong: meonjeo yuksippal beon gillo sallinaseuro ga. cheot beonjjae sageorieseo uhoejeonhae. gyesok gotjang gamyeon baegil beon gosokdoro ipguga nawa. — First take Road 68 to Salinas. Turn right at the first intersection. If you keep going straight, you will come to the entrance of Highway 101.

examples.text: 존스 일병: 거기까지는 잘 알아. 백일 번 고속도로로 얼마나 가야 해?
examples.translation: jonseu ilbyeong: geogikkajineun jal ara. baegil beon gosokdororo eolmana gaya hae? — I know that part well. How long do we have to go on Highway 101?

examples.text: 백 일병: 한 네 시간 정도. 엘에이에 도착하면 버몬트 출구가 나와. 거기 공사 중이고 복잡하기 때문에 조심해야 해.
examples.translation: baek ilbyeong: han ne sigan jeongdo. ereie dochakamyeon beomonteu chulguga nawa. geogi gongsa jungigo bokjapagi ttaemune josimhaeya hae. — About four hours. When you get to L.A., the Vermont exit comes up. It is under construction and congested there, so you have to be careful.

examples.text: 존스 일병: 응, 알았어. 그 다음에는?
examples.translation: jonseu ilbyeong: eung, arasseo. geu daeumeneun? — Okay, got it. What next?

examples.text: 백 일병: 첫 번째 신호등에서 좌회전해. 조금 더 오면 오른쪽에 편의점이 있어. 거기서 우리 집이 아주 가까워.
examples.translation: baek ilbyeong: cheot beonjjae sinhodeungeseo jwahoejeonhae. jogeum deo omyeon oreunjjoge pyeonuijeomi isseo. geogiseo uri jibi aju gakkawo. — At the first traffic light turn left. A bit farther on there is a convenience store on your right. From there our house is very close.

examples.text: 존스 일병: 그래, 알았어. 혹시 길을 잃으면 전화할게.
examples.translation: jonseu ilbyeong: geurae, arasseo. hoksi gireul ireumyeon jeonhwahalge. — Okay. If I get lost I’ll call you.

explanations.title: Pronunciation guide: ㅎ
explanations.body: At the beginning of a word, ㅎ is pronounced like the English h, as in 하나, 할머니 and 한국 사람. ㅎ is often silent in the middle of a word or when it is followed by a vowel: 실례합니다 is said /실례암니다/, 안녕히 계세요 /안녕이 게세요/, 많이 /마니/ and 넣어요 /너어요/. When ㅎ is followed or preceded by ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ or ㅈ, the two consecutive consonants are pronounced as ㅋ, ㅌ, ㅍ or ㅊ, respectively: 않고 /안코/, 넣다 /너타/, 좋지 /조치/, 입학 /이팍/.

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 출입 (出入)
explanations.body: The first syllable 출 (出) basically means (coming/going) out or leaving (a place), as in 출국 and 출항. The second syllable 입 (入) basically means (coming/going) in or entering (a place), as in 입국 and 입항. So the literal meaning of 출입 is “(coming/going) out and in”; depending on the context it can be translated as coming in and out, entrance and exit, ingress and egress, or departing and entering.

lessons.title: 150. Ch 10 · Grammar B: “because” with (-기) 때문에
lessons.subtitle: 비 때문에 · 비가 오기 때문에 · 피곤하기 때문에 · 숙제 때문에 · 주유소 이야기

explanations.title: Expressing a reason using (-기) 때문에
explanations.body: English has many words for a reason: because, because of, since, for, on account of, due to, now that. Korean has several conjunctive endings that express a reason; you learned -아서/어서 in Chapter 7. Unlike -아서/어서, which has multiple meanings, ~때문에 is used exclusively to mean “because of”. It is always preceded by a noun: 숙제 때문에 (because of the homework), 너 때문에 (because of you), 날씨 때문에 (because of the weather). To use a verb or a clause with 때문에 you must use -기 때문에, because -기 is a “gerund-maker” that turns a verb or a verbal phrase into a noun or noun phrase: 숙제를 하기 때문에 (because of doing homework), 많이 먹기 때문에 (because of eating a lot).

explanations.body: The forms below are mine, made by the book’s rule; 기 is added directly to the stem, whatever the last letter is.

explanations.title: Follow-up 3: cause and effect
explanations.body: In the book you connect seven sentences that have a cause-and-effect relation (the answers may vary), and then combine each pair with -기 때문에, as in 피곤하기 때문에 집에서 쉽니다. The sentences are the book’s; the matches below are mine. The book’s right-hand column also has 파마를 못 합니다, 중국 요리를 주문합니다 and 히터를 켭니다 (a perm, ordering Chinese food, turning on the heater): these fit as well (머리가 길기 때문에 파마를 못 합니다 is possible; 매운 음식을 못 먹기 때문에 중국 요리를 주문합니다; 날씨가 쌀쌀하기 때문에 히터를 켭니다), so the answers may vary. 시키다 and 주문하다 both mean “to order”, and 이발하다 means “to get a haircut” (mine).

rows: Because I am tired, I rest at home.
Because I am hungry, I eat a meal.
Because the weather is chilly, I wear a coat.
Because my hair is long, I get a haircut.
숙제가 어렵기 때문에 친구하고 같이 합니다.
Because the homework is difficult, I do it with a friend.
매운 음식을 못 먹기 때문에 불고기를 시킵니다.
Because I can’t eat spicy food, I order bulgogi.
Because I am bored, I call a Korean friend.

explanations.title: Follow-up 5: gas stations in America
explanations.body: The book gives two passages about gas stations, in Korea and in America, and asks you to fill in a Venn diagram in Korean and write two or three sentences comparing them. The passages are the book’s; the book writes 1갤런(gallon), 4불, 1리터, 0.22갤런 and 2,000원, which are spelled out here. The English is mine. The book also glosses 세차 (to wash a car), 직원 (an employee), 자동 (automatic), 현금 (cash).

lessons.title: 151. Ch 10 · Activities B: directions to a unit and gas stations
lessons.subtitle: 저희 부대로 오시는 길 · 경부고속도로 · 갈아타십시오 · 주유소 · 기름값이 싼 주유소

explanations.title: Activity 2 (Reading): directions to the 21st Division
explanations.body: Your unit in Korea plans a joint FTX (field training exercise) with the ROK Army at its camp next week. The directions you received are in Korean; the book asks you to translate the underlined ones into English (the underlining is not shown in my copy of the text). The Korean is the book’s; the book writes 2시간쯤, 1시간쯤 and 21사단, which are spelled out here. The English is mine.

examples.text: 안녕하십니까?
examples.translation: annyeonghasimnikka? — Hello.

examples.text: 저희 부대로 오시는 길은 다음과 같습니다.
examples.translation: jeohui budaero osineun gireun daeumgwa gatseumnida. — The way to our unit is as follows.

examples.text: 대전 방향으로 경부고속도로를 타십시오.
examples.translation: daejeon banghyangeuro gyeongbugosokdororeul tasipsio. — Take the Gyeongbu Expressway toward Daejeon.

examples.text: 두 시간쯤 후에 호남고속도로 광주 방향으로 갈아타십시오.
examples.translation: du siganjjeum hue honamgosokdoro gwangju banghyangeuro garatasipsio. — After about two hours, transfer to the Honam Expressway toward Gwangju.

examples.text: 한 시간쯤 후에 정읍 출구가 보입니다.
examples.translation: han siganjjeum hue jeongeup chulguga boimnida. — After about an hour you will see the Jeongeup exit.

examples.text: 그 출구로 나가십시오.
examples.translation: geu chulguro nagasipsio. — Take that exit.

examples.text: 첫 번째 신호등에서 좌회전 하십시오.
examples.translation: cheot beonjjae sinhodeungeseo jwahoejeon hasipsio. — Turn left at the first traffic light.

examples.text: 조금만 더 오시면 오른쪽에 우체국이 나옵니다.
examples.translation: jogeumman deo osimyeon oreunjjoge uchegugi naomnida. — If you come a little farther, a post office appears on the right.

examples.text: 그 다음 사거리에서 좌회전하시면 저희 이십일 사단이 있습니다.
examples.translation: geu daeum sageorieseo jwahoejeonhasimyeon jeohui isibil sadani itseumnida. — If you turn left at the next intersection, our 21st Division is there.

examples.text: 이십일 사단 작전과 중위 박용우
examples.translation: isibil sadan jakjeongwa jungwi bagyongu — Operations Section, 21st Division, First Lieutenant Park Yongwoo

explanations.title: Activity 2: the directions summarized (mine)
explanations.body: The book’s note box, “Directions to the 21st Division”, is blank bullets; my answers:

rows: Take the Gyeongbu Expressway toward Daejeon
After about two hours, transfer to the Honam Expressway toward Gwangju
After about an hour, you will see the Jeongeup exit
Turn left at the first traffic light
A little farther, a post office appears on the right
Turn left at the next intersection: the 21st Division is there

explanations.title: Activity 4 (Reading, writing, speaking): which gas station do you like?
explanations.body: The book lists four incentives that gas stations use to attract customers and asks you to rate each on a scale of 1 to 4 (1 = the most attractive), then to write about two gas stations you often use and say which you like better and why, using ~보다 and -기 때문에, and to interview three classmates. The incentives are the book’s (the English is mine); the two model sentences are the book’s (the English is mine; the brand names are written in Hangul as in the book).

rows: a gas station with cheap gas
a gas station with a car wash (세차장 = a car wash, the book’s gloss)
a gas station with a convenience store
a gas station close to home

examples.text: 편의점이 (더) 크기 때문에 저는 세븐 일레븐 주유소가 쉘 주유소보다 좋아요.
examples.translation: pyeonuijeomi (deo) keugi ttaemune jeoneun sebeun illebeun juyusoga swel juyusoboda joayo. — Because the convenience store is (bigger), I like the Seven Eleven gas station better than the Shell gas station.

examples.text: 가격이 (더) 싸기 때문에 저는 파일럿 주유소가 쉐브론 주유소보다 좋아요.
examples.translation: gagyeogi (deo) ssagi ttaemune jeoneun pailleot juyusoga swebeuron juyusoboda joayo. — Because the price is (cheaper), I like the Pilot gas station better than the Chevron gas station.

explanations.title: Activities left out
explanations.body: Activity 1 (listening to three students describe a weekend trip, to fill in the destination, direction and drive time), Activity 3 (two advertisements of Korean gas stations that are shown as pictures, and a conversation about two gas stations, 강남 주유소 and 서울 주유소, to listen to) and the interviews of Activity 4 are audio, picture or partner activities.

explanations.title: To take or bring: 데리고, 모시고, 가지고
explanations.body: Koreans use 가다 and 오다 to show movement from one place to another. Because “take” and “bring” involve movement, Koreans express these verbs with a compound verb that includes 가다 or 오다. Three different verbs can be used, and the type of object decides which: (~을/를) 데리고 가다/오다 for a person or an animal, (~을/를) 모시고 가다/오다 for a person you show respect to, and (~을/를) 가지고 가다/오다 for an inanimate object.

rows: take/bring (a person that you show respect to)

explanations.title: Cultural note: 환갑 (the 60th birthday)
explanations.body: 환갑 (or 회갑), the 60th birthday, is considered the most important birthday. The number 60 means completing one zodiacal cycle and beginning another in one’s lifespan. In the past the average life expectancy was much lower than today, so 환갑 also meant a celebration of longevity, and the party is a wish for an even longer and more prosperous life. In the traditional 환갑 celebration, children honor their parents by throwing a big party with a large feast and much merrymaking; children and grandchildren typically wear hanbok (한복) and bow to the parents to pay their respects. Today, with longer lives, the celebration has become simpler and less significant: many Koreans eat out with close friends and family or take a trip with the family. The 70th birthday, called 칠순 or 고희, and the 80th birthday, called 팔순, are celebrated as well.

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 부모 (父母)
explanations.body: The first syllable 부 (父) means father or paternal, as in 부자 (father and son) and 부녀 (father and daughter), while the second syllable 모 (母) means mother or maternal, as in 모자 (mother and son) and 모녀 (mother and daughter). Hence 부모 means father and mother, or parents. The book asks you to guess the meaning of 조부모 (조 祖 = grand-) and 모국; its Core Vocabulary also lists 모친, 부친 and 부자간 without meanings, so those are mine.

lessons.title: 153. Ch 10 · Grammar C: attributive forms of action verbs -는, -(으)ㄴ, -(으)ㄹ
lessons.subtitle: 공부하는 학생 · 공부한 학생 · 공부할 학생 · 먹는 음식 · 먹은 음식 · 먹을 음식

explanations.title: Attributive forms of action verbs
explanations.body: Look at the English phrases “a crying baby”, “a baby who is sleeping in the crib”, “time to sleep”, “a place for eating kimchi” and “a reason why John learned Korean”: the italicized words or phrases modify the nouns and function as adjectives. In Korean we express all of them with attributive forms. In Chapter 4 you learned the attributive forms of stative verbs (싼 컴퓨터, 좋은 컴퓨터), made by adding (으)ㄴ to the stem. Action verbs have three attributive forms, one for each tense: 공부하는 학생 (a student who studies/is studying; present), 공부한 학생 (a student who studied; past) and 공부할 학생 (a student who will study; future). Each form modifies the noun that comes right after it, and can be expanded by adding more elements in front: 공부하는 학생 → 도서관에서 공부하는 학생 → 매일 도서관에서 공부하는 학생. The modified noun is still a noun and is used as part of the sentence.

explanations.title: The three attributive forms
explanations.body: Present: verb stem + 는 (an ongoing or habitual action), as in 지금 읽는 책 and 매일 가는 카페. Past: verb stem + (으)ㄴ (a completed action): 은 after a consonant (어제 읽은 책, 어제 먹은 음식), ㄴ after a vowel (어제 만난 친구, 어제 간 곳). Future: verb stem + (으)ㄹ (an anticipated action): 을 after a consonant (내일 읽을 책, 내일 먹을 음식), ㄹ after a vowel (내일 할 일, 내일 갈 곳). A stem that ends in ㄹ drops the ㄹ before 는 and ㄴ (살다 → 사는, 산) and takes the future form as it is (살 → 살); this is the ordinary rule for ㄹ stems, not stated in the book, so the forms of 살다, 만들다, 알다 and 놀다 below are mine.

explanations.title: Activity 3 (Reading): Chaeho’s e-mail to his uncle
explanations.body: Chaeho sent this e-mail to his uncle Hyunchae, who lives in the U.S.; the subject line is 어머니 환갑여행 (a trip for my mother’s 60th birthday). The book asks you to fill in a table in English with the occasion, the time and duration, the location, the participants and the activities. The text is the book’s, with 3박 4일 and 6월 spelled out in Hangul; the sender and recipient lines with e-mail addresses are left out. The English is mine.

explanations.title: The e-mail: the table filled in
explanations.body: My key to the book’s table.

rows: Last week; three nights and four days
Eight people: his mother, father, older brother’s family (brother, sister-in-law and baby), aunt (이모), her husband (이모부) and Chaeho
Sightseeing, buying souvenirs, taking photos; no hiking because of the weather

explanations.title: Grammar and words to notice
explanations.body: The e-mail uses several things from this chapter and earlier: 환갑 (the 60th birthday); 데리고 오다 (to bring a person); the attributive form 태어난 (born) in 유월에 태어난 조카, and 좋아하시는 (that he likes, honorific) in 아버지께서 좋아하시는 등산; 동안 (during, for) in 삼박사일 동안 and 여행하는 동안; the negative 못 했어요 (couldn’t do). 이것저것 means “this and that”; 등산 is hiking and 기념품 is a souvenir (the meanings of these three are mine; the book does not gloss them here).

explanations.title: How to use this list
explanations.body:
The book’s Core Vocabulary lists the core words of the chapter with an example sentence for each (the sentences are the book’s; the book gives no English for them). The book writes pairs together (기차/열차, 항(구), 올해/금년, 값/가격, 여러 (가지), 방문(~하다), 조심(~하다), 데리고 가다/모시고 가다 (↑)); they are split here. Two of the book’s sentences have two versions (이 의자가 좀 불편해요 / 차가 없어서 불편해요; 책 살 돈이 없어요… / 결혼식에 입을 웨딩드레스를 빌렸습니다) and only the second is shown. The book’s Additional Vocabulary section is a blank list for words you add yourself.

Where a split word has no sentence of its own, it reuses the book’s sentence with the variant substituted (열차, 금년, 가격, 모시고 가다/오다 with a respected person). Digits are respelled in Hangul (1번 고속도로 → 일 번 고속도로, 101번 → 백일 번, 156번 → 백오십육 번, 10시 → 열 시, 3년 → 삼 년, 10-15% → 십 퍼센트에서 십오 퍼센트, 1달러 → 일 달러, 1987년 1월 1일 → 천구백팔십칠년 일월 일일); LA is said 엘에이, PC 피씨; the possessive 의 after a person is said 에.

explanations.title: Self-evaluation
explanations.body:
Recall the objectives of the chapter and ask yourself whether you have achieved them (the book asks you to tick Yes or No). If you tick “No” for any item, the book suggests: review that section on your own; find a study partner and review it as a pair or group; and tell your academic advisor or team leader which areas you need more help with, so that they can provide activities tailored to your learning style and needs.

Now I am able to: talk about trip planning, including the means of transportation; compare two things or people; give and understand directions; use proper kinship terms for an extended family.

Now I have a clear understanding of: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; comparative 보다 (더) (more … than; …er than); the conjunctive ending -기 때문에 (because); ~때문에 (because of); the attributive forms of action verbs -는, -(으)ㄴ and -(으)ㄹ; the Sino-Korean syllables 부 (父), 모 (母), 출 (出), 입 (入) and 구 (口).

explanations.title: Core words and phrases of Topic A
explanations.body: The meanings are the book’s (from the Core Vocabulary). The book lists ~곳, ~세(대), 근무(하다) and 사업(하다) as groups and 만 and 억 under Numbers; they are split here. -(으)ㄹ 때 and ~(으)로 are explained in their own lessons: -(으)ㄹ 때 is “when; time; at the time of”, and ~(으)로 is “(status) as”, as in 의사로 일하는 한인들이 많아요 (there are many Koreans who work as doctors).

explanations.title: Footnotes
explanations.body: 교포 means Koreans residing abroad. Thus 재미교포 means Koreans residing in the U.S.; 재일교포 means Koreans residing in Japan; and 재중교포 means Koreans residing in China. 근데 is a contracted form of 그런데, which can be translated as but, however, by the way, or and.

explanations.title: Generations: 한인 일 세, 이 세, 일 점 오 세
explanations.body: The first generation of Koreans in a new country is called 한인 1세(대), and the second generation is called 한인 2세(대). However, Koreans who immigrate to a new country before or during their early teens are called 1.5세(대) (1.5 generation). As the history of Korean immigration gets longer, the third and fourth generations and up (한인 3세/4세 and up) are rapidly increasing. The numbers are read in Sino-Korean: 일 세, 이 세, 일 점 오 세. (The table gives the digits in the first cell and the reading in the cells that are said.)

rows: the 1.5 generation: immigrated before or during the early teens
한인 삼 세, 한인 사 세
third and fourth generations and up

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 민 (民)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means people, folks, or civil(ian), as in 국민 (a people; “people of a country”), 시민 (a citizen; “people of a city”), 군민 (county people), 민병 (a militiaman; “civilian soldier”) and 이민 (immigration; emigration; “moving of people”). The Core Vocabulary also lists 민요 and 민족 under 민 without meanings; folk song and ethnic group/nation are mine.

lessons.title: 157. Ch 11 · Large numbers and decimals
lessons.subtitle: 만 · 억 · 조 · 삼십오점 일구 · 영점 구 · 사점 공팔

explanations.title: How to read large numbers
explanations.body: In the U.S. we separate every three digits with a comma and name each three-digit group thousand, million, billion, trillion, etc. 304,257,284,567 reads “three hundred four billion, two hundred fifty-seven million, two hundred eighty-four thousand, five hundred sixty-seven.” In Korean we break a number into four-digit groups and name each four-digit group based on 만 (10,000), 억 (100,000,000), 조 (1,000,000,000,000), etc.; however, commas still separate every three digits when a number is in Arabic numerals. The same number is therefore read in four-digit groups: 3,042 억 5,728 만 4,567.

tables.note: Inside a four-digit group the digits are read thousands-hundreds-tens-units; the book writes 3천4십2억 5천7백2십8만 4천5백6십7 (a digit 1 before 천, 백, 십 is not read: 천, 백, 십).

explanations.title: Large numbers from the book and from the chapter
explanations.body: The readings below follow the four-digit rule (the book’s own readings are 백구십이만 육천오백팔 for 1,926,508 and 육만 사백 for 60,400; the others are mine, worked out with the same rule). A 1 before 만 is not read (만), but a 1 before 억 or 조 is (일억, 일조).

explanations.title: How to read decimals
explanations.body: In English, 35.19 is read as “thirty-five point one nine.” Reading decimals in Korean is quite similar. “Point” is read as 점, whose literal meaning is a point or a period. Therefore 35.19 is read as 삼십오점 일구. However, there are some decimal values you should be careful with. For example, .9 and .7 are always rendered as 0.9 or 0.7 in Korean and, therefore, are read as 영점 구 and 영점 칠, respectively. When the number 0 comes after a decimal point, 0 can be read as either 공 or 영; 4.08, for example, is read as 사점 공팔 or 사점 영팔.

explanations.title: Percentages
explanations.body: The book reads percent as 퍼센트 after the number, as in the Activity 3 model: 삼점일 퍼센트 (3.1%) and, in Follow-Up Activity 3 of Topic A, 사십오 퍼센트 (45%).

explanations.title: Activity 2 (Reading): the Korean population in the U.S.
explanations.body: The book shows a news article (from Yonhap News) from the U.S. Census Bureau about the Korean population in the U.S. and asks you to write what the numbers represent and how they are written in Korean; the first row is done for you (1,926,508 → 백구십이만 육천오백팔). The headline reads 재미교포 인구 192만명…캘리포니아주에 55만 7천여 명 거주. The article is the book’s, with the numbers, ACS and LA spelled out in Hangul (the English is mine; the “see the numbers” hint tells you to ignore unknown words).

explanations.title: Part I: checking in at the Olympic Hotel
explanations.body: PV2 Kim is checking in at the front desk of the Olympic Hotel in Koreatown in L.A. The Korean is the book’s, with 120달러, 2개 and 1층 spelled out in Hangul (the English is mine).

examples.text: 호텔 직원: 어서 오세요. 어떻게 도와드릴까요?
examples.translation: hotel jigwon: eoseo oseyo. eotteoke dowadeurilkkayo? — Welcome. How can I help you?

examples.text: 김 이병: 안녕하세요? 빈 방이 있습니까?
examples.translation: gim ibyeong: annyeonghaseyo? bin bangi itseumnikka? — Hello. Do you have a vacant room?

examples.text: 호텔 직원: 네, 있습니다. 언제까지 묵으시겠어요?
examples.translation: hotel jigwon: ne, itseumnida. eonjekkaji mugeusigesseoyo? — Yes, we do. Until when will you stay?

examples.text: 김 이병: 사흘 동안 묵고 싶어요. 숙박비가 얼마예요?
examples.translation: gim ibyeong: saheul dongan mukgo sipeoyo. sukbakbiga eolmayeyo? — I want to stay for three days. How much is the lodging fee?

examples.text: 호텔 직원: 일반실은 하루에 백이십 달러입니다.
examples.translation: hotel jigwon: ilbansireun harue baegisip dalleoimnida. — A standard room is 120 dollars a day.

examples.text: 김 이병: 그 방으로 두 개 주세요. 그리고 이 호텔에 수영장이 있습니까?
examples.translation: gim ibyeong: geu bangeuro du gae juseyo. geurigo i hotere suyeongjangi itseumnikka? — Please give me two of that room. And does this hotel have a swimming pool?

examples.text: 호텔 직원: 네, 일 층 비상구 옆에 있습니다.
examples.translation: hotel jigwon: ne, il cheung bisanggu yeope itseumnida. — Yes, it is next to the emergency exit on the first floor.

explanations.title: Part II: requests and complaints
explanations.body: PFC Jones is calling the hotel front desk with requests and complaints (the book writes 303호 and 810호; spelled out here as 삼백삼 호 and 팔백십 호).

examples.translation: hotel jigwon: peureonteudeseukeuimnida. mueoseul dowadeurilkkayo? — This is the front desk. What can I help you with?

examples.text: 존스 일병: 여기 삼백삼 호입니다. 욕실에 수건이 더 필요해요.
examples.translation: jonseu ilbyeong: yeogi sambaeksam hoimnida. yoksire sugeoni deo piryohaeyo. — This is room 303. We need more towels in the bathroom.

examples.text: 호텔 직원: 네, 알겠습니다.
examples.translation: hotel jigwon: ne, algetseumnida. — Yes, certainly.

examples.text: 존스 일병: 그리고 옆 방이 시끄러워요. 다른 방으로 옮기고 싶어요.
examples.translation: jonseu ilbyeong: geurigo yeop bangi sikkeureowoyo. dareun bangeuro omgigo sipeoyo. — And the room next door is noisy. I want to move to another room.

examples.text: 호텔 직원: 잠시만요… 지금 팔백십 호가 비었습니다. 그 방으로 옮기시겠습니까?
examples.translation: hotel jigwon: jamsimanyo… jigeum palbaeksip hoga bieotseumnida. geu bangeuro omgisigetseumnikka? — Just a moment… Room 810 is vacant now. Would you like to move to that room?

examples.text: 존스 일병: 네, 감사합니다.
examples.translation: jonseu ilbyeong: ne, gamsahamnida. — Yes, thank you.

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 비 (費)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means expense or fee. The book asks you to guess the meaning of 숙박비, 택시비 and 학비; the answers are below (숙박비 is the lodging fee of the Core Vocabulary; the other two answers are mine).

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 실 (室)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means a room or chamber, as in 침실 (a bedroom) and 거실 (a living room). The book asks you to guess 세탁실, 화장실 and 교실; the answers are mine.

explanations.title: Role-play plan (Presentation Activity d)
explanations.body: Pair up: one partner plays two customers (PV2 Kim for Part I and PFC Jones for Part II), the other the hotel clerk. As a customer: ask about rooms available for ( ) nights and the room rate; ask about a swimming pool; make a complaint about noise from the next room; make requests for more towels. As a hotel clerk: a hotel room costs ( ) dollars per night; the swimming pool is located next to the emergency exit on the ground floor; accept the customer’s request for a room change. The role-play itself is a partner activity and is not reproduced.

lessons.subtitle: 숙제할 때 · 날씨가 좋을 때 · 심심할 때 · 점심 때 · 크리스마스 때

explanations.title: -(으)ㄹ 때: “when”
explanations.body: In English, when we use when as a conjunction, as in when he was a boy or when the bell rings, we can translate it as at or during the time that or at the moment that. In Korean we use the conjunctive ending -(으)ㄹ 때 to express when. The same clause is translated differently depending on the main clause: 심심할 때 is “when I am bored”, “when I am bored (in the future)” or “when I was bored”; the tense of the translation is determined by the tense of the main clause, not by 때.

explanations.title: How to form -(으)ㄹ 때
explanations.body: verb stem + (으)ㄹ 때. When a verb stem ends in a vowel, add ㄹ 때 (자다 → 잘 때; 심심하다 → 심심할 때). When a verb stem ends in a consonant, add 을 때 (있다 → 있을 때; 먹다 → 먹을 때). The book gives these two cases; the ㄹ-final stems (살다 → 살 때) and the ㅂ irregular stems (춥다 → 추울 때) follow the same pattern as the future attributive form and are mine.

rows: Verb stem ends in a vowel
자다 → 잘 때; 심심하다 → 심심할 때
Verb stem ends in a consonant
있다 → 있을 때; 먹다 → 먹을 때

tables.note: Stems that end in ㄹ keep it (살다 → 살 때), and ㅂ irregular stems change as usual (춥다 → 추울 때); these rows are mine.

explanations.title: 때 is a noun
explanations.body: Although we treat -(으)ㄹ 때 as a conjunctive ending that we often interpret as when, its literal translation is at the time that or at the time of; 때 literally means time, and -ㄹ/을 is an attributive form that modifies the noun 때. Thus, like other nouns, -(으)ㄹ 때 can take a noun marker. Also, the noun 때 is often preceded by a noun that denotes time, like 아침, 점심, 저녁, 크리스마스 and 휴가; in this case 때 can be translated at the time of or during the time of.

lessons.title: 162. Ch 11 · Grammar B: expressing a strong intention with -겠
lessons.subtitle: 저희가 하겠습니다 · 뭘 드시겠습니까? · 비가 오겠습니다 · -겠 vs -(으)ㄹ 거다

explanations.title: -겠: strong possibility and strong intention
explanations.body: In English, the modal verb will, which is used to express an event or a state in the future, implies either the strong possibility of an event/state or the strong intention of the subject: It will rain tonight (strong possibility) versus I will find you! (strong intention). Similarly, the verb suffix 겠 implies the strong possibility of an event/state or the strong intention of the speaker. In an earlier chapter, on weather forecasting, the book briefly discussed that 겠 implies a strong possibility. However, when the subject of a sentence is a person, especially the first or second person, 겠 often conveys the strong intention of the person. The 겠 that conveys the strong intention of the subject is used only with an action verb.

explanations.title: -겠 versus -(으)ㄹ 거다
explanations.body: Recall that -(으)ㄹ 거다, which you learned about in Chapter 9, is also used to express a future event. However, -(으)ㄹ 거다 is usually used to convey a future event that the speaker has prior knowledge of or that has been planned. Thus -(으)ㄹ 거다 is usually translated as “be going to”, while 겠 for intention is “will”.

explanations.body: The meanings are the book’s (from the Core Vocabulary). The book lists 배(가) 부르다 with the 가 in parentheses and -지만, -지 못하다 and -지 않다 among the words; those three have their own grammar lessons.

explanations.title: Footnotes: 전에 and 별로
explanations.body: 전에 means previously or before. 별로 means particularly and is always used in a negated sentence, as in 저는 김밥을 별로 안 좋아해요 (I do not particularly like kimbap). The book’s dialog shows both: 전에 써 봤지만 and 별로 싱겁지 않아요.

explanations.title: Types of tastes (맛의 종류)
explanations.body: The book’s table of the five basic tastes. The example sentences are from the Core Vocabulary, except for 맵다, which the book lists in this table but not in its vocabulary list; its example sentence is mine. The last column gives the attributive form used with 맛 (a stative verb’s attributive form ends in (으)ㄴ, as in Chapter 4; the book uses 단 맛, 매운 맛, 짠 맛, 신 맛 and 쓴 맛 in Activity 3).

explanations.title: Cultural notes: table manners and hospitality
explanations.body: A spirit of respect for elders is found throughout Korean culture. People are served in the order of seniority and do not pick up their chopsticks or spoon before elders begin eating. It is also a Korean hospitality custom for hosts to repeatedly urge their guests to eat more. Although the younger generation is slowly moving away from this tradition, many Koreans still practice it. If you wish to stop eating, politely tell your host that you are too full when you are asked to eat more (as PFC Jones does with 배가 불러서 더 못 먹겠어요).

lessons.title: 164. Ch 11 · Grammar C: long-form negation -지 않다 and -지 못하다
lessons.subtitle: 먹지 않아요 · 먹지 못해요 · 춥지 않아요 · 안 vs -지 않다 · 못 vs -지 못하다

explanations.title: Revisiting negation: short and long forms
explanations.body: In Chapter 7 you learned that Koreans negate a verb by placing either 안 or 못 in front of the verb: 아침을 안 먹습니다 (I do not eat breakfast), 아침을 못 먹습니다 (I cannot eat breakfast). 안 and 못 are the short forms of verb negation. In this chapter the book introduces the long forms, -지 않다 and -지 못하다. -지 못하다 is used with an action verb, but is rarely used with a stative verb; it can be used interchangeably with -(으)ㄹ 수 없다.

explanations.title: “Don’t”: verb stem + 지 않다
explanations.body: With verb stems (action verbs and stative verbs), add 지 않다: 일어나다 → 일어나지 않다; 먹다 → 먹지 않다; 춥다 → 춥지 않다.

examples.text: 아침에 일찍 일어나지 않습니다.
examples.translation: achime iljjik ireonaji anseumnida. — I don’t get up early in the morning.

examples.text: 짠 음식을 먹지 않습니다.
examples.translation: jjan eumsigeul meokji anseumnida. — I don’t eat salty foods.

examples.text: 몬트레이는 춥지 않습니다.
examples.translation: monteureineun chupji anseumnida. — It is not cold in Monterey.

explanations.title: “Can’t”: action verb stem + 지 못하다
explanations.body: With action verb stems only, add 지 못하다: 일어나다 → 일어나지 못하다; 먹다 → 먹지 못하다.

examples.text: 아침에 일찍 일어나지 못합니다.

examples.text: 짠 음식을 먹지 못합니다.
examples.translation: jjan eumsigeul meokji motamnida. — I can’t eat salty foods.

examples.text: 아침을 먹을 수 없습니다.
examples.translation: achimeul meogeul su eopseumnida. — I can’t eat breakfast. (= 먹지 못합니다)

examples.text: 저는 술을 마시지 않아요.

explanations.title: Verb tables
explanations.body: The informal polite forms (-지 않아요 and -지 못해요) of action verbs, with the honorific forms, and of stative verbs, which have no -지 못하다 form. The verb tables are mine; the endings are the book’s.

tables.note: Stative verbs are not negated with -지 못하다 (the book: they cannot be negated this way). The ㅂ irregular stems keep ㅂ before 지: 춥지, 맵지.

rows: A stative verb: only the -지 않다 form.

lessons.title: 165. Ch 11 · Grammar D: the conjunctive ending -지만 (but)
lessons.subtitle: 김치가 맵지만 맛있어요 · 한국말이 어렵지만 재미있어요 · -지만 vs 그렇지만

explanations.title: -지만: contrasting two clauses
explanations.body: In English, when contrasting two clauses we can use conjunctions like but, although and whereas (John works harder, but Jane works smarter). In Korean we contrast two clauses by using the conjunctive ending -지만, which can be interpreted as “but”. It attaches to the verb stem (the past -았/었- comes before it: 추웠지만), and works with both action and stative verbs.

examples.text: 한국이 작지만 대만은 더 작아요.
examples.translation: hangugi jakjiman daemaneun deo jagayo. — Korea is small, but Taiwan is smaller.

examples.text: 한국말이 어렵지만 재미있어요.
examples.translation: hangungmari eoryeopjiman jaemiisseoyo. — Korean is difficult, but it is fun.

examples.text: 한국말이 어렵지만 재미있어요.

examples.text: 김치가 맵지만 맛있습니다.

explanations.title: -지만 versus 그렇지만 / 하지만
explanations.body: -지만 may seem identical in meaning to 그렇지만 or 하지만, which you have encountered frequently. The book elaborates on their differences in Chapter 12; for now, know that -지만 is the conjunctive ending and is attached to the verb in the first clause, whereas 그렇지만 or 하지만 are adverbs that come between two independent clauses separated by a period.

examples.text: 한국말이 어려워요. 그렇지만 재미있어요.
examples.translation: hangungmari eoryeowoyo. geureochiman jaemiisseoyo. — Korean is difficult. However, it is fun.

examples.text: 저는 한국 음식을 좋아해요. 그렇지만 제 남편은 일식을 좋아해요.
examples.translation: jeoneun hanguk eumsigeul joahaeyo. geureochiman je nampyeoneun ilsigeul joahaeyo. — I like Korean food. However, my husband likes Japanese food. (the Core Vocabulary’s sentence)

explanations.title: How to form -지만
explanations.body: verb stem + 지만 (the ㅂ irregular stems keep ㅂ here, as before 지: 맵지만, 춥지만). For the past, add 았/었 first: 추웠지만, 비쌌지만. The table is mine.

explanations.body: The book’s passage about Korean table etiquette (the English is mine). Words glossed by the book: 손 (a hand), 어른 (an adult), 들다 (to lift), 코를 풀다 (to blow one’s nose).

explanations.title: True or false?
explanations.body: The book asks you to decide whether each English statement is true according to the passage (the answers are mine).

rows: Koreans use chopsticks for eating steamed rice.
Rice and soup are eaten with a spoon, not chopsticks.
When serving and receiving food, Koreans use both hands.
Both hands are used to give and receive food.

explanations.title: How to use this list
explanations.body:
The book’s Core Vocabulary lists the core words of the chapter with an example sentence for each (the sentences are the book’s; the book gives no English for them). The book writes pairs together (사업(~하다), ~세(대), 이용(~하다), 체크아웃(~하다), 체크인(~하다), 프런트(데스크), 근무(~하다), 할인(~하다/~받다), 배(가) 부르다); they are split here. The book’s Additional Vocabulary section is a blank list for words you add yourself.

Where a split word has no sentence of its own, it reuses the book’s sentence of the matching word (세대, 할인받다 with a military discount from the hotel review). Digits are respelled in Hangul (3만 → 삼만, 3억 → 삼억, 13억 → 십삼억, 10살 → 열 살, 203호 → 이백삼 호, 3층부터 10층까지 → 삼 층부터 십 층까지, 12층 → 십이 층, 12시 → 열두 시, 120달러 → 백이십 달러); LA is said 엘에이.

explanations.title: Self-evaluation
explanations.body:
Recall the objectives of the chapter and ask yourself whether you have achieved them (the book asks you to tick Yes or No). If you tick “No” for any item, the book suggests: review that section on your own; find a study partner and review it as a pair or group; and tell your academic advisor or team leader which areas you need more help with, so that they can provide activities tailored to your learning style and needs.

Now I am able to: identify the general profile of the Korean community in the U.S.; use large numbers and decimals in context; make hotel reservations and requests for services; talk about the five basic tastes; identify Korean table etiquette.

Now I have a clear understanding of: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; -지 않다 (do not); -지 못하다 (cannot); the conjunctive ending -지만 (but); the conjunctive ending -(으)ㄹ 때 (when); -겠 for a strong intention (will); the Sino-Korean syllables 민 (民), 비 (費) and 실 (室).

explanations.title: Notes on the spelling

explanations.body: The following text is SPC Jones’ journal entry about her shopping at a gift shop and sending parcels at a post office in L.A. The Korean is the book’s, with the prices and counted numbers spelled out in Hangul (120불 → 백이십 불, 60불, 20불, 10장 → 열 장, 2장 → 두 장, 19불 → 십구 불; the English is mine).

explanations.title: Core words and phrases of Topic A
explanations.body: The meanings are the book’s (from the Core Vocabulary). The book lists -게 (the adverb maker, explained in its own lesson), ~불 and ~장 (counters), and 포장(하다) as a group; 벨트 and 핸드백 are loan words. 친절하다 is the verb of 친절 “kindness”.

rows: to cut or shave off (price); to discount

explanations.title: Counters: 불 and 장
explanations.body: 불 counts dollars (the book also writes ~달러; in speech both are used) and 장 counts sheets of paper, cloth, postcards, stamps, etc. Both come after a number: Sino-Korean numbers with 불 (십구 불) and native numbers with 장 (열 장, 두 장). In the journal: 우표 열 장과 엽서 두 장 (ten stamps and two postcards).

examples.text: 우표 열 장과 엽서 두 장을 샀습니다.

examples.text: 엽서 열 장 주세요.
examples.translation: yeopseo yeol jang juseyo. — Please give me ten postcards. (the Core Vocabulary’s sentence)

examples.text: 이 옷은 원래 칠십 달러였어요. 그런데 세일해서 오십 불에 샀어요.
examples.translation: i oseun wollae chilsip dalleoyeosseoyo. geureonde seilhaeseo osip bure sasseoyo. — This outfit was originally 70 dollars. But it was on sale and I bought it for 50 dollars. (the Core Vocabulary’s sentence)

explanations.title: Pronunciation guide: 원래 /월래/
explanations.body: Have you noticed that 원 in 원래 sounds like 월? This is due to the influence of the consonant ㄹ in the syllable that follows. When ㄴ is followed by ㄹ, oftentimes ㄴ changes into ㄹ. This is an example of anticipatory assimilation, in which a sound becomes more like a following sound. The book’s practice words are in the table.

explanations.title: Cultural note: the Korean postal system
explanations.body: The Korean postal system is different from that in the U.S. with regard to outgoing mail. The U.S. postal system usually picks up outgoing mail from home addresses, but the postal system in Korea does not. Therefore, when Koreans have outgoing mail they go to the post office or post their letters in a red mailbox on the street, which is called 우체통.

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 우 (郵)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable 우 means post or mail, as in 우체국 (a post office), 우표 (post stamp; “post ticket”), 우편물 (mail; postal matter) and 우편번호 (the postal code; zip code; “postal number”).

rows: the postal code; zip code; “postal number”
a mailbox (the red street mailbox of the cultural note)

explanations.title: Korean verbs that express “to wear” or “to put on”
explanations.body: Korean uses a different verb depending on the kind of item. 입다 is for basic clothing items; 신다 for footwear; 쓰다 for items worn to cover the head or face; 매다 (“to tie”) for items worn by tying; 끼다 (“to insert”) for items that are snug-fitting; and 차다 (“to fasten”) for items worn by fastening them on. Some items take more than one verb (안경 can take 쓰다 or 끼다). In the book’s table 마스크 means “a mask”, 총 “a gun” and 수통 “a canteen”; the others are in the list above or in the Core Vocabulary.

explanations.title: Activity 1 (Reading and speaking): shopping for civilian clothes in Korea
explanations.body: You are stationed in Osan, Korea, and all of your moving boxes were transferred to the wrong place; it may take over two weeks for the boxes to be delivered. You brainstorm what civilian clothing you have to buy, then, with 300,000 Korean won (삼십만 원), you circle the items you decide to buy in the two flyers and tell a partner your reasons. The flyers are below as tables (the phone numbers are left out; the readings of the prices are mine; the book prints the discount rate beside each line and does not say whether the printed price is before or after the discount).

tables.note: The flyer also announces a 60% discount (육십 퍼센트 할인) on other items: 양말, 스타킹, 넥타이, 벨트, 스카프, 장갑, 모자 and so on. 반바지 (shorts) is not in the Core Vocabulary; its meaning here is mine.

explanations.title: Reading percentages and prices in a shop
explanations.body: A discount is 할인; the rate is said with 퍼센트 (삼십 퍼센트 할인). Won are counted with Sino-Korean numbers in groups of four digits (만 = 10,000): 칠만 원 is 70,000 won. A 1 before 만 is not read (만 원 = 10,000 won).

lessons.title: 173. Ch 12 · Grammar A: asking for and giving permission with -아/어도 되다
lessons.subtitle: 입어 봐도 돼요? · 먹어도 돼요? · 앉아도 되다 · 봐도 되다 · 해도 괜찮아요

explanations.title: -아/어도 되다: “may I …?”
explanations.body: In English, we use phrases such as “May I …?”, “Is it all right if …?” or “Do you mind if …?” when asking for permission; the same phrases are used when permission is granted (“You may …” or “It’s all right if …”). In Korean, we use -아/어도 되다 when asking for or giving permission to do something. 되다 literally means “to become”; it can also mean to be O.K., to be fine, to be all right or to be possible. Therefore -아/어도 좋다 and -아/어도 괜찮다 can be substituted for -아/어도 되다.

examples.text: 교실에서 영어를 해도 돼요?
examples.translation: gyosireseo yeongeoreul haedo dwaeyo? — Is it all right if I speak English in the classroom?

examples.text: 교실에서 영어를 해도 좋아요?

examples.text: 교실에서 영어를 해도 괜찮아요?
examples.translation: gyosireseo yeongeoreul haedo gwaenchanayo? — Is it all right if I speak English in the classroom? (with 괜찮다)

explanations.title: How to form it
explanations.body: verb stem + 아/어도 되다 (괜찮다/좋다). If the last syllable of the verb stem contains the vowels ㅏ or ㅗ, add 아도 되다; if it contains a vowel other than ㅏ or ㅗ, add 어도 되다. The usual contractions of the -아/어 form apply (보다 → 봐도, 마시다 → 마셔도, 하다 → 해도, 쓰다 → 써도).

rows: The last syllable of a verb stem contains ㅏ or ㅗ
의자에 앉다 → 의자에 앉아도 되다; 영화를 보다 → 영화를 봐도 되다
The last syllable of a verb stem contains a vowel other than ㅏ or ㅗ
코트를 입다 → 코트를 입어도 되다; 책을 읽다 → 책을 읽어도 되다

lessons.title: 174. Ch 12 · Grammar B: denying permission with -(으)면 안 되다
lessons.subtitle: 영어를 하면 안 됩니다 · 주차하면 안 돼요 · 앉으면 안 되다 · 놀면 안 돼

explanations.title: -(으)면 안 되다: “you may not …”
explanations.body: To express a refusal of permission or the prohibition of an action, Koreans use -(으)면 안 되다. The literal meaning of -(으)면 안 되다 is “(it) is not all right if …” or “(it) is not fine if …”. Thus, depending on the context, it can be translated as you may not, you should not, you must not or you are not allowed to.

examples.text: 교실에서 영어를 하면 안 됩니다.
examples.translation: gyosireseo yeongeoreul hamyeon an doemnida. — You should not speak English in the classroom.

examples.text: 이곳에 주차하면 안 돼요.
examples.translation: igose juchahamyeon an dwaeyo. — You may not park your car here.

examples.text: 도서관에서 음식을 먹으면 안 됩니다.
examples.translation: doseogwaneseo eumsigeul meogeumyeon an doemnida. — You must not eat in the library. (the Core Vocabulary’s sentence)

explanations.title: How to form it
explanations.body: verb stem + (으)면 안 되다. When the verb stem ends in a vowel or ㄹ, add 면 안 되다 (기숙사에 살다 → 기숙사에 살면 안 되다; 친구를 만나다 → 친구를 만나면 안 되다). When the verb stem ends in a consonant other than ㄹ, add 으면 안 되다 (여기에 앉다 → 여기에 앉으면 안 되다; 창문을 닫다 → 창문을 닫으면 안 되다). The ㄷ irregular verb 듣다 changes to 들으면 (음악을 들으면 안 되다); this is mine.

rows: The verb stem ends in a vowel or ㄹ
기숙사에 살다 → 기숙사에 살면 안 되다; 친구를 만나다 → 친구를 만나면 안 되다
The verb stem ends in a consonant other than ㄹ

explanations.body: The book gives a list of activities (음악을 듣다, 술을 마시다, 집에 전화하다, 일찍 자다) that are allowed or not allowed, asks you to add more and to take turns asking and answering with -아/어도 되다 or -(으)면 안 되다; only the first line is done for you (not allowed): A: 여기서 음악을 들어도 돼요? explanations.body: The meanings are the book’s (from the Core Vocabulary). The book lists 계산(하다) and 식품(점) as groups; they are split here (식품 is “eating item”; 식품점 is the store). -데 is a dependent noun, explained in the card below.

rows: to calculate; to compute; to count

explanations.title: Types of grocery items (식품의 종류)
explanations.body: The book’s categories of grocery items: meat (고기), fruit (과일) and seasoning (양념). The English glosses in parentheses are the book’s.

explanations.title: Dependent nouns: 데 (a place) and 것 (a thing)
explanations.body: The two nouns -데 (a place) and -것 (a thing) are called dependent nouns because they cannot stand on their own and must be accompanied by a modifier immediately preceding them. While both nouns can be modified by the attributive forms of verbs, as in 먹을 데 (a place to eat) and 먹을 것 (a thing to eat), -것 can also be modified by a demonstrative, as in 이것 (this thing) and 저것 (that thing). However, -데 cannot be modified by a demonstrative. The dialog uses both: 고기 파는 데 and 더 필요한 것.

explanations.title: Follow-Up 1 (Reading): the party shopping memo
explanations.body: Your class is having a party and you are one of the people in charge of shopping for grocery items. The book asks you to read the memo that SPC Kim, the class leader, gave you and fill in a table in English (the grocery store, the items to buy and the quantity). The memo is the book’s; 박스 means “a box”, as the book glosses (the English is mine).

lessons.title: 176. Ch 12 · Grammar C: the “adverb maker” -게
lessons.subtitle: 싸게 · 바쁘게 · 예쁘게 · 맛있게 · 예쁘게 포장해 주세요

explanations.title: -게: making an adverb
explanations.body: Adverbs are words that modify (describe) verbs, adjectives or other adverbs, as in work hard, truly happy or extremely slowly. Like truly and extremely, many English adverbs end in -ly; we know that these adverbs are derived from adjectives (true and extreme), and we make them adverbs by adding -ly, so -ly is an adverb “maker”. Korean has an adverb maker as well: 게. Simply by adding 게 to the stem of a stative verb, we make it an adverb: 싸게 (cheaply), 바쁘게 (busily).

lessons.title: 177. Ch 12 · Grammar D: connectors for sentences, verbs and nouns
lessons.subtitle: 그리고 · 그렇지만 · 하지만 · 그러나 · 그런데 · 그래서 · -고 · -지만 · -(으)면 · ~와/과 · ~(이)나

explanations.title: Three types of connectors
explanations.body: You have learned quite a few connectors so far. They are categorized into three types: sentence connectors, verb connectors (or conjunctive endings) and noun connectors.

explanations.title: 1. Sentence connectors
explanations.body: Sentence connectors connect two independent clauses: 저는 초콜렛을 좋아합니다. 그리고 제 친구도 초콜렛을 좋아합니다. / 저는 초콜렛을 좋아합니다. 하지만 제 친구는 안 좋아합니다. (I like chocolate. And my friend likes chocolate too. / I like chocolate. But my friend doesn’t.) The book’s list is below; the English meanings are the book’s.

rows: 어제 영화를 봤어요. 그리고 쇼핑도 했어요.
이 옷은 너무 비싸요. 그렇지만 마음에 들어요.
이 옷은 너무 비싸요. 하지만 마음에 들어요.
오늘은 학교에 가는 날입니다. 그러나 집에서 쉬겠습니다.
내일 산호세 가서 쇼핑하자. 그런데, 한국식품점은 몇 시에 열어?
어제 늦게까지 공부했어. 그래서 좀 피곤해.

explanations.title: 2. Verb connectors (conjunctive endings)
explanations.body: Verb connectors connect two clauses or verbs: 먹습니다 + -고 + 마십니다 → 먹고 마십니다; 저는 공부합니다 + -(으)ㄹ 때 + 음악을 듣습니다 → 저는 공부할 때 음악을 듣습니다. The book’s list is below.

rows: 이 옷은 너무 비싸지만 마음에 들어요.
저녁에 한국 식당 가서 밥 먹자. 이번 주말은 바빠서 등산 못 가요.
다음주에 시험이 있기 때문에 이번 주말에 공부를 해야 합니다.
피곤하면 오늘은 운동하지 마세요. 큰 하얀 건물이 나오면 우회전 하세요.
저는 영화 볼 때 늘 팝콘을 먹어요.

explanations.title: 3. Noun connectors
explanations.body: Noun connectors connect nouns. In English, when we enumerate two or more nouns, we tend to use and/or before the last noun. However, Koreans tend to repeat the noun connector after every noun, as in 포도하고 딸기하고 사과, which translates as “grapes and strawberries and apples”.

rows: 마켓에서 고기와 양념과 과일을 좀 샀습니다. 백화점에서 청바지하고 티셔츠를 세일해요. 생선이랑 소고기랑 닭고기가 모두 얼마에요?

explanations.title: -지만 versus 그렇지만 (from Chapter 11)
explanations.body: As the book said in Chapter 11, -지만 is a conjunctive ending attached to the verb in the first clause, whereas 그렇지만 and 하지만 are adverbs that come between two independent clauses separated by a period. The same holds for the other pairs: -고 / 그리고, -기 때문에 / 그래서.

explanations.title: How to use this list
explanations.body:
The book’s Core Vocabulary lists the core words of the chapter with an example sentence for each (the sentences are the book’s; the book gives no English for them). The book writes some words as groups (포장(~하다), 계산(~하다), 식품(점), 친절(~하다), 그럼(요)); they are split here, and a word without a sentence of its own reuses the book’s. The book’s Additional Vocabulary section is a blank list for words you add yourself.

Digits are respelled in Hangul (5분 → 오 분, 70세 → 칠십 세, 10장 → 열 장, 2파운드 → 두 파운드, 1달러는 100센트 → 일 달러는 백 센트, 50센트 → 오십 센트, 70달러 → 칠십 달러, 50불 → 오십 불, 100달러 → 백 달러, 95불 → 구십오 불); the possessive 의 after a thing is said 에 (후추의 → 후추에). 총 and 수통 are not in the Core Vocabulary; they appear in the table of the “wear” verbs.

explanations.title: What Chapter 13 teaches (한국에 오신 것을 환영합니다)
explanations.body:
Chapter 13, “Welcome to Korea”, opens Unit 4 of the Semester 1 Student’s Edition (A Visit to Korea, 한국 방문). It has three topic presentations, grammar in focus, activities, a self-evaluation and the core vocabulary.

When you finish the chapter you will be able to: talk about flight information including date, time, and flight number; comprehend and respond to flight announcements; understand the boarding procedures at an international airport; answer questions at the customs and immigration office; request in-flight services; request information about airport facilities and services; and describe the size, color, and shape of objects.

You will become familiar with: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; the noun connector ~(이)나 (or); expressing total negation with 아무 ~도; the conjunctive ending -(으)려고 (in order to; so as to); the conjunctive ending -(으)려면 (if one intends to, if one plans to); and the Sino-Korean syllables 권 (券), 승 (乘), 착 (着), and 면 (免).

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 승 (乘)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means riding or getting on (a flight, ship, bus, rollercoaster, horse, etc.), as in 탑승 (boarding; embarkation), 승객 (a passenger; “riding guest”), 승용차 (a car; “vehicle for riding use”), and 승무원 (a crew member; a flight attendant; “riding and working member”). The book asks you to guess the meaning of 승차, 승마 and 승선; my answers are in the last card.

rows: a crew member; a flight attendant; “riding and working member”

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 권 (券)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means a document, a ticket, or a bill, as in 여권 (a passport; “travel document”), 입장권 (an admission ticket; “entrance ticket”), and 상품권 (a gift certificate; “commodity bill”). The book asks you to guess the meaning of 할인권 and 탑승권.

explanations.title: Activity 2 (Reading): before boarding
explanations.body: The book shows check-in and boarding instructions written on the back of a boarding pass and asks you to put the steps in order. The four steps below are the book’s (shown here in the order of the book’s boxes, which is scrambled; digits are respelled in Hangul); the English and the order are mine.

explanations.title: Core words and phrases of Topic B
explanations.body: The meanings are the book’s (from the Core Vocabulary of the chapter). The book writes 기내(식), 신고(하다), 연착(하다/되다), 입국(하다), 착륙(하다), 출국(하다), 통과(하다) and 물어보다 / 묻다 with the optional parts in parentheses; the optional parts are kept in the meanings here.

rows: (申告) report; declaration (~하다: to report; to declare)
(延着) late arrival; delay in arrival (~하다/되다: to be delayed; to be late)
(入國) entry into a country (~하다: to enter a country)
(着陸) landing; “on the land” (~하다: to land)

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 착 (着)
explanations.body: The underlying meaning of this Sino-Korean syllable is physical contact or touch (with a larger object). Depending on the context it can translate to touch, stick to, put on (clothes, hat, shoes, etc.), or arrive, as in 착륙 (landing; “come into contact with land”), 착용 (putting on a safety belt; “putting on and using”), 도착 (arrival), 연착 (delayed arrival), etc.

rows: putting on a safety belt; “putting on and using”

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 면 (免)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means escape, avoid, or exempt, as in 면세 (tax exemption), 면역 (immunity; “exemption from diseases”), and 면허 (a license; a permit; “exempt from permission”). Note that 면허, which literally means “exempt from permission”, refers to a license or permit, as in 운전면허 (driver’s license) and 사업면허 (business license). How can this be? When you get 면허, you are exempt from further permission from authorities and you have your own license to enjoy!

lessons.title: 183. Ch 13 · Grammar A: the noun connector ~(이)나
lessons.subtitle: 한식이나 일식 · 지갑이나 벨트 · 사과나 배 · 샌프란시스코나 산호세

explanations.title: The noun connector ~(이)나 (or)
explanations.body: As the name suggests, the noun connector ~(이)나 is used to connect nouns and is translated as “or” or “either … or”: 샌프란시스코나 산호세 ((either) San Francisco or San Jose), 한국말이나 일본말 ((either) Korean or Japanese). When a noun ends in a consonant add 이나 (한식이나 일식, 지갑이나 벨트, 사과나 배); when a noun ends in a vowel add 나 (샌프란시스코나 산호세).

lessons.title: 184. Ch 13 · Grammar B: total negation with 아무 ~도
lessons.subtitle: 아무도 · 아무것도 · 아무 데도 · 아무 책도 · 하나도 · 한 명도

explanations.title: Partial and total negation
explanations.body:
Compare the two English sentences “We do not need all the apples for the pie” and “We do not need any apples for the pie”. The first indicates that some but not all apples are needed, which is a partial negation; the second indicates that no apples are needed, which is a total negation.

In Korean we can express a total negation as: 아무도 / 아무 noun도 … negative verb. Since 아무 means “anyone” or “any” and the marker 도 means “even” or “also”, the translations are “… not meet … even one person”, “… not read … even one book”, “… not go … even one place” and “… not do … even one thing”.

examples.text: 지난 주말에 아무도 안 만났어요.
examples.translation: jinan jumare amudo an mannasseoyo. — Last weekend, I didn’t meet anyone.

examples.text: 지난 주말에 아무 책도 안 읽었어요.
examples.translation: jinan jumare amu chaekdo an ilgeosseoyo. — Last weekend, I didn’t read any books.

examples.text: 지난 주말에 아무 데도 안 갔어요.
examples.translation: jinan jumare amu dedo an gasseoyo. — Last weekend, I didn’t go anywhere.

examples.text: 지난 주말에 아무것도 안 했어요.
examples.translation: jinan jumare amugeotdo an haesseoyo. — Last weekend, I didn’t do anything.

explanations.title: More examples
explanations.body: 교실에 아무도 없어요 (There is no one in the classroom); 아무도 한국말을 못해요 (No one speaks Korean); 교실에 아무것도 없어요 (There is nothing in the classroom); 저는 아무 취미도 없어요 (I don’t have any hobbies).

examples.text: 교실에 아무도 없어요.
examples.translation: gyosire amudo eopseoyo. — There is no one in the classroom.

examples.text: 아무도 한국말을 못해요.
examples.translation: amudo hangungmareul motaeyo. — No one speaks Korean.

examples.text: 교실에 아무것도 없어요.
examples.translation: gyosire amugeotdo eopseoyo. — There is nothing in the classroom.

examples.text: 저는 아무 취미도 없어요.
examples.translation: jeoneun amu chwimido eopseoyo. — I don’t have any hobbies.

explanations.title: Adding another marker
explanations.body: If we have to add an additional marker, such as 에서, 에, 한테, or (으)로, to 아무 (noun)도, the marker comes right before 도: 아무한테도 ((not) … to any one), 아무 곳에서도 ((not) … at any place), 아무 펜으로도 ((not) … with any pen).

explanations.title: 하나도 and 한 명도
explanations.body: We can also express a total negation by using 하나도 (even one), 한 명도 (even one person), etc.: 저는 취미가 하나도 없어요 (I don’t have even one hobby); 교실에 학생이 한 명도 없어요 (There isn’t even one student in the classroom).

examples.text: 저는 취미가 하나도 없어요.
examples.translation: jeoneun chwimiga hanado eopseoyo. — I don’t have even one hobby.

examples.text: 교실에 학생이 한 명도 없어요.
examples.translation: gyosire haksaengi han myeongdo eopseoyo. — There isn’t even one student in the classroom.

explanations.body: The book gives the box 아무것도 · 한 개도 · 한 명도 · 아무 데도 · 아무도 and says some sentences may have more than one answer. The sentences are the book’s; the answers are mine.

explanations.title: Activity 2 (Reading): a traveler’s guide on in-flight duty-free items
explanations.body: The excerpt is from a traveler’s guide. The book asks you to answer four questions in English: list at least four items sold in-flight; where you can find a catalog of duty-free items; when you can start buying; and to translate the underlined sentence (which one is underlined cannot be seen in the text, so all four sentences are translated below). The text is the book’s; the English is mine.

examples.text: 국제선 비행기를 타면 기내 면세점 서비스를 이용할 수 있습니다.
examples.translation: gukjeseon bihaenggireul tamyeon ginae myeonsejeom seobiseureul iyonghal su itseumnida. — If you take an international flight, you can use the in-flight duty-free shop service.

examples.text: 기내 면세품으로는 화장품이 가장 많고 액세서리(시계, 목걸이), 담배, 초콜릿, 볼펜 등도 있습니다.
examples.translation: ginae myeonsepumeuroneun hwajangpumi gajang manko aekseseori(sigye, mokgeori), dambae, chokollit, bolpen deungdo itseumnida. — Among in-flight duty-free items, cosmetics are the most, and there are also accessories (watches, necklaces), cigarettes, chocolate, ballpoint pens and so on.

examples.text: 기내 면세품 카탈로그는 좌석 앞쪽 포켓에 있습니다.
examples.translation: ginae myeonsepum katallogeuneun jwaseok apjjok pokese itseumnida. — The catalog of in-flight duty-free items is in the pocket in front of your seat.

examples.text: 면세품은 보통 첫 번째 기내식 후에 살 수 있습니다.
examples.translation: myeonsepumeun botong cheot beonjjae ginaesik hue sal su itseumnida. — You can usually buy duty-free items after the first in-flight meal.

explanations.title: The answers (mine)
explanations.body:
1. Items sold in-flight: cosmetics (the most), accessories (watches, necklaces), cigarettes, chocolate and ballpoint pens. 2. The catalog is in the pocket in front of the seat. 3. You can usually start buying after the first in-flight meal.

The book does not translate the words of the excerpt; the meanings below are mine.

lessons.title: 187. Ch 13 · Grammar C: -(으)려고 (in order to)
lessons.subtitle: 타려고 · 살려고 · 찾으려고 · 먹으려고 · 사려고 · 예약하려고

explanations.title: Conjunctive endings that express a purpose or intention: -(으)려고
explanations.body:
In Chapter 6 you learned that the conjunctive ending -(으)러 is used to express a purpose or intention, as in 식당에 식사하러 오다 (come to the restaurant to eat) and 숙제하러 도서관에 가다 (go to the library to do homework). However, -(으)러 works only with verbs like 가다, 오다 or 다니다. To express a purpose or intention that can work with any action verb (containing 가다, 오다 and 다니다 in the main clause), we can use the conjunctive ending -(으)려고, translated as “(in order) to; so as to”.

When a verb stem ends in a vowel or ㄹ add 려고 (타다 → 타려고; 살다 → 살려고); when it ends in a consonant other than ㄹ add 으려고 (찾다 → 찾으려고; 먹다 → 먹으려고).

lessons.title: 188. Ch 13 · Grammar D: -(으)려면 (if one intends to)
lessons.subtitle: 타려면 · 살려면 · 찾으려면 · 먹으려면 · 환전하려면 어떻게 해야 해요?

explanations.title: Conditional with intention or wish: -(으)려면
explanations.body:
In Chapter 9 you learned that the conjunctive ending -(으)면 expresses a conditional (“if” or “when”), as in 약을 먹으면 (if I take medicine). -(으)려면 is another conjunctive ending that expresses a conditional, but one with intention or wish; it can be translated as “if [the subject] plans to / intends to / would like to / wishes to”. It is a contraction of -(으)려고 하면.

When a verb stem ends in a vowel or ㄹ add 려면 (타다 → 타려고 하면 → 타려면; 살다 → 살려고 하면 → 살려면); when it ends in a consonant other than ㄹ add 으려면 (찾다 → 찾으려고 하면 → 찾으려면; 먹다 → 먹으려고 하면 → 먹으려면).

The book asks you to fill in a table in English (the writer’s concern, the actions requested, the items mentioned by the center, the location and the number of the center). The text is the book’s; the English and the answers are mine. The writers’ e-mail addresses and the center’s telephone number are left out, and the dates and view counts are spelled out in Hangul.

explanations.title: What Chapter 14 teaches (한국의 대중 교통)
explanations.body:
Chapter 14, “Public Transportation in Korea”, has three topic presentations, grammar in focus, activities, a self-evaluation and the core vocabulary.

When you finish the chapter you will be able to: ask for information about public transportation in Korea; read subway line maps and signs to get around using the subway system; comprehend and respond to public announcements in the subway; read traffic signs; ask for and give directions; and talk about public transportation in Korea.

You will become familiar with: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; -고 있다, which is used to express an action in progress; -기 바라다, which is used to give public instruction (please …); the conjunctive ending -(으)니까 (because); ㄷ irregular verbs; and the Sino-Korean syllables 차 (車), 금 (禁), and 도 (道).

explanations.title: Strategy: study the origins of words (etymology)
explanations.body: Sino-Korean words make up about 60% of the Korean vocabulary (H. Sohn, The Korean Language, Cambridge University Press 2001). Therefore, knowledge of Sino-Korean roots is a must for systematically expanding and retaining Korean words. Recall the Sino-Korean word 승무원 (乘務員), meaning a crew member or flight/train/bus/ship attendant, which we learned in Chapter 13. Each individual syllable of the word has a meaning: 승 (乘) means to ride, 무 (務) work, and 원 (員) a member. Once we get to know the meanings of these individual syllables, it is not difficult to figure out the meanings of newly encountered words that contain one of the syllables. For example, when we encounter the words 승차, 사무실 and 공무원, we can figure out their meanings relatively easily.

explanations.title: The same sound, different Chinese characters
explanations.body: Depending on what Chinese character the syllable comes from, however, the syllable can be interpreted differently. For example, 원 in 공무원 (a public servant) or 승무원 (a crew member) is interpreted as a member because it comes from the Chinese character 員 (원), whereas 원 in 병원 (a hospital) is interpreted as a house because it comes from the Chinese character 院 (원). Notice that both are spelled the same in Korean, although their Chinese characters are different and thus their meanings are different. This is why the book provides Hanja (Chinese characters) next to every Sino-Korean core vocabulary item in the Core Vocabulary sections from Unit 4 on. (The 病 in 병원 and the 室 in 사무실 are mine; the book gives the Hanja only for 員 and 院.)

explanations.title: Topic A: At the airport information desk
explanations.body: SPC Anderson is asking for transportation information at the Incheon International Airport information desk. (The English is mine; the book writes 30분마다, 3분에 and 지하 1층, spelled out here. Footnote of the book: 저기요 (over there) and 여기요 (over here) are commonly used to get the attention of someone you do not know. The book spells the counter 씩 with a space: 한 대 씩.)

examples.text: 앤더슨 상병: 저기요. 시청 앞 조선호텔까지 가려면 어떻게 가요?
examples.translation: aendeoseun sangbyeong: jeogiyo. sicheong ap joseonhotelkkaji garyeomyeon eotteoke gayo? — Excuse me. How do I get to the Chosun Hotel in front of City Hall?

examples.text: 안내소 직원: 대중교통을 이용하시면 편리합니다. 공항 리무진 버스, 택시, 그리고 공항철도가 있어요.
examples.translation: annaeso jigwon: daejunggyotongeul iyonghasimyeon pyeollihamnida. gonghang rimujin beoseu, taeksi, geurigo gonghangcheoldoga isseoyo. — If you use public transportation, it is convenient. There are the airport limousine bus, taxis, and the airport railroad.

examples.text: 앤더슨 상병: 음… 리무진 버스는 얼마나 자주 와요?
examples.translation: aendeoseun sangbyeong: eum… rimujin beoseuneun eolmana jaju wayo? — Hmm… how often does the limousine bus come?

examples.text: 안내소 직원: 삼십 분마다 한 대씩 운행됩니다.
examples.translation: annaeso jigwon: samsip bunmada han daessik unhaengdoemnida. — One runs every thirty minutes.

examples.text: 앤더슨 상병: 그럼, 공항철도는 어때요?
examples.translation: aendeoseun sangbyeong: geureom, gonghangcheoldoneun eottaeyo? — Then how about the airport railroad?

examples.text: 안내소 직원: 열차가 삼 분에 한 대씩 옵니다.
examples.translation: annaeso jigwon: yeolchaga sam bune han daessik omnida. — A train comes every three minutes.

examples.text: 앤더슨 상병: 그래요? 공항철도 열차는 어디에서 탑니까?
examples.translation: aendeoseun sangbyeong: geuraeyo? gonghangcheoldo yeolchaneun eodieseo tamnikka? — Is that so? Where do I get on the airport railroad train?

examples.text: 안내소 직원: 네, 지하 일 층에서 타실 수 있습니다.
examples.translation: annaeso jigwon: ne, jiha il cheungeseo tasil su itseumnida. — Yes, you can get on at the first basement floor.

examples.text: 앤더슨 상병: 거기까지 어떻게 가요?
examples.translation: aendeoseun sangbyeong: geogikkaji eotteoke gayo? — How do I get there?

examples.text: 안내소 직원: 저기 승강기로 지하까지 내려가세요. 승강기에서 내리면 바로 공항철도 표지판이 보입니다. 그 표지판을 따라가세요.
examples.translation: annaeso jigwon: jeogi seungganggiro jihakkaji naeryeogaseyo. seungganggieseo naerimyeon baro gonghangcheoldo pyojipani boimnida. geu pyojipaneul ttaragaseyo. — Go down to the basement with that elevator over there. When you get off the elevator, you will see the airport railroad sign right away. Follow that sign.

examples.text: 앤더슨 상병: 네, 감사합니다.
examples.translation: aendeoseun sangbyeong: ne, gamsahamnida. — Yes, thank you.

explanations.body: The meanings are the book’s (from the Core Vocabulary of the chapter). The book lists 승강기 / 엘리베이터 together, and 운행(하다 / 되다) and 편리하다 with their verb endings; they are split and shortened here.

rows: Excuse me. (to get the attention of someone you do not know; “over there”)

explanations.title: Topic A, Follow-up 2 (Reading): from Seoul Station to Incheon Airport
explanations.body: The book shows information from an internet portal website about the forms of transportation one can take to Incheon International Airport from Seoul Station and asks you to fill in a table in English (the strong points and weak points of each). The text is the book’s; the numbers are spelled out in Hangul and the English is mine.

examples.text: 제목: 서울역에서 인천공항까지
examples.translation: jemok: seouryeogeseo incheongonghangkkaji — Title: From Seoul Station to Incheon Airport

examples.text: 서울역에서 인천공항까지 이용할 수 있는 대중교통은 여러 가지가 있습니다.
examples.translation: seouryeogeseo incheongonghangkkaji iyonghal su inneun daejunggyotongeun yeoreo gajiga itseumnida. — There are several kinds of public transportation you can use from Seoul Station to Incheon Airport.

examples.text: 빨리 가고 싶으면 공항철도를 이용하세요.
examples.translation: ppalli gago sipeumyeon gonghangcheoldoreul iyonghaseyo. — If you want to go fast, use the airport railroad.

examples.text: 서울역에서 인천공항까지 사십삼 분 만에 도착할 수 있어요.
examples.translation: seouryeogeseo incheongonghangkkaji sasipsam bun mane dochakal su isseoyo. — You can arrive from Seoul Station to Incheon Airport in forty-three minutes.

examples.text: 그런데 공항역에서 출국장까지 멀어서 많이 걸어야 해요.
examples.translation: geureonde gonghangyeogeseo chulgukjangkkaji meoreoseo mani georeoya haeyo. — But it is far from the airport station to the departure hall, so you have to walk a lot.

examples.text: 공항철도 요금은 구천오백 원입니다.
examples.translation: gonghangcheoldo yogeumeun gucheonobaek wonimnida. — The airport railroad fare is 9,500 won.

examples.text: 짐이 많으면 서울역에서 공항 리무진 버스를 타세요.
examples.translation: jimi maneumyeon seouryeogeseo gonghang rimujin beoseureul taseyo. — If you have a lot of baggage, take the airport limousine bus from Seoul Station.

examples.text: 한 번에 공항까지 갈 수 있어서 편리해요.
examples.translation: han beone gonghangkkaji gal su isseoseo pyeollihaeyo. — It is convenient because you can go to the airport in one go.

examples.text: 요금은 만 육천 원이에요.
examples.translation: yogeumeun man yukcheon wonieyo. — The fare is 16,000 won.

examples.text: 그렇지만, 보통 이십 분마다 한 대씩 운행하기 때문에 좀 기다려야 합니다.
examples.translation: geureochiman, botong isip bunmada han daessik unhaenghagi ttaemune jom gidaryeoya hamnida. — However, a bus usually runs only every twenty minutes, so you have to wait a little.

examples.text: 그리고 택시는 편하지만 요금이 비쌉니다.
examples.translation: geurigo taeksineun pyeonhajiman yogeumi bissamnida. — And a taxi is comfortable, but the fare is expensive.

examples.text: 팔만 원 정도 나올 거예요.
examples.translation: palman won jeongdo naol geoyeyo. — It will come to about 80,000 won.

explanations.title: The table filled in (mine)
explanations.body: The book leaves the table blank; these are my answers.

rows: Fast: 43 minutes from Seoul Station to Incheon Airport; fare 9,500 won
A long walk from the airport station to the departure hall
Convenient, one ride to the airport (good for a lot of baggage); fare 16,000 won
Runs only about every 20 minutes, so you have to wait

explanations.title: Activity 2 (Reading): the Lotte Hotel’s e-mail reply
explanations.body: PFC Anderson is going to stay at the Lotte Hotel in Seoul. He e-mailed the hotel to ask about public transportation from Incheon International Airport to the hotel. The book asks you to fill in a table in English (the form of transportation, the interval of operation, the fare and the length of the trip). The text is the book’s with the numbers spelled out and KAL written 케이에이엘; the English is mine. The book’s note: 방법 means “a method; how to”.

examples.text: 답변
examples.translation: dapbyeon — Reply

examples.text: 저희 롯데호텔을 이용해 주셔서 감사합니다.
examples.translation: jeohui rotdehotereul iyonghae jusyeoseo gamsahamnida. — Thank you for using our Lotte Hotel.

examples.text: 인천공항에서 저희 호텔로 오시는 방법은 여러 가지가 있습니다.
examples.translation: incheongonghangeseo jeohui hotello osineun bangbeobeun yeoreo gajiga itseumnida. — There are several ways to come from Incheon Airport to our hotel.

examples.text: 먼저 인천공항에서 택시를 이용하실 수 있습니다.
examples.translation: meonjeo incheongonghangeseo taeksireul iyonghasil su itseumnida. — First, you can use a taxi from Incheon Airport.

examples.text: 그런데 요금이 십삼만 원으로 조금 비쌉니다.
examples.translation: geureonde yogeumi sipsamman woneuro jogeum bissamnida. — But the fare is a little expensive at 130,000 won.

examples.text: 또 인천공항에서 케이에이엘 리무진을 타실 수 있습니다.
examples.translation: tto incheongonghangeseo keieiel rimujineul tasil su itseumnida. — Also, you can take the KAL limousine from Incheon Airport.

examples.text: 케이에이엘 리무진은 공항 케이에이엘 정류장에서 타실 수 있고 삼십 분마다 출발합니다.
examples.translation: keieiel rimujineun gonghang keieiel jeongnyujangeseo tasil su itgo samsip bunmada chulbalhamnida. — You can take the KAL limousine at the airport KAL bus stop, and it leaves every thirty minutes.

examples.text: 교통이 복잡하지 않으면 호텔까지 보통 한 시간 이십 분 정도 걸립니다.
examples.translation: gyotongi bokjapaji aneumyeon hotelkkaji botong han sigan isip bun jeongdo geollimnida. — If the traffic is not congested, it usually takes about one hour and twenty minutes to the hotel.

examples.text: 요금은 만 팔천 원 정도입니다.
examples.translation: yogeumeun man palcheon won jeongdoimnida. — The fare is about 18,000 won.

examples.text: 승차권은 인천공항에 있는 케이에이엘 안내 데스크에서 사실 수 있습니다.
examples.translation: seungchagwoneun incheongonghange inneun keieiel annae deseukeueseo sasil su itseumnida. — You can buy the ticket at the KAL information desk at Incheon Airport.

examples.text: 그리고 공항철도도 이용하실 수 있습니다.
examples.translation: geurigo gonghangcheoldodo iyonghasil su itseumnida. — And you can also use the airport railroad.

examples.text: 먼저 인천공항에서 김포공항까지 공항철도를 타고 오신 후 지하철로 갈아타시면 됩니다.
examples.translation: meonjeo incheongonghangeseo gimpogonghangkkaji gonghangcheoldoreul tago osin hu jihacheollo garatasimyeon doemnida. — First, take the airport railroad from Incheon Airport to Gimpo Airport and then transfer to the subway.

examples.text: 공항철도는 십 분마다 한 대씩 운행합니다.
examples.translation: gonghangcheoldoneun sip bunmada han daessik unhaenghamnida. — The airport railroad runs one train every ten minutes.

examples.text: 호텔까지 한 시간쯤 걸립니다.
examples.translation: hotelkkaji han siganjjeum geollimnida. — It takes about an hour to the hotel.

examples.text: 요금은 칠천 원 정도입니다.
examples.translation: yogeumeun chilcheon won jeongdoimnida. — The fare is about 7,000 won.

explanations.title: The table filled in (mine)
explanations.body: The book leaves the table blank; these are my answers.

rows: About 1 hour 20 minutes if the traffic is not congested
Airport railroad (transfer to the subway at Gimpo Airport)

explanations.title: Activity 3 (Speaking): a model report
explanations.body: You and a friend decide which way to go from Incheon International Airport to Seoul (airport railroad or limousine service), using a sheet with missing information, and report your choice and your reasons to the class. The book’s model (the English is mine; 55,000원 is spelled out):

examples.text: 인천공항에서 택시를 타고 시청에 가고 싶어요.
examples.translation: incheongonghangeseo taeksireul tago sicheonge gago sipeoyo. — I want to go to City Hall from Incheon Airport by taxi.

examples.text: 시청까지 요금은 오만 오천 원이고 약 한 시간 정도 걸립니다.
examples.translation: sicheongkkaji yogeumeun oman ocheon wonigo yak han sigan jeongdo geollimnida. — The fare to City Hall is 55,000 won and it takes about an hour.

examples.text: 택시는 비싸지만 편합니다.
examples.translation: taeksineun bissajiman pyeonhamnida. — A taxi is expensive but comfortable.

explanations.title: Words in the two texts
explanations.body: The book glosses only 방법; the other meanings are mine.

rows: to be complicated; to be congested (mine)

explanations.body: Activity 1 (a SMART Board activity and listening to three announcements about public transportation from Incheon airport to Seoul), the information sheets with missing information for two partners of Activity 3 and the Useful Links (the Incheon airport traffic guide and the airport railroad) are audio, game, partner or website activities.

explanations.title: Topic B, part I: at the ticket booth
explanations.body: SPC Anderson is talking to a subway employee at a ticket booth in the Incheon International Airport Railroad station. (The English is mine; the book writes 5호선 and 2호선, spelled out as 오 호선 and 이 호선.)

examples.text: 앤더슨 상병: 저, 실례합니다. 서울대학교 입구까지 어떻게 가요?
examples.translation: aendeoseun sangbyeong: jeo, sillyehamnida. seouldaehakgyo ipgukkaji eotteoke gayo? — Excuse me. How do I get to the entrance of Seoul National University?

examples.text: 지하철 직원: 먼저 공항철도를 타고 김포공항역에서 내리세요. 거기서 광화문 방면으로 가는 지하철 오 호선으로 갈아타세요.
examples.translation: jihacheol jigwon: meonjeo gonghangcheoldoreul tago gimpogonghangyeogeseo naeriseyo. geogiseo gwanghwamun bangmyeoneuro ganeun jihacheol o hoseoneuro garataseyo. — First take the airport railroad and get off at Gimpo Airport Station. From there, transfer to the Line 5 subway that goes in the direction of Gwanghwamun.

examples.text: 앤더슨 상병: 그럼, 오 호선을 탄 후에는 어디서 내려요?
examples.translation: aendeoseun sangbyeong: geureom, o hoseoneul tan hueneun eodiseo naeryeoyo? — Then, where do I get off after taking Line 5?

examples.text: 지하철 직원: 영등포구청역에서 내려서 이 호선으로 갈아타세요.
examples.translation: jihacheol jigwon: yeongdeungpogucheongyeogeseo naeryeoseo i hoseoneuro garataseyo. — Get off at Yeongdeungpo-gu Office Station and transfer to Line 2.

examples.text: 앤더슨 상병: 그럼, 거기서 서울대학교 입구까지 얼마나 걸려요?
examples.translation: aendeoseun sangbyeong: geureom, geogiseo seouldaehakgyo ipgukkaji eolmana geollyeoyo? — Then how long does it take from there to the entrance of Seoul National University?

examples.text: 지하철 직원: 영등포구청역에서 한 여덟 정거장만 더 가시면 됩니다.
examples.translation: jihacheol jigwon: yeongdeungpogucheongyeogeseo han yeodeol jeonggeojangman deo gasimyeon doemnida. — From Yeongdeungpo-gu Office Station you only need to go about eight more stations.

examples.text: 앤더슨 상병: 아, 네. 그런데 매표소는 어디에 있어요? 승차권을 사야 해요.
examples.translation: aendeoseun sangbyeong: a, ne. geureonde maepyosoneun eodie isseoyo? seungchagwoneul saya haeyo. — Oh, I see. By the way, where is the ticket booth? I have to buy a ticket.

examples.text: 지하철 직원: 교통카드 필요하세요? 저기 자동판매기에서 사세요. 지금 줄이 길지 않네요.
examples.translation: jihacheol jigwon: gyotongkadeu piryohaseyo? jeogi jadongpanmaegieseo saseyo. jigeum juri gilji anneyo. — Do you need a transportation card? Buy it at the vending machine over there. The line isn’t long now.

explanations.title: Topic B, part II: an announcement
explanations.body: An announcement at a platform in the Gimpo Airport subway station. (The English is mine.)

examples.text: 지금 시청행 열차가 들어오고 있습니다.
examples.translation: jigeum sicheonghaeng yeolchaga deureoogo itseumnida. — A train bound for City Hall is entering the station now.

examples.text: 손님 여러분, 이 역은 전동차와 승강장 사이가 넓습니다.
examples.translation: sonnim yeoreobun, i yeogeun jeondongchawa seunggangjang saiga neolseumnida. — Passengers, at this station the gap between the train and the platform is wide.

examples.text: 타실 때 조심하시기 바랍니다.
examples.translation: tasil ttae josimhasigi baramnida. — Please be careful when you get on.

The book asks you to fill in a table in English (destination, transportation used, how the ticket was purchased, route and time to the destination). The text is the book’s with the numbers spelled out; the English is mine.

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 차 (車)
explanations.body: The Chinese character 車 of the syllable depicts the shape of a cart seen from above: the two parallel horizontal lines are wheels and the vertical line is the axle, which carries the body (box) of the cart. Thus the meaning of this syllable is a cart, car, or vehicle on wheel(s), as in 자동차 (an automobile; “self-moving car”), 전동차 (a subway; an electric car; “electricity moving car”), 기차 (a train; “steam car”), 무개차 (a convertible; “no cover car”), etc. The book asks you to guess the meaning of 차도, 차창, 차선, 소형차 and 차비; my answers are in the second table.

explanations.title: North Korea report
explanations.body: The subway is called 지하철도 (underground railroad) in North Korea. Pyongyang Metro is an important part of the transportation infrastructure in the capital of North Korea. It was constructed with close attention to security and was first opened in September 1973. It is connected to secret underground military facilities; as a result, the system can serve as a bunker. However, relatively little is known about the Metro outside the country, as few visitors are able to investigate the system.

lessons.title: 195. Ch 14 · Grammar A: an action in progress with -고 있다
lessons.subtitle: 보고 있어요 · 먹고 있어요 · 공부하고 있었어요 · 운동하고 있을 거예요 · 보고 계세요

explanations.title: Expressing an action in progress
explanations.body:
In English we commonly use “to be -ing” to express an action in progress, as in “I am working” or “Thomas is driving”. In Korean we use -고 있다 (added to the stem of an action verb): 지금 신문을 보고 있어요 (I am reading the newspaper now); 지금 점심식사를 하고 있어요 (I am having lunch now).

계시다 is the honorific form of 있다. Thus we can use -고 계시다 to describe an action being done by a person we have to show respect to: 아버님이 신문을 보고 계십니다 (Father is reading the newspaper); 선생님이 점심식사를 하고 계십니다 (The teacher is having lunch). -고 있었다 is used for a past progressive action and -고 있을 것이다 for a future progressive action.

rows: After the stem of an action verb
먹다 → 먹고 있다; 자다 → 자고 있다
