lessons.title: 196. Ch 14 · Grammar B: public instructions with -기(를) 바라다
lessons.subtitle: 이용하시기 바랍니다 · 기다리시기를 바랍니다 · 갈아타시기 바랍니다 · 건강하시기를 바랍니다

explanations.title: Giving instructions using -기(를) 바라다
explanations.body:
-기(를) 바라다 literally means “(I) hope (you) to …” and we can say it to an individual to mean “I wish you to …” or “I hope that you …”, as in 건강하시기(를) 바랍니다 (“I wish you to be healthy” or “I hope you are healthy”). However, we often hear -기(를) 바라다 in announcements made at public places like an airport, subway station, or department store. In this case, we can interpret it as an instruction that can be translated as “it is desirable that”, “we advise you that”, or “please”; for example, 에스컬레이터를 이용하시기(를) 바랍니다 (Please use the escalator) and 자동판매기를 사용하시기 바랍니다 (Please use the vending machines).

Note that the honorific form -(으)시기 바라다 is normally used for a public announcement. Note also that the object marker can be deleted (as in -기 바라다). In addition, -기를 is often contracted to -길 in speaking.

rows: 이용하다 → 이용하기(를) 바라다; 기다리다 → 기다리기(를) 바라다

lessons.title: 197. Ch 14 · Activities B: a subway trip and how to get to a restaurant
lessons.subtitle: 오산에서 이대까지 · 갈아타는 곳 표지판을 따라 · 명화당 찾아 오시는 길 · 논현역에서 칠 호선

explanations.title: Activity 1 (Reading and writing): photos of the Seoul subway
explanations.body: The book shows eight photos from the Seoul Metropolitan Subway stations and asks you to write, in Korean and English, what each photo shows. The photos are pictures; the words that go with such signs are in the Core Vocabulary lessons of this chapter (금연, 출입금지, 승강장, 매표소, 자동판매기, 계단, 줄, 정거장).

explanations.title: Activity 1b (Reading): a student’s subway trip from Osan to Ewha
explanations.body: The passage is about a student’s experience using the Seoul Metro Subway from Osan to E-Dae (Ewha Women’s University) station. The book gives the eight sentences in scrambled order and asks you to arrange them in the order in which they occurred; three are done for you (the first, 5, and the last, 8). The sentences are the book’s (the numbers 1, 2 are spelled out); the English is mine, and the order is shown here in the right sequence.

examples.text: 지난 주말에 지하철을 타고 이대 앞에 사는 친구 집에 갔습니다.
examples.translation: jinan jumare jihacheoreul tago idae ape saneun chingu jibe gatseumnida. — Last weekend I went by subway to the home of a friend who lives in front of Ewha Women’s University. (sentence 1)

examples.text: 먼저 오산 지하철역에 도착해서 자동판매기에서 승차권을 샀습니다.
examples.translation: meonjeo osan jihacheoryeoge dochakaeseo jadongpanmaegieseo seungchagwoneul satseumnida. — First I arrived at Osan subway station and bought a ticket at the vending machine. (sentence 2)

examples.text: 승차권을 산 후에 에스컬레이터를 타고 승강장으로 내려갔습니다.
examples.translation: seungchagwoneul san hue eseukeolleiteoreul tago seunggangjangeuro naeryeogatseumnida. — After buying the ticket, I went down to the platform by escalator. (sentence 3)

examples.text: 승강장에서 줄을 서서 기다린 후에 서울역 방면 일 호선 전동차를 탔습니다.
examples.translation: seunggangjangeseo jureul seoseo gidarin hue seoullyeok bangmyeon il hoseon jeondongchareul tatseumnida. — After standing in line and waiting on the platform, I took the Line 1 train toward Seoul Station. (sentence 4)

examples.text: 일 호선을 타고 한 시간쯤 후에 신도림역에서 내렸습니다.
examples.translation: il hoseoneul tago han siganjjeum hue sindorimyeogeseo naeryeotseumnida. — After about an hour on Line 1, I got off at Sindorim Station. (sentence 5)

examples.text: 신도림역에서 내린 후에 갈아타는 곳 표지판을 따라 시청방면 이 호선으로 갈아탔습니다.
examples.translation: sindorimyeogeseo naerin hue garataneun got pyojipaneul ttara sicheongbangmyeon i hoseoneuro garatatseumnida. — After getting off at Sindorim Station, I followed the transfer sign and transferred to Line 2 toward City Hall. (sentence 6)

examples.text: 이 호선을 타고 몇 정거장을 더 간 후에 이대역에서 내렸습니다.
examples.translation: i hoseoneul tago myeot jeonggeojangeul deo gan hue idaeyeogeseo naeryeotseumnida. — After riding Line 2 for a few more stations, I got off at Ewha Women’s University Station. (sentence 7)

examples.text: 이대역에서 내린 후 일 번 출구로 나갔습니다.
examples.translation: idaeyeogeseo naerin hu il beon chulguro nagatseumnida. — After getting off at Ewha Station, I went out through exit number 1. (sentence 8)

explanations.title: The order (mine)
explanations.body: The numbers below are the right order of the actions.

rows: 지난 주말에 지하철을 타고 이대 앞에 사는 친구 집에 갔습니다.
먼저 오산 지하철역에 도착해서 자동판매기에서 승차권을 샀습니다.
승차권을 산 후에 에스컬레이터를 타고 승강장으로 내려갔습니다.
승강장에서 줄을 서서 기다린 후에 서울역 방면 일 호선 전동차를 탔습니다.
일 호선을 타고 한 시간쯤 후에 신도림역에서 내렸습니다.
신도림역에서 내린 후에 갈아타는 곳 표지판을 따라 시청방면 이 호선으로 갈아탔습니다.
이 호선을 타고 몇 정거장을 더 간 후에 이대역에서 내렸습니다.
이대역에서 내린 후 일 번 출구로 나갔습니다.

explanations.title: Activity 3 (Reading and writing): how to get to a famous restaurant
explanations.body: The book shows an advertisement for a famous restaurant and asks you to circle the stations at which you should get off to get to it. The text is the book’s (the restaurant’s street address and telephone number are left out; 4호선 and 2호선 are spelled out). The answer (mine): Myeongdong-ipgu Station (Line 4) or Euljiro-ipgu Station (Line 2).

examples.text: 명화당 찾아 오시는 길
examples.translation: myeonghwadang chaja osineun gil — How to get to Myeonghwadang

examples.text: 지하철 이용시: 사 호선 명동입구역이나 이 호선 을지로입구역에서 내리시면 됩니다.
examples.translation: jihacheol iyongsi: sa hoseon myeongdongipguyeogina i hoseon euljiroipguyeogeseo naerisimyeon doemnida. — By subway: you can get off at Myeongdong-ipgu Station on Line 4 or Euljiro-ipgu Station on Line 2.

examples.text: 버스 이용시: 명동이나 외환은행 정거장에서 내리시면 됩니다.
examples.translation: beoseu iyongsi: myeongdongina oehwaneunhaeng jeonggeojangeseo naerisimyeon doemnida. — By bus: you can get off at the Myeongdong or Foreign Exchange Bank stop.

explanations.title: Giving directions to a friend (Activity 3c)
explanations.body: You want to recommend the restaurant to your friend 진수, and write the subway route he must take, using the subway map of the SMART Board activity. The book’s model begins as follows (the rest depends on the map, which is a picture; the English is mine):

examples.text: 진수야, 그 식당에 가려면, 논현역에서 먼저 칠 호선을 타고 건대입구 방면으로 가.
examples.translation: jinsuya, geu sikdange garyeomyeon, nonhyeonyeogeseo meonjeo chil hoseoneul tago geondaeipgu bangmyeoneuro ga. — Jinsu, to get to that restaurant, first take Line 7 at Nonhyeon Station and go toward Konkuk University Station.

explanations.title: Activities left out
explanations.body: Activity 2 (listening to four subway announcements to say whether they are at a platform or in a train), Activity 3b (a SMART Board activity), Activity 4 (listening to subway directions from Apgujeong Station on Line 3 to Seoul Arts Center, Millennium Shopping Center, Gyeongbokgung and Lotte Department Store, and giving directions to Seoul Station, Hongik University Station, Korea University and Yongsan; the subway map is a picture) are audio, map, game or partner activities.

lessons.subtitle: 사고가 나서 교통이 아주 복잡해요 · 횡단보도를 건너서 곧장 가세요 · 교통 안전 표지 · 금 (禁) · 도 (道)

explanations.title: Topic C: Traffic is congested because of an accident
explanations.body: SPC Anderson is talking with a taxi driver on the way to COEX (Convention and Exhibition center) in Seoul. (The English is mine; the book writes 코엑스(COEX) and 15분, here 코엑스 and 십오 분.)

examples.text: 앤더슨 상병: 도로에 차가 왜 이렇게 많아요?
examples.translation: aendeoseun sangbyeong: doroe chaga wae ireoke manayo? — Why are there so many cars on the road?

examples.text: 택시 기사: 지금 출근 시간이어서 교통이 아주 복잡해요. 그리고 사고가 나서 더 막혀요.
examples.translation: taeksi gisa: jigeum chulgeun siganieoseo gyotongi aju bokjapaeyo. geurigo sagoga naseo deo makyeoyo. — It is rush hour now, so the traffic is very congested. And because of an accident it is even more jammed.

examples.text: 앤더슨 상병: 여기서 코엑스까지 멀어요?
examples.translation: aendeoseun sangbyeong: yeogiseo koekseukkaji meoreoyo? — Is it far from here to COEX?

examples.text: 택시 기사: 아니요. 별로 안 멀어요. 걸어서 한 십오 분쯤 가면 돼요.
examples.translation: taeksi gisa: aniyo. byeollo an meoreoyo. georeoseo han sibo bunjjeum gamyeon dwaeyo. — No. It is not very far. It takes about fifteen minutes on foot.

examples.text: 앤더슨 상병: 그럼, 여기에서 내리겠습니다. 코엑스 가는 길 좀 가르쳐 주시겠어요?
examples.translation: aendeoseun sangbyeong: geureom, yeogieseo naerigetseumnida. koekseu ganeun gil jom gareucheo jusigesseoyo? — Then I will get off here. Could you tell me the way to COEX?

examples.text: 택시 기사: 여기 횡단보도를 건너서 곧장 가세요. 그리고 지하도로 내려가시면 코엑스 입구가 나옵니다.
examples.translation: taeksi gisa: yeogi hoengdanbodoreul geonneoseo gotjang gaseyo. geurigo jihadoro naeryeogasimyeon koekseu ipguga naomnida. — Cross this crosswalk and go straight. And if you go down into the underpass, you will come to the COEX entrance.

examples.text: 앤더슨 상병: 네, 감사합니다. 그런데, 오후에 제가 이태원에 가려고 하는데 코엑스에서 어떻게 가요?
examples.translation: aendeoseun sangbyeong: ne, gamsahamnida. geureonde, ohue jega itaewone garyeogo haneunde koekseueseo eotteoke gayo? — Yes, thank you. By the way, I am going to go to Itaewon in the afternoon; how do I get there from COEX?

examples.text: 택시 기사: 코엑스 앞에서 버스를 타세요. 지하철은 두 번 갈아타니까 버스가 더 편해요.
examples.translation: taeksi gisa: koekseu apeseo beoseureul taseyo. jihacheoreun du beon garatanikka beoseuga deo pyeonhaeyo. — Take a bus in front of COEX. You have to transfer twice on the subway, so the bus is more convenient.

explanations.title: Cultural notes: 교통카드
explanations.body: 교통카드 is a pre-paid card for the public transportation system in Korea. You can purchase and recharge various types of 교통카드 at many kiosks, nearly all convenience stores, and subway ticket booths.

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 금 (禁)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means forbid or ban, as in 금연 (no smoking; “forbidding smoke”), 금주 (no drinking; “forbidding liquor”), 출입 금지 (Do not enter), 주차 금지 (No parking), etc. The book asks: can you explain why 여학생 기숙사 (a dorm for female students) is often referred to as 금남의 집? My answer: 금남 means “forbidding men” (남 = male), so a 금남의 집 is a house where men are not allowed.

rows: a house where men are forbidden (mine); a women’s dormitory

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 도 (道)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means a road or way, as in 도로 (a street; “road way”), 차도 (a road; “a road for cars”), 인도 (a walkway; “a road for people”), 하수도 (sewer; “under water way”), 상수도 (water supply; “above water way”), 태권도 (tae kwon do; “way of stepping and punching”), 유도 (judo; “way of flow”), etc. The same syllable is also used for the proper names of Korean provinces, as in 경기도 and 제주도.

rows: tae kwon do; “way of stepping and punching”

explanations.title: ㄷ irregular verbs
explanations.body: There are quite a few action verbs whose stem ends in ㄷ, such as 걷다 (to walk), 싣다 (to load), and 받다 (to receive). Among these action verbs, there are a few, namely 걷다 (to walk), 묻다 (to ask), 듣다 (to hear/to listen), and 싣다 (to load), that do not follow the regular conjugation rule. When these verbs are followed by a vowel such as 아 / 어, ㄷ changes to ㄹ. They are commonly known as ㄷ irregular verbs. (The regular ㄷ verbs, such as 받다 and 믿다, keep their ㄷ.)

explanations.title: Follow-up 1: conjugate the ㄷ verbs
explanations.body: The stems of all the verbs in the first column of the book’s table end in ㄷ; some are ㄷ irregular. The book gives the verbs 묻다, 믿다, 듣다, 싣다, 걷다 and 받다 and asks you to conjugate them in -습니다/ㅂ니다, -아요/어요, -을 거예요 and -으면. The answers are mine (I added the past tense and two regular ㄷ verbs, 닫다 and 얻다). Note that 믿다 and 받다 are regular.

lessons.title: 200. Ch 14 · Grammar D: a reason with -(으)니까
lessons.subtitle: 비가 오니까 · 날씨가 좋으니까 · 추우니까 · 늦었으니까 · 길이 막히니까

explanations.title: Expressing a reason using -(으)니까
explanations.body:
Like the two conjunctive endings -아서/어서 and -기 때문에, which you learned in earlier chapters, the conjunctive ending -(으)니까 is used to express a reason, and can be translated as “because” or “since”. However, -(으)니까 is normally used to express a logical reason. In 날씨가 좋으니까 산책했어요 (I took a walk because the weather was nice), 날씨가 좋으니까 is a logical reason for taking a walk; in 피곤하니까 일찍 잤어요 (I went to bed early because I was tired), 피곤하니까 is a logical reason for going to bed early.

Therefore -(으)니까 is readily followed by a request, advice, command, or suggestion that is based on a logical reason, whereas the other two conjunctive endings are not.

After a verb stem ending with a consonant

explanations.body: The forms below are mine, made by the book’s rule; stems ending in ㄹ drop it before ㄴ (놀다 → 노니까), and the ㅂ irregular verbs 춥다, 덥다 and 어렵다 change ㅂ to 우 (추우니까, 더우니까, 어려우니까).

explanations.title: Follow-up 3: connect the sentences that have a cause-and-effect relationship
explanations.body: The book gives eight reasons on the left and eight results on the right (빨리 밥을 먹읍시다, 집에서 쉬어야겠어요, 걸어서 갈까요?, 잠바를 입으세요, 친구하고 같이 할까요?, 등산은 다음에 갑시다, 버스를 타세요, 따뜻한 커피를 마시고 싶어요) and says the answers may vary. These matches, joined with -(으)니까, are mine.

rows: Because it is cold, put on a jacket.
Because I am hungry, let’s eat quickly.
Because I am busy, let’s go hiking another time.
Because the subway broke down, take a bus.
Because the homework is difficult, shall we do it together with a friend?
Because I am tired, I think I should rest at home.
비가 오니까 따뜻한 커피를 마시고 싶어요.
Because it is raining, I want to drink hot coffee.
Because the traffic is congested, shall we go on foot?

explanations.title: Follow-up 5: a partial sentence
explanations.body: In the book each student writes the first part of a sentence with -(으)니까 and classmates add the second part. The book’s model: 오늘은 시간이 많으니까 (Because I have a lot of time today, …) → 오늘은 시간이 많으니까 백화점에 쇼핑갑시다 (Because I have a lot of time today, let’s go shopping at the department store) or 영화 볼까요? (shall we see a movie?).

The book’s Core Vocabulary lists the core words of the chapter with an example sentence for each (the sentences and the English meanings are the book’s; the book gives no English for the sentences). The Hanja of the Sino-Korean words are in parentheses before the meaning. Optional parts, such as (~하다/되다), are kept in the meanings.

The example sentences with digits or Latin letters are respelled in Hangul (1000원 → 천 원, 5번 출구 → 오 번 출구, 5명 → 다섯 명, 5분마다 → 오 분마다, 6시 → 여섯 시, 130,000원 → 십삼만 원); 몬트레이에서 PG로 → 몬트레이에서 피지로. The book’s related words (the synonyms, antonyms and related words in the last column) are not repeated. The book’s Additional Vocabulary table is empty: it is for your own words.

explanations.title: What Chapter 15 teaches (한반도와 한국전쟁)
explanations.body:
Chapter 15, “The Korean Peninsula and the Korean War”, has three topic presentations, grammar in focus, activities, a self-evaluation and the core vocabulary.

When you finish the chapter you will be able to: identify and locate provinces, major cities, and well-known tourist attractions in Korea; talk about weather; comprehend basic information about the Korean War; comprehend basic information about the Joint Security Area and its facilities in Korea; and describe a building in a simple paragraph.

You will become familiar with: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; -아/어지다, used to express changes of state or condition; the conjunctive ending -(으)ㄴ데/는데 (and; but; however); the conjunctive ending -아/어도 (even if; although); the formal blunt speech style verb ending; and the Sino-Korean syllables 해 (海) and 부 (部).

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 해 (海)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means sea, as in 해군 (navy; “sea soldier”), 동해 (East Sea), 해저 (sea bottom; seabed; “sea low”), etc. The book asks you to guess the meaning of 해수, 서해, 남해 and 해병대; the answers (and the English of 해수 and 해병대) are mine.

rows: the sea bottom; the seabed; “sea low”

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 부 (部)
explanations.body: The underlying meaning of this Sino-Korean syllable is a part, and it refers to one of several or many equal units which something is composed of or is divisible into. Depending on the context, 부 can be translated as a part, region, area, etc. This syllable is also used to refer to a part of an organization (company, government, school, etc.). When it is applied to an organization, it can be translated in various contexts as a department, ministry, or (school) club, as in 국방부, 환경부, 부장 and 유도부.

explanations.title: Note: 제주도
explanations.body: Jeju is the largest island and the smallest province of South Korea, located to the south of the mainland. However, Jeju is called 제주도, whether being referred to as Jeju Island or Jeju Province. 도 in 제주도 means both an island and a province, although they are from different Chinese characters: 島 (an island) and 道 (a province). So, whenever you hear a place name that ends in 도, other than 제주도, you know it could be either an island or a province.

explanations.title: Note: 안개가 끼었습니다
explanations.body: You will hear native speakers say 오늘은 안개가 끼었습니다, meaning it is foggy today, or 오늘은 구름이 끼었습니다, meaning it is cloudy today. Because 끼었습니다 is in the past tense, you may wonder why a Korean speaker would use the past tense to describe a present weather condition when using the verb 끼다. 끼다 literally means to form. So, when you say 구름이 낍니다, using the present tense, you are saying clouds are forming now. However, when you say 구름이 끼었습니다, the sentence implies that clouds have formed in the past and, as a result, it is cloudy.

explanations.body: The book gives a weather forecast and asks four questions, to be answered in English. The text is the book’s (the figures are spelled out in Hangul: −1도 → 영하 일 도, 3도 → 영상 삼 도, 5 도 → 오 도, 8도 → 팔 도, 10도 → 영상 십 도); the English is mine.

examples.text: 오늘은 전국이 흐리고 춥겠습니다.
examples.translation: oneureun jeongugi heurigo chupgetseumnida. — Today it will be cloudy and cold across the whole country.

lessons.title: 208. Ch 15 · Grammar A: a change of state with -아/어지다
lessons.subtitle: 따뜻해졌습니다 · 좋아질 거예요 · 추워졌어요 · 맛있어졌어요 · 싸지다 · 예뻐지다 · 빨라지다

explanations.title: Expressing a change of state or condition
explanations.body: In English, when expressing a change of state or condition, we often use the verb become or get, followed by an adjective, as in “The weather got warm” or “He became happy.” In Korean, we use -아/어지다, which is attached to the stem of a stative verb. For example: 날씨가 따뜻해졌습니다 (The weather got warm).

lessons.title: 209. Ch 15 · Grammar B: background with -(으)ㄴ데/는데
lessons.subtitle: 날씨가 좋은데 · 백화점에 가는데 · 이 옷이 큰데 · 겨울인데 · 갔는데

explanations.title: The conjunctive ending -(으)ㄴ데/는데
explanations.body:
The conjunctive ending -(으)ㄴ데/는데 is unique in its usage. This conjunctive ending signals that the first clause is background information for (or the situation or circumstance leading to) the second clause. Therefore, we can only interpret the meaning of this conjunctive ending according to the content of the second clause. For example: 날씨가 좋은데 산책합시다 (The weather is good, so let’s take a walk); 날씨가 좋은데 집에 있을 거예요? (The weather is good, but are you going to stay home?).

Note that the same conjunctive ending is interpreted differently according to how it relates to the content of the following clause. It is interpreted as so in the first sentence and as but in the second sentence. -(으)ㄴ데/는데 can also be interpreted to mean and, and thus, and then, however, or nevertheless in other contexts. Thus, from the listener’s perspective, the exact meaning of the first clause cannot be determined until the second clause is heard. For this reason, the conjunctive ending is often used as (1) an attention getter and as (2) a stage setter for the main idea the speaker is about to deliver. As a result, this conjunctive ending is used almost exclusively in speaking.

explanations.title: Forms
explanations.body: The forms below are mine, made by the book’s rule. 있다 and 없다 (and 맛있다, 재미있다) take 는데 like action verbs (mine: this is the usual form but the book’s rule table does not say it); stems ending in ㄹ drop it before ㄴ (놀다 → 노는데, 길다 → 긴데); the ㅂ irregular verbs change ㅂ to 우 (춥다 → 추운데, 어렵다 → 어려운데). The past form adds -았/었 before -는데 for every kind of verb (갔는데, 좋았는데).

explanations.title: Topic C: I have visited Panmunjom (판문점에 갔다 왔다)
explanations.body: The following text is from SPC Anderson’s journal about his weekend visit to the Joint Security Area (JSA) in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ). It is written in the formal blunt speech style (-다), which is taught later in this chapter. (The English is mine; the book gives none. The book writes 1층, spelled 일 층 here.)

explanations.title: The Joint Security Area: the words of the diagram
explanations.body: The book shows a diagram of the Panmunjom Joint Security Area with these labels (the English is the book’s).

explanations.title: Cultural notes
explanations.body: Panmunjom is a portion of the Korean Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), and includes an 800-square-meter area designated as a Joint Security Area (JSA) by the UN and North Korea. Panmunjom is also called the “Truce Village” by the media. This area is outside administrative control of both South and North Korea, but is often used for diplomatic engagements between the two countries. Currently the UN and North Korea each operate six guard posts in the JSA and 35 security guards reside there. South and North Korean forces stand face-to-face in this area but cannot enter each other’s territory.

explanations.title: Presentation Activity: the vocabulary table
explanations.body: The book gives a vocabulary table with half of the words missing and asks you to complete it with the Korean or the English word: 판문점 (Panmunjom), 공동경비구역 (Joint Security Area), 관광객 (a tourist), 주변 (surrounding; around), -아/어도 (although; even if), 가운데 (the middle), 회의실 (a conference room), 오래되다 (to be old), 인상적 (impressive), 공식적 (formal; official), 외국인 (a foreigner), 자유 (freedom), 찍다 (to take a picture) and 평화 (peace). The words are in the table above and in the exercises of this lesson.

explanations.title: The conjunctive ending -아/어도
explanations.body:
Consider the English sentences “I will learn Korean (even) though it is difficult” and “I will learn Korean even if it is difficult.” In the first sentence, the speaker knows that Korean is difficult but will learn it despite its being difficult. In the second sentence, however, the speaker does not know definitely whether or not Korean is difficult but will learn it in any event. Thus, (even) though expresses a concession and even if is a conditional.

The conjunctive ending -아/어도 is used to express both (even) though and even if. Therefore, we can express the two English sentences by using the same Korean sentence: 한국말이 어려워도 배우겠습니다. If we hear this sentence out of context, we can interpret the sentence in both ways. When a context is given, however, the meaning of the conjunctive ending is either (even) though or even if, but not both. For example:

examples.text: 오늘 날씨가 좋아도 집에 있습니다.
examples.translation: oneul nalssiga joado jibe itseumnida. — Though the weather is good today, I am staying home.

examples.text: 내일 날씨가 좋아도 집에 있겠습니다.
examples.translation: naeil nalssiga joado jibe itgetseumnida. — Even if the weather is good tomorrow, I will stay home.

explanations.title: Time words show which meaning
explanations.body: Note that both sentences have a time reference (오늘 or 내일). Thus, we know that the conjunctive ending in the first sentence is understood as a concession (though or although), whereas the same conjunctive ending in the second sentence is understood as a conditional (even if).

rows: When the last syllable of a verb stem contains the vowels ㅏ or ㅗ
좋다 → 좋아도; 오다 → 오 + 아도 → 와도
When the last syllable of a verb stem contains a vowel other than ㅏ or ㅗ
멀다 → 멀어도; 맵다 → 매우 + 어도 → 매워도

explanations.body: The forms below are mine, made by the book’s rule (the vowel contraction is the same as with -아/어요; the ㅂ irregular verbs change ㅂ to 우: 춥다 → 추워도, 어렵다 → 어려워도). The past form puts -았/었 before -어도: 힘들었어도 (the book’s example in the Core Vocabulary).

lessons.title: 212. Ch 15 · Grammar D: the formal blunt speech style -ㄴ다/는다/다
lessons.subtitle: 먹는다 · 간다 · 춥다 · 먹었다 · 대학생이다 · 산이 있다 · 일기 (journals)

explanations.title: The fourth speech style: formal blunt
explanations.body:
So far, you have learned about three different speech styles and their verb endings: 1. -ㅂ니다/습니다 (Formal Speech Style); 2. -아요/어요 (Informal Speech Style); 3. -아/어 (Informal Blunt Speech Style). Now you will learn a fourth: the Formal Blunt Speech Style,¹ which is indicated by the verb ending -ㄴ다/는다/다. As its name suggests, this style is used in formal and “blunt” settings. In written language, this speech style is typically employed in newspapers, journals, and books. In spoken language, this speech style is used among friends or by those of a higher status in age or rank.

¹ This style is also known as Formal Intimate, Formal Non-polite, or Formal Plain Speech Style.

explanations.title: The rule
explanations.body: Action verbs take -ㄴ다/는다 and stative verbs take -다. The verbs 있다, 없다, 이다 and 아니다 act like stative verbs when they are conjugated into the formal blunt speech style (준호는 이제 대학생이다; 우리 고향에는 산이 있다).

explanations.title: How to use this list
explanations.body:
The book’s Core Vocabulary lists the core words of the chapter with an example sentence for each (the sentences and the English meanings are the book’s; the book gives no English for the sentences). The Hanja of the Sino-Korean words are in parentheses before the meaning. Optional parts, such as (~하다/되다), are kept in the meanings.

The example sentences with digits or Latin letters are respelled in Hangul (9개 → 아홉 개, 90도 → 구십 도, 15° C and 86° F → 십오 도 씨 and 화씨 팔십육 도, 1950년 6월 25일 → 천구백오십년 유월 이십오일, 1964년 → 천구백육십사년, 155마일 → 백오십오 마일, 1층 → 일 층, L.A. → 엘에이, 워싱턴 D.C. → 워싱턴 디씨); the parentheses of the book’s 86° F and 30° C are left out. The book’s related words (the synonyms, antonyms and related words in the last column) are not repeated. The book’s Additional Vocabulary table is empty: it is for your own words.

explanations.title: Self-evaluation
explanations.body:
Recall the objectives of the chapter and ask yourself whether you have achieved them (the book asks you to tick Yes or No). If you tick “No” for any item, the book suggests: review that section on your own; find a study partner and review it as a pair or group; and tell your academic advisor or team leader which areas you need more help with, so that they can provide activities tailored to your learning style and needs.

Now I am able to: identify and locate provinces, major cities, well-known tourist attractions in Korea; talk about weather; comprehend basic information about the Korean War; comprehend basic information about the Joint Security Area and its facilities in Korea; describe a building in a simple paragraph.

Now I have a clear understanding of: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; -아/어지다, used to express changes of state or condition; the conjunctive ending -(으)ㄴ데/는데 (and; but; however); the conjunctive ending -아/어도 (even if; although); the formal blunt speech style verb ending; the Sino-Korean syllables 해 (海) and 부 (部).

lessons.title: 214. Ch 16 · What the chapter teaches and the Sino-Korean syllables 불/부, 형 and 적
lessons.subtitle: 한국에서 여행하기 · 불/부 (不) · 형 (型) · 적 (的) · 불법 · 소형 · 역사적

explanations.title: What Chapter 16 teaches (한국에서 여행하기)
explanations.body:
Chapter 16, “Touring in Korea”, has three topic presentations, grammar in focus, activities, a self-evaluation and the core vocabulary.

When you finish the chapter you will be able to: make a domestic flight reservation; ask for and give information about a travel package; ask for and give information about renting a car; report simple car problems; identify simple automotive parts; and talk about well-known tourist attractions in Korea.

You will become familiar with: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; 아무나 or 아무 ~(이)나 in the affirmative (any ~) and in the negative (not just any ~); -(으)ㄹ 줄 알다 (know how to) and -(으)ㄹ 줄 모르다 (not know how to); the exclamatory verb endings -군요 and -네요; the conjunctive ending -(으)면서, used to express simultaneous actions or conditions; and the Sino-Korean syllables 불/부 (不), 적 (的), and 형 (型).

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 불/부 (不)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means not or no and functions like the English prefixes in-, im-, il-, and ir-, as in inability, impossible, illegal, and irregular; for example, 불법 (illegal; “not law”), 불친절 (unkindness; “not kind”), 불합격 (failure in entrance exam; “not passing”), and 불면증 (insomnia; “no sleeping symptom”). 불 changes into 부 when the syllable comes before the consonant ㄷ or ㅈ, as in 부동산 (immovable property), 부주의 (carelessness; “no attention”), and 부족하다 (to be insufficient).

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 형 (型)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means type or model, as in 소형 (small-size; “small type”), 구형 (old type), and 원형 (prototype; “original type”). The book asks you to guess the meaning of 대형, 중형 and 신형; the answers are the book’s own meanings of the Core Vocabulary (대형, 중형) and mine (신형).

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 적 (的)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable normally means a target, as in 목적 (goal; “eye target”) and 적중 (hitting the bull’s eye; “middle of target”). However, when 적 (的) is attached to a Sino-Korean noun, it functions as an “adjective maker,” just like the English suffixes -ic or -ive, as in realistic, historic, creative, active, etc. When used this way, 적 can be translated as “of (the noun)”; for example, 역사적 (historic; historical), 인상적 (impressive), 한국적 (unique to Korea), 일시적 (temporary; “of one time”). The book asks you to guess the meaning of 세계적, 미국적 and 부분적; the answer for 세계적 is the book’s (world-renowned; worldwide), the others are mine.

explanations.body: SPC Anderson is making a reservation at a travel agency for his trip to Gyeongju. (The English is mine; the book gives none. The book writes 2박 3일, 1인당 20만 원, 15만 원 and 48시간; they are spelled out here.)

explanations.title: Topic A, Follow-up 1 (Reading): the Jeju travel advertisement
explanations.body: The book shows a travel advertisement and asks you to fill in a table in English with information about the travel package (destination, trip duration, included expenses, excluded expenses, price, terms and conditions). The text is the book’s (the figures are spelled out in Hangul, the web address is left out; the book writes 취소/환불 불가능합니다, here 취소와 환불이 불가능합니다); the English is mine. The book’s note: ~ 이상 means “~ and above” and ~미만 means “under ~”.

rows: 2 nights and 3 days; departs every Tuesday at 9:00

explanations.title: Activity 2b (Reading): a notice about the conditions of a domestic flight
explanations.body: A customer who has made a reservation for a domestic flight receives a notice about the conditions and requirements. The book asks you to read the three sentences and write their English translations; the sentences are the book’s (the figures are spelled out in Hangul), the translations are mine.

explanations.body: The book glosses only ~ 이상 and ~미만; the other meanings are mine.

explanations.body: Activity 1 (SMART Board reading and listening activities), Activity 2a (listening to three dialogs between a travel agent and a customer about what is and is not possible and filling in a table) and Activity 3 (a role-play at a travel agency in Seoul: filling out the reservation forms and acting out three situation cards for a domestic flight reservation, a change and a cancellation) are audio, computer, form or role-play activities.

explanations.title: Topic B: I would like to rent a car (차를 빌리고 싶은데요)
explanations.body: SPC Anderson is renting a car at the Ulsan airport. (The English is mine; the book gives none. The book writes 3일, 25만 원 and 낮 12시; they are spelled out here.)

examples.text: 앤더슨 상병: 저… 차를 좀 빌리고 싶어요.
examples.translation: aendeoseun sangbyeong: jeo… chareul jom billigo sipeoyo. — Um… I would like to rent a car.

examples.text: 렌터카 직원: 네, 며칠 동안 쓰실 겁니까?
examples.translation: renteoka jigwon: ne, myeochil dongan sseusil geomnikka? — Yes, for how many days will you use it?

examples.text: 앤더슨 상병: 오늘부터 삼 일 동안 빌리고 싶어요.
examples.translation: aendeoseun sangbyeong: oneulbuteo sam il dongan billigo sipeoyo. — I want to rent it for three days from today.

examples.text: 렌터카 직원: 어떤 차를 원하세요?
examples.translation: renteoka jigwon: eotteon chareul wonhaseyo? — What kind of car do you want?

examples.text: 앤더슨 상병: 아무 차나 괜찮아요. 저는 수동식도 운전할 줄 알아요.
examples.translation: aendeoseun sangbyeong: amu chana gwaenchanayo. jeoneun sudongsikdo unjeonhal jul arayo. — Any car is fine. I know how to drive a manual one, too.

examples.text: 렌터카 직원: 네, 잠시만요. 손님, 소형차도 괜찮으세요?
examples.translation: renteoka jigwon: ne, jamsimanyo. sonnim, sohyeongchado gwaenchaneuseyo? — Yes, just a moment. Sir, is a small car also OK?

examples.text: 앤더슨 상병: 네, 괜찮아요.
examples.translation: aendeoseun sangbyeong: ne, gwaenchanayo. — Yes, that’s fine.

examples.text: 렌터카 직원: 그럼 소형차로 드리겠습니다. 운전면허증 있으세요?
examples.translation: renteoka jigwon: geureom sohyeongcharo deurigetseumnida. unjeonmyeonheojeung isseuseyo? — Then I will give you a small car. Do you have a driver’s license?

examples.text: 앤더슨 상병: 네, 국제 운전면허증도 괜찮습니까?
examples.translation: aendeoseun sangbyeong: ne, gukje unjeonmyeonheojeungdo gwaenchanseumnikka? — Yes, is an international driver’s license also OK?

examples.text: 렌터카 직원: 그럼요. 보험 포함해서 모두 이십오만 원입니다.
examples.translation: renteoka jigwon: geureomyo. boheom pohamhaeseo modu isiboman wonimnida. — Of course. Including insurance, it is 250,000 won in total.

examples.text: 앤더슨 상병: 예. 그런데, 차는 몇 시까지 돌려주어야 합니까?
examples.translation: aendeoseun sangbyeong: ye. geureonde, chaneun myeot sikkaji dollyeojueoya hamnikka? — Okay. By the way, by what time do I have to return the car?

examples.text: 렌터카 직원: 낮 열두 시까지 차 열쇠하고 같이 돌려주시면 됩니다.
examples.translation: renteoka jigwon: nat yeoldu sikkaji cha yeolsoehago gachi dollyeojusimyeon doemnida. — You can return it with the car key by 12 o’clock in the daytime.

examples.text: 앤더슨 상병: 그런데 차가 고장 나면 어떻게 해야 하나요?

explanations.title: Cultural notes: 휴게소 (highway rest stops)
explanations.body: All highways in Korea charge a toll, and drivers who leave the highway are charged again to re-enter. Thus, the Korea Expressway Corporation provides rest stops on the highways for the convenience of drivers so they don’t have to exit the highway for basic services. Therefore, if you are on a highway in Korea, you will see many 휴게소 signs. The literal translation of 휴게소 is a rest place. It is a public rest area or service area where drivers and passengers can rest, eat, refuel, and shop. Most of these rest areas have good food courts, coffee shops, convenience stores, and even auto repair shops. These days, many rest areas offer additional services such as batting cages, spas, lodging, and other amenities.

lessons.title: 219. Ch 16 · Grammar A: “any” and “not just any” with 아무나 and 아무 ~(이)나
lessons.subtitle: 아무 차나 · 아무 식당이나 · 아무나 · 아무 데나 · 아무 때나 · 아무 거나 · 아무 것도

explanations.title: Expressing “any” and “not just any”
explanations.body:
In Chapter 13, you learned about the grammar feature 아무 + (noun) + 도 followed by a negative verb, which is used to express total negation. For example: 저는 아무 문제도 없어요 (I do not have any problems); 저는 방학 때 아무 데도 안 갔어요 (I did not go anywhere during the school break).

Keep in mind that 아무 ~ 도 can work only in a negative sentence (or a sentence with a negative verb). However, when 아무 ~ takes the marker (이)나, it can work with affirmative and negative sentences, though their meanings are quite different.

examples.text: 저는 아무 음식이나 잘 먹어요.
examples.translation: jeoneun amu eumsigina jal meogeoyo. — I (can) eat any food.

examples.text: 저는 아무 음식이나 안 먹어요.
examples.translation: jeoneun amu eumsigina an meogeoyo. — I do not eat just any food.

examples.text: 저는 아무 커피나 마셔요.
examples.translation: jeoneun amu keopina masyeoyo. — I drink any coffee.

examples.text: 저는 아무 커피나 안 마셔요.
examples.translation: jeoneun amu keopina an masyeoyo. — I do not drink just any coffee.

explanations.title: The two meanings
explanations.body: Note that 아무 ~(이)나 in an affirmative sentence (or a sentence that does not have a negative verb) translates to any ~, as in anyone, anything, any kimchi, any coffee, anywhere, etc. On the other hand, 아무 ~(이)나 in a negative sentence translates to not just any ~, as in not just anyone, not just anything, not just any kimchi, not just any coffee, not just any place, etc.

lessons.title: 220. Ch 16 · Grammar B: “know how to” and “not know how to” with -(으)ㄹ 줄 알다/모르다
lessons.subtitle: 수영할 줄 알아요 · 수영할 줄 몰라요 · 읽을 줄 알아요 · 고칠 줄 알아요 · 운전할 줄 알아요

explanations.title: Expressing “know how to” and “not know how to”
explanations.body: In English, we often use “know how to …” or “not know how to …” to express ability or inability to do something. Likewise, Koreans use the expressions -(으)ㄹ 줄 알다 (know how to) and -(으)ㄹ 줄 모르다 (not know how to).

rows: When a verb stem ends in a vowel
수영하다 → 수영할 줄 알다 / 수영할 줄 모르다; 차를 고치다 → 고칠 줄 알다 / 고칠 줄 모르다
When a verb stem ends in a consonant
책을 읽다 → 읽을 줄 알다 / 읽을 줄 모르다; 사전을 찾다 → 찾을 줄 알다 / 찾을 줄 모르다

Do you know how to make pasta?

explanations.title: Topic C: there are many famous tourist attractions in Gyeongju! (경주에는 유명한 관광 명소가 많네요!)
explanations.body: SPC Anderson is talking with a tour guide at Bulguksa, Gyeongju. (The English is mine; the book gives none. The book’s footnotes: 신라 is “Silla”, and 저건 is a contracted form of 저것은.)

examples.text: 안내원: 여기가 불국사입니다. 세계적인 관광 명소입니다. 신라 때 지은 절이에요.
examples.translation: annaewon: yeogiga bulguksaimnida. segyejeogin gwangwang myeongsoimnida. silla ttae jieun jeorieyo. — This is Bulguksa. It is a world-renowned tourist attraction. It is a temple built in the Silla period.

examples.text: 앤더슨 상병: 정말 인상적이군요! 경치도 아주 좋아요. 그런데 한국에는 절이 많아요?
examples.translation: aendeoseun sangbyeong: jeongmal insangjeogigunyo! gyeongchido aju joayo. geureonde hangugeneun jeori manayo? — It is really impressive! The scenery is also very good. By the way, are there many temples in Korea?

examples.text: 안내원: 네, 한국은 옛날에 불교 국가였어요.
examples.translation: annaewon: ne, hangugeun yennare bulgyo gukgayeosseoyo. — Yes, Korea was a Buddhist country in the old days.

examples.text: 앤더슨 상병: 그렇군요. 그런데, 저건 뭐예요?
examples.translation: aendeoseun sangbyeong: geureokunyo. geureonde, jeogeon mwoyeyo? — I see. By the way, what is that over there?

examples.text: 안내원: 탑입니다. 왼쪽이 다보탑이고 오른쪽이 석가탑이에요.
examples.translation: annaewon: tabimnida. oenjjogi dabotabigo oreunjjogi seokgatabieyo. — It is a pagoda. The one on the left is Dabotap and the one on the right is Seokgatap.

examples.text: 앤더슨 상병: 탑이 아주 멋있네요!
examples.translation: aendeoseun sangbyeong: tabi aju meosinneyo! — The pagodas are very cool!

examples.text: 안내원: 네. 그럼 다음에는 경주 박물관을 관광하겠습니다. 거기에는 신라 문화재가 많습니다. 또 박물관 근처에도 많은 유적지가 있습니다.
examples.translation: annaewon: ne. geureom daeumeneun gyeongju bangmulgwaneul gwangwanghagetseumnida. geogieneun silla munhwajaega manseumnida. tto bangmulgwan geuncheoedo maneun yujeokjiga itseumnida. — Yes. Then next we will tour the Gyeongju Museum. There are many Silla cultural assets there. Also there are many historic sites near the museum.

examples.text: 앤더슨 상병: 와, 오늘 경주 관광하면서 신라 역사에 대해서 많이 배우겠어요.
examples.translation: aendeoseun sangbyeong: wa, oneul gyeongju gwangwanghamyeonseo silla yeoksae daehaeseo mani baeugesseoyo. — Wow, I will learn a lot about Silla history while touring Gyeongju today.

examples.text: 안내원: 그리고 마지막으로 경주 온천을 가겠습니다.
examples.translation: annaewon: geurigo majimageuro gyeongju oncheoneul gagetseumnida. — And finally we will go to the Gyeongju hot spring.

examples.text: 앤더슨 상병: 네, 아주 좋은 경험이 되겠네요.
examples.translation: aendeoseun sangbyeong: ne, aju joeun gyeongheomi doegenneyo. — Yes, it will be a very good experience.

explanations.title: Cultural notes: Buddhism and temples
explanations.body: Buddhism was introduced to the Korean Peninsula via China in 372 c.e. 절 is the native Korean term for a Buddhist temple. Each temple has its own name, which invariably ends with 사 (a temple), as in 불국사, 해인사, 법주사, etc. There are several hundred temples scattered throughout Korea, some more than 1,500 years old. (The book also shows a map titled “The Three Kingdoms of Korea”, which is left out.)

lessons.title: 223. Ch 16 · Grammar C: simultaneous actions or conditions with -(으)면서
lessons.subtitle: 샤워하면서 노래해요 · 책을 읽으면서 커피 마셔요 · 의사이면서 교수 · 싸면서 예뻐요

explanations.title: Expressing simultaneous actions or conditions
explanations.body:
In English, we often express concurrent actions or conditions by using while or at the same time, as in “He is having breakfast while watching TV” or “He is lazy but, at the same time, smart.” In Korean, we express simultaneous actions or conditions by using the conjunctive ending -(으)면서: 저는 샤워하면서 노래해요 (I sing while taking a shower); 장 선생님은 의사이면서 교수이십니다 (Mr. Chang is a doctor and (at the same time) a professor).

Keep in mind that -(으)면서 is used only when multiple actions or conditions are done by or exist for the same subject.

rows: When a verb stem ends in a vowel
When a verb stem ends in a consonant
책을 읽다 + 커피 마시다 → 책을 읽으면서 커피 마시다

explanations.title: Forms
explanations.body: The forms below are mine, made by the book’s rule (a stem ending in ㄹ keeps it before 면서: 놀다 → 놀면서; the ㄷ irregular verbs 듣다 and 걷다 change ㄷ to ㄹ: 들으면서, 걸으면서). After a noun the copula 이다 is used: 의사이면서.

explanations.title: Follow-up 1: a chain of simultaneous actions
explanations.body: In the book the students sit in a circle: the first starts with a simple phrase like 샤워합니다; the next changes it to 샤워하면서 and adds another phrase, and so on. The book’s model, with the students A–D named 철수, 영희, 민수 and 지영 here (the English is mine):

examples.text: 철수: 샤워합니다.
examples.translation: cheolsu: syawohamnida. — I take a shower.

examples.text: 영희: 샤워하면서 음악을 듣습니다.
examples.translation: yeonghui: syawohamyeonseo eumageul deutseumnida. — I listen to music while taking a shower.

examples.text: 민수: 음악을 들으면서 커피를 마십니다.

lessons.title: 224. Ch 16 · Grammar D: realization and discovery with -(는)군요 and -네요
lessons.subtitle: 재미있군요 · 재미있네요 · 멋있네요 · 예쁘군요 · 의사이시군요 · 마시는군요

explanations.title: Verb endings that express realization or discovery
explanations.body: In English, when we come to a realization or discover a certain fact, we often say something like, “Wow, she is beautiful!” or “Wow, this is strange!” Koreans express this by using -(는)군요 or -네요. Compare the following sentences:

examples.text: 한국말이 재미있어요.
examples.translation: hangungmari jaemiisseoyo. — Korean is fun. (a simple statement: the speaker already knows)

examples.text: 한국말이 재미있군요!
examples.translation: hangungmari jaemiitgunyo! — (Wow) Korean is fun! (with -군요)

examples.text: 한국말이 재미있네요!
examples.translation: hangungmari jaemiinneyo! — (Wow) Korean is fun! (with -네요)

explanations.title: What the endings imply
explanations.body: The first sentence is a simple statement that implies the speaker already knows that Korean is fun. However, the last two sentences, which end in -(는)군요 and -네요, tell us that the speaker just realized or discovered that Korean is fun. This implies that the speaker did not know that Korean was fun until the moment of the utterance.

rows: With stative verbs and 이다/아니다 or 있다/없다
멋있다 → 멋있군요 / 멋있네요!; 예쁘다 → 예쁘군요 / 예쁘네요!; 학생이다 → 학생이군요 / 학생이네요!
With an action verb in the present tense
피아노를 잘 치다 → 피아노를 잘 치는군요 / 치네요!; 커피를 마시다 → 커피를 마시는군요 / 마시네요!

explanations.title: Forms
explanations.body: The forms below are mine, made by the book’s rule (the ending 는군요 goes after an action verb; 있다 and 없다 take 군요 as the book’s rule says; after a noun the copula 이다 gives 이군요/이네요, and after a noun that ends in a vowel the 이 can contract: 의사군요 as well as 의사이군요, mine).

explanations.title: How to use this list
explanations.body:
The book’s Core Vocabulary lists the core words of the chapter with an example sentence for each (the sentences and the English meanings are the book’s; the book gives no English for the sentences). The Hanja of the Sino-Korean words are in parentheses before the meaning. Optional parts, such as (~하다/되다), are kept in the meanings.

The example sentences with digits are respelled in Hangul (24시간 → 이십사 시간, 10,000원 → 만 원, 5,000원 → 오천 원, 5월 5일 → 오월 오일, 75만원 → 칠십오만 원, 5천 → 오천); the book’s 연기 appears twice (延期, postponement, and 煙氣, smoke) and is shown once for each meaning. The book’s related words (the synonyms, antonyms and related words in the last column) are not repeated. The book’s Additional Vocabulary table is empty: it is for your own words.

explanations.title: Self-evaluation
explanations.body:
Recall the objectives of the chapter and ask yourself whether you have achieved them (the book asks you to tick Yes or No). If you tick “No” for any item, the book suggests: review that section on your own; find a study partner and review it as a pair or group; and tell your academic advisor or team leader which areas you need more help with, so that they can provide activities tailored to your learning style and needs.

Now I am able to: make a domestic flight reservation; ask for and give information about a travel package; ask for and give information about renting a car; report simple car problems; identify simple automotive parts; talk about well-known tourist attractions in Korea.

Now I have a clear understanding of: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; 아무나 or 아무 ~(이)나 in the affirmative (any ~); 아무나 or 아무 ~(이)나 in the negative (not just any ~); -(으)ㄹ 줄 알다 (know how to); -(으)ㄹ 줄 모르다 (not know how to); the exclamatory verb endings -군요 and -네요; the conjunctive ending -(으)면서, used to express simultaneous actions or conditions; the Sino-Korean syllables 불/부 (不), 적 (的), and 형 (型).

lessons.title: 226. Ch 17 · What the chapter teaches and the Sino-Korean syllable 회

explanations.title: What Chapter 17 teaches (문화생활)
explanations.body:
Chapter 17, “Cultural Life”, has three topic presentations, grammar in focus, activities, a self-evaluation and the core vocabulary.

When you finish the chapter you will be able to: identify Koreans’ common interests and hobbies; exchange information about personal interests and hobbies; extract and talk about basic information found on posters about cultural events and movies; give simple instructions for purchasing tickets of cultural events; and elicit information at the box office for a movie.

You will become familiar with: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; the gerund or verbal ending that is used as a noun; 르 irregular verbs; the attributive form + 것 같다 (looks like …; it seems that …); and the Sino-Korean syllable 회 (會).

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 회 (會)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means meeting or gathering, as in 회사 (a company; “meeting and gathering”), 회의 (a conference; a meeting; “meeting and discussion”), 전시회 (exhibition; “display gathering”), and 교회 (church; “[religious] teaching gathering”). The book asks you to guess the meaning of 음악회, 회의실, 회비, 회사원, 회원 and 한인회장; the answers below are the book’s meanings where the Core Vocabulary gives them and mine otherwise.

explanations.title: Topic A: What do Koreans do in their spare time? (한국 사람들은 시간이 날 때 뭐 해요?)
explanations.body: David and Taehee are talking about hobbies and leisure activities that Koreans enjoy most. (The English is mine; the book gives none. The book writes 10대, 20대 and 30대; they are spelled out here.)

examples.text: 데이비드: 태희 씨는 시간이 날 때 보통 뭐 해요?
examples.translation: deibideu: taehui ssineun sigani nal ttae botong mwo haeyo? — Taehee, what do you usually do when you have free time?

examples.text: 태희: 저는 악기 연주가 취미예요. 피아노하고 바이올린을 연주해요. 데이비드 씨는 취미가 뭐예요?
examples.translation: taehui: jeoneun akgi yeonjuga chwimiyeyo. pianohago baiollineul yeonjuhaeyo. deibideu ssineun chwimiga mwoyeyo? — My hobby is playing musical instruments. I play the piano and the violin. David, what is your hobby?

examples.text: 데이비드: 저는 암벽등반하고 헬스를 좋아해요. 그런데 한국 사람들은 주로 무슨 취미활동을 해요?
examples.translation: deibideu: jeoneun ambyeokdeungbanhago helseureul joahaeyo. geureonde hanguk saramdeureun juro museun chwimihwaldongeul haeyo? — I like rock climbing and working out. By the way, what hobby activities do Koreans mainly do?

examples.text: 태희: 한국 사람들은 보통 등산과 독서를 많이 해요. 그리고 젊은 사람들은 인터넷이나 컴퓨터 게임을 좋아해요.
examples.translation: taehui: hanguk saramdeureun botong deungsangwa dokseoreul mani haeyo. geurigo jeolmeun saramdeureun inteonesina keompyuteo geimeul joahaeyo. — Koreans usually do a lot of hiking and reading. And young people like the internet and computer games.

examples.text: 데이비드: 그래요? 우리 미국 사람들은 다양한 레저와 스포츠를 즐겨요. 한국 사람들은 어떤 레저 활동을 좋아해요?
examples.translation: deibideu: geuraeyo? uri miguk saramdeureun dayanghan rejeowa seupocheureul jeulgyeoyo. hanguk saramdeureun eotteon rejeo hwaldongeul joahaeyo? — Is that so? We Americans enjoy a variety of leisure activities and sports. What kind of leisure activities do Koreans like?

examples.text: 태희: 보통 십 대나 이십 대는 운동이나 헬스를 많이 해요. 그리고 삼십 대 이상은 등산이나 낚시를 좋아해요.
examples.translation: taehui: botong sip daena isip daeneun undongina helseureul mani haeyo. geurigo samsip dae isangeun deungsanina naksireul joahaeyo. — Usually people in their 10s or 20s do a lot of sports or working out. And people in their 30s and above like hiking or fishing.

examples.text: 데이비드: 그렇군요. 그럼, 태희 씨도 운동 좋아해요?
examples.translation: deibideu: geureokunyo. geureom, taehui ssido undong joahaeyo? — I see. Then, Taehee, do you like sports, too?

examples.text: 태희: 아니요. 저는 운동을 별로 안 좋아해요. 저는 음악회나 연극 관람을 더 좋아해요.
examples.translation: taehui: aniyo. jeoneun undongeul byeollo an joahaeyo. jeoneun eumakoena yeongeuk gwallameul deo joahaeyo. — No. I don’t like sports very much. I like going to concerts and watching plays more.

explanations.title: Cultural notes
explanations.body: Before the 1990s, Koreans spent most of their time working and rarely enjoyed hobbies or leisure activities. Since the 1990s, however, Koreans have enjoyed an increase in income and free time and have come to prize their quality of living. Therefore, the percentage of Koreans enjoying various outdoor and indoor leisure activities, such as climbing, fishing, golfing, or watching movies, has been increasing.

explanations.title: Topic A, Follow-up 1 (Reading): an excerpt from a survey report
explanations.body: The book gives an excerpt from a survey report by Gallup Korea and asks you to complete a bar graph by providing the missing information. The text is the book’s (the date, the figures and the 13세 are spelled out in Hangul; the decimal point is read 점); the English is mine.

examples.text: 한국인이 좋아하는 취미
examples.translation: hangugini joahaneun chwimi — Hobbies Koreans like

examples.text: 한국갤럽이 오월 구일부터 이십오일까지 전국 만 십삼 세 이상 남녀 천칠백 명에게 가장 좋아하는 취미를 물은 결과 등산 구 퍼센트이 가장 많았고, 그다음은 음악감상 팔점삼 퍼센트이었습니다.
examples.translation: hangukgaelleobi owol guilbuteo isiboilkkaji jeonguk man sipsam se isang namnyeo cheonchilbaek myeongege gajang joahaneun chwimireul mureun gyeolgwa deungsan gu peosenteui gajang manatgo, geudaeumeun eumakgamsang paljeomsam peosenteuieotseumnida. — Gallup Korea asked 1,700 men and women nationwide aged 13 and over (full years) from May 9 to 25 about the hobby they like most, and ‘hiking’ (9.0%) was the most common, followed by ‘listening to music’ (8.3%).

examples.text: 그리고 오점이 퍼센트는 독서, 사점오 퍼센트는 영화감상을 하는 것으로 나타났습니다.
examples.translation: geurigo ojeomi peosenteuneun dokseo, sajeomo peosenteuneun yeonghwagamsangeul haneun geoseuro natanatseumnida. — And 5.2% do ‘reading’ and 4.5% do ‘watching movies’.

explanations.title: The graph filled in (mine)

explanations.title: Activities, Activity 2: sample questions
explanations.body: In the book each partner has an incomplete table of the hobbies Korean men enjoy most, and you ask each other questions to complete it. The book’s sample questions (digits spelled out; the English is mine):

examples.text: 십 대 남자들이 가장 좋아하는 취미가 무엇입니까?

examples.translation: isip dae namjadeurui gujeomsa peosenteuga joahaneun chwimiga mwoyeyo? — What hobby do 9.4% of men in their 20s like?

examples.translation: samsip dae namjadeuri du beonjjaero joahaneun chwimiga mueosimnikka? — What hobby do men in their 30s like second most?

explanations.title: Activities left out
explanations.body: Activity 1 (a SMART Board activity), the partner tables of Activity 2, Activity 3 (listening to three conversations about hobbies and filling in the hobby, the event, the day and the time) and Activity 4 (partners read passage A or B about the hobbies of Sungsoo’s and Hyojin’s families, exchange information and present; the two passages are handed out by the teacher and are not printed in the book) are audio, computer, partner or class activities.

lessons.title: 231. Ch 17 · Grammar A: the gerund with -는 것 and -기
lessons.subtitle: 한국말을 가르치는 것 · 영화 보기 · 책 읽기 · 취미는 먹는 것입니다

explanations.title: Expressing a gerund
explanations.body:
In English, the gerund refers to the usage of a verb or verbal phrase (in its -ing form) as a noun: “Teaching Korean is fun” (subject), “Mr. Kim enjoys teaching Korean” (object), “My job is teaching Korean” (subject complement). Nouns function as subjects, objects and subject complements, and the verbal phrase functions as a noun in these sentences.

In Korean, a verb or verbal phrase functions as a gerund when -는 것 or -기 is added to the stem of a verb. In a nutshell, -는 것 and -기 are the Korean equivalents of the English -ing. In the gerund that ends in -기, the object marker is deletable. This is because the gerund with -기 has more noun-like characteristics than the one with -는 것, just as “boar hunting” has more noun-like characteristics than “hunting boars” in English.

examples.text: 한국말을 가르치는 것이 쉬워요.

lessons.title: 232. Ch 17 · Grammar B: 르 irregular verbs
lessons.subtitle: 모르다 → 몰라요 · 부르다 → 불러요 · 다르다 → 달라요 · 빠르다 → 빨라요 · 고르다 · 자르다 · 누르다

explanations.title: 르 irregular verbs
explanations.body: So far you have learned quite a few verbs with stems ending in 르: 빠르다 (to be fast), 다르다 (to be different), 부르다 (to sing / call), 고르다 (to choose), 모르다 (not to know), 자르다 (to cut). These verbs are known as “르 irregular verbs” because they go through an extra step when their stem is followed by a vowel, such as -아/어요, -아/어 보다, or -았/었습니다.

rows: ㄹ moves to the bottom of the preceding syllable.
라 or 러 is added. 라 is added if the preceding syllable has a vowel ㅏ or ㅗ. Otherwise, 러 is added.

explanations.title: Cultural notes: matinee discounts
explanations.body: In the United States, an early afternoon movie is called a “matinee,” and the discounted tickets for these are called “matinee discounts.” In Korea, such discounts are called 조조할인, in which 조조 (早朝) means early morning. However, these discount prices are available only for the first showing of the day, whereas matinee discounts in the United States generally include all early afternoon showings.

Follow-up 1 is in the next lesson. The Useful Links (Cine21, Megabox) are websites.

explanations.body: The book gives two advertisements for Korean movies at two different theaters (CGV with IMAX, and MEGABOX) and asks you to fill in a table in English (movie title, first show price, first show time, age limit, discount and terms). lessons.title: 235. Ch 17 · Grammar C: “looks like” with the attributive form + 것 같다
lessons.subtitle: 오는 것 같아요 · 온 것 같아요 · 올 것 같아요 · 재미있을 것 같아요 · 더운 것 같아요

explanations.title: Expressing “looks like”
explanations.body:
In English, we often use the expressions (it) looks like …, it seems that …, or it appears that … to express speculation or conjecture, as in “Looks like the sea is calm”, followed by a tense-embedded clause: present (“looks like the sea is calm now”), past (“looks like the sea was calm then”) and future (“looks like the sea will be calm soon”).

In Korean, we use an attributive form + 것 같다 to express (it) looks like …, it seems that …, or it appears that …. 오는 것, 온 것 and 올 것 are the attributive forms of the verb 오다 that reflect the present tense, past tense and future tense. Making full use of this grammar feature requires that you be familiar with the different attributive forms of action verbs you learned about in a previous chapter.

examples.text: 지금 눈이 오는 것 같아요.
examples.translation: jigeum nuni oneun geot gatayo. — It looks like it snows or looks like it is snowing.

examples.text: 오 분 전에 눈이 온 것 같아요.
examples.translation: o bun jeone nuni on geot gatayo. — It looks like it snowed five minutes ago.

examples.text: 오늘 저녁 눈이 올 것 같아요.
examples.translation: oneul jeonyeok nuni ol geot gatayo. — It looks like it will snow tonight.

explanations.title: The rule
explanations.body: appropriate tense of attributive form + 것 같다.

examples.text: 어제 비가 많이 온 것 같아요.
examples.translation: eoje biga mani on geot gatayo. — It looks like it rained a lot yesterday.

examples.text: 지금 비가 오는 것 같아요.
examples.translation: jigeum biga oneun geot gatayo. — It looks like it is raining now.

examples.text: 한국말이 어려운 것 같아요.
examples.translation: hangungmari eoryeoun geot gatayo. — It seems that Korean is difficult.

examples.text: 내년에 한국에 갈 것 같습니다.
examples.translation: naenyeone hanguge gal geot gatseumnida. — It appears that I will go to Korea next year.

examples.text: 내일은 날씨가 따뜻해 질 것 같아요.
examples.translation: naeireun nalssiga ttatteutae jil geot gatayo. — I think that it will be warm tomorrow.

explanations.title: Follow-up 3: conversations with 것 같다
explanations.body: The book gives three conversations with a blank in each, and a box of three verbs (잘하다, 결혼하다, 없다). The answers are mine (in the third one the book’s ‘일본어도’ is followed by 잘할 것 같아요).

examples.text: 가: 김기철 씨가 결혼을 했을까?
examples.translation: ga: gimgicheol ssiga gyeolhoneul haesseulkka? — Do you think Mr. Kim Kichul got married?

examples.text: 나: 반지를 끼고 있는 것을 보니까 결혼한 것 같아.
examples.translation: na: banjireul kkigo inneun geoseul bonikka gyeolhonhan geot gata. — Seeing that he is wearing a ring, it seems he got married.

examples.text: 가: 스티브 씨한테 전화 했어?
examples.translation: ga: seutibeu ssihante jeonhwa haesseo? — Did you call Steve?

examples.text: 나: 응, 전화 했는데 전화를 안 받아. 집에 없는 것 같아.
examples.translation: na: eung, jeonhwa haenneunde jeonhwareul an bada. jibe eomneun geot gata. — Yes, I called, but he doesn’t answer. It seems he is not at home.

examples.text: 가: 김 일병, 요즘 어떻게 지내요?
examples.translation: ga: gim ilbyeong, yojeum eotteoke jinaeyo? — Private Kim, how are you these days?

examples.text: 나: 대학에서 일본어를 공부해요.
examples.translation: na: daehageseo ilboneoreul gongbuhaeyo. — I study Japanese at a university.

examples.text: 가: 김 일병은 한국어도 잘했으니까 일본어도 잘할 것 같아요.
examples.translation: ga: gim ilbyeongeun hangugeodo jalhaesseunikka ilboneodo jalhal geot gatayo. — Since you were good at Korean, too, it seems you will be good at Japanese as well.

explanations.title: Follow-up 4: speculating about your partner
explanations.body: You write three guesses about your partner’s present activities with -는 것 같다 and, on a “Lucky Card”, two lucky things that could happen to your partner with -(으)ㄹ 것 같다. The book’s models (the book writes 1년 and 2년; spelled out here; the English is mine):

examples.text: 이 일병은 요즘 공부를 열심히 하는 것 같아요.
examples.translation: i ilbyeongeun yojeum gongbureul yeolsimhi haneun geot gatayo. — Private Lee seems to be studying hard these days.

examples.text: 김 일병은 주말에 영화를 자주 보는 것 같아요.
examples.translation: gim ilbyeongeun jumare yeonghwareul jaju boneun geot gatayo. — Private Kim seems to watch movies often on weekends.

examples.text: 김 일병은 일 년 후에 예쁜 여자를 만날 것 같아요. 그리고 이 년 후에 결혼할 것 같아요.
examples.translation: gim ilbyeongeun il nyeon hue yeppeun yeojareul mannal geot gatayo. geurigo i nyeon hue gyeolhonhal geot gatayo. — Private Kim will probably meet a pretty woman in a year, and it seems he will get married in two years.

examples.text: 이 일병은 미국 대통령이 될 것 같아요.
examples.translation: i ilbyeongeun miguk daetongnyeongi doel geot gatayo. — Private Lee will probably become the President of the United States.

explanations.title: Activities left out
explanations.body: Follow-up 1 (partners draw verb cards and change them into the three forms), Follow-up 2 (b) (listening to four conversations and circling the grammar form used) and Follow-up 4 (partner speculation with a Lucky Card) are audio or partner activities.

explanations.title: How to use this list
explanations.body:
The book’s Core Vocabulary lists the core words of the chapter with an example sentence for each (the sentences and the English meanings are the book’s; the book gives no English for the sentences). The Hanja of the Sino-Korean words are in parentheses before the meaning.

The example sentences with digits or Latin letters are respelled in Hangul (40대 → 사십 대, 5세 → 오 세, 10대 → 십 대, 20대 → 이십 대, 19세 → 십구 세, 3개월 → 삼 개월, S석 → 에스석, 0번 → 영 번, 007 → 영영칠, DLI → 디엘아이); the book’s ‘13일의 금요일’ is spelled ‘십삼 일의 금요일’. The book’s example for 홈페이지 gives a web address, which is left out; the sentence shown for it is mine. The book’s related words (the synonyms, antonyms and related words in the last column) are left out; the Additional Vocabulary section of the book is blank.

explanations.title: Self-evaluation
explanations.body:
Recall the objectives of the chapter and ask yourself whether you have achieved them (the book asks you to tick Yes or No). If you tick “No” for any item, the book suggests: review that section on your own; find a study partner and review it as a pair or group; and tell your academic advisor or team leader which areas you need more help with, so that they can provide activities tailored to your learning style and needs.

Now I am able to: identify Koreans’ common interests and hobbies; exchange information about personal interests and hobbies; extract and talk about basic information found on posters about cultural events and movies; give simple instructions for purchasing tickets of cultural events; and elicit information at the box office for a movie.

Now I have a clear understanding of: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; the gerund or verbal ending that is used as a noun; 르 irregular verbs; the attributive form + 것 같다 (looks like …; it seems that …); and the Sino-Korean syllable 회 (會).

explanations.title: What Chapter 18 teaches (물건 사기)
explanations.body:
Chapter 18, “Shopping”, has three topic presentations, grammar in focus, activities, a self-evaluation and the core vocabulary.

When you finish the chapter you will be able to: inquire about basic information when shopping for items at a department store and market; ask for a refund and exchange items; place an order and request a delivery; and negotiate and bargain for a discount.

You will become familiar with: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; indicating the object in a mutual relationship with the subject; ~만큼 (as … as); -기로 하다 (to decide to); -(으)ㄹ게요 (will); and the Sino-Korean syllable 전 (電).

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 전 (電)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means electricity or electric, as in 전기 (electricity; “electric energy”) and 전자 (electron; electronics; “electric son”). The upper part of the Chinese character depicts rain. The lower part depicts lightning, or the source of natural electricity. The book asks you to guess the meaning of 전선, 전화기, 전구, 전차, 전파 and 전력, with the hints 선 (線): a line, a cord; 구 (球): a ball, a globe; 파 (波): wave; 력 (力): power. The answers are mine.

explanations.title: Activity 1 (Reading): match the Korean words with their English meanings
explanations.body: The book gives ten Korean words in the left column and ten English meanings in the right column in a different order and asks you to draw lines between them. The pairs below are the book’s words with their meanings (the answers to the matching are mine).

explanations.title: Activity 2 (Reading): customer questions on a department store’s website
explanations.body: The book gives three customer questions from the website of a department store called 아시아백화점, and three answers in a box; match each question with the appropriate response. The texts are the book’s (the dates and times are spelled out in Hangul); the English is mine.

examples.text: 작성자: 김선환, 작성 일시: 삼월 팔일 오후 네 시 삼십이 분
examples.translation: jakseongja: gimseonhwan, jakseong ilsi: samwol paril ohu ne si samsibi bun — Writer: Kim Seonhwan; written on March 8 at 4:32 p.m.

examples.text: 지난 주말에 서울에 있는 아시아 백화점에서 넥타이를 하나 구입했습니다. 그런데 디자인이 조금 마음에 안 드네요. 환불을 받고 싶은데, 저희 집이 부산이에요. 이 넥타이를 부산에 있는 아시아 백화점에서 환불을 받을 수 있습니까?
examples.translation: jinan jumare seoure inneun asia baekwajeomeseo nektaireul hana guipaetseumnida. geureonde dijaini jogeum maeume an deuneyo. hwanbureul batgo sipeunde, jeohui jibi busanieyo. i nektaireul busane inneun asia baekwajeomeseo hwanbureul badeul su itseumnikka? — Last weekend I bought a necktie at the Asia Department Store in Seoul. But I don’t like the design a little. I want a refund, but my home is in Busan. Can I get a refund for this necktie at the Asia Department Store in Busan?

examples.text: 작성자: 이선자, 작성 일시: 삼월 팔일 오후 여섯 시 팔 분
examples.translation: jakseongja: iseonja, jakseong ilsi: samwol paril ohu yeoseot si pal bun — Writer: Lee Seonja; written on March 8 at 6:08 p.m.

examples.text: 어제 아버지 생신 선물로 구두를 샀습니다. 그런데 구두가 좀 커서 다른 구두로 교환하고 싶어요. 어떻게 해야 합니까?
examples.translation: eoje abeoji saengsin seonmullo gudureul satseumnida. geureonde guduga jom keoseo dareun guduro gyohwanhago sipeoyo. eotteoke haeya hamnikka? — Yesterday I bought dress shoes as a birthday present for my father. But the shoes are a little big, so I want to exchange them for other shoes. What should I do?

examples.text: 작성자: 길용우, 작성 일시: 삼월 팔일 오후 아홉 시 이십팔 분
examples.translation: jakseongja: giryongu, jakseong ilsi: samwol paril ohu ahop si isippal bun — Writer: Gil Yongwoo; written on March 8 at 9:28 p.m.

examples.text: 얼마 전에 친구에게서 아시아 백화점 상품권을 선물 받았습니다. 이 상품권을 환불받고 싶어요. 상품권도 환불받을 수 있어요?
examples.translation: eolma jeone chinguegeseo asia baekwajeom sangpumgwoneul seonmul badatseumnida. i sangpumgwoneul hwanbulbatgo sipeoyo. sangpumgwondo hwanbulbadeul su isseoyo? — Not long ago I received an Asia Department Store gift certificate as a present from a friend. I want a refund for this gift certificate. Can I get a refund for a gift certificate, too?

explanations.title: The three answers
explanations.body: The book’s answers 1, 2 and 3 (the English is mine):

examples.text: 영수증이 있으면 상품권도 환불이 가능합니다. 구입한 날로부터 육십 일 후까지 환불받으실 수 있습니다.
examples.translation: yeongsujeungi isseumyeon sangpumgwondo hwanburi ganeunghamnida. guipan nallobuteo yuksip il hukkaji hwanbulbadeusil su itseumnida. — If you have the receipt, a refund is also possible for a gift certificate. You can get a refund until 60 days after the day of purchase.

examples.text: 교환은 아무 곳에서나 하실 수 있습니다. 하지만 환불은 구입하신 곳에서만 받으실 수 있습니다.
examples.translation: gyohwaneun amu goseseona hasil su itseumnida. hajiman hwanbureun guipasin goseseoman badeusil su itseumnida. — You can exchange at any place. But you can get a refund only at the place where you bought it.

examples.text: 아직 신지 않으셨으면 칠 일 이내에 교환이나 환불받으실 수 있습니다. 하지만 이미 신으셨으면 환불이나 교환하실 수 없습니다.
examples.translation: ajik sinji aneusyeosseumyeon chil il inaee gyohwanina hwanbulbadeusil su itseumnida. hajiman imi sineusyeosseumyeon hwanburina gyohwanhasil su eopseumnida. — If you have not worn them yet, you can get an exchange or a refund within 7 days. But if you have already worn them, you cannot get a refund or an exchange.

explanations.title: The matching (mine)
explanations.body: The book leaves the answers blank; these are my answers.

rows: Kim Seonhwan (refund for a necktie, home in Busan)
Answer 2: exchange at any place, but a refund only where you bought it
Lee Seonja (exchange shoes that are too big)
Answer 3: within 7 days if not worn yet
Gil Yongwoo (refund for a gift certificate)
Answer 1: possible with the receipt, until 60 days after purchase

explanations.title: Words of the questions and answers
explanations.body: These meanings are mine (the book does not gloss them).

explanations.title: Topic B: The quality of the product is very good (품질은 아주 좋습니다)
explanations.body: A customer is talking with a salesperson about buying a refrigerator at a home appliance store. (The English is mine; the book gives none. The book writes 120만 원 and 1년; they are spelled out here.)

examples.text: 손님: 냉장고 좀 보여주세요.
examples.translation: sonnim: naengjanggo jom boyeojuseyo. — Please show me a refrigerator.

examples.text: 판매원: 어떤 냉장고를 찾으세요?
examples.translation: panmaewon: eotteon naengjanggoreul chajeuseyo? — What kind of refrigerator are you looking for?

examples.text: 손님: 저희 집 냉장고가 너무 작아서요. 좀 큰 것이 필요해요.
examples.translation: sonnim: jeohui jip naengjanggoga neomu jagaseoyo. jom keun geosi piryohaeyo. — Our refrigerator at home is too small. I need a bigger one.

examples.text: 판매원: 그럼 이 냉장고는 어떠세요?
examples.translation: panmaewon: geureom i naengjanggoneun eotteoseyo? — Then how about this refrigerator?

lessons.title: 242. Ch 18 · Grammar A: the object in a “mutual” relationship with the subject
lessons.subtitle: 한국말은 일본말과 비슷합니다 · 와/과 · 하고 · (이)랑 · 같다 · 다르다 · 결혼하다

explanations.title: Indicating the object in a “mutual” relationship with the subject
explanations.body:
Consider the relationship between the two nouns in “Tom dates Jane” and “Korean is similar to Japanese”. Although one is the subject and the other is the object (of a verb or preposition), the nouns are in a “mutual” relationship: Tom and Jane date each other, and Korean and Japanese are similar to each other. Therefore, it is possible to reverse the two nouns without affecting the meanings of the sentences.

You can reverse the two nouns in a mutual relationship in Korean as well. In such cases, we attach the noun connector 와/과, 하고, or (이)랑 to the second noun, although the second noun is considered to be the object (of a verb or preposition).

lessons.title: 243. Ch 18 · Grammar B: first-person intention in informal settings, -(으)ㄹ게요
lessons.subtitle: 제가 전화할게요 · 제가 앉을게요 · 제가 만들게요 · 제가 살게요 · 내가 할게

explanations.title: Expressing first-person intention in informal settings
explanations.body: In Chapter 11, you learned that the verb infix 겠 is used to express the first-person speaker’s strong intention, as in 한국에 가겠습니다 (I will go to Korea) or 내년에 결혼하겠어요 (I will get married next year). In this lesson, you learn about another way to express the first-person speaker’s strong intention: the verb ending -(으)ㄹ게(요). Like 겠, -(으)ㄹ게요 expresses the speaker’s strong intention, but only in informal settings and only in statements. -(으)ㄹ게 is a blunt form of -(으)ㄹ게요, and it is used between people in close relationship.

examples.text: 제가 오늘 저녁에 전화할게요.
examples.translation: jega oneul jeonyeoge jeonhwahalgeyo. — I will give you a call tonight.

examples.text: 내가 오늘 저녁에 전화할게.
examples.translation: naega oneul jeonyeoge jeonhwahalge. — I will give you a call tonight. (blunt)

explanations.title: The rule
explanations.body: action verb stem + (으)ㄹ게요.

rows: If the verb stem ends in a consonant
여기에 앉다 → 제가 여기에 앉을게요 → 내가 여기에 앉을게
If the verb stem ends in a vowel
상을 차리다 → 제가 상을 차릴게요 → 내가 상을 차릴게

examples.text: 제가 여기에 앉을게요.
examples.translation: jega yeogie anjeulgeyo. — I will sit here.

examples.text: 내가 여기에 앉을게.
examples.translation: naega yeogie anjeulge. — I will sit here. (blunt)

examples.text: 제가 상을 차릴게요.
examples.translation: jega sangeul charilgeyo. — I will set the table.

examples.text: 내가 상을 차릴게.
examples.translation: naega sangeul charilge. — I will set the table. (blunt)

examples.text: 제 친구 수영이도 초대할게요.
examples.translation: je chingu suyeongido chodaehalgeyo. — I will invite my friend Sooyoung as well.

examples.text: 제가 케이크를 만들게요.
examples.translation: jega keikeureul mandeulgeyo. — I will make the cake.

explanations.title: Forms (mine)
explanations.body: The forms are made by the book’s rule (verbs whose stem ends in ㄹ keep the ㄹ: 만들다 → 만들게요).

explanations.title: Follow-up 3 and 5: phrases and plans
explanations.body: In Follow-up 3 partners read phrases from List A or B and make a sentence with -(으)ㄹ게요 and the subject 제가 or 저는 (the book’s model: 책을 읽다 → 제가 책을 읽을게요). In Follow-up 5 partners decide who will bring or prepare each thing for a weekend plan (models: 차는 제가 빌릴게요; 아시아 박물관 표는 제가 살게요). Sentences for eight phrases (mine):

examples.translation: jega chaegeul ilgeulgeyo. — (the book’s model for Follow-up 3) I will read the book.

examples.translation: chaneun jega billilgeyo. — I will rent the car. (the book’s model)

examples.translation: asia bangmulgwan pyoneun jega salgeyo. — I will buy the Asia Museum tickets. (the book’s model)

explanations.title: Activities left out
explanations.body: Follow-up 3 (partner activity with verb cards), Follow-up 4 (listening to three conversations about plans for the weekend and what he and she will do) and Follow-up 5 (partners plan a weekend activity and decide who prepares what) are audio or partner activities.

lessons.title: 244. Ch 18 · Topic C: I went to the open-air market to buy fruits and vegetables
lessons.subtitle: 과일하고 채소를 사러 시장에 갔다 · 수박 한 통 · 시금치 세 단 · 감자 한 상자 · 양파 한 봉지

explanations.title: Topic C: I went to the open-air market to buy fruits and vegetables (과일하고 채소를 사러 시장에 갔다)
explanations.body: The text is Michael’s journal entry about his experience at an open-air market. (The English is mine; the book gives none. The book writes 21,000원 and 1,000원; they are spelled out here.)

examples.text: 과일하고 채소를 사러 시장에 갔다.
examples.translation: gwailhago chaesoreul sareo sijange gatda. — I went to the market to buy fruits and vegetables.

examples.text: 먼저 과일 가게에 가서 수박 한 통하고 복숭아 다섯 개를 샀다.
examples.translation: meonjeo gwail gagee gaseo subak han tonghago boksunga daseot gaereul satda. — First I went to a fruit store and bought one watermelon and five peaches.

examples.text: 모두 이만 천 원이었는데 주인 아저씨가 천 원을 깎아주셨다.
examples.translation: modu iman cheon wonieonneunde juin ajeossiga cheon woneul kkakkajusyeotda. — It was 21,000 won in all, but the owner (a man) gave me a discount of 1,000 won.

examples.text: 그다음에 채소 파는 가게에 갔다.
examples.translation: geudaeume chaeso paneun gagee gatda. — Then I went to a store that sells vegetables.

examples.text: 거기에서 시금치 세 단하고 감자 한 상자를 샀다.
examples.translation: geogieseo sigeumchi se danhago gamja han sangjareul satda. — There I bought three bundles of spinach and a box of potatoes.

examples.text: 주인 아주머니께서 양파 한 봉지를 공짜로 주셨다.
examples.translation: juin ajumeonikkeseo yangpa han bongjireul gongjjaro jusyeotda. — The owner (a woman) gave me a bag of onions for free.

examples.text: 시장 물건이 백화점 물건보다 훨씬 더 쌌다.
examples.translation: sijang mulgeoni baekwajeom mulgeonboda hwolssin deo ssatda. — The goods at the market were far cheaper than the goods at the department store.

examples.text: 그렇지만 품질은 백화점 물건만큼 좋았다.
examples.translation: geureochiman pumjireun baekwajeom mulgeonmankeum joatda. — But the quality was as good as the goods at the department store.

examples.text: 그리고 가게 주인 아주머니, 아저씨들이 친절하고 좋으셨다.
examples.translation: geurigo gage juin ajumeoni, ajeossideuri chinjeolhago joeusyeotda. — And the store owners, the women and the men, were kind and nice.

examples.text: 시장 구경하는 것이 아주 재미있었다.
examples.translation: sijang gugyeonghaneun geosi aju jaemiisseotda. — Looking around the market was very fun.

examples.text: 그래서 다른 시장도 구경하기로 했다.
examples.translation: geuraeseo dareun sijangdo gugyeonghagiro haetda. — So I decided to look around other markets, too.

explanations.title: Fruits and vegetables (여러 가지 과일과 채소)
explanations.body: The book shows pictures of twelve fruits and vegetables with their names (the English is the book’s from the Core Vocabulary, except 포도, which is mine).

explanations.title: Notes: counters
explanations.body: So far, you have learned several counters used for counting nouns: 명 and 분 for counting people, 개 for counting things in general, etc. We use them in the following order: noun + number + counter. When we use a noun with a counter as a subject or an object, we can add a marker to the noun or the counter.

explanations.title: Counters of the text (the book’s, with the English mine)
explanations.body: The counters of this chapter are 통 (watermelons, heads of cabbage, etc.), 단 (a bundle), 상자 (a box), 봉지 (a bag), 송이 (a bunch of grapes, bananas, etc.) and 개.

explanations.title: Cultural notes: open-air markets
explanations.body: In Korea, an open-air market is known as (재래) 시장 (a traditional market), such as 남대문시장, 동대문시장, 광장시장, or 통인시장. Many small stores line alleyways and offer a variety of goods such as clothing, cosmetics, accessories, shoes, fabrics, foods, and agricultural products. Unlike department stores, where prices are fixed and there is no haggling, you can negotiate and bargain at an open-air market.

rows: a traditional market (the book’s 재래 시장)

Follow-up 1 is in the next lesson; Follow-up 2 (listening to four segments of a conversation between a mother and her daughter about grocery shopping, filling in the groceries and the quantities) is an audio activity.
