lessons.title: 246. Ch 18 · Grammar C: comparison of equals with ~만큼
lessons.subtitle: 중국은 미국만큼 커요 · 저 냉장고만큼 비싸요 · 안 비싸요 · 비싸지 않아요

explanations.title: Expressing comparison of equals
explanations.body:
In English, we use the grammar pattern as … as to compare two “objects” (persons, places, things or concepts) of similar or equal value, as in “China is as big as the U.S.” and “Tom eats as much as Brian (does)”. The second “object” is placed after as … as.

In Korean we use ~만큼 + verb to compare two objects of similar or equal value, and the object compared with is placed right before 만큼. Notice that in each sentence ~만큼 is followed by a verb: 미국만큼 is followed by the verb 커요, and 브라이언만큼 is followed by the verbal phrase 많이 먹어요.

examples.text: 중국은 미국만큼 커요.
examples.translation: junggugeun migungmankeum keoyo. — China is as big as the U.S.

examples.text: 톰은 브라이언만큼 많이 먹어요.
examples.translation: tomeun beuraieonmankeum mani meogeoyo. — Tom eats as much as Brian does.

explanations.title: The rule
explanations.body: noun + 만큼 + … verb.

examples.text: 이 냉장고는 저 냉장고만큼 비싸요.
examples.translation: i naengjanggoneun jeo naengjanggomankeum bissayo. — This refrigerator is as expensive as that refrigerator.

examples.text: 김 병장은 장 일병만큼 키가 커요.
examples.translation: gim byeongjangeun jang ilbyeongmankeum kiga keoyo. — SGT Kim is as tall as PFC Chang. (the book writes (키가), with the subject optional)

examples.text: 잔은 마이크만큼 한국말을 잘 해요.
examples.translation: janeun maikeumankeum hangungmareul jal haeyo. — John speaks Korean as fluently as Mike does.

explanations.title: Negation
explanations.body: We can negate these sentences by adding either 안 or -지 않다 to the verbs.

examples.text: 이 냉장고는 저 냉장고만큼 안 비싸요.
examples.translation: i naengjanggoneun jeo naengjanggomankeum an bissayo. — This refrigerator is not as expensive as that refrigerator.

examples.text: 이 냉장고는 저 냉장고만큼 비싸지 않아요.
examples.translation: i naengjanggoneun jeo naengjanggomankeum bissaji anayo. — This refrigerator is not as expensive as that refrigerator.

explanations.title: Forms (mine)
explanations.body: Nouns with 만큼 (no space; 만큼 is attached to the noun) and the negative forms of some stative verbs made by the book’s two ways.

explanations.title: Follow-up 1 (Reading and speaking)
explanations.body: Partners read a sentence aloud and the other makes a sentence of comparison by adding a noun followed by 만큼. The book’s model:

examples.text: 한국 음식이 맛있어요.
examples.translation: hanguk eumsigi masisseoyo. — Korean food is delicious. (A, the book’s model)

examples.text: 한국 음식이 멕시코 음식만큼 맛있어요.
examples.translation: hanguk eumsigi meksiko eumsingmankeum masisseoyo. — Korean food is as delicious as Mexican food. (B, the book’s model)

explanations.title: Activities left out
explanations.body: Follow-up 1 (partner sentence lists), Follow-up 2 (listening to four conversations in which a speaker compares two objects and writing the objects and the verb) and Follow-up 5 of the next grammar point (New Year’s resolutions) are audio, partner or class activities.

lessons.title: 247. Ch 18 · Grammar D: expressing a decision with -기로 하다
lessons.subtitle: 한국에 가기로 했어요 · 공부하기로 했어요 · 쉬기로 합시다 · 오늘부터 한국말만 하기로 했어요

explanations.title: Expressing a decision
explanations.body:
In English, when we express an intention or a decision that we (have) made, we say decided to or (have) decided to, followed by a verb in the infinitive form. To express this in Korean, we use -기로 했다 (the past tense form of -기로 하다).

When we want to show that both the speaker and the listener(s) must adhere to the agreed-upon decision, however, we use the present tense: 내일 여기서 모이기로 한다 (Our decision is to get together here tomorrow); 오 분만 쉬기로 합시다 (Let’s take a break for five minutes).

explanations.title: How to use this list
explanations.body:
The book’s Core Vocabulary lists the core words of the chapter with an example sentence for each (the sentences and the English meanings are the book’s; the book gives no English for the sentences). The Hanja of the Sino-Korean words are in parentheses before the meaning.

The example sentences with digits or Latin letters are respelled in Hangul (10만원 → 십만 원, 20% → 이십 퍼센트, 15,000원 → 만 오천 원, 500원 → 오백 원, 1년 → 일 년, 6층 → 육 층, 비타민 A → 비타민 에이, 10송이 → 열 송이, 5,000원 → 오천 원). The book’s (똑)같다, (무)이자, (진공)청소기, 야채/채소, 아주머니/아줌마 and 의류/~복 are shown with the forms written out (똑같다 / 같다, 무이자, 진공청소기, 야채 / 채소, 아주머니 / 아줌마, 의류 / ~복); the book’s 배 appears twice (pear here; the belly in Chapter 20). The book’s related words (the synonyms, antonyms and related words in the last column) are left out; the Additional Vocabulary section of the book is blank.

explanations.title: What Chapter 19 teaches (스포츠와 야외 활동)
explanations.body:
Chapter 19, “Sports and Outdoor Activities”, has three topic presentations, grammar in focus, activities, a self-evaluation and the core vocabulary.

When you finish the chapter you will be able to: talk about common sporting events in Korea; talk about general activities on a “weekend” farm as well as common farm animals; and talk about common “hobby” clubs and outdoor activities.

You will become familiar with: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; -(으)ㄴ 적이 있다 (to have past experience of having done something); -(으)ㄴ 적이 없다 (to have no past experience of having done something); incomplete sentences; ~에 대해(서) vs. ~에 대한 (about; regarding); ㅎ irregular verbs; and the Sino-Korean syllables 승 (勝), 패 (敗) and 농 (農).

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 승패 (勝敗)
explanations.body:
The first syllable 승 (勝) means victory or winning, as in 우승 (a victory; “excellent winning”) and 완승 (a huge victory; a complete victory), whereas the second syllable 패 (敗) means defeat or losing, as in 패배 (a defeat; a loss; “losing and running away”), 실패 (a failure) and 완패 (a crushing defeat; “complete defeat”). Thus the literal meaning of 승패 is “victory (and) defeat” or “winning or losing”. Depending on the context, the word can mean the result (of a battle, contest, match or game).

The book asks you to guess the meaning of 승자, 패자, 무승부, 패전, 승전 and 3승 2패, with the hints 자 (者): a person and 전 (戰): a war, fighting. The answers are mine.

explanations.title: Topic B: Thank you for visiting our weekend farm (저희 주말농장을 방문해 주셔서 감사합니다)
explanations.body: A visitor at a weekend farm is talking with the owner. (The English is mine; the book gives none. The book’s footnote says 뭘 is a contracted form of 무엇을.)

examples.text: 손님: 와! 농장이 아주 크네요!
examples.translation: sonnim: wa! nongjangi aju keuneyo! — Wow! The farm is very big!

examples.text: 농장주인: 네, 저희 농장에는 과수원하고 동물농장도 있습니다.
examples.translation: nongjangjuin: ne, jeohui nongjangeneun gwasuwonhago dongmullongjangdo itseumnida. — Yes, our farm has an orchard and an animal farm as well.

examples.text: 손님: 그럼 과수원에서 과일도 딸 수 있어요?
examples.translation: sonnim: geureom gwasuwoneseo gwaildo ttal su isseoyo? — Then can I pick fruit at the orchard, too?

examples.translation: nongjangjuin: mullonijo. geurigo ttan gwaireul jibe gajigo gal sudo isseoyo. — Of course. And you can take the fruit you picked home.

examples.text: 손님: 그래요? 또 뭘 할 수 있어요?
examples.translation: sonnim: geuraeyo? tto mwol hal su isseoyo? — Really? What else can I do?

examples.text: 농장주인: 밭에서 채소도 기를 수 있고 동물한테 먹이도 줄 수 있습니다.
examples.translation: nongjangjuin: bateseo chaesodo gireul su itgo dongmulhante meogido jul su itseumnida. — You can grow vegetables in the field and feed the animals, too.

examples.text: 손님: 여기에는 어떤 동물들이 있어요?
examples.translation: sonnim: yeogieneun eotteon dongmuldeuri isseoyo? — What kinds of animals are here?

examples.text: 농장주인: 저희 농장에는 토끼하고 오리, 닭, 양 등이 있습니다.
examples.translation: nongjangjuin: jeohui nongjangeneun tokkihago ori, dak, yang deungi itseumnida. — Our farm has rabbits, ducks, chickens, sheep and so on.

examples.text: 손님: 그래요? 그런데 저기 저분들은 뭐 하시는 거예요?
examples.translation: sonnim: geuraeyo? geureonde jeogi jeobundeureun mwo hasineun geoyeyo? — Really? By the way, what are those people over there doing?

examples.text: 농장주인: 네, 지금 사과 나무를 심고 있습니다.
examples.translation: nongjangjuin: ne, jigeum sagwa namureul simgo itseumnida. — Yes, they are planting apple trees now.

examples.text: 손님: 여기서 과일 나무도 기를 수 있어요?
examples.translation: sonnim: yeogiseo gwail namudo gireul su isseoyo? — Can I grow fruit trees here, too?

examples.text: 농장주인: 그럼요. 저희 주말농장에서는 다양한 체험을 해 볼 수 있습니다.
examples.translation: nongjangjuin: geureomyo. jeohui jumallongjangeseoneun dayanghan cheheomeul hae bol su itseumnida. — Of course. At our weekend farm you can try various hands-on experiences.

examples.text: 손님: 저는 시골 생활을 해 본 적이 없는데 참 재미있을 것 같아요.
examples.translation: sonnim: jeoneun sigol saenghwareul hae bon jeogi eomneunde cham jaemiisseul geot gatayo. — I have never lived in the countryside, but it seems like it would be really fun.

examples.text: 농장주인: 네. 더 구경해 보세요. 그리고 질문이 있으시면 언제든지 또 하세요.
examples.translation: nongjangjuin: ne. deo gugyeonghae boseyo. geurigo jilmuni isseusimyeon eonjedeunji tto haseyo. — Yes. Please look around more. And if you have a question, ask anytime.

explanations.title: Cultural note: 주말농장 (“Weekend” Farm)
explanations.body: 주말농장 is a farm designed for city dwellers who want to experience country life with their families on weekends. Weekend farms started around 2002 when the Korean government encouraged businesses to implement a five-day work week instead of a six-day work week. Since then, the weekend farm business has grown quickly around metropolitan areas. Many families take advantage of the farms for family activities as well as for growing healthful, organic products.

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 농 (農)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means agricultural or farming, as in 농업 (agriculture; “agricultural business”), 농지 (a farmland) and 농부 (a farmer; “farming man”). Since Korea used to be an agricultural society, many words including the same syllable are used to describe rural communities and farming businesses. The book asks you to guess the meaning of 농장, 주말 농장, 농기계 and 농산물, with the hint 산물 (産物): a product, produce. The answers are mine.

lessons.title: 254. Ch 19 · Grammar A: expressing a past experience with -(으)ㄴ 적이 있다 / 없다
lessons.subtitle: 하와이에 간 적이 있어요 · 먹은 적이 없어요 · 먹어 본 적이 있어요 · -(으)ㄴ 일이 있다

explanations.title: Expressing a past experience or event
explanations.body: In English, “Have you ever eaten kimchi before?” and “I have eaten kimchi once” are typical ways to ask about or state previous experiences. In Korean, we use the expression -(으)ㄴ 적이 있다. Because 적 in -(으)ㄴ 적이 있다 means a (past) experience or time, the whole expression literally means “a past experience of having done (something) exists”.

examples.text: 하와이에 간 적이 있어요.
examples.translation: hawaie gan jeogi isseoyo. — I have been to Hawaii.

examples.text: 하와이에 간 적이 없어요.
examples.translation: hawaie gan jeogi eopseoyo. — I have not been to Hawaii.

examples.text: 발레 공연을 관람한 적이 있어요?
examples.translation: balle gongyeoneul gwallamhan jeogi isseoyo? — Have you ever watched a ballet performance?

examples.text: 한국에 간 적이 있어요.
examples.translation: hanguge gan jeogi isseoyo. — I have been to Korea (before).

examples.text: 김치를 먹은 적이 있습니까?
examples.translation: gimchireul meogeun jeogi itseumnikka? — Have you ever eaten kimchi before? (the book’s opening question)

examples.text: 김치를 한 번 먹은 적이 있습니다.
examples.translation: gimchireul han beon meogeun jeogi itseumnida. — I have eaten kimchi once. (the book’s opening answer)

explanations.title: The rule
explanations.body: verb stem + (으)ㄴ 적이 있다 / 없다.

rows: When a verb stem ends in a consonant
심다 → 심은 적이 있다; 먹다 → 먹은 적이 없다
When a verb stem ends in a vowel
가다 → 간 적이 있다; 보다 → 본 적이 없다

explanations.title: Also -(으)ㄴ 일이 있다 / 없다, and -아/어 본 적이 있다 / 없다
explanations.body: We can also use -(으)ㄴ 일이 있다 / 없다 to express past experiences. -(으)ㄴ 적이 있다 / 없다 is commonly used in conjunction with -아/어 보다. You learned in Chapter 8 that -아/어 보다 is used to express experimentation or experience, as in 한국 음식 먹어 봤어요 (I tried eating Korean food). Therefore, the pattern -아/어 본 적이 있다 / 없다 adds the meaning of having tried something in the past.

examples.text: 발레 공연을 본 일이 있어요?
examples.translation: balle gongyeoneul bon iri isseoyo? — Have you ever watched a ballet performance?

examples.text: 한국에 간 일이 있어요.
examples.translation: hanguge gan iri isseoyo. — I have been to Korea (before).

examples.text: 김치를 먹어 본 적이 있어요.
examples.translation: gimchireul meogeo bon jeogi isseoyo. — I have tried eating kimchi.

examples.text: 스키를 타 본 적이 없어요.
examples.translation: seukireul ta bon jeogi eopseoyo. — I have not tried skiing.

explanations.title: Forms (mine)
explanations.body: The forms are made by the book’s rule (ㄹ-ending verbs lose ㄹ: 살다 → 산, 만들다 → 만든; 기르다 and 듣다 are irregular: 기른 / 길러 본, 들은 / 들어 본).

explanations.title: Follow-up 1 and 5: phrases and questions
explanations.body: In Follow-up 1 partners read a phrase card and conjugate it with -(으)ㄴ 적이 있다 / 없다 and -아/어 본 적이 있다 / 없다 (the book’s model: 한국어를 배우다 → 한국어를 배운 적이 있어요 / 없어요; 한국어를 배워 본 적이 있어요 / 없어요). In Follow-up 5 (스키를 타 본 적이 있어요?) students ask each other about the activities below (the book’s list); the models are 체조를 배운 적이 있어요? / 네, 배운 적이 있어요. / 아니요, 배운 적이 없어요. Sentences for the list (mine):

examples.translation: chejoreul baeun jeogi isseoyo? — Have you ever learned gymnastics? (the book’s model; English mine)

examples.text: 네, 배운 적이 있어요.
examples.translation: ne, baeun jeogi isseoyo. — Yes, I have learned it. (the book’s model; English mine)

examples.text: 아니요, 배운 적이 없어요.
examples.translation: aniyo, baeun jeogi eopseoyo. — No, I have not learned it. (the book’s model; English mine)

explanations.title: Activities left out
explanations.body: Follow-up 2 (listening to three dialogs in which a man asks a friend if she has ever experienced something) is an audio activity; Follow-up 1 (partner phrase cards) and Follow-up 5 (interviewing two classmates, marking O or X, writing a paragraph about one interviewee and posting it; the book’s model paragraph: 김영수 일병의 경험 — 김 일병은 한국 음식을 먹어 본 적이 있습니다. 하지만 한국에는 가 본 적이 없습니다) are partner and class activities.

lessons.title: 255. Ch 19 · Grammar B: ㅎ irregular verbs
lessons.subtitle: 빨갛다 → 빨개요 · 빨간 사과 · 하얗다 → 하얘요 · 이렇다 · 그렇다 · 어떻다 · 좋다 · 많다

explanations.title: ㅎ irregular verbs
explanations.body:
You have already learned quite a few stative verbs whose stems end in ㅎ: 빨갛다 (to be red), 노랗다 (to be yellow), 파랗다 (to be blue), 하얗다 (to be white), 까맣다 (to be black), 이렇다 (to be like this), 그렇다 (to be like it), 저렇다 (to be like that) and 어떻다 (to be like what/how).

These stative verbs are commonly known as “ㅎ irregular verbs” because they go through an extra step in their conjugation. When the stem is followed by a vowel or a consonant like ㄴ and ㄹ, the stem loses ㅎ, as if it were not part of the stem. For example, when 빨갛다 is conjugated into -아/어요 (informal style) or ㄴ (an attributive form), its stem 빨갛 loses ㅎ. It then goes through the normal conjugation: 빨갛 + 아요 → 빨가 + 아요 → 빨개요; 빨갛 + ㄴ → 빨가 + ㄴ → 빨간 (빨간 사과, a red apple).

examples.translation: sagwaneun ppalgaeyo. — An apple is red.

examples.text: 빨간 사과
examples.translation: ppalgan sagwa — a red apple; an apple which is red

examples.translation: jeo bada jom boseyo. aju paraeyo. — Look at the sea. It is very blue.

explanations.title: The exceptions
explanations.body: There are, of course, some exceptions. Even though their stems end in ㅎ, the following verbs do not lose ㅎ during the conjugation process: 좋다, 놓다 (to put; to place), 많다, 괜찮다 (to be okay / to be decent), 넣다, 낳다 (to give birth) and 싫다.

explanations.body: The book gives a table with the verb stem, -(으)ㄴ, -아/어요 and -게, and asks you to conjugate (the book gives 하얘요 and 하얗게 for 하얗다, 노란, 파래요, 이런, 그렇게, 어떤, 많게 and 좋아요; the rest are my answers). The book’s footnote: 하얗다 becomes 하얘요 because ㅑ + ㅓ is contracted to ㅒ.

lessons.title: 257. Ch 19 · Grammar C: two ways to say “about”, ~에 대해(서) and ~에 대한
lessons.subtitle: 한국에 대해서 말해 주세요 · 한국에 대한 이야기 · 대하여 · 대해서 · 대한

explanations.title: Two ways to express “about” or “regarding”
explanations.body: The postpositional phrase ~에 대해(서), ~에 대하여(서) or ~에 대한 is equivalent to the English prepositional phrase about ~, regarding ~, concerning ~, with regard to ~, of ~, on ~, etc. Thus 한국에 대해서, 한국에 대하여서 and 한국에 대한 can be translated as about Korea or regarding Korea. However, ~에 대해(서) / 대하여(서) is designated to modify verbs only, whereas ~에 대한 is designated to modify nouns only.

examples.text: 한국에 대해서 말해 주세요.
examples.translation: hanguge daehaeseo malhae juseyo. — Please tell us about Korea.

examples.text: 한국에 대한 이야기가 재미있어요.
examples.translation: hanguge daehan iyagiga jaemiisseoyo. — The story about Korea is interesting.

explanations.title: Why they differ
explanations.body: Note that ~에 대해서 in the first sentence modifies the verb 말해 주세요, whereas ~에 대한 in the second sentence modifies the noun 이야기 that immediately follows. The postpositional phrases ~에 대해(서), ~에 대하여(서) and ~에 대한 originate from the verb 대하다 (just the way the English prepositions concerning and regarding originate from the verbs concern and regard). 대해(서) or 대하여(서) is made up of the stem of the verb 대하다 and the conjunctive ending -아/어서, which has to be followed by a verb or sentence. On the other hand, 대한 is made up of the same stem of the verb 대하다 and the attributive form ㄴ, which has to be followed by a noun.

explanations.title: The rule
explanations.body: ~에 대해(서) / 대하여(서) … + verb; ~에 대한 + noun.

lessons.title: 258. Ch 19 · Grammar D: incomplete sentences and the polite 요

explanations.title: Expressing incomplete sentences
explanations.body: In casual and spontaneous conversations we frequently speak in incomplete sentences or phrases. The book gives an English exchange in which only one of the eight utterances is a complete sentence (A: Where did you say you went over the weekend? B: San Jose. A: By yourself? B: With my ex. A: You mean Sandra? B: Yup. A: Why? B: Because she wanted to.). This phenomenon is universal. In Korean, however, we add 요 to an incomplete sentence when we need to show respect to the person to whom we are speaking. Otherwise, we use the incomplete sentence without 요. (The book writes 어제 어디에서 공부했어(요)? with an optional 요.)

explanations.title: The note on 이요 and the topic marker 은/는(요)
explanations.body: The book’s footnote: 이요 is used when the preceding word is a noun that ends in a consonant (한국말이요). The topic marker 은/는(요), as in 점심은요? or 도서관에서는요?, is equivalent to “What about …?” or “How about …?” in English.

explanations.title: How to use this list
explanations.body:
The book’s Core Vocabulary lists the core words of the chapter with an example sentence for each (the sentences and the English meanings are the book’s; the book gives no English for the sentences). The Hanja of the Sino-Korean words are in parentheses before the meaning.

The example sentences with digits or Latin letters are respelled in Hangul (TV → 티브이, 100 m → 백 미터, 8대 4 → 팔 대 사, 5대 5 → 오 대 오, 10개국 → 열 개국, 3승 2패 → 삼 승 이 패). The book’s 권투 and 복싱 are listed separately here; the book’s 따다 has two example sentences (one for each meaning; both are kept, joined by a slash). explanations.title: Self-evaluation
explanations.body:
Recall the objectives of the chapter and ask yourself whether you have achieved them (the book asks you to tick Yes or No). If you tick “No” for any item, the book suggests: review that section on your own; find a study partner and review it as a pair or group; and tell your academic advisor or team leader which areas you need more help with, so that they can provide activities tailored to your learning style and needs.

Now I am able to: talk about common sporting events in Korea; talk about general activities on a “weekend” farm as well as common farm animals; and talk about common “hobby” clubs and outdoor activities.

Now I have a clear understanding of: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; -(으)ㄴ 적이 있다; -(으)ㄴ 적이 없다; incomplete sentences; ~에 대해(서) vs. ~에 대한 (about; regarding); ㅎ irregular verbs; and the Sino-Korean syllables 승 (勝), 패 (敗) and 농 (農).

lessons.subtitle: 우리 몸과 건강 · 약 (藥) · 약국 · 약사 · 감기약 · 치약 · 한약 · 농약

explanations.title: What Chapter 20 teaches (우리 몸과 건강)
explanations.body:
Chapter 20, “Body and Health”, has three topic presentations, grammar in focus, activities, a self-evaluation and the core vocabulary.

When you finish the chapter you will be able to: describe a person’s physical appearance using the names for parts of the body; describe physical discomfort and the symptoms of common illnesses; ask for basic services at a drug store; describe the causes and symptoms of common injuries; and ask for basic medical services at a doctor’s office and hospital.

You will become familiar with: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; the conjunctive ending -는 동안(에) (while; during); the conjunctive ending -자마자 (as soon as; right after); the conjunctive ending -다가 (while; in the middle of); -(으)ㄹ 뻔하다, which is used to express near misses or close calls; and the Sino-Korean syllable 약 (藥).

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 약 (藥)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means medicine or drug, as in 약국 / 약방 (a pharmacy; a drugstore; “medicine bureau / room”), 마약 (illegal drug), 한약 (Korean traditional herbal medicine; “Korean medicine”) and 양약 (Western medicine; “medicine from the ocean”). The book asks you to guess the meaning of 약사, 감기약, 치약, 한약방 and 농약, with the hint 치 (齒): tooth. The answers are mine.

explanations.title: Topic B: Take this cold medicine three times a day (이 감기약을 하루에 세 번 드세요)
explanations.body: Youngho is consulting with a pharmacist at a drugstore. (The English is mine; the book gives none. The book writes 30분; it is spelled out here. The book’s title says 이 감기약을, while the pharmacist in the dialog says 이 약을; I keep both as in the book.)

examples.text: 약사: 어떻게 오셨어요?
examples.translation: yaksa: eotteoke osyeosseoyo? — What brings you here?

examples.text: 영호: 어제부터 목이 아프고 열이 나요.
examples.translation: yeongho: eojebuteo mogi apeugo yeori nayo. — Since yesterday I have a sore throat and a fever.

examples.text: 약사: 다른 증상은 없으세요?
examples.translation: yaksa: dareun jeungsangeun eopseuseyo? — Do you have any other symptoms?

examples.text: 영호: 음, 기침도 하고 콧물도 조금 나요.
examples.translation: yeongho: eum, gichimdo hago konmuldo jogeum nayo. — Um, I cough and have a little runny nose, too.

examples.text: 약사: 요즘 유행하는 감기에 걸리셨네요!
examples.translation: yaksa: yojeum yuhaenghaneun gamgie geollisyeonneyo! — You have caught the cold that is going around these days!

examples.text: 영호: 그런 것 같아요. 약 좀 주세요.

examples.text: 약사: 네, 여기 있어요. 이 약을 하루에 세 번, 두 알씩 드세요.
examples.translation: yaksa: ne, yeogi isseoyo. i yageul harue se beon, du alssik deuseyo. — Yes, here you are. Take this medicine three times a day, two tablets at a time.

examples.text: 영호: 식전에요? 식후에요?
examples.translation: yeongho: sikjeoneyo? sikueyo? — Before meals? After meals?

examples.text: 약사: 식후 삼십 분 후에 드세요. 약을 복용하는 동안에는 술과 담배를 피하셔야 합니다.
examples.translation: yaksa: siku samsip bun hue deuseyo. yageul bogyonghaneun donganeneun sulgwa dambaereul pihasyeoya hamnida. — Take it 30 minutes after meals. While you are taking the medicine, you have to avoid alcohol and cigarettes.

examples.text: 영호: 네. 그리고 소화제도 좀 주세요.
examples.translation: yeongho: ne. geurigo sohwajedo jom juseyo. — Yes. And please give me some digestive medicine, too.

examples.text: 약사: 배탈도 나셨군요!
examples.translation: yaksa: baetaldo nasyeotgunyo! — You have an upset stomach, too!

examples.text: 영호: 네. 오늘 아침에 토하고 설사도 했어요.
examples.translation: yeongho: ne. oneul achime tohago seolsado haesseoyo. — Yes. This morning I vomited and had diarrhea, too.

examples.text: 약사: 그럼, 이 약을 드세요.
examples.translation: yaksa: geureom, i yageul deuseyo. — Then take this medicine.

examples.text: 영호: 감기약하고 같이 먹어도 돼요?
examples.translation: yeongho: gamgiyakago gachi meogeodo dwaeyo? — May I take it together with the cold medicine?

examples.text: 약사: 아니요. 이 약은 아침에 일어나자마자 드셔야 합니다. 이틀 정도 복용하시면 나으실 거예요.
examples.translation: yaksa: aniyo. i yageun achime ireonajamaja deusyeoya hamnida. iteul jeongdo bogyonghasimyeon naeusil geoyeyo. — No. You must take this medicine as soon as you get up in the morning. If you take it for about two days, you will get better.

explanations.body: The meanings are the book’s (from the Core Vocabulary of the chapter); optional parts are shortened. The book shows pictures of 해열제, 진통제, 감기약 and 소화제; the pictures are left out.

explanations.title: Presentation Activity d: the symptoms and the medicines (mine)

rows: Sore throat, fever, cough, a little runny nose, upset stomach, vomiting, diarrhea

Cold medicine: three times a day, two tablets each, 30 minutes after meals; avoid alcohol and cigarettes while taking it. Digestive medicine: take it as soon as you get up in the morning (not together with the cold medicine); about two days of taking it should cure it.

lessons.title: 266. Ch 20 · Grammar A: “while” and “during” with -는 동안(에) and ~ 동안(에)
lessons.subtitle: 한국에 있는 동안 · 이틀 동안 · 점심 시간 동안 · 여름 방학 동안 · 약을 복용하는 동안

explanations.title: Expressing “while” or “during”
explanations.body:
In English, we use the conjunction while or the preposition during to express an action or event that takes place simultaneously with another action or event: “I will learn Korean while (I stay) in Korea” and “I will learn Korean during my stay in Korea”. In Korean, we express simultaneous actions or events by using the conjunctive ending -는 동안(에).

동안 literally means an interval or a space of time. Thus the literal translation of -는 동안에 is “for an interval when” or “in the space of time when”. ~ 동안(에) also can be preceded by a noun that denotes time, as in 점심 시간 동안(에) (during the lunch hour) and 두 시간 동안 (for two hours); in this case ~ 동안(에) can be translated as during or for.

examples.text: 한국에 있는 동안에 한국말을 배우겠습니다.
examples.translation: hanguge inneun dongane hangungmareul baeugetseumnida. — I will learn Korean while (I am) in Korea.

examples.text: 친구가 운동하는 동안에 나는 공부합니다.
examples.translation: chinguga undonghaneun dongane naneun gongbuhamnida. — I study while my friend works out.

examples.text: 점심 시간 동안
examples.translation: jeomsim sigan dongan — during the lunch hour

examples.text: 두 시간 동안
examples.translation: du sigan dongan — for two hours

explanations.title: The 에
explanations.body: The time marker 에 in -는 동안에 or ~ 동안에 is optional. However, 에 has to be deleted if 동안에 is preceded by a noun that shows a time length, as in 30초 동안 (for 30 seconds), 5분 동안 (for 5 minutes), 한 시간 동안 (for 1 hour) and 이틀 동안 (for 2 days). (The book writes the digits; they are spelled out here.)

examples.text: 삼십 초 동안
examples.translation: samsip cho dongan — for 30 seconds

examples.text: 오 분 동안
examples.translation: o bun dongan — for 5 minutes

examples.text: 한 시간 동안
examples.translation: han sigan dongan — for 1 hour

examples.text: 이틀 동안
examples.translation: iteul dongan — for 2 days

explanations.title: The rule
explanations.body: action verb stem + 는 동안(에); noun + 동안(에).

rows: 공부하다 → 공부하는 동안(에); 기다리다 → 기다리는 동안(에)
연휴 → 연휴 동안(에); 수업 → 수업 동안(에); 이틀 → 이틀 동안

examples.text: 기다리시는 동안에 이 잡지 좀 보세요.
examples.translation: gidarisineun dongane i japji jom boseyo. — While waiting, please read this magazine.

examples.text: 한국에 있는 동안에 많은 것을 배웠어요.
examples.translation: hanguge inneun dongane maneun geoseul baewosseoyo. — While I was in Korea, I learned many things.

examples.text: 여름 방학 동안에 유럽에 갈 거예요.
examples.translation: yeoreum banghak dongane yureobe gal geoyeyo. — During summer vacation, I am going to Europe.

examples.text: 이 약을 이틀 동안 복용하세요.
examples.translation: i yageul iteul dongan bogyonghaseyo. — Please take this medicine for two days.

explanations.title: Forms (mine)
explanations.body: The forms are made by the book’s rule (verbs with an ㄹ-ending stem lose ㄹ before 는: 살다 → 사는, 만들다 → 만드는).

explanations.title: Follow-up 1: nouns and verbs
explanations.body: Partners pick a noun with 동안(에) and make a sentence (the book’s models below). Lists: List A: 연휴, 일주일, 사흘, 수업시간, 한 시간, 겨울방학; List B: 여름방학, 삼십 분, 주말, 한 달, 점심시간, 일 년 육 개월. In Step b, partners combine a verb of List A with a verb of List B with -는 동안(에). List A verbs: 요리하다, 공부하다, 잠을 자다, 신문을 보다, 컴퓨터 게임을 하다. List B verbs: 청소하다, 음악을 듣다, 영화를 보다, 뉴스를 듣다, 숙제를 하다. (The book writes 30분 and 1년 6개월; they are spelled out here.)

examples.text: 이십 분 동안 책을 읽었습니다.
examples.translation: isip bun dongan chaegeul ilgeotseumnida. — I read a book for 20 minutes. (the book’s model)

examples.text: 방학 동안 고향에 다녀왔습니다.
examples.translation: banghak dongan gohyange danyeowatseumnida. — During the school break I went to my hometown and came back. (the book’s model)

examples.text: 제가 책을 읽는 동안에 김 일병은 설거지를 합니다.
examples.translation: jega chaegeul ingneun dongane gim ilbyeongeun seolgeojireul hamnida. — While I read a book, PFC Kim does the dishes. (the book’s model)

explanations.title: Follow-up 2 (Reading): an e-mail from an older sister
explanations.body: The book gives an e-mail from a woman to her younger brother who lives in a college dormitory and asks you to identify five sentences that contain ~ 동안(에) or -는 동안(에), underline and number them (the first one is done for you) and translate the phrases into English. The e-mail is the book’s (the address is left out); the English is mine.

examples.text: 성수야, 잘 지내?
examples.translation: seongsuya, jal jinae? — Seongsu, are you doing well?

examples.text: 시험 공부하는 동안에 밥은 잘 먹고 있어?
examples.translation: siheom gongbuhaneun dongane babeun jal meokgo isseo? — Are you eating well while studying for your tests?

examples.translation: nunaneun iljuil dongan gamgiro apasseo. — I (your older sister) was sick with a cold for a week.

examples.text: 목도 아프고 기침도 많이 하고 그랬어.
examples.translation: mokdo apeugo gichimdo mani hago geuraesseo. — My throat hurt and I coughed a lot, and so on. (the book ends the line with an ellipsis; the wording here is mine)

examples.text: 이번 감기가 쉽게 낫지 않는 것 같아.
examples.translation: ibeon gamgiga swipge natji anneun geot gata. — It seems this cold doesn’t get better easily.

examples.text: 이번 겨울 동안 다시 감기에 걸리지 않으려면 매일 운동을 해.
examples.translation: ibeon gyeoul dongan dasi gamgie geolliji aneuryeomyeon maeil undongeul hae. — To not catch a cold again this winter, exercise every day.

examples.text: 누나도 매일 한 시간 동안 수영을 할 거야.
examples.translation: nunado maeil han sigan dongan suyeongeul hal geoya. — I am also going to swim for an hour every day.

examples.text: 다음 달이 겨울방학이니까 집에 오지?
examples.translation: daeum dari gyeoulbanghaginikka jibe oji? — Next month is the winter vacation, so you are coming home, right?

examples.text: 네가 집에 와 있는 동안 누나가 맛있는 음식을 많이 만들어 줄게.

examples.translation: bogo sipda. — I miss you.

lessons.title: 267. Ch 20 · Grammar B: “as soon as” and “right after” with -자마자
lessons.subtitle: 일어나자마자 · 도착하자마자 · 수업이 끝나자마자 · 새 핸드폰이 나오자마자

explanations.title: Expressing “as soon as” or “right after”
explanations.body: In English, we use phrases like as soon as, right after or immediately after to express an action immediately following another, as in “As soon as I am up, I take a shower” or “I take a shower right after I get up”. In Korean, we use the conjunctive ending -자마자 to express this, as in 일어나자마자 (as soon as I get up) or 샤워하자마자 (right after taking a shower).

examples.text: 아침에 일어나자마자 샤워합니다.
examples.translation: achime ireonajamaja syawohamnida. — As soon as I get up in the morning, I take a shower.

examples.text: 수업이 끝나자마자 체육관에 갔습니다.
examples.translation: sueobi kkeunnajamaja cheyukgwane gatseumnida. — Right after class (ended), I went to the gym.

explanations.title: The rule
explanations.body: action verb stem + 자마자.

examples.text: 집에 도착하자마자 비가 왔어요.
examples.translation: jibe dochakajamaja biga wasseoyo. — As soon as I arrived at home, it rained.

examples.text: 새 핸드폰이 나오자마자 샀어요.
examples.translation: sae haendeuponi naojamaja sasseoyo. — As soon as the new cell phone came out (on the market), I bought it.

explanations.title: Forms (mine)
explanations.body: The forms are made by the book’s rule.

explanations.title: Follow-up 3: the chain game, and Follow-up 5: the daily routine
explanations.body: In Follow-up 3 the class sits in a circle; each student repeats the previous student’s activity with -자마자 and adds another action. The book’s model:

examples.text: 아침에 일어납니다.
examples.translation: achime ireonamnida. — I get up in the morning. (A, the book’s model)

examples.text: 일어나자마자 아침을 먹습니다.
examples.translation: ireonajamaja achimeul meokseumnida. — As soon as I get up, I eat breakfast. (B)

examples.text: 아침을 먹자마자 학교에 갑니다.
examples.translation: achimeul meokjamaja hakgyoe gamnida. — As soon as I eat breakfast, I go to school. (C)

examples.text: 학교에 가자마자 문을 엽니다.
examples.translation: hakgyoe gajamaja muneul yeomnida. — As soon as I go to school, I open the door. (D)

explanations.title: Follow-up 5: -는 동안 and -자마자 together
explanations.body: Partners ask what the other does during the time periods (연휴, 점심시간, 방학, 주말) with ~ 동안 and what he or she does right after, with -자마자. The book’s models:

examples.text: 점심시간 동안에 뭐 해요?
examples.translation: jeomsimsigan dongane mwo haeyo? — What do you do during lunchtime? (the book’s model)

examples.text: 점심시간 동안에 밥을 먹어요.
examples.translation: jeomsimsigan dongane babeul meogeoyo. — During lunchtime I eat. (the book’s model)

examples.text: 밥 먹고 뭐 해요?
examples.translation: bap meokgo mwo haeyo? — What do you do after eating? (the book’s model)

examples.text: 밥 먹자마자 이를 닦아요.
examples.translation: bap meokjamaja ireul dakkayo. — As soon as I eat, I brush my teeth. (the book’s model)

examples.text: 김 일병은 점심시간 동안에 밥을 먹어요. 그리고 밥을 먹자마자 이를 닦아요.
examples.translation: gim ilbyeongeun jeomsimsigan dongane babeul meogeoyo. geurigo babeul meokjamaja ireul dakkayo. — PFC Kim eats during lunchtime. And as soon as he eats, he brushes his teeth. (the book’s model for reporting)

explanations.title: Activities left out
explanations.body: Follow-up 3 (a class chain game), Follow-up 4 (listening to three dialogs and writing the two actions of the -자마자 sentence in English) and Follow-up 5 (partner and class work, tables of two actions) are class, audio or partner activities.

explanations.title: Topic C: I fell while going down the stairs (계단을 내려가다가 넘어졌어요)
explanations.body: Woojin is seeing a doctor at a clinic for his physical discomfort. (The English is mine; the book gives none. The book writes 한 2주, 3, 4일간 and 2주 후에; they are spelled out here. The book’s title says 넘어졌어요, while in the dialog Woojin says 넘어질 뻔했어요; I keep both as in the book. The book marks the doctor’s next lines as “(later)”.)

examples.text: 의사: 어디가 불편하세요?
examples.translation: uisa: eodiga bulpyeonhaseyo? — Where does it bother you?

examples.text: 우진: 어제 아침에 지하철 계단을 내려가다가 넘어질 뻔했어요. 그때 발을 다친 것 같아요.
examples.translation: ujin: eoje achime jihacheol gyedaneul naeryeogadaga neomeojil ppeonhaesseoyo. geuttae bareul dachin geot gatayo. — Yesterday morning I almost fell while going down the subway stairs. I think I hurt my foot then.

examples.text: 의사: 발이 부었군요! 많이 아프세요?
examples.translation: uisa: bari bueotgunyo! mani apeuseyo? — Your foot is swollen! Does it hurt a lot?

examples.text: 우진: 네, 너무 아파서 걷기가 힘들어요.
examples.translation: ujin: ne, neomu apaseo geotgiga himdeureoyo. — Yes, it hurts so much that walking is hard.

examples.text: 의사: 먼저 발목 엑스레이를 찍어 봅시다. 다행히 뼈는 부러지지 않았습니다. 발목을 심하게 삐었습니다.
examples.translation: uisa: meonjeo balmok ekseureireul jjigeo bopsida. dahaenghi ppyeoneun bureojiji anatseumnida. balmogeul simhage ppieotseumnida. — First let’s take an x-ray of the ankle. Fortunately the bone is not broken. You sprained your ankle badly. (the book marks a pause, “later”, after the first sentence)

examples.text: 우진: 깁스를 해야 합니까?
examples.translation: ujin: gipseureul haeya hamnikka? — Do I have to wear a cast?

examples.text: 의사: 네. 한 이 주 정도 하는 것이 좋겠습니다.
examples.translation: uisa: ne. han i ju jeongdo haneun geosi joketseumnida. — Yes. It would be good to wear it for about two weeks.

examples.text: 우진: 외출할 때는 어떻게 해야 합니까?
examples.translation: ujin: oechulhal ttaeneun eotteoke haeya hamnikka? — What should I do when I go out?

examples.text: 의사: 목발을 쓰시면 됩니다.
examples.translation: uisa: mokbareul sseusimyeon doemnida. — You can use crutches.

examples.text: 우진: 통증은 어떻게 해요? 어제는 아파서 잠도 못 잤어요.
examples.translation: ujin: tongjeungeun eotteoke haeyo? eojeneun apaseo jamdo mot jasseoyo. — What about the pain? Yesterday it hurt so much that I couldn’t even sleep.

examples.text: 의사: 진통제를 처방해 드리겠습니다. 삼사 일간 드시면 괜찮아질 겁니다.
examples.translation: uisa: jintongjereul cheobanghae deurigetseumnida. samsa ilgan deusimyeon gwaenchanajil geomnida. — I will prescribe a painkiller. If you take it for three or four days, you will be fine.

examples.text: 우진: 알겠습니다. 언제 병원에 다시 올까요?
examples.translation: ujin: algetseumnida. eonje byeongwone dasi olkkayo? — I understand. When should I come to the hospital again?

examples.text: 의사: 이 주 후에 깁스 풀러 오세요.
examples.translation: uisa: i ju hue gipseu pulleo oseyo. — Come in two weeks to take the cast off.

lessons.title: 270. Ch 20 · Grammar C: “switching gears” with -다(가)
lessons.subtitle: 저녁을 먹다가 전화를 받았어요 · 스키를 타다가 다쳤습니다 · 갔다가 · 읽다가 잤어요

explanations.title: The conjunctive ending -다(가) expressing “switching gears” or changing direction
explanations.body:
The conjunctive ending -다(가), which is usually translated as while or in the middle of, is used to express “switching gears” or “changing direction”. It is used to express the idea that the first action in progress switches to the second action without the first being completed.

The first sentence implies the speaker was eating, which he stopped doing to answer the phone call. The second sentence implies the speaker was skiing and got hurt in the process. The third sentence implies the speaker was going down the road before he came to the intersection, where he turned left.

examples.text: 저녁을 먹다가 전화를 받았어요.
examples.translation: jeonyeogeul meokdaga jeonhwareul badasseoyo. — While eating dinner, I got a phone call.

examples.text: 스키를 타다가 다쳤습니다.
examples.translation: seukireul tadaga dacheotseumnida. — While skiing, I got hurt.

examples.text: 가다가 사거리에서 왼쪽으로 돌았어요.
examples.translation: gadaga sageorieseo oenjjogeuro dorasseoyo. — While going (down the road), I turned left at the intersection.

explanations.title: The rule
explanations.body: verb stem + 다(가).

rows: When a verb is an action verb
샤워를 하다 → 샤워를 하다(가); 비가 오다 → 비가 오다(가)

examples.text: 음악을 듣다가 잠이 들었어요.

examples.text: 운전을 하다가 사고를 냈어요.

examples.text: 학교에 가다가 친구를 만났어요.
examples.translation: hakgyoe gadaga chingureul mannasseoyo. — On the way to school, I bumped into a friend.

explanations.title: Note: 았/었 before -다가
explanations.body: There are a few occasions when 았/었 is inserted before the conjunctive ending -다가 (e.g. 갔다가 or 왔다가). In these cases the conjunctive ending indicates that the second action takes place after the first action has been completed. Compare 학교에 가다(가) 친구를 만났어요 (On the way to school, I ran into a friend) and 학교에 갔다(가) 친구를 만났어요 (I went to school, and (there) I ran into a friend).

lessons.title: 271. Ch 20 · Grammar D: near misses with -(으)ㄹ 뻔하다
lessons.subtitle: 넘어질 뻔했어요 · 늦을 뻔했어 · 크게 다칠 뻔했어요 · 앞차와 부딪칠 뻔했어요

explanations.title: Expressing near misses or close calls
explanations.body: In English, we often use adverbs such as nearly, almost and barely to indicate a close call, as in “The car almost ran over my foot” or “I almost failed the test”. In Korean, we convey this meaning by using -(으)ㄹ 뻔하다, as in 앞차와 부딪칠 뻔했어요 (I almost hit the car in front of me).

examples.text: 앞차와 부딪칠 뻔했어요.
examples.translation: apchawa buditchil ppeonhaesseoyo. — I almost hit the car in front of me.

explanations.title: The rule
explanations.body: action verb stem + (으)ㄹ 뻔하다.

rows: When an action verb stem ends in a vowel
넘어지다 → 넘어질 뻔하다; 경기에 지다 → 경기에 질 뻔하다
When an action verb stem ends in a consonant
잃다 → 잃을 뻔하다; 먹다 → 먹을 뻔하다

examples.text: 아침에 늦게 일어나서 학교에 늦을 뻔했어.
examples.translation: achime neutge ireonaseo hakgyoe neujeul ppeonhaesseo. — I got up late, so I was almost late for school.

examples.text: 어제 교통사고가 나서 크게 다칠 뻔했어요.
examples.translation: eoje gyotongsagoga naseo keuge dachil ppeonhaesseoyo. — A car accident occurred yesterday, and I was almost seriously hurt.

examples.text: 영화를 보다가 울 뻔했어요.
examples.translation: yeonghwareul bodaga ul ppeonhaesseoyo. — While watching a movie, I almost wept. (the book’s translation says TV)

explanations.title: Forms (mine)
explanations.body: The forms are made by the book’s rule (verbs with an ㄹ-ending stem keep a single ㄹ: 울다 → 울 뻔하다).

explanations.title: Follow-up 3: the verb lists

explanations.title: How to use this list
explanations.body:
The book’s Core Vocabulary lists the core words of the chapter with an example sentence for each (the sentences and the English meanings are the book’s; the book gives no English for the sentences). The Hanja of the Sino-Korean words are in parentheses before the meaning.

The example sentences with digits are respelled in Hangul (30분 → 삼십 분). The book’s 부딪치다/부딪히다 and ~(에) 걸리다 are shown with the forms written out; the book’s 며칠 has two example sentences (both kept, joined by a slash). The book’s related words (the synonyms, antonyms and related words in the last column) are left out; the book’s Additional Vocabulary section is blank. The book’s Glossary at the end of the unit (the word index for Chapters 17 to 20) repeats these words.

explanations.title: Self-evaluation
explanations.body:
Recall the objectives of the chapter and ask yourself whether you have achieved them (the book asks you to tick Yes or No). If you tick “No” for any item, the book suggests: review that section on your own; find a study partner and review it as a pair or group; and tell your academic advisor or team leader which areas you need more help with, so that they can provide activities tailored to your learning style and needs.

Now I am able to: describe a person’s physical appearance using the names for parts of the body; describe physical discomfort and the symptoms of common illnesses; ask for basic services at a drug store; describe the causes and symptoms of common injuries; and ask for basic medical services at a doctor’s office and hospital.

Now I have a clear understanding of: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; the conjunctive ending -는 동안(에) (while; during); the conjunctive ending -자마자 (as soon as; right after); the conjunctive ending -다가 (while; in the middle of); -(으)ㄹ 뻔하다, which is used to express near misses or close calls; and the Sino-Korean syllable 약 (藥).

explanations.title: What Chapter 21 teaches (집 구하기와 이사하기)
explanations.body:
Chapter 21, “House Hunting and Moving”, has three topic presentations, grammar in focus, activities, a self-evaluation and the core vocabulary.

When you finish the chapter you will be able to: talk about two major types of housing, single-family homes and apartments; describe in a simple paragraph rooms and other components of a house or apartment; ask for basic information about renting a house; ask for basic information about moving, including moving services and types of moves; and give simple instructions about how to prepare for moving.

You will become familiar with: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; -(으)려고 하다 (to intend to; to plan to); -(으)ㄴ/는 편이다 used to make a nonassertive statement; -(으)ㄹ까 하다 used to imply a speaker’s uncertainty; 좋다 vs. 좋아하다 (to like); 싫다 vs. 싫어하다 (to dislike); and the Sino-Korean syllables 다 (多), 동 (動) and 이 (移).

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 다 (多)
explanations.body:
This Sino-Korean syllable means many, much or numerous, as in 다수 (a large number) and 다량 (a large amount). If you look at the Chinese character 多, you will notice that the same shape 夕 repeats twice vertically. The shape alone stands as a complete character, with 석 (夕) meaning evening. 夕 originated from the shape of the crescent moon in the evening. Thus the meaning of 다 (多) came from “evening after evening, time after time, or a lot of time”. When the syllable is used as a prefix, it can be translated as multi-, as in 다자회담 (a multiparty conference) and 다국적 기업 (a multinational enterprise).

The book asks you to guess the meaning of 다문화 가정, 다용도실, 다소 and 최다. The answers are mine, except 다용도실, which is a core word.

explanations.title: Cultural note: Ondol and the sitting culture
explanations.body: 온돌 is a traditional Korean under-floor heating system that uses direct heat transfer from the kitchen fireplace or stove to the underside of a stone floor. 온돌 has long been an integral part of Korean culture and may date back to as early as 37 b.c.e.; it has remained in use for millennia in Korea and continues to be a typical feature of the Korean home. Nowadays, 온돌 refers to any type of under-floor heating system. 온돌 is widely credited for distinctive Korean customs, such as removing one’s shoes upon entering a home and sitting on the floor.

lessons.title: 275. Ch 21 · Topic A, Follow-up 2 and Activities A: housing types and a parents’ apartment
lessons.subtitle: 아파트와 단독주택 · 마당 · 주차장 · 녹원 아파트 · 거실 바닥은 마루 · 전세 아파트

explanations.title: Follow-up 2 (Reading): an article on housing preferences
explanations.body: The book gives an article about preferences for different types of housing and the reasons, and asks you to fill in a table in English (the percent of Korean people preferring each type, and the reasons). The text is the book’s (the percentages are spelled out in Hangul); the English is mine.

examples.text: 아파트와 단독주택
examples.translation: apateuwa dandokjutaek — Apartments and single-family houses

examples.text: 한국 사람들이 살고 싶어 하는 집은 아파트 오십 점 일 퍼센트, 단독주택 삼십이 점 일 퍼센트, 그리고 오피스텔 육 점 이 퍼센트, 빌라 십일 점 육 퍼센트 순이다.
examples.translation: hanguk saramdeuri salgo sipeo haneun jibeun apateu osip jeom il peosenteu, dandokjutaek samsibi jeom il peosenteu, geurigo opiseutel yuk jeom i peosenteu, billa sibil jeom yuk peosenteu sunida. — The homes Korean people want to live in are, in order, apartments 50.1%, single-family houses 32.1%, and officetels 6.2% and villas 11.6%. (the book’s order of the last two is as printed)

examples.text: 사람들이 아파트를 좋아하는 이유는 무엇일까?
examples.translation: saramdeuri apateureul joahaneun iyuneun mueosilkka? — Why do people like apartments?

examples.text: 무엇보다 아파트는 편리하다.
examples.translation: mueotboda apateuneun pyeollihada. — Above all, apartments are convenient.

examples.text: 아파트 단지에는 주차장이 있고 상가와 여러 가지 편의시설이 있다.
examples.translation: apateu danjieneun juchajangi itgo sanggawa yeoreo gaji pyeonuisiseori itda. — In an apartment complex there is a parking lot, and there are shops and various amenities.

examples.text: 그럼, 사람들이 단독주택을 좋아하는 이유는 무엇일까?
examples.translation: geureom, saramdeuri dandokjutaegeul joahaneun iyuneun mueosilkka? — Then why do people like single-family houses?

examples.text: 단독주택은 마당이 있어서 꽃이나 나무를 심을 수 있다.
examples.translation: dandokjutaegeun madangi isseoseo kkochina namureul simeul su itda. — A single-family house has a yard, so you can plant flowers or trees.

examples.text: 또 아이들이 마당에서 놀 수 있다.
examples.translation: tto aideuri madangeseo nol su itda. — Also, children can play in the yard.

examples.text: 그리고 집에서는 동물도 기를 수 있다.
examples.translation: geurigo jibeseoneun dongmuldo gireul su itda. — And you can also raise animals at home.

explanations.title: The table filled in (mine)
explanations.body: The book leaves the table blank; these are my answers.

rows: A yard for planting flowers or trees; children can play in the yard; you can raise animals at home
Convenient; parking lot, shops and various amenities in the complex

explanations.title: Activity 2 (Reading): Sungjoon’s parents’ apartment
explanations.body: The passage is Sungjoon’s description of his parents’ apartment; the book asks three questions in English (how he describes the floor and walls of the living room; where the bathroom is; how he describes the multi-use room). The text is the book’s (17층 is spelled out); the English is mine.

examples.text: 저희 집은 녹원 아파트 십칠 층입니다.
examples.translation: jeohui jibeun nogwon apateu sipchil cheungimnida. — Our home is on the 17th floor of the Nokwon Apartments.

examples.text: 방은 세 개 있고 욕실은 한 개 있습니다.
examples.translation: bangeun se gae itgo yoksireun han gae itseumnida. — There are three rooms and one bathroom.

examples.text: 먼저 현관으로 들어가면 앞에 거실이 보입니다.
examples.translation: meonjeo hyeongwaneuro deureogamyeon ape geosiri boimnida. — First, if you go in through the entrance, you see the living room in front.

examples.text: 거실 바닥은 마루이고 벽은 노란색입니다.
examples.translation: geosil badageun maruigo byeogeun noransaegimnida. — The living room floor is a wooden floor and the walls are yellow.

examples.text: 현관에서 오른쪽에 욕실이 있고 왼쪽에는 제 여동생 방이 있습니다.
examples.translation: hyeongwaneseo oreunjjoge yoksiri itgo oenjjogeneun je yeodongsaeng bangi itseumnida. — From the entrance, the bathroom is on the right, and my younger sister’s room is on the left.

examples.text: 제 여동생 방 바로 옆에 부엌이 있습니다.
examples.translation: je yeodongsaeng bang baro yeope bueoki itseumnida. — Right next to my younger sister’s room is the kitchen.

examples.text: 부엌 뒤쪽에 다용도실이 있는데 조금 작고 어둡습니다.
examples.translation: bueok dwijjoge dayongdosiri inneunde jogeum jakgo eodupseumnida. — Behind the kitchen is a utility room, which is a little small and dark.

examples.text: 또 부엌 옆에는 제 방이 있습니다.
examples.translation: tto bueok yeopeneun je bangi itseumnida. — Also, next to the kitchen is my room.

examples.text: 제 방 건너편에 부모님 방이 있습니다.
examples.translation: je bang geonneopyeone bumonim bangi itseumnida. — On the opposite side of my room is my parents’ room.

explanations.title: The answers (mine)
explanations.body: The book leaves the answers blank; these are my answers.

rows: How does he describe the floor and walls of the living room?
The floor is wooden and the walls are yellow
To the right as you come in from the entrance
How does he describe the multi-use room?
It is behind the kitchen, and it is a little small and dark

explanations.title: Activity 4: renting an apartment (the model)
explanations.body: In the role-play of Activity 4 (realtors and prospective renters visit each other’s booths) the book gives this model (the English is mine; the book writes 50평, spelled out here):

examples.text: 방 네 개짜리 전세 아파트 있어요?
examples.translation: bang ne gaejjari jeonse apateu isseoyo? — Do you have a four-room 전세 apartment? (A)

examples.text: 네, 있습니다. 오십 평 아파트가 하나 나왔어요. 방이 네 개, 화장실이 두 개예요.
examples.translation: ne, itseumnida. osip pyeong apateuga hana nawasseoyo. bangi ne gae, hwajangsiri du gaeyeyo. — Yes, we do. A 50-pyeong apartment has come up. It has four rooms and two bathrooms. (B)

examples.text: 그 지역 교통은 편리한가요?
examples.translation: geu jiyeok gyotongeun pyeollihangayo? — Is the transportation in that area convenient? (A)

examples.text: 그럼요. 지하철 역이 아주 가까워요.
examples.translation: geureomyo. jihacheol yeogi aju gakkawoyo. — Of course. The subway station is very close. (B)

explanations.title: Activities left out
explanations.body: Activity 1 (a SMART Board activity and listening to three short dialogs about a new home) and Activity 3 (listening to three conversations between a home owner and a visitor) are computer or audio activities. Activity 4 of this chapter’s first part (민박집 찾기: two homestay flyers for Jeju Island, whose texts are not in the book’s text, with a table of type of housing, number and size of rooms, house features, surrounding environment and additional information, in pairs) and the rental role-play with situation cards are partner and class activities.

explanations.title: Cultural note: 전세 and 월세
explanations.body: In Korea, there are two major types of rental arrangements for a house, an apartment, a store, a building, etc.: 전세 and 월세. 전세, whose literal meaning is exclusive rent, is the more common rental arrangement in which the renter pays approximately 60 to 80% of the property price as a deposit but pays no monthly rent. The deposit is paid back when the lease contract expires. 월세, which literally means monthly rent, is the combination of 전세 and a typical monthly rental in the U.S. You pay about 20% of the market value of the house as a deposit and a fixed amount each month as a rental charge.

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 동 (動)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means move or mobile, as in 자동차 (an automobile; “self-moving car”) and 부동산 (real estate; “not movable property”). The shape of the Chinese character gives you some indication of the meaning, if you understand that 重 (중) means heavy and 力 (역/력) means power. In order to “move” heavy stuff, you need to add power. The book asks you to guess the meaning of 동물, 행동, 동력, 전동차, 운동장 and 동영상. The answers are mine, except those marked as the book’s.

lessons.title: 278. Ch 21 · Grammar A: “intend to” and “plan to” with -(으)려고 하다
lessons.subtitle: 한국말을 공부하려고 해요 · 고향에 가려고 해요 · 집을 팔려고 해요 · 양복을 사려고 해요

explanations.title: Expressing “intend to” or “plan to”
explanations.body: In Chapter 13, you learned that the conjunctive endings -(으)려고 and -(으)려면 are used to express a purpose or intention, as in 한국말을 공부하려고 (in order to learn Korean) and 핸드폰을 빌리려면 (if you intend to rent a cell phone). However, when the conjunctive ending -(으)려고 is immediately followed by 하다, it functions as an auxiliary verb that can be interpreted as intend to or plan to.

examples.text: 한국에서 한국말을 공부하려고 해요.
examples.translation: hangugeseo hangungmareul gongbuharyeogo haeyo. — I intend to study Korean in Korea.

examples.text: 이번 주말에 고향에 가려고 해요.
examples.translation: ibeon jumare gohyange garyeogo haeyo. — I plan to go to my hometown this weekend.

explanations.title: The rule
explanations.body: action verb stem + (으)려고 하다.

rows: When a verb stem ends in a vowel or ㄹ
가다 → 가려고 하다; 팔다 → 팔려고 하다
When a verb stem ends in a consonant other than ㄹ
찾다 → 찾으려고 하다; 먹다 → 먹으려고 하다

examples.text: 올해 집을 팔려고 해요.
examples.translation: olhae jibeul pallyeogo haeyo. — I plan to sell my house this year.

examples.text: 자바 카페에서 점심을 먹으려고 해요.
examples.translation: jaba kapeeseo jeomsimeul meogeuryeogo haeyo. — I plan to eat lunch at the Java Cafe.

examples.text: 백화점에서 양복을 사려고 해요.
examples.translation: baekwajeomeseo yangbogeul saryeogo haeyo. — I intend to buy a suit at a department store.

explanations.title: Forms (mine)
explanations.body: The forms are made by the book’s rule.

explanations.title: Follow-up 1 and 5: phrases and plans
explanations.body: In Follow-up 1 partners read a verb phrase and the other conjugates it with -(으)려고 하다, adding adverbs if they like (the book’s model: 친구를 방문하다 → 이번 주말에 친구를 방문하려고 해요). In Follow-up 5 (이번 여름에 해수욕장에 가려고 해요) you think about summer plans for your family and exchange them with classmates using -(으)려고 하다 and -(으)ㄴ/는 편이다. The book’s model:

examples.translation: jeohui gajokdeuri syopingeul joahaneun pyeonieyo. geuraeseo garyeogo haeyo. — My family tends to like shopping. So I plan to go. (B)

lessons.title: 279. Ch 21 · Grammar B: the nonassertive statement with -(으)ㄴ/는 편이다
lessons.subtitle: 작은 편입니다 · 자주 먹는 편입니다 · 머리가 긴 편이에요 · 잘하는 편이에요

explanations.title: The usage of -(으)ㄴ/는 편이다
explanations.body:
The expression -(으)ㄴ/는 편이다, which is attached to the stem of a verb, literally means “to be on the side of” or “to be in the group of” because 편 means a side, group or direction. 몬트레이가 작은 편입니다 means Monterey is “on the smaller side”; 저는 한국 음식을 자주 먹는 편입니다 means I am “on the side of” eating Korean food often.

This expression can be best understood in the context of two sides or two categories: right or wrong, big or small, good or bad, etc. The first sentence, for example, implies that there are two categories, bigger places and smaller places, and Monterey belongs to the latter. Likewise, the second sentence implies that there are two categories, those who eat Korean food often and those who don’t, and the speaker belongs in the former.

examples.text: 몬트레이가 작은 편입니다.
examples.translation: monteureiga jageun pyeonimnida. — Monterey is rather small.

examples.text: 저는 한국 음식을 자주 먹는 편입니다.
examples.translation: jeoneun hanguk eumsigeul jaju meongneun pyeonimnida. — I tend to eat Korean food often.

explanations.title: Nonassertive, not conclusive
explanations.body: Neither of the sentences is as assertive or conclusive as 몬트레이가 작아요 (Monterey is small) and 저는 한국 음식을 자주 먹어요 (I eat Korean food often). Therefore, this expression is mainly used to make a nonassertive or non-conclusive statement about some factual information. When the expression is attached to a stative verb, depending on the context, it can be translated as fairly, rather, kind of or somewhat. When it is used with an action verb, it can be translated as tend to or be inclined to.

examples.text: 몬트레이가 작아요.
examples.translation: monteureiga jagayo. — Monterey is small. (more assertive)

examples.text: 저는 한국 음식을 자주 먹어요.
examples.translation: jeoneun hanguk eumsigeul jaju meogeoyo. — I eat Korean food often. (more assertive)

explanations.title: The rule
explanations.body: verb stem + (으)ㄴ/는 편이다.

rows: When a stative verb stem ends in a vowel
크다 → 큰 편이다; 예쁘다 → 예쁜 편이다
When a stative verb stem ends in a consonant
넓다 → 넓은 편이다; 작다 → 작은 편이다
잘하다 → 잘하는 편이다; 듣다 → 듣는 편이다

examples.text: 제 여자 친구는 머리가 긴 편이에요.
examples.translation: je yeoja chinguneun meoriga gin pyeonieyo. — My girlfriend has fairly long hair.

examples.text: 우리 교실은 작은 편입니다.
examples.translation: uri gyosireun jageun pyeonimnida. — Our classroom is rather small.

examples.text: 박 일병은 한국말을 잘하는 편이에요.
examples.translation: bak ilbyeongeun hangungmareul jalhaneun pyeonieyo. — PFC Park speaks Korean fairly well.

examples.text: 저는 음악을 자주 듣는 편이에요.
examples.translation: jeoneun eumageul jaju deunneun pyeonieyo. — I tend to listen to music a lot.

explanations.title: Forms (mine)
explanations.body: The forms are made by the book’s rule (stems with ㄹ lose it before ㄴ and 는: 길다 → 긴, 살다 → 사는).

explanations.title: Follow-up 3 and 4: questions and an ad
explanations.body: In Follow-up 3 partners ask and answer questions with -(으)ㄴ/는 편이다 (the book’s model: 김 일병, 커피를 많이 마시는 편입니까? / 아니요. 저는 커피를 잘 안 마시는 편입니다. / 네, 커피를 많이 마시는 편입니다). In Follow-up 4 you read an ad for a studio apartment, circle all the verbal phrases that contain -(으)ㄴ/는 편이다 and translate them. The ad is the book’s (the figures are spelled out; the telephone number is left out; the book glosses 오피스텔 as “a type of apartment; from the words office + hotel” and 원룸 as “a studio apartment; one room”); the English is mine.

explanations.title: Notes: moving companies and the inserted ㅅ
explanations.body:
1. Moving companies are called 이삿짐 센터, which literally means “moving load center”. Names for moving companies usually end with one of the following: … 이사 (moving), … 익스프레스 (express), … 통운 (transport), … 용달 이사 (small truck moving) or 트랜스 (transport).

2. 이삿짐 is a compound noun derived from 이사 and 짐. As with 이삿짐, ㅅ is inserted in a compound noun when the following two conditions exist: a. At least one of the words is a native Korean word. b. The first word ends in a vowel and the second word begins with a stop sound. Examples: 어젯밤, 빗길 and 나뭇가지 (tree branch).

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 이 (移)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means move or transfer, as in 이사 (“house-moving”) and 이식 (transplantation; “moving and planting”). Note that the Chinese character is made up of 禾 (화) and 多 (다). 禾, depicting a rice plant (its ear, stem and roots), means rice. 多 means many or multiple, as you learned in the earlier part of this chapter. Thus the character 移 originated from the rice farming tradition of mass-transplanting rice seedlings from a rice seedbed to a rice field. The more seedlings you move or transfer in spring, the more harvest you get in fall. The book asks you to guess the meaning of 이민, 이주, 이동 and 이동 통신; the answers are mine.

lessons.title: 282. Ch 21 · Grammar C: the speaker’s uncertainty with -(으)ㄹ까 하다
lessons.subtitle: 등산을 할까 합니다 · 영화를 볼까 합니다 · 이사할까 해요 · 컴퓨터를 살까 해요

explanations.title: Auxiliary verbs -(으)ㄹ까 하다
explanations.body:
Consider the following two sentences, both of which show the speaker’s intention of going hiking this weekend. -(으)려고 하다 in the first sentence implies the speaker has made up his mind about going hiking this weekend. However, -(으)ㄹ까 하다 in the second sentence implies the speaker has the intention of going hiking this weekend but has not made up his mind.

As shown in the example, the auxiliary verb -(으)ㄹ까 하다 is used to imply a speaker’s uncertainty. For this reason, the auxiliary verb is often translated as may, might, could or (I’m) thinking about. Keep in mind that this auxiliary verb is not used in interrogatives.

lessons.title: 283. Ch 21 · Grammar D: likes and dislikes in two ways, 좋다 / 좋아하다 and 싫다 / 싫어하다
lessons.subtitle: 아이스크림이 좋아요 · 아이스크림을 좋아해요 · 매운 음식이 싫어요 · 매운 음식을 싫어해요

explanations.title: Expressing likes and dislikes in two different ways
explanations.body:
Consider the structural differences of 나는 아이스크림을 좋아해요 and 나는 아이스크림이 좋아요, both of which mean “I like ice cream”. In the first sentence, 좋아해요, whose dictionary form is 좋아하다 (to like), is an action verb that takes an object. Therefore the object 아이스크림 takes the object marker 을. In the second sentence, however, 좋아요, whose dictionary form is 좋다 (to be good; to be pleasant), is a stative verb. Thus 아이스크림 takes the subject marker 이, and the literal translation of the sentence is “For me, ice cream is good”. These two sentences are perfectly interchangeable.

The same pattern is found in ~을/를 싫어하다 and ~이/가 싫다, both of which are used to mean “I do not like ~”.

explanations.title: Self-evaluation
explanations.body:
Recall the objectives of the chapter and ask yourself whether you have achieved them (the book asks you to tick Yes or No). If you tick “No” for any item, the book suggests: review that section on your own; find a study partner and review it as a pair or group; and tell your academic advisor or team leader which areas you need more help with, so that they can provide activities tailored to your learning style and needs.

Now I am able to: talk about two major types of housing, single-family homes and apartments; describe in a simple paragraph rooms and other components of a house or apartment; ask for basic information about renting a house; ask for basic information about moving, including moving services and types of moves; and give simple instructions about how to prepare for moving.

Now I have a clear understanding of: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; -(으)려고 하다; -(으)ㄴ/는 편이다; -(으)ㄹ까 하다; 좋다 vs. 좋아하다; 싫다 vs. 싫어하다; and the Sino-Korean syllables 다 (多), 동 (動) and 이 (移).

explanations.title: What Chapter 22 teaches (가정 생활)
explanations.body:
Chapter 22, “Home Life”, has three topic presentations, grammar in focus, activities, a self-evaluation and the core vocabulary.

When you finish the chapter you will be able to: talk about common household chores; report malfunctions and request services for home maintenance; express emotions in a simple way; and express concerns and give suggestions on household expenses.

You will become familiar with: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; -지, the verb ending in an interrogative clause; -기 위해(서) (in order to; so as to); the conjunctive ending -거나/-든지 (or); and the Sino-Korean syllable 비 (費).

explanations.title: Note 1: expressing “sharing” using 나눠서
explanations.body: Koreans use 나눠서 + an action verb to express sharing something like food, drink or chores: 나눠서 먹다 (to share food), 나눠서 마시다 (to share a drink) and 집안일을 나눠서 하다 (to share household chores). The expression literally means “divide and eat” (or “drink” or “do”).

rows: to share a drink; “divide and drink”
to share household chores; “divide and do”

explanations.title: Note 2: ~질
explanations.body: The suffix ~질 (attached to a noun) indicates a repetitive action, as in 걸레질 (mopping), 다림질 (ironing), 양치질 (brushing one’s teeth), etc. It can also indicate an undesirable or socially unacceptable action done repetitively, as in 도둑질 (theft), 싸움질 (fighting), etc.

explanations.body: The listening activity (Follow-up 1) names these household chores in English. The Korean is mine, except for the core words (걸레질, 다림질, 쓰레기, 장보기, 돌보다, 쓸다).

explanations.title: Topic A: We share the household chores (집안일을 나눠서 해요)
explanations.body: Jungwoo describes each of his family members’ responsibilities for household chores. (The English is mine; the book gives none.)

examples.text: 우리 가족은 집안일을 나눠서 합니다.

examples.translation: eomeonikkeseoneun jangbogiwa yori deung bueok sallimeul hasimnida. — My mother does the kitchen housework, such as grocery shopping and cooking.

explanations.title: Follow-up 2 (Reading): who does more housework?
explanations.body: The book gives an article about spouses sharing household chores and asks you to write in English what each percentage (70.5%, 26.6%, 2.9%) refers to. The text is the book’s (the percentages are spelled out in Hangul); the English is mine. The book glosses 똑같이: equally, evenly.

examples.text: 집안일, 누가 더 많이 할까?
examples.translation: jibannil, nuga deo mani halkka? — Who does more housework?

examples.text: 한 조사에 따르면 집안일을 여성 혼자 다 하는 가족이 칠십 점 오 퍼센트, 그리고 이십육 점 육 퍼센트의 가족은 여성과 남성이 집안일을 똑같이 나누어서 하는 것으로 나타났다.
examples.translation: han josae ttareumyeon jibanireul yeoseong honja da haneun gajogi chilsip jeom o peosenteu, geurigo isimnyuk jeom yuk peosenteuui gajogeun yeoseonggwa namseongi jibanireul ttokgachi nanueoseo haneun geoseuro natanatda. — According to one survey, in 70.5% of families a woman does all the housework alone, and in 26.6% of families women and men share the housework equally.

examples.text: 나머지 이 점 구 퍼센트는 남편이 집안일을 하는 것으로 조사되었다.
examples.translation: nameoji i jeom gu peosenteuneun nampyeoni jibanireul haneun geoseuro josadoeeotda. — In the remaining 2.9%, the husband was found to do the housework.

explanations.title: The table filled in (mine)
explanations.body: The book leaves the table blank; these are my answers.

rows: Families in which the woman does all the housework alone
Families in which women and men share the housework equally
Families in which the husband does the housework

explanations.title: Activity 2 (Reading): a man’s concerns on an online counseling site
explanations.body: The text is from an online counseling site, in which a man is expressing his concerns about household chores. The book asks you to fill in a table in English (personal information about the man, what his spouse wants, the man’s dilemma). The text is the book’s (3년 → 삼 년); the English is mine.

examples.text: 안녕하세요? 저는 김수철이라고 합니다.
examples.translation: annyeonghaseyo? jeoneun gimsucheorirago hamnida. — Hello? My name is Kim Suchul.

examples.text: 삼 년 전에 결혼했고 두 살 된 아이가 하나 있습니다.
examples.translation: sam nyeon jeone gyeolhonhaetgo du sal doen aiga hana itseumnida. — I got married three years ago and have one child who is two years old.

examples.text: 저는 아내하고 사이가 좋은데 가끔 집안일 때문에 싸웁니다.
examples.translation: jeoneun anaehago saiga joeunde gakkeum jibannil ttaemune ssaumnida. — I get along well with my wife, but sometimes we fight because of the housework.

examples.text: 결혼 초에는 제가 자주 집안일을 도와주었습니다.
examples.translation: gyeolhon choeneun jega jaju jibanireul dowajueotseumnida. — At the beginning of our marriage I often helped with the housework.

examples.text: 하지만 요즘은 제 회사 일이 너무 바빠서 평일에는 집안일을 도와주지 못합니다.
examples.translation: hajiman yojeumeun je hoesa iri neomu bappaseo pyeongireneun jibanireul dowajuji motamnida. — But these days my work at the company is too busy, so I cannot help with the housework on weekdays.

examples.text: 그래서 주말이나 휴일에만 집안청소를 해줍니다.
examples.translation: geuraeseo jumarina hyuireman jibancheongsoreul haejumnida. — So I do the house cleaning only on weekends or holidays.

examples.text: 그런데 아내는 제가 평일에도 장보기와 설거지, 아이 돌보는 것을 도와주기를 바랍니다.
examples.translation: geureonde anaeneun jega pyeongiredo jangbogiwa seolgeoji, ai dolboneun geoseul dowajugireul baramnida. — But my wife wants me to help with grocery shopping, washing the dishes and looking after the child on weekdays, too.

examples.text: 제가 집안일을 너무 안 도와주고 있나요?
examples.translation: jega jibanireul neomu an dowajugo innayo? — Am I not helping with the housework too little?

explanations.title: The table filled in (mine)
explanations.body: The book leaves the table blank; these are my answers.

rows: Kim Suchul; married three years ago; one two-year-old child
She wants him to help with grocery shopping, washing the dishes and looking after the child on weekdays, too
He gets along well with his wife but sometimes they fight about housework; his job is too busy on weekdays, so he can only clean on weekends and holidays

explanations.title: Activity 4: “Please clean thoroughly” (the model)
explanations.body: In the role-play of Activity 4 (깨끗이 청소해 주세요: a home owner who needs to hire a helper for an upcoming family event and a domestic helper), the students first write down the chores in Korean and then use -아/어 주다 for requesting services. The book gives this model (the English is mine):

examples.text: 일층은 거실하고 부엌, 욕실, 현관을 청소해 주세요.
examples.translation: ilcheungeun geosilhago bueok, yoksil, hyeongwaneul cheongsohae juseyo. — On the first floor, please clean the living room, the kitchen, the bathroom and the entrance. (home owner)

examples.text: 거실은 어떻게 청소할까요?
examples.translation: geosireun eotteoke cheongsohalkkayo? — How shall I clean the living room? (helper)

examples.text: 청소기로 먼저 청소하고 걸레질을 해 주세요.
examples.translation: cheongsogiro meonjeo cheongsohago geollejireul hae juseyo. — Please clean with the vacuum cleaner first and then mop. (home owner)

explanations.title: Activities left out
explanations.body: Activity 1 (a SMART Board activity and a video clip from MBC America in which a household helper is instructed to do chores; one chore, sterilizing baby bottles, is given) is a computer and video activity. Activity 3 (a family meeting at which Jitae’s parents make suggestions about sharing the chores; two listening tables of suggestions, with “feed the dog” and “clean the veranda” given) is an audio activity. Activity 4’s role-play (with situation cards) is a partner activity.

explanations.title: Topic B: The toilet leaks (변기에서 물이 새요)
explanations.body: Sunah is complaining to the manager of the apartment management office. (The English is mine; the book gives none. The book writes 111동 1007호 and 30일; they are spelled out here. The book’s footnote says the literal translation of 어떻게 오셨습니까? is “How did you come?”; in conversation it is an opening remark meaning “How can I help you?”)

examples.translation: seona: byeongieseo muri saeyo. — Water leaks from the toilet.

examples.text: 소장: 아, 그래요?
examples.translation: sojang: a, geuraeyo? — Oh, really?

examples.text: 선아: 그리고 이미 여러 번 관리사무소에 전화했는데 직원들이 전화를 잘 안 받아요. 전화를 받아도 직원들이 불친절해서 기분이 나빠요.
examples.translation: seona: geurigo imi yeoreo beon gwallisamusoe jeonhwahaenneunde jigwondeuri jeonhwareul jal an badayo. jeonhwareul badado jigwondeuri bulchinjeolhaeseo gibuni nappayo. — And I have already called the management office several times, but the staff don’t often answer the phone. Even when they answer, the staff are unfriendly, so I feel bad.

examples.text: 소장: 정말 죄송합니다. 다른 문제는 없으십니까?
examples.translation: sojang: jeongmal joesonghamnida. dareun munjeneun eopseusimnikka? — I am really sorry. Is there no other problem?

examples.text: 선아: 보일러도 고장 난 것 같아요. 어젯밤에 난방이 잘 안 돼서 추웠어요.
examples.translation: seona: boilleodo gojang nan geot gatayo. eojetbame nanbangi jal an dwaeseo chuwosseoyo. — The boiler seems to be broken, too. Last night the heating didn’t work well, so it was cold.

examples.text: 소장: 알겠습니다. 화장실, 보일러 둘 다 곧 수리해 드리겠습니다.
examples.translation: sojang: algetseumnida. hwajangsil, boilleo dul da got surihae deurigetseumnida. — I understand. We will repair both the bathroom and the boiler soon.

examples.text: 선아: 참, 관리비는 언제 나오는지 알고 싶어요.
examples.translation: seona: cham, gwallibineun eonje naoneunji algo sipeoyo. — Oh, I would like to know when the management fee comes out.

examples.text: 소장: 관리비는 매달 삼십 일에 나옵니다.
examples.translation: sojang: gwallibineun maedal samsip ire naomnida. — The management fee comes out on the 30th of every month.

examples.text: 선아: 관리비에 수도요금하고 전기요금이 포함돼요?
examples.translation: seona: gwallibie sudoyogeumhago jeongiyogeumi pohamdwaeyo? — Are the water bill and the electricity bill included in the management fee?

examples.text: 소장: 네, 포함됩니다.
examples.translation: sojang: ne, pohamdoemnida. — Yes, they are included.

examples.text: 선아: 알겠습니다. 그럼, 직원 좀 빨리 보내 주세요.
examples.translation: seona: algetseumnida. geureom, jigwon jom ppalli bonae juseyo. — I see. Then please send a staff member quickly.

explanations.title: Cultural note: the management fee
explanations.body: In Korea, those who live in an apartment complex normally pay 관리비 (a management fee) every month to help maintain the apartment complex. This is similar to association fees for condominiums in the U.S. However, when you receive the bill for 관리비, a statement of each unit’s electricity, gas and water expenses is often included on the bill.

lessons.title: 290. Ch 22 · Grammar: the interrogative clause with -지
lessons.subtitle: 어디에서 먹는지 몰라요 · 먹었는지 · 먹을지 · 있는지 없는지

explanations.title: Expressing an interrogative clause
explanations.body:
Look at the following English clauses: I don’t know where David is (derived from Where is David?); I know what you ate last night (derived from What did you eat last night?); I wonder if he lives in Seaside (derived from Does he live in Seaside?). These clauses are all derived from questions but are now part of a sentence. They are called interrogative clauses. When a question becomes an interrogative clause, the typical interrogative word order changes (where is David → where David is), and in a yes/no question, if or whether is added (Does he live in Seaside → if he lives in Seaside).

In Korean, when a question becomes an interrogative clause, the verb changes to -지. Depending on the tense of the verb, -지 has a different form.

examples.text: 데이비드가 어디에서 식사하는지 몰라요.
examples.translation: deibideuga eodieseo siksahaneunji mollayo. — I don’t know where David eats.

examples.text: 데이비드가 여기에서 식사하는지 몰라요.
examples.translation: deibideuga yeogieseo siksahaneunji mollayo. — I don’t know if David eats here.

explanations.title: The rule: the verb ending in an interrogative clause -지
explanations.body: In the book’s table (the arrow in 가다 → 가았는지 → 갔는지 shows the contraction).

rows: When the action verb is in present tense
add 는지 to the verb stem
When the stative verb is in present tense
When the verb is in past tense
add 았/었는지 to the verb stem
When the verb is in future tense

examples.text: 데이비드가 어디에서 먹는지 몰라요.
examples.translation: deibideuga eodieseo meongneunji mollayo. — I don’t know where David eats.

examples.text: 데이비드가 어디에서 먹었는지 몰라요.
examples.translation: deibideuga eodieseo meogeonneunji mollayo. — I don’t know where David ate.

examples.text: 데이비드가 어디에서 먹을지 몰라요.

explanations.title: More examples
explanations.body: The book’s examples:

examples.text: 수업이 몇 시에 시작하는지 아세요?
examples.translation: sueobi myeot sie sijakaneunji aseyo? — Do you know when class starts?

examples.text: 어제 무엇을 배웠는지 말해주세요.
examples.translation: eoje mueoseul baewonneunji malhaejuseyo. — Please tell me what you learned yesterday.

examples.text: 델몬티 쇼핑센터가 어디에 있는지 알아요.
examples.translation: delmonti syopingsenteoga eodie inneunji arayo. — I know where Del Monte Shopping Center is.

examples.text: 왜 이 일병이 김치를 안 먹는지 모르겠어요.
examples.translation: wae i ilbyeongi gimchireul an meongneunji moreugesseoyo. — I don’t know why PFC Lee does not eat kimchi.

explanations.title: “Whether or not …” (or “if”)
explanations.body: You can express “whether or not …” (or “if”) in the following way (repeat the verb in its affirmative and negative form):

examples.text: 책이 교실에 있는지 없는지 몰라요.
examples.translation: chaegi gyosire inneunji eomneunji mollayo. — I don’t know whether or not my book is in the classroom.

examples.text: 김 일병이 이라크에 갔는지 안 갔는지 아세요?
examples.translation: gim ilbyeongi irakeue ganneunji an ganneunji aseyo? — Do you know if PFC Kim went to Iraq (or not)?

examples.text: 제 아내가 한국에 갈지 안 갈지 몰라요.
examples.translation: je anaega hanguge galji an galji mollayo. — I don’t know whether or not my wife will go to Korea.

explanations.title: Topic C: We will have to reduce living expenses (생활비를 줄여야겠어요)
explanations.body: Two women are chatting about their household expenses. (The English is mine; the book gives none. The book writes 35만 원; it is spelled out here. The book’s footnotes: 2. ~이나 can be used to express a number or an amount that is more than what the speaker expects. It means as many as or as much as. 3. 저희 집, which literally means “our house”, can be interpreted as my family in this context.)

examples.text: 정수 엄마: 민지네는 이번 달 관리비가 얼마 나왔어요?
examples.translation: jeongsu eomma: minjineneun ibeon dal gwallibiga eolma nawasseoyo? — How much was Minji’s family’s management fee this month?

examples.text: 민지 엄마: 삼십오만 원이나 나왔어요. 지난달보다 많이 나왔어요.
examples.translation: minji eomma: samsiboman wonina nawasseoyo. jinandalboda mani nawasseoyo. — It came to as much as 350,000 won. It was more than last month.

examples.text: 정수 엄마: 저희도요. 특히 난방비가 많이 나왔어요.
examples.translation: jeongsu eomma: jeohuidoyo. teuki nanbangbiga mani nawasseoyo. — Ours, too. The heating bill in particular came out high.

examples.text: 민지 엄마: 남편 월급은 오르지 않는데 물가는 자꾸 오르네요.
examples.translation: minji eomma: nampyeon wolgeubeun oreuji anneunde mulganeun jakku oreuneyo. — My husband’s salary doesn’t go up, but prices keep going up.

examples.translation: jeongsu eomma: majayo. geuraeseo yojeumeun jeochukdo mani mo taeyo. — That’s right. So these days I can’t save much, either.

examples.text: 민지 엄마: 정수네는 저금도 해요? 저희는 저축할 돈이 없어요.
examples.translation: minji eomma: jeongsuneneun jeogeumdo haeyo? jeohuineun jeochukal doni eopseoyo. — Does Jungsu’s family save, too? We have no money to save.

examples.text: 정수 엄마: 그래도 아이들을 위해서 조금씩 저축해야 해요.
examples.translation: jeongsu eomma: geuraedo aideureul wihaeseo jogeumssik jeochukaeya haeyo. — Still, we have to save a little at a time for the children.

examples.text: 민지 엄마: 어떻게요?
examples.translation: minji eomma: eotteokeyo? — How?

examples.text: 정수 엄마: 대중교통을 이용하거나 걸어 다녀요.

explanations.title: Cultural note: addressing parents and families
explanations.body: The way men and women are addressed often changes once a child is born into the family. Family members or close acquaintances generally address the new parents by their children’s first names instead of their own. For example, in 정수 엄마 and 지현이 아빠, 정수 and 지현 refer to the children’s names. In addition, to refer to the family, Koreans often add ~(이)네 to one of their children’s names, as in 정수네 and 지현이네, or their titles, as in 김 씨네, 박 선생님네 or 이 중위님네.

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 비 (費)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means expense, cost, fee or expenditure, as in 비용 (expense), 병원비 (medical expenses; “hospital expense”), 학비 (tuition; “expense for schooling”) and 치료비 (money for treatment). The book asks you to guess the meaning of 교통비, 회비, 학원비, 식비, 관리비 and 잡비 (잡 (雜): odds and ends, mixed). The answers are mine, except 식비 and 관리비, which are core words.

a management fee (the book’s core word)
miscellaneous expenses (mine; 잡 (雜): odds and ends, mixed)
