lessons.subtitle: 생활비 · 교육비 · 외식비 · 오락비 · 교통비 · 저축 · 무엇을 절약해야 할까요

explanations.title: Activity 1a: match the expenses with the types of expense
explanations.body: The book lists six groups of expenses and six types of expense and asks you to draw lines between them. The lists are the book’s; the matches are mine (the book leaves them blank). The English is mine.

explanations.title: Activity 2 (Reading): a woman asks about her home finances
explanations.body: The text is extracted from a Q&A section on a website where a woman asks about her home finances. The book asks you to identify what expense each amount of money is associated with, fill in a table in English, and then underline the woman’s request for advice and translate it into English. The text is the book’s (the amounts are spelled out in Hangul; the book’s 5백50만, 2억 8,000만 etc. are respelled); the English is mine.

examples.text: 남편이랑 저랑 매달 오백오십만 원쯤 법니다.
examples.translation: nampyeonirang jeorang maedal obaegosimman wonjjeum beomnida. — My husband and I earn about 5,500,000 won every month.

examples.text: 남편이랑 삼 년 전에 결혼했고 십오 개월 된 아기가 있어요.
examples.translation: nampyeonirang sam nyeon jeone gyeolhonhaetgo sibo gaewol doen agiga isseoyo. — My husband and I got married three years ago, and we have a 15-month-old baby.

examples.text: 지금 저희는 전세 이억 팔천만 원짜리 이십삼 평 아파트에서 살고 있습니다.
examples.translation: jigeum jeohuineun jeonse ieok palcheonman wonjjari isipsam pyeong apateueseo salgo itseumnida. — Now we live in a 23-pyeong apartment with a 전세 of 280,000,000 won.

examples.text: 매달 전기요금, 수도요금, 전화요금, 관리비 등으로 한 구십만 원 정도 들어요.
examples.translation: maedal jeongiyogeum, sudoyogeum, jeonhwayogeum, gwallibi deungeuro han gusimman won jeongdo deureoyo. — Every month about 900,000 won goes to the electricity bill, the water bill, the phone bill, the management fee and so on.

examples.text: 또, 교통비 십오만 원, 오락비 이십만 원, 식비와 외식비로 백만 원 정도 들어요.
examples.translation: tto, gyotongbi siboman won, orakbi isimman won, sikbiwa oesikbiro baengman won jeongdo deureoyo. — Also, 150,000 won for transportation, 200,000 won for entertainment, and about 1,000,000 won for food and eating out.

examples.text: 그리고 시어머니가 아기를 돌봐 주시기 때문에 시어머니에게 오십만 원 정도 드리고 있어요.
examples.translation: geurigo sieomeoniga agireul dolbwa jusigi ttaemune sieomeoniege osimman won jeongdo deurigo isseoyo. — And because my mother-in-law looks after the baby, I give her about 500,000 won.

examples.text: 그리고 매달 팔십만 원 정도 저축하고 있어요.
examples.translation: geurigo maedal palsimman won jeongdo jeochukago isseoyo. — And I save about 800,000 won every month.

examples.text: 집을 사기 위해서 물건도 많이 사지 않으려고 하고 외식도 자주 하지 않으려고 해요.
examples.translation: jibeul sagi wihaeseo mulgeondo mani saji aneuryeogo hago oesikdo jaju haji aneuryeogo haeyo. — In order to buy a house, I try not to buy many things and not to eat out often.

examples.text: 하지만 저축을 많이 못 해요.
examples.translation: hajiman jeochugeul mani mo taeyo. — But I can’t save much.

examples.text: 돈을 많이 쓰는 편은 아니에요.
examples.translation: doneul mani sseuneun pyeoneun anieyo. — I am not on the side of spending a lot of money.

examples.text: 하지만 저축을 더 많이 하기 위해서 어떻게 해야 하는지 좀 알려주세요.
examples.translation: hajiman jeochugeul deo mani hagi wihaeseo eotteoke haeya haneunji jom allyeojuseyo. — But please tell me what I should do in order to save even more. (the request for advice)

examples.text: 그럼, 수고하세요.
examples.translation: geureom, sugohaseyo. — Well, take care.

explanations.title: Activity 3: What should we save on? (the model)
explanations.body: In Activity 3 (무엇을 절약해야 할까요?) you jot down last month’s expenses in English, categorize them on a form, write in Korean sentences about one area where you spent sparingly or lavishly, and then tell your partner and give advice. The book’s models (the English is mine):

examples.text: 지난 달에 저는 택시를 타지 않고 버스를 타서 교통비를 아꼈습니다.
examples.translation: jinan dare jeoneun taeksireul taji anko beoseureul taseo gyotongbireul akkyeotseumnida. — Last month I didn’t take taxis but took the bus, so I saved on transportation costs.

examples.text: 지난달에 저는 비디오 게임을 많이 해서 오락비에 돈을 많이 썼습니다.
examples.translation: jinandare jeoneun bidio geimeul mani haeseo orakbie doneul mani sseotseumnida. — Last month I played a lot of video games, so I spent a lot of money on entertainment expenses.

explanations.title: Activities left out
explanations.body: Activity 1b (listening to three conversations between two women sharing their concerns about household expenses) is an audio activity. Activity 3’s expense forms and partner exchange are written and partner activities.

lessons.title: 294. Ch 22 · Grammar A: expressing a purpose with -기 위해(서)
lessons.subtitle: 먹기 위해서 · 차를 사기 위해 저축을 합니다 · 살기 위해서 먹습니다

explanations.title: Expressing a purpose using -기 위해(서)
explanations.body:
Recall the two grammar features -(으)러 and -(으)려고 you learned about in earlier chapters: 불고기를 먹으러 한국 식당에 갔어요 (I went to a Korean restaurant to eat bulgogi) and 불고기를 먹으려고 젓가락을 들었어요 (I picked up my chopsticks to eat bulgogi). Both convey the same purpose: to eat bulgogi. -(으)러, however, works only with verbs like 가다, 오다 and 다니다. We can also express the same purpose by replacing the two grammar features with -기 위해(서).

Koreans tend to use this grammar feature to emphasize a purpose; -기 위해(서) is often translated as in order to or so as to.

examples.text: 불고기를 먹으러 한국 식당에 갔어요.
examples.translation: bulgogireul meogeureo hanguk sikdange gasseoyo. — I went to a Korean restaurant to eat bulgogi.

examples.text: 불고기를 먹으려고 젓가락을 들었어요.
examples.translation: bulgogireul meogeuryeogo jeotgarageul deureosseoyo. — I picked up my chopsticks to eat bulgogi.

examples.text: 불고기를 먹기 위해서 한국 식당에 갔어요.
examples.translation: bulgogireul meokgi wihaeseo hanguk sikdange gasseoyo. — I went to a Korean restaurant (in order) to eat bulgogi.

examples.text: 불고기를 먹기 위해서 젓가락을 들었어요.
examples.translation: bulgogireul meokgi wihaeseo jeotgarageul deureosseoyo. — I picked up my chopsticks (in order) to eat bulgogi.

explanations.title: “In order to” / “So as to”
explanations.body: verb stem + 기 위해(서).

rows: 먹다 → 먹기 위해(서); 사다 → 사기 위해(서)

examples.text: 차를 사기 위해 저축을 합니다.
examples.translation: chareul sagi wihae jeochugeul hamnida. — I am saving money in order to buy a car.

examples.text: 살기 위해서 먹습니다.
examples.translation: salgi wihaeseo meokseumnida. — I eat in order to live.

examples.text: 한국말을 배우기 위해 한국에 갔습니다.
examples.translation: hangungmareul baeugi wihae hanguge gatseumnida. — I went to Korea in order to learn Korean.

explanations.title: With nouns: ~을/를 위해(서)
explanations.body: The core vocabulary also has ~을/를 위해(서) (for (the sake of); for (the benefit of)) for nouns, and -기 위해(서) for verbs. The book’s examples:

examples.text: 운동하기 위해서 체육관에 갑니다.
examples.translation: undonghagi wihaeseo cheyukgwane gamnida. — I go to the gym in order to exercise.

examples.text: 저축하기 위해서 외식을 줄였어요.
examples.translation: jeochukagi wihaeseo oesigeul juryeosseoyo. — I cut down on eating out in order to save.

examples.text: 부모님을 위해서 선물을 샀습니다.
examples.translation: bumonimeul wihaeseo seonmureul satseumnida. — I bought a present for my parents.

examples.text: 김 선생님은 아이들 교육을 위해 서울로 이사하려고 해요.
examples.translation: gim seonsaengnimeun aideul gyoyugeul wihae seoullo isaharyeogo haeyo. — Teacher Kim plans to move to Seoul for the children’s education.

lessons.title: 295. Ch 22 · Grammar B: the conjunctive ending -거나/든지 (or)
lessons.subtitle: 친구를 만나거나 영화를 볼 거예요 · 골프를 치든지 등산을 합니다 · 일본사람이거나

explanations.title: The conjunctive ending -거나/든지
explanations.body:
Recall the noun connector ~(이)나, which translates to or or either…or and is often used to indicate a choice or an alternative. As its name indicates, a noun connector connects only nouns: 오렌지나 바나나를 주세요; 저는 한국이나 일본에 가고 싶어요.

When we connect verbs, however, we use the conjunctive ending (a.k.a. verb connector) -거나 or -든지 instead. The two are interchangeable in the book’s examples.

examples.text: 오렌지나 바나나를 주세요.
examples.translation: orenjina bananareul juseyo. — Please give me an orange or a banana.

examples.text: 저는 한국이나 일본에 가고 싶어요.
examples.translation: jeoneun hangugina ilbone gago sipeoyo. — I’d like to go to Korea or Japan.

explanations.title: “Or”
explanations.body: verb stem + 거나 / 든지.

rows: 만나다 → 만나거나 / 만나든지; 하다 → 하거나 / 하든지

explanations.title: Forms (mine)
explanations.body: The forms are made by the book’s rule.

explanations.title: Follow-up 3 and 5: weekend plans
explanations.body: In Follow-up 3 Student A asks what Student B will do over the coming weekend; Student B chooses two actions from the words in the box and answers using -거나/든지. The words (the book’s list; the English is mine) are below. In Follow-up 5 you plan two things to do with each family member. The book’s models:

examples.text: 이번 주말에 뭐 할 거예요?
examples.translation: ibeon jumare mwo hal geoyeyo? — What are you going to do this weekend? (A)

examples.text: 쇼핑가거나 영화를 볼 거예요.
examples.translation: syopinggageona yeonghwareul bol geoyeyo. — I will go shopping or watch a movie. (B)

examples.text: 쇼핑가든지 영화를 볼 거예요.
examples.translation: syopinggadeunji yeonghwareul bol geoyeyo. — I will go shopping or watch a movie. (B)

examples.text: 남동생하고 같이 야구를 하거나 영화를 보러 갈 거예요.
examples.translation: namdongsaenghago gachi yagureul hageona yeonghwareul boreo gal geoyeyo. — I will play baseball with my younger brother or go to see a movie. (the Follow-up 5 model)

explanations.title: The box of phrases (Follow-up 3)
explanations.body: The English is mine.

explanations.title: Activities left out
explanations.body: Follow-up 4 (listening to three conversations about household chores and noting two chores in each) is an audio activity; Follow-up 3 and 5 (partner exchanges and a class presentation) are partner and class activities.

explanations.title: How to use this list
explanations.body:
The book’s Core Vocabulary lists the core words of the chapter with an example sentence for each (the sentences and the English meanings are the book’s; the book gives no English for the sentences). The Hanja of the Sino-Korean words are in parentheses before the meaning.

The example sentences with digits or Latin letters are respelled in Hangul (30일 → 삼십 일, 15일 → 십오 일, TV → 티브이). The book’s related words (the synonyms, antonyms and related words in the last column) are left out; the book’s Additional Vocabulary section is blank.

explanations.title: Self-evaluation
explanations.body:
Recall the objectives of the chapter and ask yourself whether you have achieved them (the book asks you to tick Yes or No). If you tick “No” for any item, the book suggests: review that section on your own; find a study partner and review it as a pair or group; and tell your academic advisor or team leader which areas you need more help with, so that they can provide activities tailored to your learning style and needs.

Now I am able to: talk about common household chores; report malfunctions and request services for home maintenance; express emotions in a simple way; and express concerns and give suggestions on household expenses.

Now I have a clear understanding of: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; -지, the verb ending in an interrogative clause; -기 위해(서) (in order to; so as to); the conjunctive ending -거나/-든지 (or); and the Sino-Korean syllable 비 (費).

explanations.title: What Chapter 23 teaches (한국의 명절과 기념일)
explanations.body:
Chapter 23, “Traditional Korean Holidays and Observances”, has three topic presentations, grammar in focus, activities, a self-evaluation and the core vocabulary.

When you finish the chapter you will be able to: identify and talk about important Korean holidays and observances; identify and talk about activities done on traditional Korean holidays; and express gratitude to teachers and parents.

You will become familiar with: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; -지요 used to ask for confirmation or to seek agreement; -았었다 or -었었다 (used to [do/not do something]); -다고 하다 or -라고 하다 used to quote indirectly; and the Sino-Korean syllables 객 (客) and 절 (節).

explanations.title: Korean national holidays and observances (한국의 국경일과 기념일)
explanations.body: The book’s table of Korean national holidays and observances, with the date and the English meaning. The book’s footnotes: 설날 and 추석 are three-day holidays; 음력: (by the) lunar calendar. (The dates are written 1월 1일 etc. in the book; the Korean reading is in the next card.)

explanations.title: The dates read aloud (Korean)
explanations.body: How the dates are read (months and days in Sino-Korean; June is 유월 and October is 시월).

explanations.title: Notes: historical events named by their dates
explanations.body: Historical events in Korea are often referred to by the date on which the event occurred. For example, 광복절 (Independence Day) is often called 8·15 (팔일오) and the Independence Movement of March 1 is officially named 3·1절 (삼일절). 6·25 (육이오) refers to June 25, 1950, the day the Korean War broke out.

The book’s footnote: 이런 literally translates to “(things) like this”. It is used as an exclamation and has a meaning similar to Oh my! or Darn it! in English.)

examples.text: 지훈: 다은 씨, 내년 달력이 나왔어요.
examples.translation: jihun: daeun ssi, naenyeon dallyeogi nawasseoyo. — Daeun, next year’s calendar has come out.

examples.text: 다은: 그래요? 그럼 휴일 좀 확인해 봐요.
examples.translation: daeun: geuraeyo? geureom hyuil jom hwaginhae bwayo. — Is that so? Then let’s check the holidays.

examples.text: 지훈: 네. 이런! 내년에는 설날과 추석연휴가 너무 짧네!
examples.translation: jihun: ne. ireon! naenyeoneneun seollalgwa chuseogyeonhyuga neomu jjalle! — Yes. Oh my! Next year the Lunar New Year and Chuseok holidays are too short!

examples.text: 다은: 어, 정말이군요! 그런데 다른 연휴는 없어요?
examples.translation: daeun: eo, jeongmarigunyo! geureonde dareun yeonhyuneun eopseoyo? — Oh, so they are! But is there no other long holiday?

examples.text: 지훈: 다행히 팔월에 하나 있어요. 광복절이 금요일이어서 그때는 사흘 동안 쉴 수 있어요.
examples.translation: jihun: dahaenghi parwore hana isseoyo. gwangbokjeori geumyoirieoseo geuttaeneun saheul dongan swil su isseoyo. — Fortunately there is one in August. Independence Day falls on a Friday, so we can rest for three days then.

examples.text: 다은: 잘 됐네요! 지훈 씨, 시월 달력 좀 볼까요?
examples.translation: daeun: jal dwaenneyo! jihun ssi, siwol dallyeok jom bolkkayo? — That’s great! Jihoon, shall we look at the October calendar?

examples.text: 지훈: 시월이요? 왜요?
examples.translation: jihun: siworiyo? waeyo? — October? Why?

examples.text: 다은: 시월에 중요한 국경일이 많으니까요. 국군의 날, 개천절, 한글날 그리고 또…
examples.translation: daeun: siwore jungyohan gukgyeongiri maneunikkayo. gukgunui nal, gaecheonjeol, hangeullal geurigo tto… — Because there are many important national holidays in October: Armed Forces Day, National Foundation Day, Hangeul Day, and also…

examples.text: 지훈: 그렇지만 개천절과 한글날만 공휴일이에요. 국군의 날은 이제 쉬지 않아요.
examples.translation: jihun: geureochiman gaecheonjeolgwa hangeullalman gonghyuirieyo. gukgunui nareun ije swiji anayo. — But only National Foundation Day and Hangeul Day are legal holidays. We don’t take a day off on Armed Forces Day any more.

examples.text: 다은: 그렇군요. 그런데 올해는 추석이 언제예요?
examples.translation: daeun: geureokunyo. geureonde olhaeneun chuseogi eonjeyeyo? — I see. By the way, when is Chuseok this year?

examples.text: 지훈: 구월 초순입니다.
examples.translation: jihun: guwol chosunimnida. — It is in early September.

examples.text: 다은: 잘 됐다! 우리 아버지 생신도 구월 초순이니까 그때 꼭 고향에 가야겠어요.
examples.translation: daeun: jal dwaetda! uri abeoji saengsindo guwol chosuninikka geuttae kkok gohyange gayagesseoyo. — Great! My father’s birthday is also in early September, so I must go to my hometown then.

explanations.title: North Korea Report
explanations.body: North Korea has eight national holidays: Kim Il-sung’s birthday, known as 태양절 (“the Sun Day”), 2월절 (Kim Jung-il’s birthday), 국제 노동자절 (International Labor Day), 조국해방 기념일 (Independence Day), 인민정권 창건일 (People’s Party Foundation Day), 노동당 창건일 (Labor Party Day), 사회주의 헌법절 (Communist Constitution Day) and 설 (New Year’s Day). The first seven holidays are called 사회주의 7대 명절 (Seven Socialists’ National Holidays). Among these holidays, the most important is Kim Il-sung’s birthday on April 15, called either 태양절 or 4·15 명절.

rows: Seven Socialists’ National Holidays (written 사회주의 7대 명절)
the 4·15 holiday: another name of 태양절

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 절 (節)
explanations.body: The original meaning of this Sino-Korean syllable is section or part (of something), as in 음절 (a syllable; “sound sect”) and 예절 (etiquette; manners; “polite parts”). When it is used in the context of time, 절 (節) refers to a section of time, that is, a season or festival day, as in 광복절 (Korea’s Independence day; “regain light/freedom day”) and 성탄절 (Christmas; “sacred birth day”). The book asks you to guess the meaning of 명절 and 사계절 (명 (名): name, fame, celebration); the answers are mine.

rows: a traditional holiday (mine; 명 (名): name, fame, celebration)

explanations.title: Topic B: I offered a big bow to my friend’s parents on New Year’s Day (설날에 친구 부모님께 세배를 드렸습니다)
explanations.body: Sarah, an American student attending a language school in Korea, is reporting in class about the traditional Korean New Year’s Day. (The English is mine; the book gives none. The book writes 음력 1월 1일; it is spelled out here. The book’s footnotes: 4. When quoting directly, 라고 (말)하다 is added after the quotation. 5. 한 해 동안 잘 지내라 is a common blessing given on New Year’s Day and literally means “stay healthy during the year.” 6. The traditional games introduced in this chapter are also called 전통민속놀이 (traditional folk games).)

examples.text: 음력 일월 일일은 설입니다.
examples.translation: eumnyeok irwol irireun seorimnida. — The first day of the first month by the lunar calendar is 설.

examples.text: 설은 한국의 가장 큰 명절입니다.
examples.translation: seoreun hangugui gajang keun myeongjeorimnida. — 설 is Korea’s biggest traditional holiday.

examples.text: 설에는 가족과 친척들과 함께 시간을 보냅니다.
examples.translation: seoreneun gajokgwa chincheokdeulgwa hamkke siganeul bonaemnida. — On 설 people spend time with their family and relatives.

examples.text: 그래서 고향을 찾아가는 사람들이 많습니다.
examples.translation: geuraeseo gohyangeul chajaganeun saramdeuri manseumnida. — So many people visit their hometowns.

examples.text: 기차역과 고속버스 터미널, 공항 등은 귀성객들로 붐빕니다.
examples.translation: gichayeokgwa gosokbeoseu teomineol, gonghang deungeun gwiseonggaekdeullo bumbimnida. — Train stations, express bus terminals, airports and so on are crowded with people heading to their hometowns.

examples.text: 그리고 고속도로도 많이 막힙니다.
examples.translation: geurigo gosokdorodo mani makimnida. — And the expressways are also heavily congested.

examples.text: 설날 아침에는 가족들이 모두 일찍 일어나서 제일 먼저 한복을 입습니다.
examples.translation: seollal achimeneun gajokdeuri modu iljjik ireonaseo jeil meonjeo hanbogeul ipseumnida. — On the morning of the Lunar New Year, all the family members get up early and first of all put on hanbok.

examples.text: 그리고 조상님께 차례를 지내고 어른들께 세배도 드립니다.
examples.translation: geurigo josangnimkke charyereul jinaego eoreundeulkke sebaedo deurimnida. — And they hold a memorial service for their ancestors and also make a formal bow to the elders.

examples.text: 세배를 하면서 보통 새해 복 많이 받으세요 라고 말합니다.
examples.translation: sebaereul hamyeonseo botong saehae bok mani badeuseyo rago malhamnida. — While bowing, they usually say “Happy New Year!” (literally “Receive many blessings in the new year!”).

examples.text: 그러면 어른들께서는 세뱃돈을 주시면서 한 해 동안 건강하게 잘 지내라고 하십니다.
examples.translation: geureomyeon eoreundeulkkeseoneun sebaetdoneul jusimyeonseo han hae dongan geonganghage jal jinaerago hasimnida. — Then the elders give New Year’s money and say, “Stay healthy during the year.”

examples.text: 세배를 드린 후에는 가족이 다 같이 모여서 떡국을 먹습니다.
examples.translation: sebaereul deurin hueneun gajogi da gachi moyeoseo tteokgugeul meokseumnida. — After the bows, the whole family gathers together and eats rice cake soup.

examples.text: 설날에는 보통 성묘를 가거나 전통 놀이를 합니다.
examples.translation: seollareneun botong seongmyoreul gageona jeontong norireul hamnida. — On the Lunar New Year they usually visit ancestral graves or play traditional games.

explanations.title: Note 1: 세뱃돈
explanations.body: 세뱃돈 is the money people receive on 설날 when they bow to their parents or other older family members. 세뱃돈 is a compound noun made of 세배 and 돈.

explanations.title: Note 2: 전통민속놀이 (traditional folk games)
explanations.body: There are several traditional outdoor games Koreans enjoy during the holiday seasons. 팽이치기 (top spinning) on a frozen river or pond is a favorite for boys. 제기차기 (hacky sack) is another popular game among boys. In 제기차기 contests, the winner is determined by the number of kicks made in succession without letting the 제기 (hacky sack) hit the ground. 연날리기 (kite flying) is a popular activity young boys and girls can enjoy, and it dates back to the Shilla Dynasty. For young women, games like 널뛰기 (seesaw jumping) and 그네뛰기 (swinging) are popular during the holiday seasons. In 널뛰기, two people stand on opposite ends of a long wooden board balanced on a tightly folded bag of straw and take turns jumping on their respective ends of the board.

explanations.title: Cultural note: 효도 관광
explanations.body: Korea has long been influenced by Confucianism, an ethical and philosophical belief system developed from the teachings of Confucius. According to Confucianism, filial piety (효 or 효도), a respect for parents and ancestors, is considered the most important virtue. Therefore, 효도 is prevalent in Korean society, and 효도 관광 (literally “filial piety sightseeing”) is one way adult children show respect to their parent(s) or grandparent(s). The children arrange a vacation for them and pay all the travel expenses. This is known as 효도관광, and many travel agencies offer various 효도관광 programs.

explanations.title: Follow-up 1 (Reading): three special occasion cards
explanations.body: The book shows three handwritten cards and asks you to identify the occasion and, in English, write the occasion and the suggested plans in a table. The book glosses 제자: a student, an apprentice, a disciple; 사랑(하다): love. The texts were read from the page image; the English is mine. Card 1:

examples.text: 보고 싶은 박 선생님께,
examples.translation: bogo sipeun bak seonsaengnimkke, — To Teacher Park, whom I miss,

examples.text: 선생님, 그 동안 잘 지내셨어요?
examples.translation: seonsaengnim, geu dongan jal jinaesyeosseoyo? — Teacher, have you been well all this time?

examples.text: 선생님 수업시간이 아직도 생각나요.
examples.translation: seonsaengnim sueopsigani ajikdo saenggangnayo. — I still remember your class time.

examples.text: 선생님 시간은 늘 재미있었어요.
examples.translation: seonsaengnim siganeun neul jaemiisseosseoyo. — Your lessons were always fun.

examples.text: 잘 가르쳐 주셔서 감사합니다.
examples.translation: jal gareucheo jusyeoseo gamsahamnida. — Thank you for teaching me well.

examples.text: 보고 싶어요. 다음 주에 선생님을 모시고 식사 한번 하고 싶어요.
examples.translation: bogo sipeoyo. daeum jue seonsaengnimeul mosigo siksa hanbeon hago sipeoyo. — I miss you. Next week I would like to take you out for a meal once.

examples.text: 전화 드릴게요.
examples.translation: jeonhwa deurilgeyo. — I will call you.

examples.text: 제자 승민 올림
examples.translation: jeja seungmin ollim — Your student Seungmin

explanations.title: Card 2
explanations.body: The second card (the English is mine):

examples.text: 정수야!
examples.translation: jeongsuya! — Jungsu!

examples.text: 어린이 날 축하해!
examples.translation: eorini nal chukahae! — Happy Children’s Day!

examples.text: 엄마, 아빠가 늘 바빠서 많이 못 놀아줬지? 미안해.
examples.translation: eomma, appaga neul bappaseo mani mot norajwotji? mianhae. — Mom and Dad are always busy, so we couldn’t play with you much, could we? We’re sorry.

examples.text: 그렇지만 엄마아빠는 우리 정수를 많이 많이 사랑해.
examples.translation: geureochiman eommaappaneun uri jeongsureul mani mani saranghae. — But Mom and Dad love our Jungsu very, very much.

examples.text: 우리 이번 어린이 날에는 어린이 대공원에 같이 가서 놀자.
examples.translation: uri ibeon eorini nareneun eorini daegongwone gachi gaseo nolja. — This Children’s Day, let’s go to the Children’s Grand Park together and play.

examples.text: 사랑해, 우리 아들!
examples.translation: saranghae, uri adeul! — I love you, our son!

examples.text: 엄마아빠가
examples.translation: eommaappaga — From Mom and Dad

explanations.title: Card 3
explanations.body: The third card (the English is mine):

examples.text: 엄마, 아빠
examples.translation: eomma, appa — Mom, Dad,

examples.text: 늘 바빠서 부모님하고 같이 시간을 많이 못 보냈네요. 죄송해요.
examples.translation: neul bappaseo bumonimhago gachi siganeul mani mot bonaenneyo. joesonghaeyo. — I have always been busy, so I couldn’t spend much time with my parents. I’m sorry.

examples.text: 올해는 엄마, 아빠 모시고 좋은 곳에 많이 갈게요.
examples.translation: olhaeneun eomma, appa mosigo joeun gose mani galgeyo. — This year I will take you, Mom and Dad, to many nice places.

examples.text: 엄마, 아빠, 사랑해요!
examples.translation: eomma, appa, saranghaeyo! — Mom, Dad, I love you!

examples.text: 이번 어버이날에는 엄마, 아빠 모시고 좋은 식당에 가서 외식해요.
examples.translation: ibeon eobeoinareneun eomma, appa mosigo joeun sikdange gaseo oesikaeyo. — This Parents’ Day, let’s take you, Mom and Dad, to a nice restaurant and eat out.

examples.text: 소정 올림
examples.translation: sojeong ollim — From Sojeong

explanations.title: Activity 3 (Reading): a survey about Parents’ Day
explanations.body: The book gives an article about the results of a survey on a Korean celebration and asks you to (a) skim it and identify the occasion, (b) list the 11 gift items in order of preference in English (one answer is given: underwear is no. 7), and (c) summarize in English the plans of the respondents (52.1%: spending time with parents, given). The text is the book’s (the figures are spelled out in Hangul); the English is mine.

examples.text: 어버이날 선물은 현금이 최고
examples.translation: eobeoinal seonmureun hyeongeumi choego — Cash is the best Parents’ Day present

examples.text: 한국사람들은 어버이날 부모님에게 어떤 선물을 드리고 싶을까?
examples.translation: hanguksaramdeureun eobeoinal bumonimege eotteon seonmureul deurigo sipeulkka? — What kind of present do Korean people want to give their parents on Parents’ Day?

examples.text: 그리고 어버이날 어떤 계획이 있을까?
examples.translation: geurigo eobeoinal eotteon gyehoegi isseulkka? — And what plans do they have for Parents’ Day?

examples.text: 한 여론조사에 따르면 현금을 가장 선호한다고 한다.
examples.translation: han yeoronjosae ttareumyeon hyeongeumeul gajang seonhohandago handa. — According to an opinion poll, they say they prefer cash most.

examples.text: 오백 명의 응답자 중 육십사 퍼센트가 어버이날 선물로 부모님에게 현금을 드리고 싶다고 했다.
examples.translation: obaek myeongui eungdapja jung yuksipsa peosenteuga eobeoinal seonmullo bumonimege hyeongeumeul deurigo sipdago haetda. — Of 500 respondents, 64% said they wanted to give their parents cash as a Parents’ Day present.

examples.text: 현금에 이어 건강식품 십육 퍼센트, 옷 칠 퍼센트, 꽃 사 퍼센트, 화장품 이 점 이 퍼센트, 넥타이 일 점 팔 퍼센트, 속옷 일 점 오 퍼센트, 상품권 일 점 삼 퍼센트, 여행상품 영 점 팔 퍼센트, 공연티켓 영 점 칠 퍼센트, 지갑 영 점 칠 퍼센트 등으로 조사됐다.
examples.translation: hyeongeume ieo geongangsikpum simnyuk peosenteu, ot chil peosenteu, kkot sa peosenteu, hwajangpum i jeom i peosenteu, nektai il jeom pal peosenteu, sogot il jeom o peosenteu, sangpumgwon il jeom sam peosenteu, yeohaengsangpum yeong jeom pal peosenteu, gongyeontiket yeong jeom chil peosenteu, jigap yeong jeom chil peosenteu deungeuro josadwaetda. — After cash: health food 16%, clothes 7%, flowers 4%, cosmetics 2.2%, neckties 1.8%, underwear 1.5%, gift certificates 1.3%, travel packages 0.8%, performance tickets 0.7%, wallets 0.7% and so on.

examples.text: 어버이날 계획에 대해서는 응답자 오십이 점 일 퍼센트가 부모님과 함께 시간을 보내겠다고 응답했다.
examples.translation: eobeoinal gyehoege daehaeseoneun eungdapja osibi jeom il peosenteuga bumonimgwa hamkke siganeul bonaegetdago eungdapaetda. — As for Parents’ Day plans, 52.1% of respondents answered that they would spend time with their parents.

examples.text: 응답자 이십구 점 구 퍼센트는 선물을 보내겠다고 답했고, 응답자 십오 점 삼 퍼센트는 부모님과 전화통화만 하겠다고 답했으며, 이 점 육 퍼센트는 아무것도 안 하겠다고 했다.
examples.translation: eungdapja isipgu jeom gu peosenteuneun seonmureul bonaegetdago dapaetgo, eungdapja sibo jeom sam peosenteuneun bumonimgwa jeonhwatonghwaman hagetdago dapaesseumyeo, i jeom yuk peosenteuneun amugeotdo an hagetdago haetda. — 29.9% of respondents answered that they would send a present, 15.3% answered that they would only talk with their parents by phone, and 2.6% said they would do nothing.

explanations.body: The book leaves the tables blank except the two given answers; these are my answers.

explanations.body: Activity 2 (a video clip from the Korean TV drama 거침없이 하이킥 (MBC America) in which an elderly woman tells her housekeeper what her family members will do for her on Parents’ Day) is a video activity; Activity 1 is a SMART Board activity; Activity 4 (이날에는 무엇을 할까요?: reading three texts about occasions Koreans celebrate and discussing creative ideas, in groups) is a group activity whose texts are not in the book’s text.

lessons.title: 304. Ch 23 · Grammar A: indirectly quoted statements with -다고 하다 / -라고 하다
lessons.subtitle: 한국말이 쉽다고 해요 · 비가 오겠다고 해요 · 군인이라고 합니다 · 의사가 아니라고 합니다

explanations.title: Expressing indirectly quoted statements
explanations.body:
In English, when we want to report or quote someone else’s statement indirectly, we normally use the phrase (the subject) says [that] …, as in He says [that] Korean is easy or My mom says [that] she is retiring next year. The presence of that can be optional.

In Korean, when we want to report or quote someone’s statement indirectly, we use the phrase -다고 하다, which is the English equivalent of (the subject) says [that]. Note that the verb in each indirectly quoted statement ends in the formal blunt form -다. (Refer to the Grammar in Focus of Chapter 15 if you feel unfamiliar with the formal blunt form.) The statement is immediately followed by 고 하다, which can be interpreted as to say [that] …, to state [that] …, to comment [that] …, etc. 고 functions as an object marker and indicates that the quoted statement is the object of the verb 하다. (When a declarative clause becomes the object of a verb, it takes 고, not 을/를, as an object marker.)

When an indirectly quoted statement ends with the verb 이다 or 아니다, however, -다고 하다 changes to -라고 하다.

examples.text: 한국말이 쉽다고 해요.
examples.translation: hangungmari swipdago haeyo. — (Someone) says that Korean is easy.

examples.text: 내일 비가 오겠다고 해요.
examples.translation: naeil biga ogetdago haeyo. — (Someone) says that it will rain tomorrow.

examples.text: 마크 씨가 군인이라고 합니다.
examples.translation: makeu ssiga guninirago hamnida. — (Someone) says that Mark is a serviceman.

examples.text: 민재 씨가 의사가 아니라고 합니다.
examples.translation: minjae ssiga uisaga anirago hamnida. — (Someone) says that Minjae is not a doctor.

explanations.title: Who says it
explanations.body: Keep in mind that the speaker who is reporting the indirectly quoted statement is usually not named. If you want to be sure the listener understands who the reporting speaker is, you can express it as follows:

examples.text: 김 선생님은 한국말이 쉽다고 해요.
examples.translation: gim seonsaengnimeun hangungmari swipdago haeyo. — Mr. Kim says that Korean is easy.

explanations.title: The rule: formal blunt form + 고 하다
explanations.body: In the book’s table (the arrows show the change).

rows: When the quoted statement ends in a verb other than 이다 and 아니다
When the quoted statement ends with the verb 이다 or 아니다
change 다 to 라 and add 고 하다
… 군인이다 → … 군인이라고 하다; … 군인이 아니다 → … 군인이 아니라고 하다

examples.translation: sin seonsaengnimui agiga yeppeudago hamnida. — (Someone) says that Mr. Shin’s baby is cute.

examples.text: 정수가 열심히 공부했다고 합니다.
examples.translation: jeongsuga yeolsimhi gongbuhaetdago hamnida. — (Someone) says that Jungsoo studied hard.

examples.text: 정 이병이 자동차가 있다고 합니다.

examples.translation: geu keompyuteoneun bissan geosirago hamnida. — (Someone) says that the computer is an expensive one.

explanations.title: Forms (mine)
explanations.body: The forms are made by the book’s rule (the formal blunt form: an action verb takes ㄴ다/는다, a stative verb takes 다, the past takes 았/었다, and the future takes 겠다).

explanations.title: More examples and the Follow-up 1 model
explanations.body: The core vocabulary’s example and the footnote’s examples with 고, and the model of Follow-up 1 (What does he say?), in which a group of three plays a game: Student A makes a statement, Student B pretends to have a problem hearing and asks Student C what the statement was, and Student C reports it using -다고 합니다:

examples.text: 아버님은 오늘 늦게 오신다고 말했습니다.
examples.translation: abeonimeun oneul neutge osindago malhaetseumnida. — My father said that he will come late today. (the core vocabulary’s example)

examples.text: 나는 미국이 크다고 생각해요.
examples.translation: naneun migugi keudago saenggakaeyo. — I think that America is big. (the book’s footnote on 고)

examples.text: 신이 있다고 믿습니까?
examples.translation: sini itdago mitseumnikka? — Do you believe that there is a god? (the book’s footnote on 고)

examples.text: 한국말이 재미있습니다.
examples.translation: hangungmari jaemiitseumnida. — Korean is interesting. (A)

examples.text: 뭐라고요?
examples.translation: mworagoyo? — What did he say? (B, playing a person who has a problem hearing)

examples.text: 한국말이 재미있다고 합니다.
examples.translation: hangungmari jaemiitdago hamnida. — He says that Korean is interesting. (C)

explanations.title: Activities left out
explanations.body: Follow-up 1 (a group game), Follow-up 4 (“Spread the Rumor!”, a team game) are group and class activities; Follow-up 2 and 3 are in the next lesson.

lessons.title: 306. Ch 23 · Grammar B: asking for confirmation or seeking agreement with -지요
lessons.subtitle: 오늘 날씨가 좋지요? · 좋죠? · 좋지? · 어제 친구를 방문했지요?

explanations.title: Asking for confirmation or seeking agreement
explanations.body:
In English, we use a tag question to ask for confirmation or to seek agreement, as in “It’s a beautiful day, isn’t it?” and “You are going to New York this summer, aren’t you?”

In Korean, we use the verb ending -지요 or -죠 (abbreviated form of 지요) to ask for confirmation or to seek agreement. 요 in 지요 is omitted by people who do not maintain social distance. If we were to use the above expressions among friends, the verb ending is shortened to -지.

examples.text: 오늘 날씨가 좋지요?
examples.translation: oneul nalssiga jochiyo? — Today’s weather is good, isn’t it?

examples.text: 오늘 날씨가 좋죠?
examples.translation: oneul nalssiga jocho? — Today’s weather is good, isn’t it?

examples.text: 한국말이 쉽지 않지요?
examples.translation: hangungmari swipji anchiyo? — Korean is not easy, is it?

examples.text: 한국말이 쉽지 않죠?
examples.translation: hangungmari swipji ancho? — Korean is not easy, is it?

examples.text: 오늘 날씨가 좋지?
examples.translation: oneul nalssiga jochi? — Today’s weather is good, isn’t it? (among friends)

examples.text: 한국말이 쉽지 않지?
examples.translation: hangungmari swipji anchi? — Korean is not easy, is it? (among friends)

explanations.title: The rule
explanations.body: -지요? or -죠?

rows: When creating a tag question and social distance needs to be maintained
1. 오늘 날씨가 좋지요? 2. 내일 뉴욕에 가지요?
1. 오늘 날씨가 좋죠? 2. 내일 뉴욕에 가죠?

lessons.title: 307. Ch 23 · Grammar C: “used to” with -았었 / -었었
lessons.subtitle: 수영했었어요 · 하와이에 살았었어요 · 책을 많이 읽었었어요 · 입대 전에 게임을 많이 했었지요

explanations.title: Expressing “used to”
explanations.body:
In English, the expression “used to + verb” implies past actions that no longer occur or past conditions that no longer exist. For example: I used to eat at the chow hall (but I no longer eat there); My brother used to be nice to his girlfriend (but he is no longer nice to her).

In Korean, adding the syllable 었 to a past tense verb takes care of this. Note that 었 is inserted between the past tense marker 았/었 and the verb ending 어요.

examples.text: 호텔 수영장에서 수영했었어요.
examples.translation: hotel suyeongjangeseo suyeonghaesseosseoyo. — I used to swim in the hotel swimming pool (but I no longer do that).

examples.text: 날씨가 좋았었어요.
examples.translation: nalssiga joasseosseoyo. — The weather used to be good (but is not any more).

explanations.title: Stative verbs and 이다, 아니다, 있다, 없다
explanations.body: However, the past tense of stative verbs (e.g., 좋다, 예쁘다, 춥다) and the past tense of the verbs 이다, 아니다, 있다 and 없다 can also imply that past conditions no longer exist. Thus, depending on the context, 날씨가 좋았어요 can simply mean “The weather was good” or “The weather used to be good (but is not any more).”

examples.text: 여기에 극장이 있었어요.
examples.translation: yeogie geukjangi isseosseoyo. — There was a theater here or There used to be a theater here.

examples.text: 여기에 극장이 있었었어요.
examples.translation: yeogie geukjangi isseosseosseoyo. — There used to be a theater here. (the book’s contrast)

explanations.title: The rule
explanations.body: verb stem + past tense marker 았/었 + 었 (+ 어요).

examples.text: 어렸을 때 하와이에 살았었어요.
examples.translation: eoryeosseul ttae hawaie sarasseosseoyo. — I used to live in Hawaii when I was young.

examples.text: 김 일병이 사무실에 왔었어요.
examples.translation: gim ilbyeongi samusire wasseosseoyo. — PFC Kim visited the office. (But now he is gone).

examples.text: 채소를 잘 안 먹었었어요.
examples.translation: chaesoreul jal an meogeosseosseoyo. — I used to not eat vegetables very often.

examples.text: 책을 많이 읽었었어요.
examples.translation: chaegeul mani ilgeosseosseoyo. — I used to read books a lot.

explanations.title: Forms (mine)
explanations.body: The forms are made by the book’s rule.

explanations.title: More examples and the models of Follow-up 3 and 5
explanations.body: The core vocabulary’s example and the example from Topic C, and the models of Follow-up 3 (changing a verb phrase into one with -았었 or -었었 and translating it) and Follow-up 5 (입대 전에 게임을 많이 했었지요?: asking and answering about what you used to do or did not use to do before enlisting). The English is mine.

explanations.title: Self-evaluation
explanations.body:
Recall the objectives of the chapter and ask yourself whether you have achieved them (the book asks you to tick Yes or No). If you tick “No” for any item, the book suggests: review that section on your own; find a study partner and review it as a pair or group; and tell your academic advisor or team leader which areas you need more help with, so that they can provide activities tailored to your learning style and needs.

Now I am able to: identify and talk about important Korean holidays and observances; identify and talk about activities done on traditional Korean holidays; and express gratitude to teachers and parents.

Now I have a clear understanding of: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; -지요 used to ask for confirmation or seek agreement; -았었다 or -었었다 (used to [do/not do something]); -다고 하다 or -라고 하다 used to quote indirectly; and the Sino-Korean syllables 객 (客) and 절 (節).

explanations.title: What Chapter 24 teaches (한국의 군대 생활)
explanations.body:
Chapter 24, “Military Life in Korea”, has three topic presentations, grammar in focus, activities, a self-evaluation and the core vocabulary.

When you finish the chapter you will be able to: identify and talk about general military terms, branch specialties or military occupational specialties; identify and talk about basic military training, military gear, equipment and weaponry; and describe the military organizational structure, such as unit assignments and duty sections.

You will become familiar with: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; -(으/느)냐고 하다 to quote a question indirectly; -(으)라고 하다 to quote a request or command indirectly; -자고 하다 to quote a suggestion indirectly; a Sino-Korean noun + 하다 vs. 되다; ~밖에 + a negative verb (only); and the Sino-Korean syllables 무 (務), 체 (體), 대 (隊) and 과 (課).

explanations.title: 육군 병과 (Army branch specialties)
explanations.body: The book shows pictures of six army branch specialties with these labels. The English is the book’s (from the Core Vocabulary), except 기갑병 and 정보통신병, which are mine.

explanations.title: Cultural note: 여군
explanations.body: Unlike men in South Korea, women are not required to serve in the military. However, women over the age of 18 can volunteer to serve in the military as sergeants or officers. Korean women first joined the military during the Korean War. They are now permitted to serve in every service branch.

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 무 (務)
explanations.body: The Sino-Korean syllable means work or service, as in 의무병 (a medic; “medical work soldier”), 근무 (service; duty; work; “diligent work”), and 복무 (public service; “service in [official] dress”).

explanations.title: North Korea Report
explanations.body: North Korea has the world’s fourth largest military force, known as 조선인민군 (the Korean People’s Army or KPA). The armed forces, under the control of supreme commander of the KPA (국방위원장) Kim Jong-un, have five branches: the Army Ground Forces, the Navy, the Air Force and Air Defense Forces, Strategic Forces (missile forces), and Special Forces (special operations forces). It is mandatory for both men and women to serve in the armed forces starting from the age of 17. The service obligation is 10 years for men, while women serve until the age of 23 (but the service requirement was reportedly reduced in 2021 to 7-8 years for men and 5 years for women).

explanations.body: Sejoon, on leave from military duty, is talking with Junghwan, who is about to join the military. (The English is mine; the book gives none. The book writes 6개월; it is spelled out here. The book’s footnote: the kinship terms 형/오빠 (older brother) and 누나/언니 (older sister) are often used by young people to address their older friends.)

explanations.title: Topic B: I had basic training at the Nonsan Army Training Center (논산 훈련소에서 신병훈련을 받았어요)
explanations.body: The following report is about Minsoo’s basic training experiences. (The English is mine; the book gives none. The book writes 5주; it is spelled out here. The book’s footnote: ~(와/과) 같은 means like ~ or such as ~. In English we say “Asian languages like Korean” or “services such as the navy and air force.” Thus, 군복과 군화(와) 같은 보급품 means supplies like a military uniform and military boots.)

examples.text: 저는 논산 훈련소에서 오 주 동안 신병훈련을 받았습니다.
examples.translation: jeoneun nonsan hullyeonsoeseo o ju dongan sinbyeonghullyeoneul badatseumnida. — I received recruit training at the Nonsan training center for five weeks.

examples.text: 훈련소에 도착한 후 먼저 신체검사를 받았습니다.
examples.translation: hullyeonsoe dochakan hu meonjeo sinchegeomsareul badatseumnida. — After arriving at the training center, I first had a physical examination.

examples.text: 그 다음에 교관들이 군복과 군화 같은 보급품을 나누어 주었습니다.
examples.translation: geu daeume gyogwandeuri gunbokgwa gunhwa gateun bogeuppumeul nanueo jueotseumnida. — Then the instructors handed out supplies like military uniforms and military boots.

examples.text: 우리는 매일 아침 일찍 집합을 해서 팔 굽혀 펴기와 달리기 등 체력훈련을 받았습니다.
examples.translation: urineun maeil achim iljjik jipabeul haeseo pal gupyeo pyeogiwa dalligi deung cheryeokullyeoneul badatseumnida. — Every morning we fell into formation early and had physical training such as push-ups and running.

examples.text: 아침 식사 후에는 사격훈련, 전투훈련, 화생방훈련, 제식훈련을 받았습니다.
examples.translation: achim siksa hueneun sagyeokullyeon, jeontuhullyeon, hwasaengbanghullyeon, jesikullyeoneul badatseumnida. — After breakfast we had marksmanship training, combat training, CBR training and drill and ceremony training.

examples.text: 전투훈련을 받을 때는 완전무장을 하고 행군도 했습니다.
examples.translation: jeontuhullyeoneul badeul ttaeneun wanjeonmujangeul hago haenggundo haetseumnida. — During combat training we put on full-battle dress and also marched.

examples.text: 또 밤에는 보초도 섰습니다.
examples.translation: tto bameneun bochodo seotseumnida. — Also at night we stood guard.

examples.text: 교관이 보초를 두 시간마다 교대 하라고 했습니다.
examples.translation: gyogwani bochoreul du siganmada gyodae harago haetseumnida. — The instructor told us to rotate the guard every two hours.

examples.text: 훈련 받는 동안 행군과 유격훈련이 제일 힘들었습니다.
examples.translation: hullyeon banneun dongan haenggungwa yugyeokullyeoni jeil himdeureotseumnida. — During the training, marching and the obstacle course were the hardest.

examples.text: 그렇지만 소총 쏘기와 수류탄 던지기는 재미있었습니다.
examples.translation: geureochiman sochong ssogiwa suryutan deonjigineun jaemiisseotseumnida. — But shooting the rifle and throwing hand grenades were fun.

explanations.title: Core words and phrases of Topic B
explanations.body: The meanings are the book’s (from the Core Vocabulary of the chapter); optional parts are shortened. (The core list of Topic B also has the grammar patterns -(으/느)냐고 하다, -(으)라고 하다 and -자고 하다, which are in the grammar lessons.)

rows: (交代) (~하다) an alternation; a shift (to take turns; to alternate; to rotate)
to carry (a thing on one’s shoulder)

(手榴彈) a hand grenade; “hand pomegranate explosive”
(身體檢査) (~하다) a physical examination; checkup (to have a physical exam)
(完全武裝) (~하다) full-battle dress; “completely armed” (to wear full-battle dress)
(集合) (~하다) a formation; gathering; assembly (to fall into formation)
(體力訓鍊) physical training; “body strength training”
(化生放訓鍊) chemical, biological, and radiological (CBR) training

explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means a body. The book asks you to guess the meaning of 체육관, 체중 and 체력 (중 (重): weight, heaviness; 력 (力): ability, power). The answers are mine; 체험 is in the core vocabulary.

explanations.title: Notes: 카투사 (KATUSA)
explanations.body: KATUSA is an acronym for Korean Augmentation to the United States Army. The term (known as 카투사 or 카추사) refers to either the program that provides the U.S. military in Korea with bilingual Korean soldiers or to a KATUSA soldier. With few exceptions, all men serve in the R.O.K. Army, and many young men who speak English apply to be 카투사. Once selected, they complete six-week R.O.K. Army basic training and work with a United States Army unit garrisoned in Korea. 카추사 soldiers serve as translators for the local populace and the U.S. Army. They also help the U.S. Army maneuver in unfamiliar terrain. The program symbolizes friendship and mutual support between the two nations.

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 대 (隊)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means organized (military) unit or military. The book asks you to guess the meaning of 군대, 입대, 부대 and 대대; the answers are the core words’ meanings (부대 is mine).

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 과 (課)
explanations.body: The Chinese character of this syllable depicts a government official’s word (言) on a fruit tree (果) for taxation. Thus the Sino-Korean syllable means levying a tax on or taxation, as in 과세 (taxation; imposition of taxes). However, the syllable has evolved to mean routine task (by a government official) or department/section (of government officials), as in 일과 (a daily task; daily work), 정보과 (an intelligence section), 학과 (a [college] department; “school department”) and 과장 (a section chief; a department chair).

explanations.title: Activity 3 (Reading): the new commander of the 8th U.S. Army
explanations.body: The excerpt is from a news article about the new commander of the 8th U.S. Army. The book asks you to (1) write, using only the headline, what the article is about, and (2) identify his previous assignments for 1986–1987, 2000–2002 and 2005–2006, in English. The text is the book’s (the years and the numbers are spelled out in Hangul); the English is mine.

lessons.title: 316. Ch 24 · Grammar A: indirectly quoted questions with -(으/느)냐고 하다
lessons.subtitle: 날씨가 좋으냐고 합니다 · 무엇을 먹느냐고 합니다 · 영화를 봤느냐고 합니다 · 농구했냐고 합니다

explanations.title: Indirectly quoting questions, requests and suggestions
explanations.body: In the previous chapter, you learned about -다고 하다, which is used to indirectly report or quote a statement, as in 한국말이 쉽다고 해요 (People) say that Korean is easy. In this lesson, you will learn about three more patterns for indirectly reporting or quoting: (1) -냐고 하다 for questions, (2) -라고 하다 for requests, and (3) -자고 하다 for suggestions.

explanations.title: Indirectly quoted questions
explanations.body: When quoting or reporting a question indirectly, we can use the pattern -(으/느)냐고 하다. Depending on the type of verb, -(으)냐고 하다 or -냐고 하다 is used.

examples.text: 나에게 오늘 날씨가 좋으냐고 합니다.
examples.translation: naege oneul nalssiga joeunyago hamnida. — [He] asks me if the weather is good today.

examples.text: 나에게 어제 날씨가 좋았느냐고 합니다.
examples.translation: naege eoje nalssiga joanneunyago hamnida. — [He] asks me if the weather was good yesterday.

explanations.title: The rule: -(으/느)냐고 하다
explanations.body: In the book’s table.

rows: When the stative verb ends in a consonant
좋다 → 좋(으)냐고 하다; 작다 → 작(으)냐고 하다
When the stative verb ends in a vowel or ㄹ
예쁘다 → 예쁘냐고 하다; 크다 → 크냐고 하다; 길다 → 기냐고 하다
When the verb is an action verb including 있다 and 없다, or when the stative verb is in the future or past tense
먹다 → 먹(느)냐고 하다; 자다 → 자(느)냐고 하다; 있다 → 있(느)냐고 하다; 좋았다 → 좋았(느)냐고 하다; 좋겠다 → 좋겠(느)냐고 하다

examples.text: 나에게 무엇을 먹느냐고 합니다.
examples.translation: naege mueoseul meongneunyago hamnida. — [He] asks me what I am eating or what I eat.

examples.text: 나에게 무슨 영화를 봤느냐고 합니다.
examples.translation: naege museun yeonghwareul bwanneunyago hamnida. — [He] asks me what movie I saw.

examples.text: 친구에게 무슨 영화를 보겠느냐고 합니다.
examples.translation: chinguege museun yeonghwareul bogenneunyago hamnida. — [He] asks my friend what movie he will see.

explanations.title: Forms (mine)
explanations.body: The forms are made by the book’s rule (the 느 is often dropped in speech: 먹냐고, 있냐고; stems with ㄹ lose it before 느 and 냐고: 살다 → 사느냐고, 길다 → 기냐고).

explanations.title: More examples and the Follow-up 1 model
explanations.body: The core vocabulary’s example and the model of Follow-up 1, in which the teacher asks the class a question and the partners take turns conveying it using -냐고 합니다:

lessons.title: 317. Ch 24 · Grammar A: quoting requests and suggestions with -(으)라고 하다 and -자고 하다
lessons.subtitle: 창문을 닫으라고 했습니다 · 숙제하라고 했습니다 · 도서관에 가자고 하십니다

explanations.title: Indirectly quoted requests/commands: -(으)라고 하다
explanations.body: When quoting or reporting a request/command indirectly, we can use the pattern -(으)라고 하다. The pattern can translate to ask/request/tell/command a person to [do something].

rows: When the stem of a verb ends in a consonant
닫다 → 닫으라고 하다; 먹다 → 먹으라고 하다
When the stem of a verb ends in a vowel or ㄹ
가다 → 가라고 하다; 보다 → 보라고 하다; 열다 → 열라고 하다

examples.text: 선생님이 나에게 창문을 닫으라고 했습니다.

explanations.title: Indirectly quoted suggestions: -자고 하다
explanations.body: When indirectly quoting or reporting a suggestion like “… (으)ㅂ시다” or “… (으)ㄹ까요”, we can use the pattern -자고 하다. The pattern can be translated as suggest (to a person) that we/they …

lessons.title: 318. Ch 24 · Grammar B: Sino-Korean noun + 하다 (active) vs. 되다 (passive)
lessons.subtitle: 번역하다 · 번역되다 · 준비했습니다 · 준비되었습니다 · 복잡하다

explanations.title: ~하다 (active voice) vs. ~되다 (passive voice)
explanations.body: You may notice that in a chapter glossary there are a number of Sino-Korean nouns with (~하다/~되다), for example 번역 (translation; to translate/to be translated) and 통역. The noun 번역 (translation) can be used as a verb when it is followed by 하다 or 되다 (e.g., 번역하다 and 번역되다). Note, however, that 번역하다 means to translate, whereas 번역되다 means to be translated. In other words, ~하다 is in the active voice and ~되다 is in the passive voice.

examples.text: 해리포터 시리즈가 한국말로 번역되었습니다.

explanations.title: Stative verbs with 하다
explanations.body: Some Sino-Korean words can be used with ~하다 but not with ~되다. When ~하다 is a stative verb, 되다 cannot be used. For example, 복잡하다 (to be congested; to be crowded) and 죄송하다 (to be sorry) are stative verbs. Thus, there is no such verb as *복잡되다 or *죄송되다.

examples.translation: gyotongi bokjapaeyo. — The traffic is congested. (복잡하다 is a stative verb; there is no 복잡되다)

lessons.title: 319. Ch 24 · Grammar C: expressing “only” with ~밖에 + a negative verb
lessons.subtitle: 테니스밖에 안 칩니다 · 채소밖에 안 먹어요 · 한 번밖에 안 가봤어요 · 영어밖에 못 합니다

explanations.title: Expressing “only” using ~밖에
explanations.body:
Recall the marker ~만 (only), which you learned about in an earlier chapter. It can be attached to a noun or phrase, as in 저는 테니스만 칩니다 and 주말에만 영화를 봅니다. We can replace ~만 in these two sentences with ~밖에, without affecting the meaning at all.

Note, however, that ~밖에 is always followed by a negative verb. This is because 밖에 means outside, and 저는 테니스밖에 안 칩니다 literally means “I don’t play (any sports) outside tennis.”

examples.text: 저는 테니스만 칩니다.
examples.translation: jeoneun teniseuman chimnida. — I play tennis only.

examples.text: 주말에만 영화를 봅니다.
examples.translation: jumareman yeonghwareul bomnida. — [I] watch movies only on weekends.

examples.text: 저는 테니스밖에 안 칩니다.
examples.translation: jeoneun teniseubakke an chimnida. — I play tennis only.

examples.text: 주말에밖에 영화를 안 봅니다.
examples.translation: jumarebakke yeonghwareul an bomnida. — [I] watch movies only on weekends.

explanations.title: The rule
explanations.body: noun + 밖에 + negative verb.

The book’s Core Vocabulary lists the core words of the chapter with an example sentence for each (the sentences and the English meanings are the book’s; the book gives no English for the sentences). The Hanja of the Sino-Korean words are in parentheses before the meaning.

explanations.title: Self-evaluation
explanations.body:
Recall the objectives of the chapter and ask yourself whether you have achieved them (the book asks you to tick Yes or No). If you tick “No” for any item, the book suggests: review that section on your own; find a study partner and review it as a pair or group; and tell your academic advisor or team leader which areas you need more help with, so that they can provide activities tailored to your learning style and needs.

Now I am able to: identify and talk about general military terms, branch specialties or military occupational specialties; identify and talk about basic military training, military gear, equipment and weaponry; and describe the military organizational structure, such as unit assignments and duty sections.

Now I have a clear understanding of: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; -(으/느)냐고 하다 to quote a question indirectly; -(으)라고 하다 to quote a request or command indirectly; -자고 하다 to quote a suggestion indirectly; a Sino-Korean noun + 하다 vs. 되다; ~밖에 + a negative verb (only); and the Sino-Korean syllables 무 (務), 체 (體), 대 (隊) and 과 (課).

explanations.title: What Chapter 25 teaches (한국의 가족)
explanations.body:
Chapter 25, “The Korean Family”, has three topic presentations, grammar in focus, activities, a self-evaluation and the core vocabulary.

When you finish the chapter you will be able to: identify and talk about family types and use kinship terms; identify and talk about changes in Korean family life; and describe a person’s appearance and personality.

You will become familiar with: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary section; the verb ending –잖아요; nouns derived from native Korean verbs; past tense verbs for a present state or condition; contractions of the topic marker 는 and the object marker 를; and the Sino-Korean syllables 장 (長), 차 (次), 조 (祖), 처 (妻) and 가 (家).

explanations.title: Notes 1: terms for children and siblings
explanations.body: Koreans often use the ordinal numbers in informal speech to refer to their children or siblings: 우리 집 첫째 (literally, “our family’s first”), 둘째 (second child), 셋째 (third child), etc. The youngest child is called (우리 집) 막내 (our youngest child). Koreans also use the following kinship terms to refer to their children (the book’s table: first, second, third and youngest son and daughter; the English is the book’s).

the oldest daughter (also 큰딸, 첫째 딸)
the youngest child (also 막내 아들, 막내 딸)

explanations.title: Notes 2 and 3: the number of children and family relationships
explanations.body:
Koreans often use the Sino-Korean syllables ~남 (男) (man or boy) and ~녀 (女) (woman or girl) preceded by a Sino number when they refer to a specific number of children: 삼남사녀 (three sons and four daughters); 일남이녀 (one son and two daughters). When a family has only one son, he is called 독자 (獨子) or 외아들; when a family has only a daughter and no other children, she is called 무남독녀 (無男獨女).

Koreans often use the Sino-Korean words ~(지)간 (之間) to refer to a relationship between family members: 부부(지)간 (husband-wife relationship; between husband and wife) and 부자(지)간 (father-son relationship; between father and son).

rows: an only daughter and no other children (無男獨女)

explanations.title: Cultural note: the oldest son
explanations.body: Heavily influenced by Confucianism, a traditional Korean family held its oldest son in highest esteem. Once married, he was responsible for carrying on the family name and lineage, keeping property in the family, and taking care of ancestral rites as well as aging parents. For this reason, the oldest son enjoyed a special status with an added bonus: He usually received the largest share of the family’s inheritance. Since the 1970s, however, when Korean society began to become industrialized, this tradition has been fading away. Nowadays, all siblings are expected to share in the responsibility of taking care of aging parents, and the number of parents who live with their second/third sons or daughters has increased. Despite these changes, however, an increasing number of elderly people prefer to live independently.

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 장 (長)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means long or big, as in 장거리 (long distance), 장기간 (a long period), 장화 (a boot; “long [leathered] shoe”), and 장남 (the eldest son; “big man”). The syllable also means the chief or head (of a group or an organization), as in 사장 (a company president; a business owner; “company head”), 병장 (a sergeant; “head of soldiers”), and 학장 (a dean; “school head”). The book asks you to guess 장녀 and 부대장; the answers (mine): 장녀 is the oldest daughter, 부대장 is a unit commander.

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 차 (次) and 조 (祖)
explanations.body: 차 (次) means next, second, or sequence. 조 (祖) means ancestor.

explanations.title: Topic A: A large family of four generations (대가 모여 사는 대가족)
explanations.body: A TV reporter is interviewing the head of a family spanning four generations. (The English is mine; the book gives none. The book writes 4대가; it is spelled out here. The book’s footnote: ~을/를 모시고 살다 literally means “to serve and live.” This expression is used when people live with parents, grandparents, or others who are considered superior in social status.)

examples.text: 기자: 안녕하십니까? 가족 소개를 해 주시겠습니까?
examples.translation: gija: annyeonghasimnikka? gajok sogaereul hae jusigetseumnikka? — How do you do? Would you introduce your family?

examples.text: 대철: 네. 조부모님, 부모님, 제 아내와 저 그리고 아이들이 같이 살고 있습니다.
examples.translation: daecheol: ne. jobumonim, bumonim, je anaewa jeo geurigo aideuri gachi salgo itseumnida. — Yes. My grandparents, my parents, my wife and I, and the children live together.

examples.text: 기자: 네. 요즘 흔하지 않은 대가족이군요!
examples.translation: gija: ne. yojeum heunhaji aneun daegajogigunyo! — I see. It’s an extended family, which is not common these days!

examples.text: 대철: 네. 저희 아버지가 장남이십니다. 그래서 항상 조부모님과 같이 살았어요. 그리고 저도 장남이어서 지금 어른들을 모시고 삽니다.
examples.translation: daecheol: ne. jeohui abeojiga jangnamisimnida. geuraeseo hangsang jobumonimgwa gachi sarasseoyo. geurigo jeodo jangnamieoseo jigeum eoreundeureul mosigo samnida. — Yes. My father is the oldest son. So he has always lived with my grandparents. And I am also the oldest son, so I now live serving the elders.

examples.text: 기자: 아, 네. 그럼 사 대가 같이 살고 계시는데, 불편한 점은 없으십니까?
examples.translation: gija: a, ne. geureom sa daega gachi salgo gyesineunde, bulpyeonhan jeomeun eopseusimnikka? — Oh, I see. Then four generations live together; are there any inconvenient points?

examples.text: 대철: 식구가 많으니까 불편할 때도 있어요. 다 같이 차를 타고 나갈 때 조금 불편해요. 그렇지만, 좋은 점이 더 많아요.
examples.translation: daecheol: sikguga maneunikka bulpyeonhal ttaedo isseoyo. da gachi chareul tago nagal ttae jogeum bulpyeonhaeyo. geureochiman, joeun jeomi deo manayo. — Since there are many family members, it is sometimes inconvenient. It’s a little inconvenient when we all go out in a car together. But there are more good points.

examples.text: 기자: 어떤 점이 좋으세요?
examples.translation: gija: eotteon jeomi joeuseyo? — What points are good?

examples.text: 대철: 어른들이 아이들을 잘 돌봐 주시니까 좋아요. 그리고 어려운 일이 있으면 어른들과 의논할 수 있어서 좋습니다.
examples.translation: daecheol: eoreundeuri aideureul jal dolbwa jusinikka joayo. geurigo eoryeoun iri isseumyeon eoreundeulgwa uinonhal su isseoseo joseumnida. — It’s good because the elders take good care of the children. And when there is a difficult matter, I can talk it over with the elders, which is good.

examples.text: 기자: 보통 여자분들은 따로 살고 싶어하는데, 부인은 어떠십니까?
examples.translation: gija: botong yeojabundeureun ttaro salgo sipeohaneunde, buineun eotteosimnikka? — Women usually want to live separately; how about your wife?

examples.text: 대철: 제 아내는 어른들과 같이 사는 것을 아주 좋아합니다.
examples.translation: daecheol: je anaeneun eoreundeulgwa gachi saneun geoseul aju joahamnida. — My wife likes living with the elders very much.

lessons.title: 323. Ch 25 · Topic A, Follow-up 2 and Activity 3: two family stories
lessons.subtitle: 대가족 · 핵가족 · 집안일 · 시집갔을 때 · 따로 살고 있습니다

explanations.title: Follow-up 2 (Reading): a married woman describes her family
explanations.body: The book asks you to read a family description written by a married woman, tick the family type (extended or nuclear family) and fill in a table in English (family members; positive and/or negative aspects). The text is the book’s (1살 is spelled out); the English is mine.

examples.text: 우리 가족은 요즘 흔하지 않은 대가족입니다.
examples.translation: uri gajogeun yojeum heunhaji aneun daegajogimnida. — My family is an extended family, which is not common these days.

examples.text: 조부모님과 부모님, 남편과 저, 그리고 저희 아이들까지 사 대가 한 집에 살고 있어요.
examples.translation: jobumonimgwa bumonim, nampyeongwa jeo, geurigo jeohui aideulkkaji sa daega han jibe salgo isseoyo. — Four generations live in one house: my grandparents, my parents, my husband and me, and our children.

examples.text: 저희는 아이가 셋인데, 아들 하나 딸 둘이 있습니다.
examples.translation: jeohuineun aiga sesinde, adeul hana ttal duri itseumnida. — We have three children: one son and two daughters.

examples.text: 아들은 중학생, 첫째 딸은 초등학생, 그리고 막내딸은 한 살입니다.
examples.translation: adeureun junghaksaeng, cheotjjae ttareun chodeunghaksaeng, geurigo mangnaettareun han sarimnida. — The son is a middle school student, the first daughter is an elementary school student, and the youngest daughter is one year old.

examples.text: 식구가 많아서 집안일이 많지만 온 가족이 다 함께 집안일을 합니다.
examples.translation: sikguga manaseo jibaniri manchiman on gajogi da hamkke jibanireul hamnida. — Since there are many family members there is a lot of housework, but the whole family does the housework together.

examples.text: 어른들께서는 막내딸을 잘 돌봐 주시고 남편과 큰아이들은 집 청소와 빨래를 도와줍니다.
examples.translation: eoreundeulkkeseoneun mangnaettareul jal dolbwa jusigo nampyeongwa keunaideureun jip cheongsowa ppallaereul dowajumnida. — The elders take good care of the youngest daughter, and my husband and the older children help with cleaning the house and the laundry.

examples.text: 그래서 집안일이 조금도 힘들지 않습니다.
examples.translation: geuraeseo jibaniri jogeumdo himdeulji anseumnida. — So the housework is not hard at all.

examples.text: 그렇지만, 집이 작고 화장실이 하나밖에 없어서 불편합니다.
examples.translation: geureochiman, jibi jakgo hwajangsiri hanabakke eopseoseo bulpyeonhamnida. — However, the house is small and there is only one bathroom, so it is inconvenient.

explanations.title: The table filled in (mine)
explanations.body: The book leaves the table blank; these are my answers.

rows: Grandparents, parents, husband and wife, a son, two daughters
Positive: the whole family does the housework; the elders take care of the youngest daughter; the husband and older children help. Negative: the house is small and there is only one bathroom

explanations.title: Activity 3 (Reading): changes in a man’s family two years ago
explanations.body: The book asks you to read a story in which a man talks about changes in his family that occurred two years ago and to fill in a table in English. The text is the book’s (7년, 5년, 2년 are spelled out); the English is mine.

examples.text: 저는 칠 년 전에 결혼해서 아들 하나, 딸 하나가 있습니다.
examples.translation: jeoneun chil nyeon jeone gyeolhonhaeseo adeul hana, ttal hanaga itseumnida. — I got married seven years ago and have one son and one daughter.

examples.text: 결혼하고 처음 오 년 동안 부모님을 모시고 살았습니다.
examples.translation: gyeolhonhago cheoeum o nyeon dongan bumonimeul mosigo saratseumnida. — For the first five years after marriage I lived with my parents.

examples.text: 결혼하지 않은 여동생도 같이 살았습니다.
examples.translation: gyeolhonhaji aneun yeodongsaengdo gachi saratseumnida. — My unmarried younger sister also lived with us.

examples.text: 이 년 전, 여동생이 시집갔을 때 부모님이 고향에서 살고 싶어 하셨습니다.
examples.translation: i nyeon jeon, yeodongsaengi sijipgasseul ttae bumonimi gohyangeseo salgo sipeo hasyeotseumnida. — Two years ago, when my younger sister got married, my parents wanted to live in their hometown.

examples.text: 그래서 이 년 전부터 저는 아내와 아이들하고만 따로 살고 있습니다.
examples.translation: geuraeseo i nyeon jeonbuteo jeoneun anaewa aideulhagoman ttaro salgo itseumnida. — So since two years ago I have been living separately with only my wife and children.

examples.text: 제 가족이 부모님과 여동생과 함께 살았을 때는 집안일이 많았습니다.
examples.translation: je gajogi bumonimgwa yeodongsaenggwa hamkke sarasseul ttaeneun jibaniri manatseumnida. — When my family lived with my parents and younger sister, there was a lot of housework.

examples.text: 그래서 아내에게 늘 미안했습니다.
examples.translation: geuraeseo anaeege neul mianhaetseumnida. — So I always felt sorry toward my wife.

examples.text: 그렇지만 부모님과 동생이 아이들과 잘 놀아 주었습니다.
examples.translation: geureochiman bumonimgwa dongsaengi aideulgwa jal nora jueotseumnida. — But my parents and my sibling played well with the children.

examples.text: 지금은 식구가 적으니까 조금 심심합니다.
examples.translation: jigeumeun sikguga jeogeunikka jogeum simsimhamnida. — Now there are few family members, so it is a little boring.

examples.text: 그렇지만 집안일도 많지 않고 여행도 자주 갈 수 있습니다.
examples.translation: geureochiman jibanildo manchi anko yeohaengdo jaju gal su itseumnida. — But there is not much housework and we can travel often.

explanations.title: The table filled in (mine)
explanations.body: The book leaves the table blank; these are my answers.

rows: Wife, two children, his parents and his unmarried younger sister
The parents and the sibling played well with the children
Not much housework; can travel often
A lot of housework; he felt sorry toward his wife
A little boring because there are few family members

explanations.title: Activities left out
explanations.body: Activity 1 (a SMART Board activity), Activity 2 (listening to three conversations asking about the other speaker’s family) and Activity 4 (어버이날 기념 효행상 추천: listening to interviews about two finalists for an exemplary-filial-conduct award from the Ministry of National Defense and choosing one, in pairs) are computer, audio and partner activities.

explanations.title: Notes: North Korea
explanations.body: In North Korea, 장인 and 장모 are called 가시아버지 and 가시어머니, respectively; 아내 is called 안해.

explanations.title: Cultural note: kinship terms of in-laws
explanations.body: Koreans have long valued the importance of family beyond their immediate and extended family. Therefore, kinship terms for non-blood relations are extensive and diverse. For example, when a man is married, he refers to his wife’s family as 처가/처가댁 (↑), which literally means “wife’s home.” A married man refers to his in-laws (except his father-in-law 장인 and mother-in-law 장모) with a word that begins with 처 (妻) wife, as in 처형 wife’s older sister, 처제 wife’s younger sister, 처남 wife’s brothers, etc. When a woman is married, she refers to her husband’s family as 시집/시댁 (↑). A married woman refers to her in-laws with a word that begins with 시 (媤) husband’s home, as in 시아버지 husband’s father, 시어머니 husband’s mother, 시누이 husband’s sister, 시동생 husband’s younger brother, etc. Once married, a woman refers to her own parents’ family with a word that begins with 친정 (親庭), as in 친정 아버지, 친정 어머니, 친정 동생, etc. Terms like 장가 (literally, “man’s in-laws’ home”) and 시집 (literally, “woman’s in-laws’ home”) are also used to express “tying the knot.” Although Koreans use the term 결혼하다, they also use 장가가다 or 장가들다, whose literal meaning is go to the (man’s) in-laws’ home or get in the in-laws’ home, when a man gets married. For a woman who marries, Koreans say 시집가다, which literally means go to the husband’s home. 친정 (親庭) literally means “true garden” or “biological garden” and refers to a married woman’s parents’ home, as in 친정 아버지, 친정 동생, 친정집, etc.

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 처 (妻)
explanations.body: The Chinese character of this Sino-Korean syllable describes a woman with a broom in her hand, implying woman working at home. So this syllable means wife, as in 처가 (one’s wife’s home), 처남 (one’s wife’s brother), 처제 (one’s wife’s younger sister; “wife’s younger sibling”), and 전처 (one’s ex-wife; “previous wife”). The book asks you to guess 처삼촌, 처형 and 처조카; the answers are mine (처형 is in the cultural note).

explanations.title: Follow-up 2 (Reading): survey results on families living with parents
explanations.body: The text is an excerpt from survey results about families living with their parents. The book asks you to fill in a table in English (positive aspects, negative aspects and solutions to the negative aspects). The text is the book’s; the English is mine. The book glosses 갈등: conflict, discord; 대화: a dialog, a conversation.

examples.text: 맞벌이 부부가 늘어나면서 시댁이나 처가에서 함께 사는 가족이 늘어나고 있다.
examples.translation: matbeori bubuga neureonamyeonseo sidaegina cheogaeseo hamkke saneun gajogi neureonago itda. — As the number of dual-income couples increases, families living together at the husband’s family’s or the wife’s family’s home are increasing.

examples.text: 야후 미디어 조사에 따르면 시댁이나 처가에서 부모를 모시고 사는 대부분의 가정은 부모와 같이 살면 아이를 키우는 데 도움을 받고, 생활비를 절약할 수 있어서 좋다고 대답했다.
examples.translation: yahu midieo josae ttareumyeon sidaegina cheogaeseo bumoreul mosigo saneun daebubunui gajeongeun bumowa gachi salmyeon aireul kiuneun de doumeul batgo, saenghwalbireul jeoryakal su isseoseo jotago daedapaetda. — According to a Yahoo Media survey, most families who live with their parents at the husband’s or wife’s family’s home answered that living with the parents is good because they get help raising the children and can save living expenses.

examples.text: 그러나 나쁜 점으로는 장모와 사위간의 갈등, 시어머니와 며느리간의 갈등이라고 대답했다.
examples.translation: geureona nappeun jeomeuroneun jangmowa sawiganui galdeung, sieomeoniwa myeoneuriganui galdeungirago daedapaetda. — However, as the bad points they answered the conflict between mother-in-law and son-in-law and the conflict between mother-in-law and daughter-in-law.

examples.text: 그리고 이러한 문제는 서로 다른 성격 때문이며, 더 많은 가족간의 대화가 필요하다고 말했다.
examples.translation: geurigo ireohan munjeneun seoro dareun seonggyeok ttaemunimyeo, deo maneun gajokganui daehwaga piryohadago malhaetda. — And they said that these problems are due to different personalities, and that more conversation among family members is needed.

explanations.title: Activity 2 (Reading): a news article on college students’ opinions on marriage
explanations.body: The book asks you to (a) translate the headline into English, (b) match each of the four paragraphs with its topic, and (c) correlate the percents with who responded, the response and the reason. The text is the book’s (the figures are spelled out in Hangul; the quotation marks are left out); the English is mine. The book glosses 대상으로: as subjects (of a survey); 응답: a response; 이유: a reason.

examples.text: 남자 대학생 육십삼 퍼센트 처가에 사는 것 좋아
examples.translation: namja daehaksaeng yuksipsam peosenteu cheogae saneun geot joa — Sixty-three percent of male college students like living with the wife’s family (the headline; the book writes 63%)

examples.text: 한 아르바이트 전문 사이트는 대학생 구백십팔 명을 대상으로 결혼에 대해 조사했다.
examples.translation: han areubaiteu jeonmun saiteuneun daehaksaeng gubaeksippal myeongeul daesangeuro gyeolhone daehae josahaetda. — A part-time job specialty site surveyed 918 college students about marriage.

examples.text: 조사에서 전체 응답자의 오십사 퍼센트가 결혼 후 처가나 시집에서 살 수 있다고 응답했다.
examples.translation: josaeseo jeonche eungdapjaui osipsa peosenteuga gyeolhon hu cheogana sijibeseo sal su itdago eungdapaetda. — In the survey, 54 percent of all respondents answered that they could live at the wife’s or husband’s family’s home after marriage.

examples.text: 특히, 남자 대학생의 육십삼 점 삼 퍼센트는 결혼 후 처가에 살 수 있다고 말했다.
examples.translation: teuki, namja daehaksaengui yuksipsam jeom sam peosenteuneun gyeolhon hu cheogae sal su itdago malhaetda. — In particular, 63.3 percent of male college students said they could live at the wife’s family’s home after marriage.

examples.text: 시집에 살 수 있다는 여대생은 사십오 점 팔 퍼센트로, 처가에 살겠다는 남학생보다 적었다.
examples.translation: sijibe sal su itdaneun yeodaesaengeun sasibo jeom pal peosenteuro, cheogae salgetdaneun namhaksaengboda jeogeotda. — The female college students who said they could live at the husband’s family’s home were 45.8 percent, fewer than the male students who said they would live at the wife’s family’s home.

examples.text: 처가나 시집에 살고 싶어하는 이유도 남학생과 여학생은 달랐다.
examples.translation: cheogana sijibe salgo sipeohaneun iyudo namhaksaenggwa yeohaksaengeun dallatda. — The reasons for wanting to live at the wife’s or husband’s family’s home also differed between male and female students.

examples.text: 시집에 살겠다는 여대생의 사십삼 점 구 퍼센트가 남편의 부모님도 부모님이기 때문이라는 이유를 말했다.
examples.translation: sijibe salgetdaneun yeodaesaengui sasipsam jeom gu peosenteuga nampyeonui bumonimdo bumonimigi ttaemuniraneun iyureul malhaetda. — 43.9 percent of the female college students who would live at the husband’s family’s home gave the reason that the husband’s parents are also parents.

examples.text: 하지만 처가에 살겠다는 남학생 삼십오 점 오 퍼센트는 돈을 절약하기 위해서라고 그 이유를 말했다.
examples.translation: hajiman cheogae salgetdaneun namhaksaeng samsibo jeom o peosenteuneun doneul jeoryakagi wihaeseorago geu iyureul malhaetda. — But 35.5 percent of the male students who would live at the wife’s family’s home gave their reason as to save money.

examples.text: 처가나 시집에 살지 않겠다고 응답한 대학생의 삼십 점 삼 퍼센트가 독립된 생활을 즐기기 위해서라고 말했다.
examples.translation: cheogana sijibe salji anketdago eungdapan daehaksaengui samsip jeom sam peosenteuga dongnipdoen saenghwareul jeulgigi wihaeseorago malhaetda. — 30.3 percent of the college students who answered that they would not live at the wife’s or husband’s family’s home said it was to enjoy an independent life.

lessons.title: 326. Ch 25 · Grammar A: past tense verbs for a present state or condition
lessons.subtitle: 결혼했습니다 · 안경을 꼈습니다 · 말랐습니다 · 결혼했었습니다

explanations.title: A. Past tense verbs for a present state or condition
explanations.body: Look at the literal meanings of the following sentences that contain a verb in the past tense. Note that these sentences all imply that an action that took place in the past is still in effect. There are quite a few verbs in Korean that “behave” this way. For now, however, we will focus on the verbs in this chapter for practice. These verbs can be broken into three categories.

examples.text: 산에 안개가 끼었습니다.
examples.translation: sane angaega kkieotseumnida. — Fog formed on the mountain (at one point in the past and it is foggy now).

examples.text: 나는 작년에 결혼했습니다.
examples.translation: naneun jangnyeone gyeolhonhaetseumnida. — Last year I got married (and I am married now).

examples.text: 저는 이 월에 입대했습니다.
examples.translation: jeoneun i wore ipdaehaetseumnida. — I joined the military in February (and I am in the military now).

examples.text: 김 선생님은 삼 월에 약혼했습니다.
examples.translation: gim seonsaengnimeun sam wore yakonhaetseumnida. — Mr. Kim got engaged in March (and he is engaged).

explanations.title: More examples
explanations.body: In the book’s examples:

examples.text: 책상에 먼지가 끼었습니다.

examples.text: 그 영화배우는 잘 생겼습니다.
examples.translation: geu yeonghwabaeuneun jal saenggyeotseumnida. — The actor “formed” well (and he is handsome).

examples.text: 제 아내는 말랐습니다.
examples.translation: je anaeneun mallatseumnida. — My wife is skinny.

examples.text: 여동생은 안경을 꼈습니다.
examples.translation: yeodongsaengeun angyeongeul kkyeotseumnida. — My younger sister put on glasses (and she is wearing glasses).

explanations.title: A past state that is no longer in effect
explanations.body: To imply a present state or condition that is no longer in effect, we add 었 to the past tense of the verb. For example:

examples.text: 김 선생님은 결혼했었습니다.
examples.translation: gim seonsaengnimeun gyeolhonhaesseotseumnida. — Mr. Kim was married once (and no longer is).

examples.text: 아침에 안개가 꼈었습니다.
examples.translation: achime angaega kkyeosseotseumnida. — It was foggy in the morning (and no longer is).

examples.text: 제 아내는 말랐었습니다.
examples.translation: je anaeneun mallasseotseumnida. — My wife was skinny (and no longer is).

lessons.title: 327. Ch 25 · Grammar B: contractions of the topic marker 는 and the object marker 를

explanations.title: B. Contractions of the topic marker and the object marker
explanations.body: Contracted forms like I’m, you’re, it’s, I’d, she’s, I’ve, etc., are frequently used in English, especially in informal settings. Likewise, Korean has two contracted forms commonly used in colloquial speaking: ~ㄴ and ~ㄹ. The topic marker 는 and the object marker 를 can be contracted into simple consonants, ~ㄴ and ~ㄹ, respectively. (The ㄴ or ㄹ is written under the last syllable of the noun, which therefore must have no final consonant of its own.)

explanations.title: Sentences with the contractions
