explanations.title: Topic C: Changes in Korean families (한국 가정의 변화)
explanations.body: James, an exchange student, is discussing changes in Korean families with his Korean classmate. (The English is mine; the book gives none. The book’s footnote: 국제결혼, which literally means “international marriage,” refers to a marriage between people of different nationalities or with different cultural/racial backgrounds.)

examples.text: 제임스: 은영 씨, 요즘 한국 가정이 예전과 많이 달라요?
examples.translation: jeimseu: eunyeong ssi, yojeum hanguk gajeongi yejeongwa mani dallayo? — Eunyoung, are Korean families these days very different from before?

examples.text: 은영: 네, 전에는 주로 대가족이었는데 요즘은 핵가족이 대부분이에요.
examples.translation: eunyeong: ne, jeoneneun juro daegajogieonneunde yojeumeun haekgajogi daebubunieyo. — Yes, before they were mostly extended families, but these days most are nuclear families.

examples.text: 제임스: 그래요? 또 어떤 변화가 있어요?
examples.translation: jeimseu: geuraeyo? tto eotteon byeonhwaga isseoyo? — Is that so? What other changes are there?

examples.text: 은영: 음, 요즘에는 결혼을 늦게 하거나 안 하는 사람들도 많아요. 그리고 대부분 자녀를 한 명이나 두 명만 낳아요.
examples.translation: eunyeong: eum, yojeumeneun gyeolhoneul neutge hageona an haneun saramdeuldo manayo. geurigo daebubun janyeoreul han myeongina du myeongman naayo. — Well, these days there are many people who marry late or don’t marry. And most have only one or two children.

examples.text: 제임스: 또, 아이를 갖지 않는 부부도 늘어나고 있죠?
examples.translation: jeimseu: tto, aireul gatji anneun bubudo neureonago itjo? — Also, couples who don’t have children are increasing, right?

examples.text: 은영: 맞아요. 그래서 한국 인구 수가 줄어들고 있대요.
examples.translation: eunyeong: majayo. geuraeseo hanguk ingu suga jureodeulgo itdaeyo. — That’s right. So they say the population of Korea is decreasing.

examples.text: 제임스: 그렇군요! 한국도 미국처럼 맞벌이 부부가 많죠?
examples.translation: jeimseu: geureokunyo! hangukdo migukcheoreom matbeori bubuga mancho? — I see! Korea also has many dual-income couples, like America, right?

examples.text: 은영: 네. 맞벌이 부부와 직장 여성이 많아져서 여성들의 삶이 많이 달라졌어요. 예를 들면, 전에는 집안일을 여자들만 했는데, 요즘에는 남자들도 같이 해요.
examples.translation: eunyeong: ne. matbeori bubuwa jikjang yeoseongi manajeoseo yeoseongdeurui salmi mani dallajeosseoyo. yereul deulmyeon, jeoneneun jibanireul yeojadeulman haenneunde, yojeumeneun namjadeuldo gachi haeyo. — Yes. As dual-income couples and working women have increased, women’s lives have changed a lot. For example, before, only women did the housework, but these days men do it together.

examples.text: 제임스: 그리고 요즘에는 한국사람들도 국제결혼을 많이 하는 것 같아요. 그렇죠?
examples.translation: jeimseu: geurigo yojeumeneun hanguksaramdeuldo gukjegyeolhoneul mani haneun geot gatayo. geureocho? — And these days it seems Koreans also have many international marriages. Right?

examples.text: 은영: 그래요. 그래서 한국 사회에 다문화가정이 늘어나고 있잖아요.
examples.translation: eunyeong: geuraeyo. geuraeseo hanguk sahoee damunhwagajeongi neureonago itjanayo. — That’s right. So multicultural families are increasing in Korean society, you know.

explanations.title: Cultural note: 다문화가정
explanations.body: Living in Korea, you will often see 다문화가정 (multicultural family). This term refers to a family of Korean nationals (usually men), immigrant spouses, and their children. The number of these families has been growing rapidly since 2000 because of the huge influx of foreign nationals seeking the “Korean dream” and the growing number of Koreans in rural areas marrying people of different races or nationalities. According to the Statistics Agency, approximately 7.2 % of all marriages in Korea in 2021 were “international,” and among them, 62.1% were between Korean men and foreign wives.

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 가 (家)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means home, family, or household, as in 처가 (one’s wife’s [parents’] home; “wife’s house”), 가장 (a household head; “family head”), 가옥 (a house; “family home”), and 가축 (a domestic animal; cattle; livestock; “household animal”). This Sino-Korean syllable is also used to mean (professional) man or person, which is equivalent to -er or -or in English, as in 화가 (a painter; “person who draws pictures”), 작가 (a writer; an author; “person who creates/makes”), and 발명가 (an inventor; “person who invents”). The book asks you to guess 대가족, 조각가, 가출 and 전문가; the answers are mine.

lessons.title: 329. Ch 25 · Topic C, Follow-up 2 and Activity 3: modern and traditional families, an article
lessons.subtitle: 다문화가정 · 대가족 · 직장 여성 · 한국 가정 이렇게 변하고 있다

explanations.title: Follow-up 2 (Reading): modern or traditional?
explanations.body: The book asks you to read three stories and write “Modern” if the story is about a modern trend or “Traditional” if it is about traditional Korean practices, and then to circle or underline the parts that describe the trend or tradition. The text is the book’s; the English is mine.

examples.text: 박태수 씨 가정은 다문화가정입니다.
examples.translation: baktaesu ssi gajeongeun damunhwagajeongimnida. — Mr. Park Taesu’s family is a multicultural family.

examples.text: 박태수 씨는 몇 년 전에 베트남에서 온 여성하고 결혼했어요.
examples.translation: baktaesu ssineun myeon nyeon jeone beteunameseo on yeoseonghago gyeolhonhaesseoyo. — Mr. Park married a woman from Vietnam a few years ago.

examples.text: 시골에서 부인과 작년에 낳은 딸하고 살고 있어요.
examples.translation: sigoreseo buingwa jangnyeone naeun ttalhago salgo isseoyo. — He lives in the countryside with his wife and the daughter born last year.

examples.text: 박태수 씨 부인은 한국 사람이 아니지만 한국 음식을 아주 좋아하고 한국말도 잘 합니다.
examples.translation: baktaesu ssi buineun hanguk sarami anijiman hanguk eumsigeul aju joahago hangungmaldo jal hamnida. — Mr. Park’s wife is not Korean, but she likes Korean food very much and also speaks Korean well.

examples.text: 그리고 시부모님하고도 잘 지내서 박태수 씨는 늘 기쁩니다.
examples.translation: geurigo sibumonimhagodo jal jinaeseo baktaesu ssineun neul gippeumnida. — And she gets along well with her parents-in-law, so Mr. Park is always happy.

examples.text: 정병국 씨 가족은 대가족입니다.
examples.translation: jeongbyeongguk ssi gajogeun daegajogimnida. — Mr. Jeong Byeongguk’s family is an extended family.

examples.text: 그래서 식구 수도 아주 많아요.
examples.translation: geuraeseo sikgu sudo aju manayo. — So the number of family members is also very large.

examples.text: 조부모님과 부모님 그리고 부인과 아들 둘, 딸 하나, 모두 아홉 명입니다.
examples.translation: jobumonimgwa bumonim geurigo buingwa adeul dul, ttal hana, modu ahop myeongimnida. — There are nine in all: grandparents, parents, his wife, two sons and one daughter.

examples.text: 정병국 씨는 집안의 장남이어서 여러 가지 일들을 해야 합니다.
examples.translation: jeongbyeongguk ssineun jibanui jangnamieoseo yeoreo gaji ildeureul haeya hamnida. — Mr. Jeong is the oldest son of the family, so he has to do various things.

examples.text: 또 정병국 씨 부인도 큰 며느리니까 집안살림으로 항상 바쁩니다.
examples.translation: tto jeongbyeongguk ssi buindo keun myeoneurinikka jibansallimeuro hangsang bappeumnida. — Also Mr. Jeong’s wife is the oldest daughter-in-law, so she is always busy with the household.

examples.text: 이세나 씨는 늦게 결혼한 직장 여성입니다.
examples.translation: isena ssineun neutge gyeolhonhan jikjang yeoseongimnida. — Ms. Lee Sena is a working woman who married late.

examples.text: 그런데 부부가 같이 일을 해서 아이 가질 계획을 아직 못 하고 있어요.
examples.translation: geureonde bubuga gachi ireul haeseo ai gajil gyehoegeul ajik mot hago isseoyo. — But since the couple both work, they are still not able to plan to have a child.

examples.text: 집안일은 보통 남편과 같이 합니다.
examples.translation: jibanireun botong nampyeongwa gachi hamnida. — She usually does the housework together with her husband.

examples.text: 아침 식사 준비와 설거지는 남편이 하고 이세나 씨는 저녁 식사를 준비합니다.
examples.translation: achim siksa junbiwa seolgeojineun nampyeoni hago isena ssineun jeonyeok siksareul junbihamnida. — Her husband does the breakfast preparation and the dishes, and Ms. Lee prepares dinner.

examples.text: 집안 청소는 주말에 남편하고 같이 합니다.
examples.translation: jiban cheongsoneun jumare nampyeonhago gachi hamnida. — She cleans the house together with her husband on weekends.

explanations.title: The answers (mine)
explanations.body: The book leaves the blanks empty; these are my answers.

rows: A multicultural family: he married a woman from Vietnam
An extended family; he is the oldest son and his wife the oldest daughter-in-law, with many duties
A late marriage; a working woman who shares the housework with her husband

explanations.title: Activity 2: the four topics
explanations.body: In Activity 2 (listening) you choose, for each of three conversations between colleagues, the relevant topic; one topic has no match. The book’s topics:

rows: a couple who do the housework together
a couple who do not have children

explanations.title: Activity 3 (Reading): an article about changes in present-day Korean families
explanations.body: Before reading, you write in English what you think the article will be about; then you read it and write down the changes noted. The text is the book’s (30세 is spelled out; the plus signs and quotation marks are left out); the English is mine. The book glosses 형태: a type; 사례: an example; 시기: timing.

examples.text: 한국 가정 이렇게 변하고 있다
examples.translation: hanguk gajeong ireoke byeonhago itda — Korean families are changing like this (the headline)

examples.text: 한국 가정의 가족 수는 매년 줄어 들고 있다.
examples.translation: hanguk gajeongui gajok suneun maenyeon jureo deulgo itda. — The number of members in Korean families is decreasing every year.

examples.text: 대부분의 가정은 부부 자녀 형태의 핵가족이다.
examples.translation: daebubunui gajeongeun bubu janyeo hyeongtaeui haekgajogida. — Most families are nuclear families of the “couple and children” type. (the book writes ‘부부+자녀’)

examples.text: 그러나, 요즘은 이런 부부 자녀 가족 형태도 줄고 있다.
examples.translation: geureona, yojeumeun ireon bubu janyeo gajok hyeongtaedo julgo itda. — However, these days this “couple and children” type of family is also decreasing.

examples.text: 부부 가정과 일 인 가정이 늘고 있다.
examples.translation: bubu gajeonggwa il in gajeongi neulgo itda. — “Couple” households and “one-person” households are increasing. (the book writes ‘1인’)

examples.text: 결혼 연령과 첫 자녀를 낳는 연령이 매년 올라가고 있다.
examples.translation: gyeolhon yeollyeonggwa cheot janyeoreul nanneun yeollyeongi maenyeon ollagago itda. — The age at marriage and the age of having the first child are rising every year.

examples.text: 삼십 세 이상 여성이 첫 아이를 낳는 사례를 주변에서 쉽게 찾아 볼 수 있다.
examples.translation: samsip se isang yeoseongi cheot aireul nanneun saryereul jubyeoneseo swipge chaja bol su itda. — Cases of women aged 30 or over having their first child can be easily found around us.

examples.text: 또한, 첫 아이를 가지는 시기가 늦어지면서 자녀도 한 두 명만 낳는 부부가 늘어나고 있다.
examples.translation: ttohan, cheot aireul gajineun sigiga neujeojimyeonseo janyeodo han du myeongman nanneun bubuga neureonago itda. — Also, as the timing of having the first child gets later, couples who have only one or two children are increasing.

examples.text: 그리고 맞벌이 부부가 늘어나면서 집안일을 부부가 함께 하는 가정이 많아지고 있다.
examples.translation: geurigo matbeori bubuga neureonamyeonseo jibanireul bubuga hamkke haneun gajeongi manajigo itda. — And as dual-income couples increase, families in which the couple do the housework together are becoming more common.

examples.text: 청소, 빨래, 아이 돌보기, 요리 등의 집안일이나 자녀 교육을 부부가 함께 하는 가정이 늘어나고 있다.
examples.translation: cheongso, ppallae, ai dolbogi, yori deungui jibanirina janyeo gyoyugeul bubuga hamkke haneun gajeongi neureonago itda. — Families in which the couple together do housework such as cleaning, laundry, childcare and cooking, or the children’s education, are increasing.

explanations.title: The changes noted (mine)
explanations.body: The book leaves the blanks empty; these are my answers.

rows: The number of members per family is decreasing every year
The “couple and children” nuclear family is decreasing; couple-only and one-person households are increasing
The age of marriage and of having the first child keeps rising; couples with only one or two children are increasing
Couples increasingly do the housework (cleaning, laundry, childcare, cooking) and the children’s education together

explanations.title: Activity 4: the model
explanations.body: In Activity 4 (한국 가정의 과거와 현재) you listen to the stories of two families, one recorded 60 years ago and one a year ago, and compare how the Korean family has changed. The book’s model for the flip chart:

rows: the number of family members is large
the number of family members is small

explanations.title: Activities left out
explanations.body: Activity 1 (a SMART Board activity), Activity 2’s listening and Activity 4’s listening, group work and presentation are computer, audio and group activities.

lessons.title: 330. Ch 25 · Grammar C: the verb ending -잖아요 reminds of what is obvious
lessons.subtitle: 토요일이잖아요 · 맛있잖아요 · 제가 한국사람이잖아요 · 어렵잖아요

explanations.title: A. The verb ending -잖아요
explanations.body:
Compare the exchanges 오늘이 무슨 요일이에요? 토요일이에요. and 왜 직장에 안 가세요? 토요일이잖아요. Note that Speaker B’s response in the first exchange ends in 이에요. The response simply provides information Speaker A does not have. However, Speaker B’s response in the second exchange ends in 이잖아요. Thus, the response implies that the answer to the question is obvious to both parties. In other words, the verb ending –잖아(요) is used when the speaker reminds the listener of what is obvious to both parties. The ending is often translated as you know.

Keep in mind that –잖아(요) is different from –지 않아(요), which is used to negate a verb.

examples.text: 오늘이 무슨 요일이에요?
examples.translation: oneuri museun nyoilieyo? — What day is it today?

examples.text: 토요일이에요.
examples.translation: toyoirieyo. — It is Saturday.

examples.text: 왜 직장에 안 가세요?
examples.translation: wae jikjange an gaseyo? — How come you are not going to work?

examples.text: 토요일이잖아요.
examples.translation: toyoirijanayo. — (You know) it is Saturday!

examples.text: 내가 김치를 먹잖아요.
examples.translation: naega gimchireul meokjanayo. — You know that I eat kimchi.

examples.text: 내가 김치를 먹지 않아요.
examples.translation: naega gimchireul meokji anayo. — I do not eat kimchi. (negation)

explanations.title: The rule: verb stem + 잖아요
explanations.body: Verb Ending 잖아요 Used to Remind What Is Obvious: verb stem + 잖아요.

examples.text: 왜 김치를 자주 먹어요?
examples.translation: wae gimchireul jaju meogeoyo? — Why do you often eat kimchi?

examples.text: 맛있잖아요.
examples.translation: masitjanayo. — You know [it] is tasty.

examples.text: 제가 한국사람이잖아요.
examples.translation: jega hanguksaramijanayo. — You know I am Korean.

examples.text: 한국말이 어렵잖아요.
examples.translation: hangungmari eoryeopjanayo. — You know Korean is difficult.

examples.text: 그래서 열심히 공부해요.
examples.translation: geuraeseo yeolsimhi gongbuhaeyo. — So I am studying hard.

examples.text: 올해가 벌써 다 갔잖아요.
examples.translation: olhaega beolsseo da gatjanayo. — You know this year has already gone by. (the core vocabulary’s example)

explanations.title: Forms (mine)
explanations.body: The forms are made by the book’s rule: the verb stem plus 잖아요 (for a noun, 이잖아요 after a final consonant and 잖아요 after a vowel); in the past, the past stem plus 잖아요, as in 갔잖아요.

explanations.title: Follow-up 1 and 5: the models
explanations.body: In Follow-up 1 the teacher asks questions with obvious answers and the class answers with -잖아요. In Follow-up 5 (몬트레이에 대해 알아봅시다) you exchange information about your favorite places and the reasons. The book’s models (the English is mine):

examples.text: 왜 군인식당에서 점심을 먹어요?
examples.translation: wae guninsikdangeseo jeomsimeul meogeoyo? — Why do you eat lunch at the military dining facility? (Teacher’s question, the book’s model)

examples.text: 한국학교에서 가깝잖아요.
examples.translation: hangukakgyoeseo gakkapjanayo. — You know it is close to the Korean school. (A)

examples.text: 무료로 먹을 수 있잖아요.
examples.translation: muryoro meogeul su itjanayo. — You know we can eat there for free. (B)

examples.text: 주말에 보통 어디에 가세요?
examples.translation: jumare botong eodie gaseyo? — Where do you usually go on weekends? (the book’s model for Follow-up 5)

examples.text: 저는 몬트레이 파인스 골프장에 가요.
examples.translation: jeoneun monteurei painseu golpeujange gayo. — I go to the Monterey Pines golf course.

examples.text: 왜요?
examples.translation: waeyo? — Why?

examples.text: 제가 골프를 좋아하잖아요.
examples.translation: jega golpeureul joahajanayo. — You know I like golf.

examples.text: 그리고 그 골프장이 싸잖아요.
examples.translation: geurigo geu golpeujangi ssajanayo. — And you know that golf course is cheap.

explanations.title: Activities left out
explanations.body: Follow-up 1 (class questions), Follow-up 2 (listening to three conversations in which a woman states what is obvious to both speakers) and Follow-up 5 (a partner exchange) are audio and partner activities.

explanations.title: The rule: verb stem + (으)ㅁ
explanations.body: Note that all these nouns are formed from the stems of the verbs and (으)ㅁ. If the verb stems end in a vowel, the nouns end in ㅁ, as in 잠 and 춤. If the verb stems end in a consonant, the nouns end in 음, as in 죽음 and 웃음. If the nouns are derived from stative verbs ending in ㅂ, as in 고맙다 and 밉다, however, we drop ㅂ, add 우, and then add ㅁ: 고맙다 → 고맙 → 고마 → 고마우 → 고마움; 밉다 → 밉 → 미 → 미우 → 미움. One exception to the previous rules is 삶 (life), which is derived from 살다.

The book’s Core Vocabulary lists the core words of the chapter with an example sentence for each (the sentences and the English meanings are the book’s; the book gives no English for the sentences). The Hanja of the Sino-Korean words are in parentheses before the meaning. Where the book writes two forms together (for example 며느리/며느님 or 장모(님)), the forms are written with a slash and the honorific form is noted in the meaning.

The example sentences with digits are respelled in Hangul (3대 → 삼 대, 100점 → 백 점, 1인 → 일 인). The book’s related words (the synonyms, antonyms and related words in the last column) are left out; the book’s Additional Vocabulary section is blank.

explanations.title: Self-evaluation
explanations.body:
Recall the objectives of the chapter and ask yourself whether you have achieved them (the book asks you to tick Yes or No). If you tick “No” for any item, the book suggests: review that section on your own; find a study partner and review it as a pair or group; and tell your academic advisor or team leader which areas you need more help with, so that they can provide activities tailored to your learning style and needs.

Now I am able to: identify and talk about family types and use kinship terms; identify and talk about changes in Korean family life; and describe a person’s appearance and personality.

Now I have a clear understanding of: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary section; the verb ending –잖아요; nouns derived from native Korean verbs; past tense verbs for a present state or condition; contractions of the topic marker 는 and the object marker 를; and the Sino-Korean syllables 장 (長), 차 (次), 조 (祖), 처 (妻) and 가 (家).

explanations.title: What Chapter 26 teaches (가정행사와 결혼 문화)
explanations.body:
Chapter 26, “Family Events and Marriage”, has three topic presentations, grammar in focus, activities, a self-evaluation and the core vocabulary.

When you finish the chapter you will be able to: identify and talk about important birthdays like the 1st, 70th, and 80th; identify and talk about events related to courting and a wedding, and one’s ideal type of partner; and offer an invitation to an important family event.

You will become familiar with: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary section; –는 중이다 / ~중이다 (to be in the middle of; to be –ing); –아/어(서) 죽겠다 used to exaggerate feelings about a condition; –(으)ㄴ/는 대신(에) and ~대신(에) (instead of; rather than; in place of); –(으)ㄹ 계획/생각/예정이다 (plan to; intend to; be going to); and the Sino-Korean syllables 애 (愛), 축 (祝) and 식 (式).

explanations.title: Notes: the Asian zodiac (띠)
explanations.body: 띠 means birth year according to the Asian zodiac. The book’s picture shows the twelve signs with a birth year each (the years are spelled out in the second column; the English animal names of the signs the book does not gloss are mine).

explanations.title: Cultural note: the first birthday
explanations.body: Koreans traditionally have a large celebration, called 첫돌 or 돌, for a child’s first birthday. This practice originates from the fact that in the past many infants did not survive their first year. For their child’s first birthday, parents prepare a 돌상 (first birthday table). This table is laden with various foods, such as rice cakes, fruits, and other items. The table is stacked high, symbolizing the wish for the child’s prosperous future. The highlight of the event is 돌잡이 (“first birthday grabbing”), where people watch what item the child grabs first. The chosen item is believed to predict the child’s future. Parents usually use money or rice to symbolize wealth, silk thread for longevity, and a pencil for learning. These days, many parents use more varied objects, such as a microphone, a golf ball, a computer mouse, or a stethoscope.

lessons.title: 335. Ch 26 · Topic A Activity 2: a news article about a famous couple’s wedding
lessons.subtitle: 한류스타 소식 · 열애 · 결혼식을 올렸다 · 연애 중 · 부인하다 · 데이트

explanations.title: Activity 2 (Reading): an article about a famous Korean actor and actress couple
explanations.body: The book asks you to read the article (dated March 31, 2022) and answer four questions in English. The text is the book’s (the digits are spelled out; the parentheses with the ages and the characters’ actors and the quotation marks around the titles are left out); the English is mine. The book glosses 열애: passionate love; 부인하다: to deny.

examples.text: 한류스타 소식
examples.translation: hallyuseuta sosik — Hallyu star news (the section)

examples.text: 톱스타 커플 현빈 마흔 살과 손예진 마흔 살이 지난 삼 월 삼십일 일 서울 광진구 그랜드워커힐 호텔에서 결혼식을 올렸다.
examples.translation: topseuta keopeul hyeonbin maheun salgwa sonyejin maheun sari jinan sam wol samsibil il seoul gwangjingu geuraendeuwokeohil hotereseo gyeolhonsigeul ollyeotda. — The top-star couple Hyun Bin (40) and Son Ye-jin (40) held their wedding on March 31 at the Grand Walkerhill Hotel in Gwangjin-gu, Seoul. (the book writes the ages 40 in parentheses)

examples.text: 이천이십 년 삼 월 열애를 시작한 후 이 년 만이다.
examples.translation: icheonisip nyeon sam wol yeoraereul sijakan hu i nyeon manida. — It is two years after they started their passionate love in March 2020.

examples.text: 현빈과 손예진은 이천십팔 년 영화 협상을 찍을 때 처음 연애 중이라는 기사가 나왔었지만 두 사람 모두 이를 부인했었다.
examples.translation: hyeonbingwa sonyejineun icheonsippal nyeon yeonghwa hyeopsangeul jjigeul ttae cheoeum yeonae jungiraneun gisaga nawasseotjiman du saram modu ireul buinhaesseotda. — When Hyun Bin and Son Ye-jin were filming the movie Negotiation in 2018, an article first appeared saying they were dating, but both of them denied it.

examples.text: 그 후 두 사람은 이천십구 년 드라마 사랑의 불시착에서 남녀 주연으로 다시 만났다.
examples.translation: geu hu du sarameun icheonsipgu nyeon deurama sarangui bulsichageseo namnyeo juyeoneuro dasi mannatda. — After that, the two met again in 2019 as the male and female leads in the drama Crash Landing on You.

examples.text: 두 사람은 사랑의 불시착이 끝난 후 약 이 년간 사귀어 왔다고 한다.
examples.translation: du sarameun sarangui bulsichagi kkeunnan hu yak i nyeongan sagwieo watdago handa. — They are said to have been going out for about two years after Crash Landing on You ended.

examples.text: 국내 뿐 아니라 일본, 인도 등 해외에서도 높은 인기를 얻은 사랑의 불시착은 남한 여자 윤세리가 우연한 사고로 북한에 떨어져 북한 장교 리정혁을 만나 서로 사랑하게 되는 이야기이다.
examples.translation: gungnae ppun anira ilbon, indo deung haeoeeseodo nopeun ingireul eodeun sarangui bulsichageun namhan yeoja yunseriga uyeonhan sagoro bukane tteoreojeo bukan janggyo rijeonghyeogeul manna seoro saranghage doeneun iyagiida. — Crash Landing on You, which gained great popularity not only in Korea but also abroad in Japan, India and elsewhere, is the story of a South Korean woman, Yoon Seri (Son Ye-jin), who falls into North Korea by an accidental accident, meets a North Korean officer, Ri Jeong-hyeok (Hyun Bin), and they fall in love.

examples.text: 손예진은 현빈과 연애를 시작할 때 나이도 같고 취미도 비슷해서 같이 있으면 편하고 재미있었다고 한다.
examples.translation: sonyejineun hyeonbingwa yeonaereul sijakal ttae naido gatgo chwimido biseutaeseo gachi isseumyeon pyeonhago jaemiisseotdago handa. — Son Ye-jin is said to have found it comfortable and fun to be with Hyun Bin when they started dating because they were the same age and had similar hobbies.

examples.text: 운동이 취미인 현빈은 손예진이 골프를 배울 때 골프 연습장에서 직접 가르쳐 주었다.
examples.translation: undongi chwimiin hyeonbineun sonyejini golpeureul baeul ttae golpeu yeonseupjangeseo jikjeop gareucheo jueotda. — Hyun Bin, whose hobby is sports, taught Son Ye-jin himself at the driving range when she was learning golf.

examples.text: 두 사람은 시간이 날 때면 강원도의 한 골프장에서 골프를 같이 치거나 주로 서로의 집에서 데이트를 했다고 한다.
examples.translation: du sarameun sigani nal ttaemyeon gangwondoui han golpeujangeseo golpeureul gachi chigeona juro seoroui jibeseo deiteureul haetdago handa. — When they had time, the two are said to have played golf together at a golf course in Gangwon-do or mostly dated at each other’s homes.

examples.text: 백 선생님: 네. 그래서 사람들이 아직도 맞선을 많이 봐요. 옛날엔 가족이나 친척, 친구들이 중매를 섰어요. 그런데 요즘엔 전문적으로 중매를 서는 결혼정보회사들이 많아요.
examples.translation: baek seonsaengnim: ne. geuraeseo saramdeuri ajikdo matseoneul mani bwayo. yennaren gajogina chincheok, chingudeuri jungmaereul seosseoyo. geureonde yojeumen jeonmunjeogeuro jungmaereul seoneun gyeolhonjeongbohoesadeuri manayo. — Yes. So people still go on a lot of arranged meetings. In the old days, family, relatives and friends acted as go-betweens. But these days there are many marriage agencies that professionally act as matchmakers.

examples.text: 백 선생님: 내일 만나는 소개팅 상대가 피에르 씨 마음에 들면 좋겠네요.

explanations.title: Cultural note: 미팅, 소개팅 and 맞선
explanations.body: 미팅, 소개팅, and 맞선 commonly relate to an arranged meeting between single men and women. 미팅, borrowed from the English word meeting, roughly translates to “a group blind date.” The 미팅 organizer is usually a senior student in college or a senior employee of a company. 소개팅 is a compound word using 소개 (referral; introduction) and the last syllable of 미팅 (meeting). Both 소개팅 and 맞선 mean a one-on-one blind date. 소개팅 is more casual and for those who want to meet a person for a possible relationship. On the other hand, 맞선 is for those who are more serious and looking specifically for a spouse.

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 애 (愛)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means love or loving, as in 애인 (one’s lover; one’s boyfriend/girlfriend; “lover”), 애국 (patriotism; love of one’s country), and 애연가 (a habitual smoker; a chain smoker; “a person who loves smoking”). The book asks you to find out the meanings of 열애, 모성애 and 애사심; the answers are mine (열애: passionate love, as the book glosses it in an article of this chapter).

lessons.title: 338. Ch 26 · Grammar A: expressing progressive action with -는 중이다 / ~중이다
lessons.subtitle: 아침식사를 하는 중입니다 · 식사 중입니다 · 공사 중입니다 · 통화 중이십니다 · 회의 중입니다

explanations.title: A. Expressing progressive action with 중이다
explanations.body:
Recall the auxiliary verb –고 있다, which is used to express a progressive (or continuing) action, as in 아침 식사를 하고 있어요 (I am having breakfast) and 은행에 가고 있어요 (I am going to the bank). We can also express a progressive action by using –는 중이다, which literally translates as to be in the middle of. 중이다 can also be preceded by a noun.

Expressing progressive action: action verb stem + 는 중이다; noun + 중이다.

examples.text: 아침식사를 하는 중입니다.
examples.translation: achimsiksareul haneun jungimnida. — I am in the middle of having breakfast, or I am having breakfast.

examples.text: 은행에 가는 중입니다.
examples.translation: eunhaenge ganeun jungimnida. — I am in the middle of going to the bank, or I am going to the bank.

examples.text: 식사 중입니다.
examples.translation: siksa jungimnida. — I am in the middle of a meal, or I am having a meal.

examples.text: 이 도로가 공사 중입니다.
examples.translation: i doroga gongsa jungimnida. — This road is in the middle of construction, or this road is under construction.

explanations.title: Forms (mine)
explanations.body: The forms are made by the book’s rule: the present attributive form -는 of the action verb (ㄹ stems drop the ㄹ: 팔다 → 파는, 만들다 → 만드는) plus 중이다; a noun takes 중이다 directly.

explanations.title: Follow-up 1 (Writing): -고 있다 → -는 중이다
explanations.body: The book asks you to change the –고 있다 sentences into the –는 중이다 or ~ 중이다 form; the first one has been done. The second column is my answer key (the English is mine).

rows: I am going to the academy.
I am waiting for a friend.
I am taking care of a baby.
We are having a company dinner at a restaurant.
I am cleaning the dormitory room.
Home appliances are being sold cheaply.

explanations.title: Follow-up 5: the excuse model
explanations.body: You have an annoying acquaintance you want to avoid. When he calls, you make excuses with –는 중이다 or ~ 중이다. The book’s model (the English is mine):

examples.text: 돈이 없어서 점심을 못 먹었어요. 배고파 죽겠어요. 지금 점심 좀 사 주세요.
examples.translation: doni eopseoseo jeomsimeul mot meogeosseoyo. baegopa jukgesseoyo. jigeum jeomsim jom sa juseyo. — I had no money, so I couldn’t eat lunch. I’m starving to death. Please buy me lunch now. (A, the annoying friend)

examples.text: 어, 제가 지금 병원에 가는 중이에요. 그래서 안 돼요. 미안해요.
examples.translation: eo, jega jigeum byeongwone ganeun jungieyo. geuraeseo an dwaeyo. mianhaeyo. — Oh, I am on my way to the hospital now. So I can’t. I’m sorry. (B, the excuse)

lessons.title: 339. Ch 26 · Grammar B: expressing strong feelings about a condition with -아/어(서) 죽겠다
lessons.subtitle: 피곤해 죽겠어요 · 배고파 죽겠어요 · 행복해 죽겠어요 · 졸려 죽겠어요 · 추워 죽겠어요

explanations.title: B. Expressing strong feelings about a condition, using -아/어(서) 죽겠다
explanations.body: Koreans often use –아/어(서) 죽겠다 to exaggerate their feelings about a certain condition they are in, as in 피곤해서 죽겠어요 (I am extremely tired), 배 고파서 죽겠어요 (I am really hungry), and 행복해서 죽겠어요 (I am extremely happy). –아/어(서) 죽겠다 literally means “and thus I will die” or “so I will die,” and it is somewhat similar to an English speaker saying, “I am freezing to death.” We can translate the phrase as extremely, really, truly, to death, etc., depending on the context. Note that 서 in –아/어서 죽겠다 can be omitted.

explanations.body: The forms are made by the book’s rule: the -아/어 form of the stative verb plus 죽겠어요 (with or without 서); the ㅂ irregular verbs change as usual (춥다 → 추워).

explanations.title: Cultural note: 혼수 (婚需)
explanations.body: The Korean word 혼수 (婚需) means items needed for marriage. This refers to items essential to a marriage ceremony or to marriage expenses. Customarily in the past the bride’s side of family bought everything from large furniture items to kitchenware. On the other hand, the groom’s family traditionally bought or put down a large deposit (전세) to rent a house in which the couple would live after their wedding. However, with the cost of housing expense soaring in Korea recently, more and more couples are focusing their resources on meeting their housing needs together rather than sticking to traditional arrangements of women spending money on 혼수 while men take care of their housing.

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 축 (祝) and 식 (式)
explanations.body: 축 (祝) means congratulation, celebration, or wishing. 식 (式) means ceremony, style, or way. The book asks you to guess the meanings of 졸업식, 약혼식 and 수동식; the answers are mine.

explanations.title: Activity 2 (Reading): a young couple’s wedding plans
explanations.body: The text is about a young couple’s wedding plans. The book asks you to identify what the couple has done and what they will do for their wedding and to complete a table in English. The text is the book’s (2주 and 7박8일 are spelled out); the English is mine.

examples.text: 이 주 전에 지환 씨와 영미 씨는 약혼했습니다.
examples.translation: i ju jeone jihwan ssiwa yeongmi ssineun yakonhaetseumnida. — Two weeks ago, Jihwan and Yeongmi got engaged.

examples.text: 두 사람은 한 달 후에 결혼할 계획입니다.
examples.translation: du sarameun han dal hue gyeolhonhal gyehoegimnida. — The two plan to marry in a month.

examples.text: 그래서 두 사람은 결혼식 준비 때문에 요즘 아주 바쁩니다.
examples.translation: geuraeseo du sarameun gyeolhonsik junbi ttaemune yojeum aju bappeumnida. — So the two are very busy these days because of the wedding preparations.

examples.text: 지난주에는 예식장을 예약하고 백화점에 가서 결혼 예물을 샀습니다.
examples.translation: jinanjueneun yesikjangeul yeyakago baekwajeome gaseo gyeolhon yemureul satseumnida. — Last week they reserved the wedding hall and went to a department store and bought the wedding gifts.

examples.text: 이번 주말에는 신혼여행 비행기표를 사고 호텔을 예약할 생각입니다.
examples.translation: ibeon jumareneun sinhonnyeohaeng bihaenggipyoreul sago hotereul yeyakal saenggagimnida. — This weekend they intend to buy the honeymoon plane tickets and reserve a hotel.

examples.text: 지환 씨와 영미 씨는 칠 박 팔 일로 하와이에 신혼여행을 가기로 했습니다.
examples.translation: jihwan ssiwa yeongmi ssineun chil bak pal illo hawaie sinhonyeohaengeul gagiro haetseumnida. — Jihwan and Yeongmi have decided to go on a honeymoon to Hawaii for seven nights and eight days.

examples.text: 다음 주말에는 청첩장을 만들고 영미 씨 웨딩드레스와 지환 씨 양복을 고를 예정입니다.
examples.translation: daeum jumareneun cheongcheopjangeul mandeulgo yeongmi ssi wedingdeureseuwa jihwan ssi yangbogeul goreul yejeongimnida. — Next weekend they are going to make the wedding invitations and choose Yeongmi’s wedding dress and Jihwan’s suit.

examples.text: 지환 씨와 영미 씨는 결혼준비로 바쁘지만 다가올 결혼식 때문에 너무 행복합니다.
examples.translation: jihwan ssiwa yeongmi ssineun gyeolhonjunbiro bappeujiman dagaol gyeolhonsik ttaemune neomu haengbokamnida. — Jihwan and Yeongmi are busy with the wedding preparations, but they are very happy because of the coming wedding.

explanations.title: Activity 3 (Reading): a newspaper article on congratulatory money
explanations.body: Read the article and complete three tasks: choose the best title, mark two statements true or false, and write what each category of the pie chart indicates. The text is the book’s (the digits are spelled out; the quotation marks are left out); the English is mine.

examples.text: 결혼식 비용과 피로연 음식 값이 오르면서 축의금도 오르고 있는 것으로 나타났다.
examples.translation: gyeolhonsik biyonggwa piroyeon eumsik gapsi oreumyeonseo chuguigeumdo oreugo inneun geoseuro natanatda. — It has been found that as wedding costs and the price of reception food rise, congratulatory money is also rising.

examples.text: 조사결과 한국인들이 내는 결혼식 축의금의 평균은 칠만 구천 원인 것으로 조사됐다.
examples.translation: josagyeolgwa hangugindeuri naeneun gyeolhonsik chuguigeumui pyeonggyuneun chilman gucheon wonin geoseuro josadwaetda. — The survey found that the average congratulatory money Koreans give for a wedding is 79,000 won.

examples.text: 이는 코로나 유행 전 이천십구 년 평균 칠만 칠천 원에서 이천 원이 늘어난 금액이다.
examples.translation: ineun korona yuhaeng jeon icheonsipgu nyeon pyeonggyun chilman chilcheon woneseo icheon woni neureonan geumaegida. — This is an amount that has increased by 2,000 won from the average of 77,000 won in 2019, before the spread of COVID.

examples.text: 결혼정보회사 듀오가 지난 이천이십이 년 사 월 미혼남녀 삼백여 명을 대상으로 설문조사한 결과 평균 축의금 액수는 칠만 구천 원인 것으로 나타났다.
examples.translation: gyeolhonjeongbohoesa dyuoga jinan icheonisibi nyeon sa wol mihonnamnyeo sambaegyeo myeongeul daesangeuro seolmunjosahan gyeolgwa pyeonggyun chuguigeum aeksuneun chilman gucheon wonin geoseuro natanatda. — In a survey the marriage agency Duo conducted last April 2022 of about 300 unmarried men and women, the average congratulatory money was found to be 79,000 won.

examples.text: 그 밖에 오만 원 사십팔 퍼센트가 가장 많았고, 그 다음은 십만 원 사십 퍼센트였다.
examples.translation: geu bakke oman won sasippal peosenteuga gajang manatgo, geu daeumeun simman won sasip peosenteuyeotda. — Besides that, 50,000 won (48%) was the most common, followed by 100,000 won (40%).

examples.text: 친한 친구나 가족에게는 이십만 원 이상을 한다고 한 답변도 사 퍼센트였다.
examples.translation: chinhan chinguna gajogegeneun isimman won isangeul handago han dapbyeondo sa peosenteuyeotda. — There was also an answer of 4% that said they give 200,000 won or more to close friends or family.

examples.text: 결혼식장에 어떤 기분으로 가느냐는 질문에 대해서는 오십오 점 칠 퍼센트가 결혼을 축하하러라고, 이십육 점 칠 퍼센트가 돈을 내러라고, 십칠 점 칠 퍼센트가 반반이라고 답했다.
examples.translation: gyeolhonsikjange eotteon gibuneuro ganeunyaneun jilmune daehaeseoneun osibo jeom chil peosenteuga gyeolhoneul chukahareorago, isimnyuk jeom chil peosenteuga doneul naereorago, sipchil jeom chil peosenteuga banbanirago dapaetda. — To the question of what feeling people go to a wedding hall with, 55.7% answered “to congratulate the marriage,” 26.7% “to pay money,” and 17.7% “half and half.”

explanations.title: The answers (mine)
explanations.body: The book leaves the answers blank; these are my answers.

rows: 4. 결혼 축의금 (congratulatory money for a wedding)
b. 1. The average amount increased by 77,000 won compared with 2019
False: it increased by 2,000 won (from 77,000 won to 79,000 won)
b. 2. Most people give the couple 50,000 won or more
True: 48% give 50,000 won, 40% give 100,000 won and 4% give 200,000 won or more
People who go to a wedding to congratulate the couple
People who go to pay (congratulatory) money
People who go half to congratulate and half to pay money

lessons.title: 342. Ch 26 · Grammar C: expressing a future plan with -(으)ㄹ 계획 / 생각 / 예정이다
lessons.subtitle: 갈 계획입니다 · 이사할 생각입니다 · 결혼할 예정입니다 · 읽을 생각이다

explanations.title: A. Expressing a future plan: -(으)ㄹ 계획 / 생각 / 예정이다
explanations.body: Koreans often express a future plan by using one of the following grammar features: –(으)ㄹ 계획 / 생각 / 예정이다, any of which can be translated as plan to, intend to, or be going to. Note that the future attributive form of a verb –(으)ㄹ precedes 계획 / 생각 / 예정.

examples.text: 내년에 유럽 여행을 갈 계획입니다.
examples.translation: naenyeone yureop yeohaengeul gal gyehoegimnida. — I plan to go sightseeing in Europe next year.

examples.text: 한 달 후에 아파트로 이사할 생각입니다.
examples.translation: han dal hue apateuro isahal saenggagimnida. — I plan to move to an apartment in a month.

examples.text: 다음 달에 결혼할 예정입니다.
examples.translation: daeum dare gyeolhonhal yejeongimnida. — I am going to marry next month.

explanations.title: Expressing future plans: -(으)ㄹ 계획 / 생각 / 예정이다
explanations.body: The book’s examples (the English is the book’s):

examples.text: 삼 년 후에 미국으로 이민 갈 계획이에요.
examples.translation: sam nyeon hue migugeuro imin gal gyehoegieyo. — I plan to immigrate to the U.S. in three years.

examples.text: 다음 달에 결혼할 예정이야.
examples.translation: daeum dare gyeolhonhal yejeongiya. — I am going to marry next month. (casual)

examples.text: 이번 방학에 책을 많이 읽을 생각이다.
examples.translation: ibeon banghage chaegeul mani ilgeul saenggagida. — I intend to read a lot of books during this vacation.

examples.text: 제 생일 파티를 호텔에서 할 예정이에요.
examples.translation: je saengil patireul hotereseo hal yejeongieyo. — I am going to have my birthday party at a hotel. (the core vocabulary’s example)

explanations.title: Forms (mine)
explanations.body: The forms are made by the book’s rule: the future attributive form -(으)ㄹ (ㄹ stems keep ㄹ: 만들다 → 만들, 살다 → 살; the ㅂ irregular 돕다 → 도울) plus 계획 / 생각 / 예정이다. The three are used the same way.

lessons.title: 343. Ch 26 · Grammar D: expressing “instead of” with 대신(에)
lessons.subtitle: 생선 대신에 닭고기를 · 가는 대신에 · 값이 싼 대신 · 이메일 대신 전화로

explanations.title: B. Expressing “instead of”
explanations.body: In English, when we have two available options and choose one over the other, we use expressions like instead of, rather than, or in place of, as in “I will eat chicken rather than fish.” In Korean, this choice of two options is expressed by using 대신(에). Note that 대신(에) can be preceded by a noun, as in 생선 대신에 (instead of fish), or by a verbal phrase in the attributive form, as in 가는 대신에 (instead of going).

examples.text: 생선 대신에 닭고기를 먹겠습니다.
examples.translation: saengseon daesine dalgogireul meokgetseumnida. — I will eat chicken rather than fish.

examples.text: 콜라 대신에 물을 마실게요.
examples.translation: kolla daesine mureul masilgeyo. — I will drink water instead of Coke.

examples.text: 병원에 가는 대신에 약을 사서 먹었습니다.
examples.translation: byeongwone ganeun daesine yageul saseo meogeotseumnida. — I bought and took some medicine instead of going to the doctor’s office.

explanations.title: 대신(에) in the sense of “in compensation for”
explanations.body: 대신(에) is also used to mean in compensation for or to make up for, as in the following examples:

examples.text: 저 책 대신에 이 펜을 줄게.
examples.translation: jeo chaek daesine i peneul julge. — I will give you this pen for that book.

examples.text: 이 컴퓨터는 값이 싼 대신 질이 나쁩니다.
examples.translation: i keompyuteoneun gapsi ssan daesin jiri nappeumnida. — This computer is cheap, but the quality is bad.

examples.text: 이메일 대신 전화로 연락합시다.
examples.translation: imeil daesin jeonhwaro yeollakapsida. — Let’s keep in touch by phone instead of e-mail.

explanations.title: More examples
explanations.body: From the core vocabulary:

examples.text: 커피 대신에 차를 마셔보세요.
examples.translation: keopi daesine chareul masyeoboseyo. — Try drinking tea instead of coffee. (the core vocabulary’s example)

examples.text: 시험을 볼 때는 펜 대신에 연필을 사용하세요.
examples.translation: siheomeul bol ttaeneun pen daesine yeonpireul sayonghaseyo. — When you take the test, use a pencil instead of a pen. (the core vocabulary’s example)

explanations.title: Forms (mine)
explanations.body: The forms are made by the book’s rule: a noun + 대신에, or the present attributive form -는 of an action verb + 대신에 (ㄹ stems drop the ㄹ: 놀다 → 노는).

rows: a pencil instead of a pen

explanations.title: How to use this list
explanations.body:
The book’s Core Vocabulary lists the core words of the chapter with an example sentence for each (the sentences and the English meanings are the book’s; the book gives no English for the sentences). The Hanja of the Sino-Korean words are in parentheses before the meaning. Where the book writes two forms together (for example 상대(방) or 소개팅/미팅), the forms are written with a slash.

The example sentences with digits are respelled in Hangul (1988년 → 천구백팔십팔 년, 3장 → 세 장). The book’s related words (the synonyms, antonyms and related words in the last column) are left out; the book’s Additional Vocabulary section is blank.

explanations.title: Self-evaluation
explanations.body:
Recall the objectives of the chapter and ask yourself whether you have achieved them (the book asks you to tick Yes or No). If you tick “No” for any item, the book suggests: review that section on your own; find a study partner and review it as a pair or group; and tell your academic advisor or team leader which areas you need more help with, so that they can provide activities tailored to your learning style and needs.

Now I am able to: identify and talk about important birthdays like the 1st, 70th, and 80th; identify and talk about events related to courting and a wedding, and one’s ideal type of partner; and offer an invitation to an important family event.

Now I have a clear understanding of: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary section; –는 중이다 / ~ 중이다 (to be in the middle of; to be –ing); –아/어(서) 죽겠다 used to exaggerate feelings about a condition; –(으)ㄴ/는 대신(에) and ~ 대신(에) (instead of; rather than; in place of); –(으)ㄹ 계획/생각/예정이다 (plan to; intend to; be going to); and the Sino-Korean syllables 애 (愛), 축 (祝) and 식 (式).

explanations.title: What Chapter 27 teaches (친목 모임)
explanations.body:
Chapter 27, “Social Gatherings”, has three topic presentations, grammar in focus, activities, a self-evaluation and the core vocabulary.

When you finish the chapter you will be able to: identify and talk about social events such as housewarming parties, company lunches/dinners, alumni reunions, and end-of-year parties; talk about organizing social events; and accept or decline an invitation to a social event.

You will become familiar with: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary section; contracted forms for reported speech; –(으)ㄹ래(요) used to indicate a speaker’s intention or desire in casual situations; the auxiliary verb –아/어 버리다 used to imply a completed action; and the Sino-Korean syllables 친 (親) and 선 (先).

explanations.title: Cultural note: the housewarming party (집들이)
explanations.body: Koreans often host a housewarming party (집들이) to present their new home to their friends and relatives after getting married or moving. When invited to a housewarming party, Koreans have traditionally brought soaps, detergent, or matches as presents (집들이 선물). These gifts express hope that the new residents will become rich as quickly as detergent or soap bubbles up or a match lights. Though soaps and detergent remain favorite gift items, people today also bring home appliances or items necessary for a new home.

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 친 (親)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means close or intimate (in relationship), as in 친구 (a friend), 친목회 (a social gathering). When the syllable comes before a kinship term, it means real or true, as in 친어머니 (one’s real mother), 친동생 (one’s real brother), 친부모 (one’s real parents; one’s own parents), and 친손자 (one’s own grandson; “real grandson”). This syllable is used to refer to a relative on one’s father’s side, as in 친할아버지 (one’s paternal grandfather; “real grandfather”) and 친삼촌 (one’s paternal uncle; “real uncle”). The syllable 외 is used to refer to a relative on one’s mother’s side, as in 외할아버지 (one’s maternal grandfather) and 외삼촌 (one’s maternal uncle). When the Sino-Korean syllable 친 comes before a non-kinship term, it normally means pro- or favoring, as in 친미 (pro-American) and 친북 (pro-North Korean; “pro-North”).

explanations.title: Topic A: I will go to a housewarming party this Saturday (이번 주 토요일에 집들이에 갈 거예요)
explanations.body: The following text is from a woman’s blog entry about a housewarming party. (The English is mine; the book gives none. The book’s footnote: In Chapter 22 you learned that –(으)ㄹ지 expresses an indirect question embedded in a sentence, as in 무엇을 해야 할지 모르겠다 (I don’t know what I should do).)

examples.text: 한 달 전에 남편의 친구 가족이 새 아파트로 이사를 갔다.
examples.translation: han dal jeone nampyeonui chingu gajogi sae apateuro isareul gatda. — A month ago, my husband’s friend’s family moved to a new apartment.

examples.text: 그래서 이번 주 토요일에 집들이 겸 친목회를 한다.
examples.translation: geuraeseo ibeon ju toyoire jipdeuri gyeom chinmokoereul handa. — So this Saturday there will be a housewarming party and social gathering together.

examples.text: 남편들끼리는 한 달에 한 번 친목 모임을 해서 자주 만난다.
examples.translation: nampyeondeulkkirineun han dare han beon chinmok moimeul haeseo jaju mannanda. — The husbands have a social gathering once a month, so they often meet.

examples.text: 그렇지만, 부인들은 오랜만에 만나기 때문에 이번 주 토요일이 아주 기대된다.
examples.translation: geureochiman, buindeureun oraenmane mannagi ttaemune ibeon ju toyoiri aju gidaedoenda. — However, the wives meet after a long time, so I am really looking forward to this Saturday.

explanations.title: Follow-up 2 (Reading and Writing): an invitation to a housewarming party
explanations.body: The e-mail is an invitation to your friend’s housewarming party. The book asks you to fill in the blanks with words from a box (정리, 세제, 고민, 기대, 휴지, 친목회, 새, 집들이; the answers may vary). The text below is the e-mail with the blanks filled (my answer key; the digit is spelled out; the e-mail address and the ellipsis are left out; the English is mine).

examples.text: 잘 있었니?
examples.translation: jal isseonni? — How have you been?

examples.text: 내가 지난달에 새 아파트로 이사 간 것 알지?
examples.translation: naega jinandare sae apateuro isa gan geot alji? — You know I moved to a new apartment last month, right?

examples.text: 다음 주 토요일 저녁 다섯 시에 우리 집에서 집들이 겸 친목회를 하려고 해.
examples.translation: daeum ju toyoil jeonyeok daseot sie uri jibeseo jipdeuri gyeom chinmokoereul haryeogo hae. — I am going to have a housewarming party and social gathering at my house next Saturday at five in the evening.

examples.text: 참, 집들이 선물로 무엇을 가져올까 고민하지 마.
examples.translation: cham, jipdeuri seonmullo mueoseul gajeoolkka gominhaji ma. — Oh, and don’t worry about what to bring as a housewarming gift.

examples.text: 세제도 많고 휴지도 많으니까 사오지 말고.
examples.translation: sejedo manko hyujido maneunikka saoji malgo. — I have lots of detergent and lots of toilet paper, so don’t buy any and bring it.

examples.text: 다음 주 토요일이 너무 기대된다.
examples.translation: daeum ju toyoiri neomu gidaedoenda. — I am really looking forward to next Saturday.

examples.text: 참, 그날 올 수 있는지 없는지 미리 알려줘.
examples.translation: cham, geunal ol su inneunji eomneunji miri allyeojwo. — Oh, and let me know in advance whether you can come that day or not.

explanations.title: The blanks (mine)
explanations.body: The blanks in order are 새, 집들이, 친목회, 고민, 세제, 휴지 and 기대; 정리 is the word left over.

explanations.title: Activity 3 (Reading): a man’s concern about a housewarming present
explanations.body: You read a man’s concerns about a housewarming present, posted on a website’s Q&A section, and fill in a table in English. The text is the book’s (3년 and 6개월 and 10만 원 are spelled out; the emoticon is left out); the English is mine.

examples.text: 집들이 선물 추천 바랍니다.
examples.translation: jipdeuri seonmul chucheon baramnida. — Please recommend a housewarming gift. (the question’s title)

examples.text: 다음 주 토요일에 아는 형이 집들이를 하는데요.
examples.translation: daeum ju toyoire aneun hyeongi jipdeurireul haneundeyo. — Next Saturday a guy I know, an older brother figure, is having a housewarming party.

examples.text: 형은 삼 년 전에 결혼했고 육 개월쯤 된 아들이 하나 있습니다.
examples.translation: hyeongeun sam nyeon jeone gyeolhonhaetgo yuk gaewoljjeum doen adeuri hana itseumnida. — He got married three years ago and has a son who is about six months old.

examples.text: 예전부터 저하고 아주 친한 형이어서 색다른 선물을 하고 싶어요.
examples.translation: yejeonbuteo jeohago aju chinhan hyeongieoseo saekdareun seonmureul hago sipeoyo. — He has been very close to me for a long time, so I want to give an unusual gift.

examples.text: 그래서 무슨 선물을 해야 할지 고민입니다.
examples.translation: geuraeseo museun seonmureul haeya halji gominimnida. — So I am torn over what gift to give.

examples.text: 선물은 십만 원 정도로 생각하고 있습니다.
examples.translation: seonmureun simman won jeongdoro saenggakago itseumnida. — I am thinking of about 100,000 won for the gift.

examples.text: 어떤 선물이 좋을지 추천해 주세요.
examples.translation: eotteon seonmuri joeulji chucheonhae juseyo. — Please recommend what kind of gift would be good.

examples.text: 선물을 구입할 수 있는 웹사이트도 알려주시면 고맙겠습니다.
examples.translation: seonmureul guipal su inneun wepsaiteudo allyeojusimyeon gomapgetseumnida. — I would be grateful if you could also tell me a website where I can buy the gift.

examples.translation: maikeul: a, geureokunyo! geureom, hoesigeneun uri buseo jigwondeulman moineun geoyeyo? — Oh, I see! Then is it only our department’s staff who gather at the dinner?

examples.text: 주연: 네, 그런데 이번에는 사장님과 부장님도 참석하신대요.
examples.translation: juyeon: ne, geureonde ibeoneneun sajangnimgwa bujangnimdo chamseokasindaeyo. — Yes, but this time they say the president and the general manager will also attend.

examples.text: 마이클: 저는 회식은 처음인데, 이런 모임에서는 주로 뭘 해요?
examples.translation: maikeul: jeoneun hoesigeun cheoeuminde, ireon moimeseoneun juro mwol haeyo? — It is my first company dinner; what do people mainly do at this kind of gathering?

examples.text: 주연: 보통 음식점에 가서 식사하고, 그 후에 술집이나 노래방에 가요. 동료들과 음식도 먹고 편하게 이야기할 수 있는 기회예요.
examples.translation: juyeon: botong eumsikjeome gaseo siksahago, geu hue suljibina noraebange gayo. dongnyodeulgwa eumsikdo meokgo pyeonhage iyagihal su inneun gihoeyeyo. — Usually we go to a restaurant and eat, and after that go to a bar or a karaoke room. It is an opportunity to eat with colleagues and talk comfortably.

examples.text: 마이클: 그럼 술을 마셔야 해요? 저는 술을 못 마셔요.
examples.translation: maikeul: geureom sureul masyeoya haeyo? jeoneun sureul mon masyeoyo. — Then do I have to drink alcohol? I can’t drink.

examples.text: 주연: 걱정하지 마세요. 이번에는 술 마시는 대신에 연극 보러 간대요.
examples.translation: juyeon: geokjeonghaji maseyo. ibeoneneun sul masineun daesine yeongeuk boreo gandaeyo. — Don’t worry. This time they say they are going to see a play instead of drinking.

examples.text: 마이클: 그럼 좋아요. 주연 씨도 가시는 거죠?

explanations.title: Cultural note: 회식
explanations.body:
회식 literally means “gathering and eating.” It refers to a company lunch or dinner at a restaurant. Korean companies or organizations often host and pay for these events because the culture places high value on human relationships, unity, and solidarity. The events are frequently held throughout the year for special occasions such as promotions, an employee’s retirement, and welcoming new employees. If 회식 is held after work, it often evolves into after-dinner activities, called 2차 (second round), 3차 (third round), and so forth. These after-dinner activities often involve entertainment and drinking at places like 노래방 (a karaoke bar). However, new activity trends like bowling, playing pool, and drinking tea have emerged.

In recent years with the emergence of ‘work and life balance’ values - especially among young people, 회식 practices and after work entertainment culture have significantly decreased in Korea. The persistent Covid 19 pandemic and subsequent ‘work from home’ trend also contributed to the substantial social change around 회식 culture. Instead, an increasing number of people are pursuing their individual leisure activities after work.

lessons.title: 348. Ch 27 · Grammar A: contracted forms of reported speech (-답니다, -냡니다, -랍니다, -잡니다)
lessons.subtitle: 간답니다 · 간대요 · 가냡니다 · 가냬요 · 가랍니다 · 가래요 · 가잡니다 · 가재요 · 군인이랍니다

explanations.title: Reported speech: contracted forms
explanations.body: In Chapters 23 and 24, you learned about reported speech: –다고 하다 for statements, –냐고 하다 for questions, –라고 하다 for commands, and –자고 하다 for suggestions. In this lesson, you will learn the contracted forms of each. Contracted forms are used when speaking.

explanations.title: Examples
explanations.body: The book’s examples (the English is the book’s). Note that 이라고 합니다 and 아니라고 합니다 are the full forms of 이랍니다 / 이래요 and 아니랍니다 / 아니래요.

examples.text: 김일병이 저한테 도서관에 간답니다.
examples.translation: gimilbyeongi jeohante doseogwane gandamnida. — PFC Kim says (to me) [that] he is going to the library.

examples.text: 김일병이 저한테 도서관에 간대요.
examples.translation: gimilbyeongi jeohante doseogwane gandaeyo. — PFC Kim says (to me) [that] he is going to the library.

examples.text: 김일병이 저한테 어디 가냡니다.
examples.translation: gimilbyeongi jeohante eodi ganyamnida. — PFC Kim asks (me) where I am going.

examples.text: 김일병이 저한테 어디 가냬요.
examples.translation: gimilbyeongi jeohante eodi ganyaeyo. — PFC Kim asks (me) where I am going.

explanations.title: Forms (mine)
explanations.body: The forms are made by the book’s rule. In the full form a statement of an action verb ends in -ㄴ다 / -는다 (the ㄹ stems drop ㄹ: 만들다 → 만든다고), a command in -(으)라고 and a suggestion in -자고.

explanations.title: Follow-up 1: the model
explanations.body: Partner A reads a full-form reported speech sentence; Partner B changes it into the contracted form and translates it into English. The book’s two models:

rows: PFC Kim says [that] he is going to school.
My friend suggests (to me) [that] we should study together.

explanations.title: Follow-up 3 (Reading and Writing): a phone conversation retold
explanations.body: Text A is the transcription of a phone conversation in which two friends, Youngmee and Jimin, arrange a meeting on the weekend. Text B is the conversation in which Jimin tells her mother about it; the book asks you to complete Text B by reporting Youngmee’s speech with the appropriate contracted form. The text is the book’s (the blanks are my answers); the English is mine.

examples.text: 지민아, 이번 일요일에 등산 가자.
examples.translation: jimina, ibeon iryoire deungsan gaja. — Jimin, let’s go hiking this Sunday. (Youngmee)

examples.text: 그래, 근데 뭘 준비해야 해?
examples.translation: geurae, geunde mwol junbihaeya hae? — OK, but what should I prepare? (Jimin)

examples.text: 어디서 만나?

examples.text: 지하철 서울대 입구에서 만나재요.
examples.translation: jihacheol seouldae ipgueseo mannajaeyo. — She says let’s meet at Seoul National University Station of the subway. (Jimin; my answer)

examples.text: 뭘 준비해야 해?

explanations.title: Topic C: We will have the alumni reunion and end-of-year party together (동창회 겸 송년회를 같이 할 거야)
explanations.body: Two friends who have not seen each other since they graduated from college are having a conversation at a reunion. (The English is mine; the book gives none. The book’s footnotes: 학번 literally means “class number.” 학번 is a label assigned to each class. It consists of the two digits of the year in which the students in the class entered college; this designator is used for college only, not for high school. Since 네가 and 내가 have almost the same pronunciation, people often pronounce 네가 as 니가 to make it less confusing. The book writes 17학번; it is spelled out here.)

explanations.title: Notes: 선배와 후배
explanations.body: 선배 (先輩) literally means “(person who is) front in a group” and 후배 (後輩) means “(person who is) back in a group.” 선배 refers to a person who is senior or an elder in an organization, whereas 후배 refers to a person who is junior or younger in an organization. In Korea, if someone in the same social group (school, company, club, etc.) is senior to you in starting date or experience, he becomes your 선배, and you address the person as 선배(님), as in 김 선배(님), 박 선배(님), etc. You may call the person 형, 오빠, 누나, or 언니 if you share a closer relationship. Someone in the same group who is junior to you is your 후배, and you use the person’s first name.

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 선 (先)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means before(hand), ahead, or front, as in 선생님 (a teacher; Mr.; Mrs.; “[person] born ahead”), 선약 (a previous engagement; a previous appointment), 선례 (a precedent; “preceding example”), 선착 (first arrival; “beforehand” arrival), and 선진국 (an advanced nation; “nation moving ahead”).

lessons.title: 350. Ch 27 · Grammar B: expressing a speaker’s intention or desire with -(으)ㄹ래(요)
lessons.subtitle: 비빔밥 먹을래요 · 뭐 시킬래? · 지금 먹을래요 · 도와줄래? · 올래요?

explanations.title: A. Expressing a speaker’s intention or desire in casual situations
explanations.body: In earlier chapters, you learned how to express an intention or desire by using grammar features like –겠다, –(으)ㄹ 거다, and –고 싶다. For example:

examples.text: 저는 내년에 한국에 가겠어요.
examples.translation: jeoneun naenyeone hanguge gagesseoyo. — I will go to Korea next year.

examples.text: 저는 내년에 한국에 갈 거예요.
examples.translation: jeoneun naenyeone hanguge gal geoyeyo. — I am going to go to Korea next year.

examples.text: 저는 내년에 한국에 가고 싶어요.
examples.translation: jeoneun naenyeone hanguge gago sipeoyo. — I want to go to Korea next year.

explanations.title: The verb ending -(으)ㄹ래(요)
explanations.body: In this lesson, you will learn the verb ending –(으)ㄹ래(요), which is used in casual conversation to express the speaker’s intention or desire. If used in a question, however, the verb ending indicates the listener’s intention or desire. Look at the following casual conversation between a mother and a daughter at a restaurant (the English is the book’s):

examples.text: 영미야, 뭐 시킬래?
examples.translation: yeongmiya, mwo sikillae? — Youngmi, what would you like to order? (A, the mother)

examples.text: 전 비빔밥 먹을래요. 엄마는요?
examples.translation: jeon bibimbap meogeullaeyo. eommaneunyo? — I’ll have bibimbap. What about you, Mom? (B)

examples.text: 난 김치찌개 먹을래.
examples.translation: nan gimchijjigae meogeullae. — I’ll have kimchi stew. (A)

explanations.title: Translation and use
explanations.body: Note that the mother uses the verb ending –(으)ㄹ래 to ask what the daughter wants to order. The daughter uses the same verb ending plus 요 to express her own desire for 비빔밥. For this reason, –(으)ㄹ래 can be translated as will, would like to, or want to. Keep in mind that this verb ending works only with action verbs.

examples.text: 저녁은 나중에 먹을래요?
examples.translation: jeonyeogeun najunge meogeullaeyo? — Will you eat dinner later?

examples.text: 지금 먹을래요.
examples.translation: jigeum meogeullaeyo. — I will have it now.

explanations.title: A request with -(으)ㄹ래
explanations.body: The verb ending –(으)ㄹ래 can be also used when the speaker makes a request. For example:

examples.text: 지현아, 내 숙제 좀 도와줄래?
examples.translation: jihyeona, nae sukje jom dowajullae? — Would you help me with my homework?

examples.text: 그래, 알았어.
examples.translation: geurae, arasseo. — OK, I will.

examples.text: 오늘 저녁에 우리 집에 올래요?
examples.translation: oneul jeonyeoge uri jibe ollaeyo? — Would you like to come to my house this evening? (the core vocabulary’s example)

explanations.title: Forms (mine)
explanations.body: The forms are made by the book’s rule: the future attributive form -(으)ㄹ (ㄹ stems keep it: 놀다 → 놀, 만들다 → 만들; the ㅂ irregular 돕다 → 도울) plus 래 (and 요 in polite speech).

explanations.title: Follow-up 1: the model and my sentences
explanations.body: The book gives ten sentence strips, which are not in the text; its model, and my own sentences in the same pattern (the English is mine):

rows: I’ll watch a movie on the weekend. (mine)

explanations.title: Activities left out
explanations.body: Follow-up 1’s sentence strips (a partner activity) and Follow-up 2 (listening to three conversations between family members and noting what the female speaker wants) are audio and partner activities.

lessons.title: 351. Ch 27 · Grammar C: the auxiliary verb -아/어 버리다 implies a completed action
lessons.subtitle: 먹어 버렸어요 · 써 버렸어요 · 날아가 버렸어요 · 해 버릴 거예요 · 사 버렸어요 · 잊어버렸어요

explanations.title: B. The auxiliary verb -아/어 버리다
explanations.body: So far you have learned auxiliary verbs that start with 아/어: –아/어 보다, as in 김치를 먹어보세요 (sense of experiment), and –아/어 주다, as in 문을 열어 주세요 (sense of service). All these auxiliary verbs add “flavor” to the main verb. Likewise, the auxiliary verb –아/어 버리다 adds “flavor” to the main verb. Because 버리다 in –아/어 버리다 means to throw away or discard, this auxiliary verb is used to imply that an action is completed and thus it is irreversible or no longer available. Compare the following two sentences:

examples.text: 동생이 내 피자를 먹었어요.
examples.translation: dongsaengi nae pijareul meogeosseoyo. — My younger brother ate my pizza.

examples.text: 동생이 내 피자를 먹어 버렸어요.
examples.translation: dongsaengi nae pijareul meogeo beoryeosseoyo. — My younger brother ate my pizza (and it’s gone). / My younger brother ended up eating my pizza.

explanations.title: Meaning
explanations.body: The verb in the first sentence is 먹었어요 (ate), and the speaker tells us that his younger brother ate his pizza. The verb in the second sentence ends with the auxiliary verb –아/어 버리다. The speaker implies that the action of his brother eating his pizza was completed and is irreversible. In a certain context, the sentence can imply that the speaker is upset that his pizza is gone. Look at the following sentences that use –아/어 버리다:

examples.text: 돈을 다 써 버렸어요.

examples.text: 숙제를 다 해 버릴 거예요.

examples.text: 새 컴퓨터를 사 버렸어요.

explanations.title: How to use this list
explanations.body:
The book’s Core Vocabulary lists the core words of the chapter with an example sentence for each (the sentences and the English meanings are the book’s; the book gives no English for the sentences). The Hanja of the Sino-Korean words are in parentheses before the meaning. Where the book writes two forms together (for example 동문/동창 or 화장지/휴지), the forms are written with a slash.

The example sentences with digits are respelled in Hangul (12월 31일 → 십이 월 삼십일 일, 20명 → 스무 명, 07학번 → 공칠 학번). The book’s related words (the synonyms, antonyms and related words in the last column) are left out; the book’s Additional Vocabulary section is blank.

explanations.title: Self-evaluation
explanations.body:
Recall the objectives of the chapter and ask yourself whether you have achieved them (the book asks you to tick Yes or No). If you tick “No” for any item, the book suggests: review that section on your own; find a study partner and review it as a pair or group; and tell your academic advisor or team leader which areas you need more help with, so that they can provide activities tailored to your learning style and needs.

Now I am able to: identify and talk about social events such as housewarming parties, company lunches/dinners, alumni reunions, and end-of-year parties; talk about organizing social events; and accept or decline an invitation to a social event.

Now I have a clear understanding of: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary section; contracted forms for reported speech; –(으)ㄹ래(요) used to indicate a speaker’s intention or desire in casual situations; the auxiliary verb –아/어 버리다 used to imply a completed action; and the Sino-Korean syllables 친 (親) and 선 (先).

lessons.title: 353. Ch 28 · What the chapter teaches, 례/예 (禮) and 음 (音), and Korean dialects
lessons.subtitle: 예의 바른 한국인 · 무례 · 실례 · 예의 · 예절 · 음악 · 음성 · 표준말 · 사투리

explanations.title: What Chapter 28 teaches (예의 바른 한국인)
explanations.body:
Chapter 28, “Polite Koreans”, has three topic presentations, grammar in focus, activities, a self-evaluation and the core vocabulary.

When you finish the chapter you will be able to: identify different generations and talk about them; identify and use two different language registers, 존댓말 and 반말; and identify and talk about Korean manners and etiquette.

You will become familiar with: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary section; a summary of speech styles; the verb ending –지(요); the interrogative ending –나(요); and the Sino-Korean syllables 례/예 (禮) and 음 (音).

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 례/예 (禮)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means manners, etiquette, or courtesy, as in 무례 (impoliteness; rudeness; “no manners”), 실례 (rudeness; impoliteness; “loss of manners”), 예의 (courtesy; decorum; civility; etiquette), and 예절 (decorum; courtesy; etiquette). Note that 례 becomes 예 when it is placed at the beginning of a word.

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 음 (音)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means sound or sonic-, as in 고음 (high-pitched sound; “high sound”), 저음 (low-pitched sound), 음악 (music; “merry sound”), 음량 (sound volume), 음성 (a voice; a sound), 음속 (the speed of sound; sonic speed; “sound speed”), 음질 (the quality of sound), and 음파 (sound wave).

rows: the speed of sound; sonic speed; “sound speed”

explanations.title: Notes: Korean dialects
explanations.body: Like most languages in the world, Korean has dialects (사투리 or 방언). Korean dialects are not extreme and do not block basic communication the way Mandarin and Cantonese do in China. Differences are found in intonation, verbal endings, and some vocabulary. 서울말 is considered a standard dialect (표준말) in South Korea and 평양말 is a standard dialect in North Korea. South Korean regional dialects include, as you may have guessed, 강원도 사투리, 충청도 사투리, 전라도 사투리, 경상도 사투리 and 제주도 사투리. The last two (경상도 and 제주도) carry a relatively strong accent when compared with 서울 표준말. (The book’s picture shows various words for “dragonfly” in the dialects; the standard Korean word is 잠자리.)

lessons.subtitle: 한국 사람들은 예의가 바른 것 같아요 · 자리를 양보했어요 · 어른을 공경 · 신세대 · 기성세대

explanations.title: Topic A: Korean people seem to be courteous (한국 사람들은 예의가 바른 것 같아요)
explanations.body: Mr. Kim and Michael are talking about the manners of the younger generation after Michael observed a high school student giving his seat to an elderly man on a subway train. (The English is mine; the book gives none. The book writes 아… with an ellipsis; it is left out.)

examples.text: 마이클: 지하철에서 한 고등학생이 나이 드신 분께 자리를 양보했어요.
examples.translation: maikeul: jihacheoreseo han godeunghaksaengi nai deusin bunkke jarireul yangbohaesseoyo. — On the subway, a high school student gave up his seat to an elderly person.

examples.text: 김 선생님: 한국에서는 흔한 일이에요. 한국 사람들은 어릴 때부터 어른을 공경해야 한다고 배워요.
examples.translation: gim seonsaengnim: hangugeseoneun heunhan irieyo. hanguk saramdeureun eoril ttaebuteo eoreuneul gonggyeonghaeya handago baewoyo. — In Korea, that is a common thing. Koreans learn from the time they are young that they should respect their elders.

examples.text: 마이클: 아, 그래서 한국 사람들이 예의가 바르군요. 근데, 요즘 신세대들도 예전처럼 예의를 잘 지켜요?
examples.translation: maikeul: a, geuraeseo hanguk saramdeuri yeuiga bareugunyo. geunde, yojeum sinsedaedeuldo yejeoncheoreom yeuireul jal jikyeoyo? — Oh, so that’s why Koreans are polite. By the way, do the younger generation these days also keep good manners like before?

examples.text: 김 선생님: 네. 그렇지만 신세대들은 개성이 강해요. 그리고 자기 의견을 솔직하게 말하는 편이에요. 그래서 어떤 기성세대들은 신세대들이 버릇이 없다고 생각해요.
examples.translation: gim seonsaengnim: ne. geureochiman sinsedaedeureun gaeseongi ganghaeyo. geurigo jagi uigyeoneul soljikage malhaneun pyeonieyo. geuraeseo eotteon giseongsedaedeureun sinsedaedeuri beoreusi eopdago saenggakaeyo. — Yes. But the younger generation has strong individuality. And they tend to state their opinions frankly. So some of the older generation think the younger generation has no manners.

examples.text: 마이클: 김 선생님은 어떻게 생각하세요?
examples.translation: maikeul: gim seonsaengnimeun eotteoke saenggakaseyo? — What do you think, Mr. Kim?

examples.text: 김 선생님: 글쎄요. 세대간에 생각하는 방식이 좀 다른 것 같아요. 가끔 신세대들이 버릇이 없어 보여요. 그렇지만 어른을 존경하는 마음은 여전히 있는 것 같아요.
examples.translation: gim seonsaengnim: geulsseyo. sedaegane saenggakaneun bangsigi jom dareun geot gatayo. gakkeum sinsedaedeuri beoreusi eopseo boyeoyo. geureochiman eoreuneul jongyeonghaneun maeumeun yeojeonhi inneun geot gatayo. — Well. It seems the way of thinking differs a little between generations. Sometimes the younger generation seems to have no manners. But it seems they still have a heart that respects elders.

examples.text: 마이클: 그렇군요. 그럼, 기성세대와 신세대가 서로를 이해하려고 노력해야겠네요.
examples.translation: maikeul: geureokunyo. geureom, giseongsedaewa sinsedaega seororeul ihaeharyeogo noryeokaeyagenneyo. — I see. Then the older and younger generations will have to try to understand each other.

examples.text: 김 선생님: 그렇죠. 대화가 제일 좋은 방법인 것 같아요.
examples.translation: gim seonsaengnim: geureocho. daehwaga jeil joeun bangbeobin geot gatayo. — That’s right. It seems conversation is the best way.

lessons.subtitle: 존댓말을 써야 해요 · 표준말 · 사투리 · 반말 · 실수 · 자연스럽게 쓸 수 있어요

explanations.title: Topic B: You should use an honorific expression (존댓말을 써야 해요)
explanations.body: Peter, who is learning Korean in Korea, is talking to Jungmee about his language-learning experience. (The English is mine; the book gives none. The book’s footnote: 자연스럽게 (naturally) is from 자연스럽다 (to be natural). The quotation marks and the stage direction “(웃으면서)”, laughing, are left out of the spoken lines.)

examples.text: 피터: 정미 씨, 한국말이 지방마다 조금씩 달라요?
examples.translation: piteo: jeongmi ssi, hangungmari jibangmada jogeumssik dallayo? — Jungmee, does Korean differ a little by region?

examples.text: 정미: 그럼요. 서울말이 표준말이고 지방마다 사투리가 있어요. 근데, 왜요?
examples.translation: jeongmi: geureomyo. seoulmari pyojunmarigo jibangmada saturiga isseoyo. geunde, waeyo? — Of course. The Seoul dialect is the standard language and every region has a dialect. But why?

examples.text: 피터: 네, 어제 텔레비전에서 우연히 제주도 말을 들었는데 정말 어려웠어요.
examples.translation: piteo: ne, eoje tellebijeoneseo uyeonhi jejudo mareul deureonneunde jeongmal eoryeowosseoyo. — Well, yesterday I happened to hear the Jeju dialect on television and it was really difficult.

examples.text: 정미: 맞아요. 특히 제주도 말은 이해하기가 힘들어요. 또 발음하기도 어려워요.
examples.translation: jeongmi: majayo. teuki jejudo mareun ihaehagiga himdeureoyo. tto bareumhagido eoryeowoyo. — That’s right. In particular, the Jeju dialect is hard to understand. It is also hard to pronounce.

examples.text: 피터: 아, 그렇군요.
examples.translation: piteo: a, geureokunyo. — Oh, I see.

examples.text: 정미: 그런데, 피터 씨는 존댓말을 아주 잘하시네요?
examples.translation: jeongmi: geureonde, piteo ssineun jondaenmareul aju jalhasineyo? — By the way, you speak honorific language very well, Peter.

examples.text: 피터: 아, 그래요? 그래도, 자주 틀려요. 지난번에는 선생님, 잘 잤어요? 라고 말해서 반 친구들이 많이 웃었어요.
examples.translation: piteo: a, geuraeyo? geuraedo, jaju teullyeoyo. jinanbeoneneun seonsaengnim, jal jasseoyo? rago malhaeseo ban chingudeuri mani useosseoyo. — Oh, really? Still, I often get it wrong. Last time I said, “Teacher, did you sleep well?” (in the wrong form) and my classmates laughed a lot.

examples.text: 정미: 아, 네. 근데, 피터 씨는 반말보다 존댓말이 더 쉬워요?
examples.translation: jeongmi: a, ne. geunde, piteo ssineun banmalboda jondaenmari deo swiwoyo? — Oh, I see. By the way, is honorific language easier for you than blunt language?

examples.text: 피터: 네. 저는 존댓말이 더 쉬워요. 그렇지만, 댁이나 연세처럼 단어가 아주 다른 존댓말은 아직 잘 몰라요. 외워야 할 단어가 많은 것 같아요.
examples.translation: piteo: ne. jeoneun jondaenmari deo swiwoyo. geureochiman, daegina yeonsecheoreom daneoga aju dareun jondaenmareun ajik jal mollayo. oewoya hal daneoga maneun geot gatayo. — Yes. Honorific language is easier for me. But I still don’t know well the honorific words that are very different, like 댁 and 연세. It seems there are many words to memorize.

examples.text: 정미: 피터 씨, 걱정하지 마세요. 부지런히 공부하면 그런 표현들도 다 자연스럽게 쓸 수 있어요.
examples.translation: jeongmi: piteo ssi, geokjeonghaji maseyo. bujireonhi gongbuhamyeon geureon pyohyeondeuldo da jayeonseureopge sseul su isseoyo. — Don’t worry, Peter. If you study diligently, you will be able to use those expressions all naturally, too.

The text is the book’s (10년 and 8년 are spelled out; the quotation marks are left out); the English is mine. The book glosses 실수: an error, a mistake.

examples.text: 저는 필리핀에서 온 니에베스 쿠발란입니다.
examples.translation: jeoneun pillipineseo on niebeseu kuballanimnida. — I am Nieves Cuballan, who came from the Philippines.

examples.text: 저는 십 년 전에 한국에 공부하러 왔습니다.
examples.translation: jeoneun sip nyeon jeone hanguge gongbuhareo watseumnida. — I came to Korea to study ten years ago.

examples.text: 그때 지금의 남편을 만났습니다.
examples.translation: geuttae jigeumui nampyeoneul mannatseumnida. — At that time I met my present husband.

examples.text: 그리고 팔 년 전에 결혼했습니다.
examples.translation: geurigo pal nyeon jeone gyeolhonhaetseumnida. — And I got married eight years ago.

examples.text: 지금은 제주시에서 시부모님을 모시고 살고 있습니다.
examples.translation: jigeumeun jejusieseo sibumonimeul mosigo salgo itseumnida. — Now I live in Jeju City with my parents-in-law.

examples.text: 처음에는 한국말을 잘 몰라서 실수한 적도 많았습니다.
examples.translation: cheoeumeneun hangungmareul jal mollaseo silsuhan jeokdo manatseumnida. — At first, I did not know Korean well, so there were many times I made mistakes.

examples.text: 결혼해서 시댁에 살게 된 첫날이었습니다.
examples.translation: gyeolhonhaeseo sidaege salge doen cheonnarieotseumnida. — It was the first day after I got married and came to live at my husband’s family’s home.

examples.text: 아침에 일어나서 시부모님께 잘 잤어라고 인사를 했습니다.
examples.translation: achime ireonaseo sibumonimkke jal jasseorago insareul haetseumnida. — In the morning I got up and greeted my parents-in-law with “Did you sleep well?” (in blunt language).

examples.text: 그랬더니 시부모님께서 많이 웃으셨습니다.
examples.translation: geuraetdeoni sibumonimkkeseo mani useusyeotseumnida. — Then my parents-in-law laughed a lot.

examples.text: 남편이 어른께는 반말을 써서는 안 된다고 가르쳐 주었습니다.
examples.translation: nampyeoni eoreunkkeneun banmareul sseoseoneun an doendago gareucheo jueotseumnida. — My husband taught me that I must not use blunt language to elders.

examples.text: 또, 이웃에 사는 초등학생 아이에게 저녁 잡수셨어요라고 존댓말을 써서 웃은 적도 있습니다.
examples.translation: tto, iuse saneun chodeunghaksaeng aiege jeonyeok japsusyeosseoyorago jondaenmareul sseoseo useun jeokdo itseumnida. — Also, there was a time people laughed because I used honorific language, saying “Did you have dinner?”, to an elementary school child living nearby.

examples.text: 지금은 한국말이 많이 늘어서 이런 실수는 안 합니다.
examples.translation: jigeumeun hangungmari mani neureoseo ireon silsuneun an hamnida. — Now my Korean has improved a lot, so I don’t make this kind of mistake.

examples.text: 하지만, 아직도 제주도 사투리는 어렵습니다.
examples.translation: hajiman, ajikdo jejudo saturineun eoryeopseumnida. — But the Jeju dialect is still difficult.

examples.text: 시부모님께서 제주도 말을 하시면 이해하기 어렵습니다.
examples.translation: sibumonimkkeseo jejudo mareul hasimyeon ihaehagi eoryeopseumnida. — When my parents-in-law speak the Jeju dialect, it is hard to understand.

examples.text: 한국말이 어려워도 한국말이 참 아름답다는 생각을 저는 자주 합니다.
examples.translation: hangungmari eoryeowodo hangungmari cham areumdapdaneun saenggageul jeoneun jaju hamnida. — Even though Korean is difficult, I often think that Korean is truly beautiful.

examples.text: 앞으로도 한국말을 열심히 배워서 더 잘할 수 있도록 노력할 겁니다.
examples.translation: apeurodo hangungmareul yeolsimhi baewoseo deo jalhal su itdorok noryeokal geomnida. — In the future, too, I will learn Korean hard and make an effort so that I can do it better.
