lessons.title: 519. Ch 41 · Grammar D: the scope of comparisons in the superlative, ~ 중에서/가운데서 and ~에서
lessons.subtitle: 가장 · 제일 · ~ 중에서 · ~ 가운데서 · ~에서 · 우리 반에서 · 식구 중에서 · 가족에 대한 이야기

explanations.title: Recall the superlative
explanations.body: Recall the superlative in which the adjective (or stative verb) or adverb is preceded by 가장 or 제일. For example (the English is the book’s):

examples.text: 러시아가 가장 큰 나라예요.
examples.translation: reosiaga gajang keun narayeyo. — Russia is the largest country.

examples.text: 최 병장이 제일 빨리 말해요.
examples.translation: choe byeongjangi jeil ppalli malhaeyo. — Sgt. Choi speaks the fastest.

explanations.title: The scope of comparisons
explanations.body: Note that 제일 is more frequently used than 가장, especially in spoken language. Because the superlative is used for comparing more than two things or people, we often express the scope of comparisons using one of the following two phrases: (1) ~에서, as in 직장에서 (in my workplace) and 뉴욕에서 (in New York); (2) ~ 중에서/가운데서, as in 한국인 중에서 (among Koreans) and 책 가운데서 (among books). For example (the English is the book’s):

examples.text: 제가 우리 학교에서 성적이 제일 좋아요.
examples.translation: jega uri hakgyoeseo seongjeogi jeil joayo. — I have the highest GPA in my school.

examples.text: 제가 학생 중에서 가장 빨리 달려요.
examples.translation: jega haksaeng jungeseo gajang ppalli dallyeoyo. — Of (all) the students, I run the fastest.

explanations.title: Which one follows what
explanations.body: Note that ~에서 is preceded by a place and ~ 중에서/가운데서 is preceded by things or people. More examples (the English is the book’s):

examples.text: 우리 식구 중에서 제 남동생이 제일 커요.
examples.translation: uri sikgu jungeseo je namdongsaengi jeil keoyo. — My younger brother is the tallest of (all) my family members.

examples.text: 언어 가운데서 한국말이 제일 어려워요.
examples.translation: eoneo gaundeseo hangungmari jeil eoryeowoyo. — Of (all) the languages, Korean is the most difficult.

examples.text: 이 식당에서 불고기가 제일 비싸요.
examples.translation: i sikdangeseo bulgogiga jeil bissayo. — Bulgogi is the most expensive (food) at this restaurant.

examples.text: 우리 반에서 이 병장이 노래를 제일 잘해요.
examples.translation: uri baneseo i byeongjangi noraereul jeil jalhaeyo. — SFC Lee is the best singer in our class.

explanations.title: Follow-up 3 (Listening, reading and speaking): the model
explanations.body: On the teacher’s cue, Partner A reads a sentence aloud to Partner B (e.g. 에베레스트 산이 높다). Then Partner B makes it a superlative sentence, using ~ 중에서/가운데서. Partner A repeats the superlative sentence, this time using the ~에서 phrase. The book’s model (the English is mine):

examples.text: 가: 에베레스트 산이 높다
examples.translation: ga: ebereseuteu sani nopda — Mount Everest is high.

examples.text: 나: 산 중에서 에베레스트 산이 제일 높아요.
examples.translation: na: san jungeseo ebereseuteu sani jeil nopayo. — Of mountains, Mount Everest is the highest.

examples.text: 가: 세계에서 에베레스트 산이 제일 높아요.
examples.translation: ga: segyeeseo ebereseuteu sani jeil nopayo. — In the world, Mount Everest is the highest.

explanations.title: Follow-up 5 (Listening and speaking): talk about your family
explanations.body: Think about three family members who are good at something; ask about each other’s family members and discuss what each is good at in comparison with the others, using ~ 중에서/가운데에서/에서 with 가장/제일. The book’s model (the English is mine):

examples.text: 가: 가족이 어떻게 되세요?
examples.translation: ga: gajogi eotteoke doeseyo? — How many are in your family?

examples.text: 나: 어머니, 아버지, 저 셋입니다.
examples.translation: na: eomeoni, abeoji, jeo sesimnida. — My mother, my father and I, three.

examples.text: 가: 가족에 대해서 얘기해 주세요.
examples.translation: ga: gajoge daehaeseo yaegihae juseyo. — Please tell me about your family.

examples.text: 나: 네. 저희 어머니는 식구 중에서 가장 노래를 잘 부르세요. 어머니 직장에서도 노래를 제일 잘 부르세요. 저희 아버지는 취미로 자동차 수리와 낚시, 음악감상을 하십니다. 그중에서 차 수리하는 것을 제일 좋아하세요. 저는 사진 찍기를 좋아해요. 제 친구들 중에서 사진을 제일 잘 찍어요.
examples.translation: na: ne. jeohui eomeonineun sikgu jungeseo gajang noraereul jal bureuseyo. eomeoni jikjangeseodo noraereul jeil jal bureuseyo. jeohui abeojineun chwimiro jadongcha suriwa naksi, eumakgamsangeul hasimnida. geujungeseo cha surihaneun geoseul jeil joahaseyo. jeoneun sajin jjikgireul joahaeyo. je chingudeul jungeseo sajineul jeil jal jjigeoyo. — Yes. My mother sings the best of the family. She sings the best at her workplace too. My father does car repair, fishing and listening to music as hobbies. Among them he likes repairing cars the most. I like taking photos. Among my friends, I take photos the best.

explanations.title: More sentences (mine)
explanations.body: Sample sentences of my own (the English is mine):

examples.translation: uri gajok jungeseo halmeoniga jeil bujireonhaseyo. — Of my family, my grandmother is the most diligent.

examples.text: 우리 회사에서 김 과장님이 제일 일찍 오십니다.
examples.translation: uri hoesaeseo gim gwajangnimi jeil iljjik osimnida. — In our company, Section Chief Kim comes the earliest.

examples.text: 과일 중에서 저는 딸기를 제일 좋아해요.
examples.translation: gwail jungeseo jeoneun ttalgireul jeil joahaeyo. — Of fruits, I like strawberries the most.

examples.text: 우리 반에서 제 친구가 한국어를 제일 잘해요.
examples.translation: uri baneseo je chinguga hangugeoreul jeil jalhaeyo. — In our class, my friend speaks Korean the best.

explanations.title: Activity 1: making sentences with two new words
explanations.body: The book asks you to get a card with two words from the teacher, make a sentence with them at the bottom of the card and have it checked (the model: 전통찻집, 차); then to read your sentence aloud to a partner until the partner translates it correctly, and to repeat with other students. A sample sentence of my own for the model (the English is mine):

examples.text: 전통찻집에서 전통차를 마셨어요.
examples.translation: jeontongchatjibeseo jeontongchareul masyeosseoyo. — I drank traditional tea at a traditional teahouse.

explanations.title: Activity 2: a tour of a traditional village in Jeonju
explanations.body: Myung-su and a friend toured a traditional village in Jeonju last week. The book asks you to listen to his narration, number the order of the sites (Handicraft Gallery, Traditional Liquor Museum, Traditional Paper Museum, Traditional Teahouse, Restaurant [3]) and write what they did at each place. This is an audio activity and is left out.

explanations.title: Activity 3: Which house would you like to live in?
explanations.body: With a partner, compare two houses in Seoul and decide which you would like to live in: two groups each receive a description of a Korean house (House A or House B; information to fill in: house type, when built/repaired, location; number of rooms, specific features; positive aspects; negative aspects), listen to the missing information, exchange information in Korean with a student from the other group, choose a house, and present the reasons in Korean. The descriptions and audio are not in the printed text I have, so this activity is left out.

explanations.title: Self-evaluation
explanations.body:
Recall the objectives of the chapter and ask yourself whether you have achieved them (the book asks you to tick Yes or No). If you tick “No” for any item, the book suggests: review that section on your own; find a study partner and review it as a pair or group; and tell your academic advisor or team leader which areas you need more help with.

Now I am able to: identify and extract information about traditional and modern clothing in Korea, and describe a person’s outfit; discuss food-related culture in Korea, including making kimchi; talk about basic cooking methods; and identify traditional and modern Korean houses, and compare them.

Now I have a clear understanding of: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary section; ~을/를 포함해(서) (including); ~와/과 달리 or ~하고 달리 (unlike); transitive verbs with a causative infix; ~ 중에서/가운데서 (among) and ~에서 (at; on; in) in the superlative form; and the Sino-Korean syllables within 서양 (西洋), 음식 (飮食), and 한옥 (韓屋).

explanations.title: How to use this list
explanations.body:
The book’s Core Vocabulary lists the core words of the chapter with an example sentence for each (the sentences and the English meanings are the book’s; the book gives no English for the sentences). The Hanja of the Sino-Korean words are in parentheses before the meaning. The book’s related words (synonyms, antonyms and related words in the last column) are left out, and the book’s Additional Vocabulary section is blank. 스타일 and 캐주얼 are listed also as loan words; the last section lists the Sino-Korean related words of 서양, 음식 and 한옥 as the book gives them.

The example sentences with digits are respelled in Hangul (물 8컵 → 물 여덟 컵; 11월 → 십일월; 200여 명 → 이백여 명; 50채 → 오십 채).

explanations.title: What Chapter 42 teaches (한국의 문화 2)
explanations.body:
Chapter 42, “Korean Culture II”, has a vocabulary builder, three topic presentations (festivals, tourist attractions, the Korean Folk Village) with grammar in focus, activities, a self-evaluation and the core vocabulary.

When you finish the chapter you will be able to: identify and discuss tourist attractions, festivals, transportation, and lodging; identify and describe cultural events, including traditional weddings and folk games; provide directions to a location; and narrate a past event in a simple paragraph.

You will become familiar with: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary section; ~뿐(만) 아니라 ~도 (not only … but also …); –(으)ㄹ 수 밖에 없다 (there is no choice but; cannot help -ing); stative verbs that are interpreted as transitive verbs; the adverbial suffix 으로; and the Sino-Korean syllables within 해산물 (海産物), 무명 (無名), 혼례 (婚禮), and 민속촌 (民俗村).

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 해산물 (海産物)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean word means sea food or marine products. The first syllable 해 (海) means sea or marine, as in 남해 (the South Sea), 해녀 (a female diver; “marine woman”) and 해군 (navy; a sailor; “sea military”). The second syllable 산 (産) means producing or giving birth, as in 산모 (a woman who has [recently] given birth to a child; “birth-giving mother”) and 중국산 (Chinese products). The last syllable 물 (物) means object or thing, as in 동물 (animal; “moving object”) and 고물 (an antique; secondary goods; “old thing”). Thus the literal meaning of the word 해산물 is “things that the sea produces,” and the word refers to seafood or edible marine products, such as fish, shellfish, or seaweed. The book asks you to guess the meaning of 농산물, 동해, 지중해, 서해, 해상 도시, 식물, 물품, 생산 and (생)산지 (my answers):

rows: a woman who has recently given birth; “birth-giving mother”
the West Sea; the Yellow Sea
a city on the sea; a floating city

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 무명 (無名)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean word means nameless or unknown, as in 무명 용사 (an unknown soldier; “nameless warrior”) and 무명 작가 (an obscure writer; a nameless writer). The first syllable 무 (無) means nonexistent, not having, or without, and it is similar to the English prefix a- in amoral, asexual, etc. In many combinations, this syllable contrasts with 유 (有), which means existing, having, or with. Some examples of contrasting pairs are 유료 vs. 무료 (paid vs. free of charge), 유인 vs. 무인 (manned vs. unmanned), and 유해 vs. 무해 (hazardous vs. nonhazardous). The second syllable 명 (名) means name, as in 성명 (one’s full name) and 유명하다 (to be famous; “to have a name”). Thus the literal meaning of the word is “not having a name” or “without a name.” The book asks you to guess the meaning of 무선 전화, 인명, 무관심, 가명, 무사고 and 명단 (the book glosses 가 [假]: fake, pseudo-; my answers):

rows: an obscure writer; a nameless writer
to be famous; “to have a name”
a wireless phone; a cordless phone
a person’s name (not 人命, human life)
a list of names; a roster

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 혼례 (婚禮)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean word means a wedding (ceremony), a wedding, or nuptials. The first syllable 혼 (婚) means marriage, nuptial, or conjugal, as in 이혼 (a divorce; “leaving one’s marriage”), 약혼 (an engagement; “promising a marriage”), 재혼 (a second marriage; a remarriage), 미혼 (single; unmarried; “not married”), and 기혼 (married; “already married”). The second syllable 례/예 (禮) means ceremony or manners, as in 경례 (salutation; a military salute; “respect with manners”) and 예물 (a wedding gift; “ceremony object”). Note that 례 turns into 예 at the beginning of a word. Thus the literal meaning of the word is “marriage ceremony.” The book asks you to guess the meaning of 결혼, 미혼모, 기혼자, 예절, 예복 and 무례 (my answers):

rows: salutation; a military salute; “respect with manners”

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 민속촌 (民俗村)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean word means a folk village, a living museum type of tourist attraction. The first syllable 민 (民) means people or folk (of a country, nation, or kingdom), as in 국민 (a nation; a people; “people of a nation”), 시민 (a citizen; an inhabitant of a city), and 민요 (a folk song). The second syllable 속 (俗) means custom or secular, as in 속어 (slang; secular language). The last syllable 촌 (村) means village or -ville, as in 산촌 (a mountain village), 강촌 (a riverside village), and 부촌 (a rich village; a wealthy village). Just as there are American cities or towns whose names end in -ville (e.g., Castroville or Watsonville), there are Korean towns or cities whose names end in 촌, as in 점촌, 상촌, and 대촌. Thus the literal meaning of the word 민속촌 is “folk customs village,” and it refers to the Korean Folk Village, a living museum tourist attraction in the city of 용인. The village displays various elements of traditional Korean life and culture with numerous replicas of traditional houses of the different social classes and various regions. The book asks you to guess the meaning of 군민, 도민, 어촌, 농촌, 장수촌 and 속담 (the book glosses 어 [漁]: fishing, fishery; 담 [談]: saying, words; my answers):

a citizen; an inhabitant of a city
a rich village; a wealthy village
county residents; people of a county
a farming village; a rural village
a longevity village; a village known for long-living people

explanations.title: Topic A: Go to the cherry blossom festival (벚꽃 축제에 가 보세요)
explanations.body: The following blog entry is about the Cherry Blossom Festival in Jinhae. (The English is mine; the book gives none; 15 km and “1일” are spelled out in Hangul; the printed text has a blank before 호텔, which I left out.)

examples.text: 봄 가족여행으로 진해의 벚꽃 축제는 어떠세요?

explanations.title: 한국에서는: 1. The units of measure
explanations.body: Korea uses the metric system to measure length, weight, and volume. 미터 (meter) is for measuring length, 그램 (gram) for weight, and 리터 (liter) for volume. 1 킬로미터 = 1000 미터 = 0.62 마일; 1 킬로그램 = 1000 그램 = 2.2 파운드; 1 리터 = 1000 밀리리터 = 0.26 갤론.

explanations.title: 한국에서는: 2. 벚꽃축제 (the Cherry Blossom Festival)
explanations.body: In Korea, cherry trees are in full bloom in early spring (late March and early April). During this period, many local governments (cities and towns) celebrate the cherry blossoms and sponsor festivals (벚꽃축제) that include various events. Many Koreans attend the cherry blossom festivals. The most popular cherry blossom festival is held in the City of Jinhae, home of the Korean Navy headquarters. Each spring, several hundred thousand people visit the city to see 벚꽃축제.

explanations.title: 북한에서는
explanations.body: In North Korea, large-scale cultural events are held to commemorate specific days, including the birthdays of the leaders Kim Il-Sung and Kim Jung-Il. These events are called 축전, which means festival. Often held as political propaganda, these events require people to participate in mass dances or mass games to show their support for the government and promote its political agenda. 연환모임 is closer to the Western notion of a festival. At these gatherings, which are more open and free, people share food and enjoy leisurely activities.

explanations.body: The following travel magazine article is about a famous festival held in a city on Korea’s east coast; the book asks you to fill in a table in English (Name of festival and date; Events; Location; Lodging information). The book glosses 예상하다: to expect, to anticipate, to predict. The article is the book’s with the date spelled out; the English is mine.

explanations.title: Activity 2 (Reading): a high school student’s blog
explanations.body: The following high school student’s blog is about his family’s trip to a festival held in Jindo (진도). The book asks you to locate Jindo on an online map and fill in a table in English (Means of transportation; Lodging information; Events and activities offered; Family’s activities), with some answers given. The blog is the book’s with the numbers spelled out; the English is mine.

explanations.title: Activity 3 (Planning): a festival tour
explanations.body: You are planning to attend a festival and are leaving from Seoul. With a partner you visit the home page of the festival the teacher assigns (경남 진해 벚꽃축제, 충남 보령 머드축제, 전남 진도 바닷길축제 or 경북 안동 국제탈춤축제), fill in a table in English (basic festival information: time, place, admission fee, etc.; available transportation; available lodging; events and activities) and report your plan to the class. This needs the festival web sites and a partner and is left out.

explanations.title: Topic B: Daehak-ro and Insa-dong (대학로와 인사동)
explanations.body: The following general information is about two tourist attractions in Seoul: Daehak-ro and Insa-dong. (The English is mine; the book gives none. The book’s footnotes: ~로 [路] means street or boulevard and indicates the street name, as in 종로, 대학로, or 을지로; see 한국어에는 below for 즐겨.)

examples.text: 문화예술의 거리로서 대학로는 젊은이들이 즐겨 찾는다.
examples.translation: munhwayesurui georiroseo daehangnoneun jeolmeunideuri jeulgyeo channeunda. — As a street of culture and the arts, Daehak-ro is a place that young people enjoy visiting.

examples.text: 무명 가수나 배우, 무용가들이 야외 공연장이나 길거리에서 공연한다.
examples.translation: mumyeong gasuna baeu, muyonggadeuri yaoe gongyeonjangina gilgeorieseo gongyeonhanda. — Unknown singers, actors and dancers perform at outdoor stages or on the street.

examples.text: 또, 그림을 그리는 화가나 춤과 노래를 연습하는 젊은이들도 볼 수 있다.
examples.translation: tto, geurimeul geurineun hwagana chumgwa noraereul yeonseupaneun jeolmeunideuldo bol su itda. — Also, you can see painters drawing pictures and young people practicing dance and song.

examples.text: 대학로 중심에 있는 마로니에 공원 근처에는 소극장뿐만 아니라 맛집이나 카페도 많다.
examples.translation: daehangno jungsime inneun maronie gongwon geuncheoeneun sogeukjangppunman anira matjibina kapedo manta. — Near Marronnier Park at the center of Daehak-ro there are not only small theaters but also many well-known restaurants and cafes.

examples.text: 그래서 대학로는 연인들의 데이트 장소로 유명하다.
examples.translation: geuraeseo daehangnoneun yeonindeurui deiteu jangsoro yumyeonghada. — So Daehak-ro is famous as a dating place for lovers.

examples.text: 인사동은 서울의 대표적인 전통문화의 거리로 외국인들이 많이 찾는다.
examples.translation: insadongeun seourui daepyojeogin jeontongmunhwaui georiro oegugindeuri mani channeunda. — Insa-dong is a representative street of traditional culture in Seoul and many foreigners visit it.

examples.text: 골동품 가게와 화랑 등이 많고 한국의 이색적인 문화를 체험할 수 있다.
examples.translation: goldongpum gagewa hwarang deungi manko hangugui isaekjeogin munhwareul cheheomhal su itda. — There are many antique shops, galleries, etc., and you can experience Korea’s exotic culture.

examples.text: 전통 찻집에서 차도 마실 수 있고 떡집에서 떡도 직접 만들어 볼 수 있다.
examples.translation: jeontong chatjibeseo chado masil su itgo tteokjibeseo tteokdo jikjeop mandeureo bol su itda. — You can drink tea at traditional teahouses and also try making rice cakes yourself at rice cake shops.

examples.text: 그래서 외국인들이 인사동을 좋아할 수밖에 없다.
examples.translation: geuraeseo oegugindeuri insadongeul joahal subakke eopda. — So foreigners cannot help liking Insa-dong.

examples.text: 일요일에는 인사동 거리에서 다양한 축제도 열린다.
examples.translation: iryoireneun insadong georieseo dayanghan chukjedo yeollinda. — On Sundays various festivals are also held on the street in Insa-dong.

examples.text: 인사동에 가면 평생 잊지 못할 추억을 만들 수 있다.
examples.translation: insadonge gamyeon pyeongsaeng itji motal chueogeul mandeul su itda. — If you go to Insa-dong, you can make memories you will never forget in your life.

explanations.title: 한국어 발음은: reciprocal assimilation
explanations.body: When the stop consonants ㄱ, ㄷ, and ㅂ come before ㄹ, they are nasalized and become ㅇ, ㄴ, and ㅁ, respectively. The ㄹ sound is also nasalized into ㄴ, because of the influence of the new nasalized sound. This phenomenon is called reciprocal assimilation. (See the Introductory Unit Appendix, page A.4, for more information.) Thus, 대학로 sounds like /대항노/. The book gives 율곡로 and 사직로 to listen to (audio); by the same rule they sound like /율공노/ and /사징노/ (my note).

explanations.title: 한국어에는: 집 and 즐겨
explanations.body:
1. 집 literally means “a house.” However, it often refers to a business, store, shop, or restaurant in different contexts, as in 꽃집 (a flower shop), 빵집 (a bakery), 찻집 (a teahouse), 맛집 (a restaurant well known for tasty food), and 떡집 (a rice cake store). 이 집이 음식을 잘 합니다 (This restaurant makes good food. / “This house does food well.”)

2. 즐겨 + action verb. 즐겨 comes from the verb 즐기다, which means to enjoy, as in 저는 쇼핑을 즐겨요 (I enjoy shopping). 즐겨 is used to express “enjoy doing something” when it is combined with verbs such as 먹다, 보다, 듣다, or 입다.

explanations.title: 한국에서는: 대학로 and 인사동
explanations.body:
대학로 (Daehak-ro), known as a street for young people, is located on the former campus of the Seoul National University. The school moved out in 1975 and many theater groups started moving to Daehak-ro in the 1980s as it developed into a cultural center. The center of Daehak-ro, Marronnier Park, is the site of live performances by young people.

인사동 (Insa-dong), located at the heart of the capital, is a favorite shopping area because its main street branches into countless alleys of antique stores, galleries, traditional restaurants, teahouses, and cafes. In fact, more than 40% of the nation’s antique stores are in Insa-dong. Every Sunday, selected streets are blocked off from traffic. Insa-dong is especially popular with foreign tourists because they can experience traditional Korean culture and festivities.

lessons.title: 527. Ch 42 · Grammar A: expressing “cannot help -ing”, –(으)ㄹ 수밖에 없다 and –지 않을 수 없다
lessons.subtitle: -(으)ㄹ 수밖에 없다 · -지 않을 수 없다 · 숙제가 많아서 늦게 잘 수밖에 없어요

explanations.title: Expressing “cannot help -ing”
explanations.body: In English, expressions like “cannot help -ing” or “have no choice but to” emphasize that there is no alternative, as in “I cannot help laughing” or “I have no choice but to sell it.” The Korean equivalents are the auxiliary verbs –(으)ㄹ 수밖에 없다 and –지 않을 수 없다. For example (the English is the book’s):

examples.text: 숙제가 많아서 늦게 잘 수밖에 없어요.
examples.translation: sukjega manaseo neutge jal subakke eopseoyo. — There is so much homework, I have no choice but to go to bed late.

examples.text: 숙제가 많아서 늦게 자지 않을 수 없어요.
examples.translation: sukjega manaseo neutge jaji aneul su eopseoyo. — There is so much homework, I can’t help going to bed late.

explanations.title: The patterns
explanations.body: verb stem + (으)ㄹ 수밖에 없다; verb stem + 지 않을 수 없다. More examples (the English is the book’s):

examples.text: 신용카드 빚이 많아서 돈을 아낄 수밖에 없어.
examples.translation: sinyongkadeu biji manaseo doneul akkil subakke eopseo. — I have so much credit card debt, I have no choice but to be frugal with money.

examples.text: 약을 먹기 싫지만 먹을 수밖에 없다.
examples.translation: yageul meokgi silchiman meogeul subakke eopda. — I hate to take a pill, but I have no choice but to do it.

explanations.title: Follow-up 1 (Listening, reading and speaking): the model
explanations.body: Partner A chooses a verbal phrase from List A and reads it aloud to Partner B. Then Partner B makes a sentence using the auxiliary verb –(으)ㄹ 수밖에 없다 and adds reasons. The book’s model (the English is mine):

examples.text: 가: 회의에 늦게 참석하다
examples.translation: ga: hoeuie neutge chamseokada — Attend the meeting late

examples.text: 나: 길이 많이 막혀서 회의에 늦게 참석할 수밖에 없었어요.
examples.translation: na: giri mani makyeoseo hoeuie neutge chamseokal subakke eopseosseoyo. — The roads were so jammed that I had no choice but to attend the meeting late.

explanations.title: More sentences (mine)
explanations.body: Sample sentences of my own (the English is mine):

examples.text: 비가 많이 와서 집에 있을 수밖에 없었어요.
examples.translation: biga mani waseo jibe isseul subakke eopseosseoyo. — It rained a lot, so I had no choice but to stay home.

examples.text: 시험이 내일이라서 밤을 새울 수밖에 없어요.
examples.translation: siheomi naeiriraseo bameul saeul subakke eopseoyo. — The exam is tomorrow, so I have no choice but to stay up all night.

examples.text: 차가 고장 나서 버스를 탈 수밖에 없었어요.
examples.translation: chaga gojang naseo beoseureul tal subakke eopseosseoyo. — My car broke down, so I had no choice but to take the bus.

examples.text: 아파서 병원에 가지 않을 수 없었어요.
examples.translation: apaseo byeongwone gaji aneul su eopseosseoyo. — I was sick, so I could not help going to the hospital.

lessons.title: 528. Ch 42 · Grammar B: expressing “not only … but also …”, ~뿐(만) 아니라 ~도
lessons.subtitle: ~뿐(만) 아니라 ~도 · -(으)ㄹ 뿐(만) 아니라 -기도 하다 · 김 병장뿐만 아니라 · 내 고향의 관광지

explanations.title: Not only … but also …
explanations.body: In English, the correlative conjunction “not only … but also …” expresses two ideas of the same importance. For example: I like not only bananas but also apples. She is not only clever but also hardworking. I speak Korean not only at work but also at home. Note that the two italicized ideas in the conjunctive structures above can be nouns, adjectives, verbs, phrases, etc. The Korean equivalent of the correlative conjunction “not only … but also …” is ~뿐(만) 아니라 ~도. For example (the English is the book’s):

examples.text: 나는 한국음식뿐만 아니라 멕시코음식도 좋아해요.
examples.translation: naneun hangugeumsikppunman anira meksikoeumsikdo joahaeyo. — I like not only Korean food but also Mexican food.

examples.text: 직장에서뿐만 아니라 집에서도 한국말을 합니다.
examples.translation: jikjangeseoppunman anira jibeseodo hangungmareul hamnida. — I speak Korean not only at work but also at home.

explanations.title: Two verbs
explanations.body: To express two verbs of the same importance, however, we use –(으)ㄹ 뿐(만) 아니라 –기도 하다. For example (the English is the book’s):

examples.text: 나는 한국음식을 좋아할 뿐만 아니라 만들기도 합니다.
examples.translation: naneun hangugeumsigeul joahal ppunman anira mandeulgido hamnida. — I not only like Korean food but also make it.

explanations.title: Notes on the forms
explanations.body:
–(으)ㄹ in –(으)ㄹ 뿐(만) 아니라 is the attributive form of a verb and –기 in –기도 하다 is a gerund. If the second verb is made up of a noun and 하다, as in 공부하다, 운동하다, etc., we can use ~도 하다 instead of –기도 하다.

noun + 뿐(만) 아니라 noun + 도; verb stem + (으)ㄹ 뿐(만) 아니라 verb stem + 기도 하다. More examples (the English is the book’s):

examples.text: 김 선생님은 제주도뿐 아니라 하와이도 가 봤어요.
examples.translation: gim seonsaengnimeun jejudoppun anira hawaido ga bwasseoyo. — Mr. Kim has been not only to Jeju Island but also to Hawaii.

examples.text: 불고기는 어른뿐만 아니라 아이들도 좋아합니다.
examples.translation: bulgogineun eoreunppunman anira aideuldo joahamnida. — Not only do adults like bulgogi, but children do as well.

examples.text: 김 일병은 춤을 잘 출 뿐만 아니라 노래도 잘 합니다.
examples.translation: gim ilbyeongeun chumeul jal chul ppunman anira noraedo jal hamnida. — PFC Kim not only dances well but also sings well.

examples.text: 이 식당 음식은 맛있을 뿐 아니라 가격도 쌉니다.
examples.translation: i sikdang eumsigeun masisseul ppun anira gagyeokdo ssamnida. — The food in this restaurant is not only tasty but also cheap.

explanations.title: Follow-up 3 (Listening and speaking): the models
explanations.body: a. One student says a set of words to the other (e.g. 김 병장/이 상병/운동); the second student creates a complete sentence using ~뿐(만) 아니라 ~도. The sets are: 손/발/크다; 미국/중국/가보다; 꽃/초콜릿/사다; 인사동/대학로/유명하다. The book’s model and my answers for the four sets (the English is mine):

examples.text: 김 병장뿐만 아니라 이 상병도 운동을 잘 한다.
examples.translation: gim byeongjangppunman anira i sangbyeongdo undongeul jal handa. — Not only Sgt. Kim but also Cpl. Lee is good at sports.

examples.text: 손뿐만 아니라 발도 커요.
examples.translation: sonppunman anira baldo keoyo. — Not only the hands but also the feet are big.

examples.text: 미국뿐만 아니라 중국도 가 봤어요.
examples.translation: migukppunman anira junggukdo ga bwasseoyo. — I have been not only to America but also to China.

examples.text: 꽃뿐만 아니라 초콜릿도 샀어요.
examples.translation: kkotppunman anira chokollitdo sasseoyo. — I bought not only flowers but also chocolate.

examples.text: 인사동뿐만 아니라 대학로도 유명해요.
examples.translation: insadongppunman anira daehangnodo yumyeonghaeyo. — Not only Insa-dong but also Daehak-ro is famous.

explanations.title: Follow-up 3 b (the second set)
explanations.body: b. The second set uses both ~뿐(만) 아니라 ~도 and –(으)ㄹ 뿐(만) 아니라 –기도 하다: the book’s model is 동생/공부를 잘 하다/가르치다. The sets are: 이 호텔/시끄럽다/비싸다; 지하철/싸다/빠르다; 내 핸드폰/예쁘다/편리하다; 몬트레이/날씨가 좋다/경치가 좋다. The book’s model and my answers (the English is mine):

examples.text: 동생은 공부를 잘 할 뿐 아니라 가르치기도 잘한다.
examples.translation: dongsaengeun gongbureul jal hal ppun anira gareuchigido jalhanda. — My younger brother is not only good at studying but also good at teaching.

examples.text: 이 호텔은 시끄러울 뿐만 아니라 비싸기도 해요.
examples.translation: i hotereun sikkeureoul ppunman anira bissagido haeyo. — This hotel is not only noisy but also expensive.

examples.text: 지하철은 쌀 뿐만 아니라 빠르기도 해요.
examples.translation: jihacheoreun ssal ppunman anira ppareugido haeyo. — The subway is not only cheap but also fast.

examples.text: 내 핸드폰은 예쁠 뿐만 아니라 편리하기도 해요.
examples.translation: nae haendeuponeun yeppeul ppunman anira pyeollihagido haeyo. — My cell phone is not only pretty but also convenient.

examples.text: 몬트레이는 날씨가 좋을 뿐만 아니라 경치도 좋아요.
examples.translation: monteureineun nalssiga joeul ppunman anira gyeongchido joayo. — Monterey not only has good weather but also good scenery.

explanations.title: Follow-up 5 (Listening and speaking): two tourist attractions of your hometown
explanations.body: Think of two tourist attractions in your hometown and two reasons each is famous (fill in a table in English); go around the classroom and exchange information with at least three classmates, using ~뿐만 아니라 ~도 and –(으)ㄹ 뿐만 아니라 –기도 하다; then present one attraction you learned about. The book’s model (the English is mine):

examples.text: 제 고향은 뉴욕주입니다.
examples.translation: je gohyangeun nyuyokjuimnida. — My hometown is New York State.

examples.text: 뉴욕은 브로드웨이뿐만 아니라 타임스퀘어도 유명합니다.
examples.translation: nyuyogeun beurodeuweippunman anira taimseukweeodo yumyeonghamnida. — New York is famous for not only Broadway but also Times Square.

examples.text: 타임스퀘어에는 구경할 것이 많을 뿐만 아니라 좋은 식당도 많습니다.
examples.translation: taimseukweeoeneun gugyeonghal geosi maneul ppunman anira joeun sikdangdo manseumnida. — In Times Square there are not only many things to see but also many good restaurants.

lessons.title: 529. Ch 42 · Activities B: Insoo’s day in Daehak-ro
lessons.subtitle: 대학로 · 마로니에 공원 · 소극장 · 뮤지컬 · 찻집 · 자동차 없는 거리 · 일기

explanations.title: Activity 2 (Reading): Insoo’s blog
explanations.body: The following blog entry is written by Insoo, who recently met a friend from high school. The book asks you to (1) fill in a table in English (time; what Insoo did; related comments) and (2) answer what Insoo wrote about visiting Insa-dong next time (the text actually says 대학로; see my answer). The book glosses 조각: sculpture; 헤어지다: to part from, to bid farewell. The blog is the book’s with the times spelled out in Hangul; the English is mine.

examples.text: 토요일에 고등학교 동창을 만나서 오랜만에 대학로에 갔다.
examples.translation: toyoire godeunghakgyo dongchangeul mannaseo oraenmane daehangnoe gatda. — On Saturday I met a high school classmate and went to Daehak-ro after a long time.

examples.text: 날씨는 따뜻했고 거리는 젊은이들로 붐볐다.
examples.translation: nalssineun ttatteutaetgo georineun jeolmeunideullo bumbyeotda. — The weather was warm and the streets were crowded with young people.

examples.text: 우리는 열 시쯤 마로니에 공원으로 갔다.
examples.translation: urineun yeol sijjeum maronie gongwoneuro gatda. — We went to Marronnier Park at about 10 o’clock.

examples.text: 거기서 야외 조각 전시회와 전통춤 공연을 무료로 관람했다.
examples.translation: geogiseo yaoe jogak jeonsihoewa jeontongchum gongyeoneul muryoro gwallamhaetda. — There we watched an outdoor sculpture exhibition and a traditional dance performance free of charge.

examples.text: 열두 시에 어떤 맛집에 갔는데 손님이 많아서 이십 분 정도 기다려야 했다.
examples.translation: yeoldu sie eotteon matjibe ganneunde sonnimi manaseo isip bun jeongdo gidaryeoya haetda. — At 12 o’clock we went to a well-known restaurant, and there were many customers, so we had to wait about 20 minutes.

examples.text: 점심을 먹고 두 시에 소극장에 가서 뮤지컬을 봤다.
examples.translation: jeomsimeul meokgo du sie sogeukjange gaseo myujikeoreul bwatda. — After lunch, at 2 o’clock, we went to a small theater and saw a musical.

examples.text: 무명배우들의 공연이었지만 아주 인상적이었다.
examples.translation: mumyeongbaeudeurui gongyeonieotjiman aju insangjeogieotda. — It was a performance by unknown actors, but it was very impressive.

examples.text: 다섯 시에 공연이 끝나 우리는 극장 옆에 있는 찻집에 가서 차를 마시고 떡도 먹었다.
examples.translation: daseot sie gongyeoni kkeunna urineun geukjang yeope inneun chatjibe gaseo chareul masigo tteokdo meogeotda. — At 5 o’clock the performance ended, and we went to a teahouse next to the theater and drank tea and ate rice cakes.

examples.text: 인테리어가 이색적이어서 데이트 장소로 사랑받는 곳이라고 했다.
examples.translation: interieoga isaekjeogieoseo deiteu jangsoro sarangbanneun gosirago haetda. — The interior was exotic, so they said it is a place loved as a dating spot.

examples.text: 일곱 시쯤 친구와 헤어져서 집으로 왔다.
examples.translation: ilgop sijjeum chinguwa heeojeoseo jibeuro watda. — At about 7 o’clock I parted from my friend and came home.

examples.text: 오랜만에 동창하고 시간을 보내서 좋았다.
examples.translation: oraenmane dongchanghago siganeul bonaeseo joatda. — It was nice to spend time with a classmate after a long time.

examples.text: 매월 마지막 토요일 오후 한 시부터 일곱 시까지 대학로는 자동차 없는 거리가 된다고 하니까 다음에 갈 때는 이 시간에 가야겠다.
examples.translation: maewol majimak toyoil ohu han sibuteo ilgop sikkaji daehangnoneun jadongcha eomneun georiga doendago hanikka daeume gal ttaeneun i sigane gayagetda. — I heard that Daehak-ro becomes a car-free street from 1 p.m. to 7 p.m. on the last Saturday of every month, so next time I go I should go at this time.

rows: Went to Marronnier Park; watched an outdoor sculpture exhibition and a traditional dance performance
Free of charge (N/A in the book’s first row)
Had lunch at a well-known restaurant; saw a musical at a small theater
The restaurant was crowded (about a 20-minute wait); the actors were unknown, but the performance was very impressive
Went to a teahouse next to the theater and drank tea and ate rice cakes; parted from the friend at about 7:00 and went home
The interior was exotic; it is loved as a dating spot; he enjoyed time with a classmate after a long time

explanations.title: The answer to question 2 (mine)
explanations.body: The text says that Daehak-ro becomes a car-free street from 1 p.m. to 7 p.m. on the last Saturday of every month, so next time Insoo plans to go at this time. (The book’s question says “Insa-dong”, but the text is about Daehak-ro.)

explanations.title: Activities left out
explanations.body: Activity 1 (the “story-chaining” game in which students sit in a circle, add sentences using the new words from Topic B and vote for the best story) and Activity 3 (listening to a Korean friend’s voice mail message, finding and recommending a place for a one-day tour of Seoul on the websites 서울 관광 명소, 서울시 추천 코스 10선 and 외국인의 추천 코스, summarizing it in Korean and presenting it) are audio, online and group activities.

explanations.title: Topic C: I went to the Korean Folk Village (한국민속촌에 갔다 왔다)
explanations.body: This journal entry is about Yongsu’s visit to the Korean Folk Village. (The English is mine; the book gives none; the times are spelled out in Hangul. The book’s footnote: –기 in 널뛰기, 줄타기, and 그네타기 is a gerund “maker”; its English equivalent is -ing. The printed text has a stray blank after the line about bowing to each other, which I left out.)

examples.text: 전통 혼례복을 입은 신랑 신부가 서로 절을 하고 술잔을 주고받았다.
examples.translation: jeontong hollyebogeul ibeun sillang sinbuga seoro jeoreul hago suljaneul jugobadatda. — The bride and groom in traditional wedding clothes bowed to each other and exchanged wine cups.

explanations.title: 한국에서는: 정월 대보름
explanations.body: (정월) 대보름, which literally means “the great 15th day (of January),” is a traditional Korean holiday that celebrates the first full moon of the lunar new year. Koreans used to practice some unique traditions on this holiday. For example, people cracked nuts with their teeth. This practice, known as 부럼 깨기, is believed to make one’s teeth strong for the rest of the year. In the countryside, people climbed mountains to try to catch sight of the first full moonrise of the year. It is said that the first person to see the moonrise will have good luck all year. When the first full moon is near, people burn the dry grass on the slopes between the rice fields while children whirl cans full of burning charcoal. The whirling of many fire cans makes an impressive scene on a moonlit night. 쥐불놀이 (“rat fire play”) is a practice in which the cans are tossed high in the air and into the field. The resulting fire fertilizes the fields and destroys harmful pests, including rats.

lessons.title: 531. Ch 42 · Grammar C: the adverbial suffix 으로 (~적으로 and ~식으로)
lessons.subtitle: ~적으로 · ~식으로 · 규칙적으로 · 긍정적으로 · 세계적으로 · 한국식으로

explanations.title: Recall ~적, then add 으로
explanations.body:
Recall that the syllable 적 (的) turns a Sino-Korean noun into an adjective when it is attached to the noun: 역사적 (historical), 세계적 (worldwide; global), 국제적 (international), 교육적 (educational), etc. In other words, any Sino-Korean word that ends with the syllable 적 is equivalent to an English adjective that ends with -ic or -ive.

These adjectives can be turned into adverbs by adding 으로. For example (the English is the book’s):

explanations.title: Sentences with adverbs ending in 으로
explanations.body: Here are some sentences containing adverbs that end with 으로 (the English is the book’s):

examples.text: 독서는 교육적으로 좋습니다.
examples.translation: dokseoneun gyoyukjeogeuro joseumnida. — Reading is good educationally.

examples.text: 나는 매일 규칙적으로 운동합니다.
examples.translation: naneun maeil gyuchikjeogeuro undonghamnida. — I exercise regularly every day.

examples.text: 동아리 활동에 적극적으로 참여합니다.
examples.translation: dongari hwaldonge jeokgeukjeogeuro chamyeohamnida. — I actively participate in club activities.

examples.text: 태권도는 세계적으로 유명합니다.
examples.translation: taegwondoneun segyejeogeuro yumyeonghamnida. — Taekwondo is “globally famous.”

explanations.title: 참고: ~식으로
explanations.body: When 으로 is added to a word ending with 식 (式), it means in the style of: 한국식 → 한국식으로; 자동식 → 자동식으로. (The English is the book’s.)

examples.text: 한국식으로 절을 했습니다.
examples.translation: hanguksigeuro jeoreul haetseumnida. — I bowed in the Korean style.

explanations.title: Follow-up 1 (Listening and speaking): the model
explanations.body: Student A studies the Sino-Korean nouns in List A and Student B those in List B. On the teacher’s cue, Student A makes an adverb with a noun from the list, using ~적으로, and reads it aloud to Student B. Then Student B makes a sentence that includes the adverb. The book’s model is 긍정적으로 → 저는 항상 긍정적으로 생각합니다. My sample sentences (the English is mine):

examples.text: 저는 항상 긍정적으로 생각합니다.
examples.translation: jeoneun hangsang geungjeongjeogeuro saenggakamnida. — I always think positively.

examples.text: 저는 역사적으로 중요한 곳을 좋아해요.
examples.translation: jeoneun yeoksajeogeuro jungyohan goseul joahaeyo. — I like historically important places.

examples.text: 한국 음식은 세계적으로 인기가 있어요.
examples.translation: hanguk eumsigeun segyejeogeuro ingiga isseoyo. — Korean food is popular worldwide.

examples.text: 저는 습관적으로 아침에 커피를 마십니다.
examples.translation: jeoneun seupgwanjeogeuro achime keopireul masimnida. — I habitually drink coffee in the morning.

explanations.title: Follow-up 2 (Reading): a grandmother
explanations.body: Read the following paragraph and circle the adverbs; then translate the sentences containing ~적으로 into English. The paragraph is the book’s with the age spelled out; the English is mine.

examples.text: 저희 할머니는 지금 연세가 백육 세이시다.
examples.translation: jeohui halmeonineun jigeum yeonsega baegyuk seisida. — My grandmother is now 106 years old.

examples.text: 할머니께서는 항상 아침 일찍 일어나서 규칙적으로 운동하신다.
examples.translation: halmeonikkeseoneun hangsang achim iljjik ireonaseo gyuchikjeogeuro undonghasinda. — She always gets up early in the morning and exercises regularly.

examples.text: 또 매일 채소를 가꾸는 일을 하시면서 습관적으로 몸을 부지런히 움직이신다.
examples.translation: tto maeil chaesoreul gakkuneun ireul hasimyeonseo seupgwanjeogeuro momeul bujireonhi umjigisinda. — Also, while doing the work of growing vegetables every day, she habitually moves her body diligently.

examples.text: 그리고 손자, 손녀들을 보면서 늘 웃으며 아주 낙천적으로 사신다.
examples.translation: geurigo sonja, sonnyeodeureul bomyeonseo neul useumyeo aju nakcheonjeogeuro sasinda. — And she lives very optimistically, always smiling as she looks at her grandsons and granddaughters.

explanations.title: The adverbs (mine)
explanations.body: The adverbs are 규칙적으로 (regularly), 습관적으로 (habitually) and 낙천적으로 (optimistically). Also 항상, 일찍, 부지런히 and 늘 are adverbs, but they do not end with ~적으로. The sentences with ~적으로 are the second, third and fourth sentences above.

lessons.title: 532. Ch 42 · Grammar D: stative verbs that are interpreted as transitive verbs (좋다 · 싫다 · 그립다)
lessons.subtitle: ~이/가 좋다 · ~이/가 싫다 · ~이/가 그립다 · ~이/가 밉다 · ~이/가 아쉽다 · ~이/가 고맙다 · ~이/가 필요하다

explanations.title: Compare the English and Korean sentences
explanations.body: Carefully compare the grammatical differences between the following English sentences and their Korean counterparts (the English is the book’s).

examples.text: 나는 한국말이 좋다.
examples.translation: naneun hangungmari jota. — I like Korean.

examples.text: 나는 매운 김치가 싫다.
examples.translation: naneun maeun gimchiga silta. — I dislike spicy kimchi.

examples.text: 나는 우리 가족이 그립다.
examples.translation: naneun uri gajogi geuripda. — I miss my family.

explanations.title: Two differences
explanations.body:
There are two noticeable grammatical differences in the examples above.

1. Verb Type: In the English sentences, the verbs are all transitive verbs (verbs that take an object). In the Korean sentences, their counterparts are all stative verbs (or adjectives). Note that the verbs in blunt formal form are made up of their stems and 다, a common feature of stative verbs.

2. Functions of the Nouns: In the English sentences, Korean, spicy kimchi, and my family are objects of the verb. In the Korean sentences, their counterparts are all subjects, and the nouns are marked by the subject marker 이/가.

explanations.title: More verbs that “behave” this way
explanations.body: There are a few more Korean stative verbs that “behave” like 좋다, 싫다, and 그립다. They are 밉다 (to hate a person; to be hateful), 아쉽다 (to be left wanting; to have a sense of regret), 고맙다 (to thank a person; to be thankful), and 필요하다 (to need a person/thing; to be necessary). examples.text: 나는 내 친구가 고맙다.
examples.translation: naneun nae chinguga gomapda. — I am thankful to my friend.

examples.text: 시간과 돈이 필요해요.
examples.translation: sigangwa doni piryohaeyo. — I need time and money.

explanations.title: Activity 1 (Reading): where can each activity be done?
explanations.body: The following sentences are about activities held at the Korean Folk Village (한국민속촌). The book asks you to read each sentence and identify, from the box, where each activity can be done: a. 장터 민속 음식점; b. 공연장; c. 기념품 가게; d. 민속마을; e. 민속촌 주차장; f. 전통 혼례식장. explanations.title: Self-evaluation
explanations.body:
Recall the objectives of the chapter and ask yourself whether you have achieved them (the book asks you to tick Yes or No). If you tick “No” for any item, the book suggests: review that section on your own; find a study partner and review it as a pair or group; and tell your academic advisor or team leader which areas you need more help with.

Now I am able to: identify and discuss tourist attractions, festivals, transportation, and lodging; identify and describe cultural events, including traditional weddings and folk games; provide directions to a location; and narrate a past event in a simple paragraph.

Now I have a clear understanding of: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary section; ~뿐(만) 아니라 ~도 (not only … but also …); –(으)ㄹ 수 밖에 없다 (there is no choice but; cannot help -ing); stative verbs that are interpreted as transitive verbs; the adverbial suffix 으로; and the Sino-Korean syllables within 해산물 (海産物), 무명 (無名), 혼례 (婚禮), and 민속촌 (民俗村).

explanations.title: How to use this list
explanations.body:
The book’s Core Vocabulary lists the core words of the chapter with an example sentence for each (the sentences and the English meanings are the book’s; the book gives no English for the sentences). The Hanja of the Sino-Korean words are in parentheses before the meaning. The book’s related words (synonyms, antonyms and related words in the last column) are left out, and the book’s Additional Vocabulary section is blank. 데이트, 카페, 킬로미터, 펜션 and 퍼레이드 are listed also as loan words; the last section lists the Sino-Korean related words of 해(산)물, 무명, 혼례 and 민속촌 as the book gives them.

The example sentences with digits or Latin letters are respelled in Hangul (약 20킬로미터 → 약 이십 킬로미터; 오늘 저녁 10시 → 오늘 저녁 열 시; 무용가가 3명 → 세 명; L.A. → 엘에이; 음력 1월 15일 → 음력 일월 십오 일; 한국인 무용가가 3명 → 세 명).

explanations.title: What Chapter 43 teaches (종교와 사회)
explanations.body:
Chapter 43, “Religion and Society”, has a vocabulary builder, three topic presentations (religion and volunteer work, life of foreigners in Korea, women’s status and roles) with grammar in focus, activities, a self-evaluation and the core vocabulary.

When you finish the chapter you will be able to: identify major religions and beliefs in Korea; discuss volunteer work; understand the lives of foreigners in Korea and their typical concerns; discuss the social status and role of women in Korea; and talk about more occupations.

You will become familiar with: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary section; ~ (도)중에/(–는/던) (도)중에 (in the middle of doing something); the sentence ending –(으)ㄴ/는데(요); 반면(에) (on the other hand; whereas; while); the auxiliary verb −곤 하다 for common or routine occurrences of an action/event; and the Sino-Korean syllables within 천주교 (天主敎), 대륙 (大陸), and 전문직 (專門職).

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 천주교 (天主敎)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean word means the (Roman) Catholic Church or Catholicism. The first syllable 천 (天) means heaven or sky, as in 천문학 (astronomy; “study of the sky”), 천국 (heaven; paradise; the kingdom of heaven), 천하 (the world; the whole country; “below the heavens”), 천사 (an angel; “heavenly messenger”), and 천지 (heaven and earth; the world). The second syllable 주 (主) means lord, master, or host, as in 주인 (the master [of a house]; the head [of a family]; “master person”), 주일 (the Sabbath; the Lord’s day; Sunday), 주객 (host and guest), and 주권 (sovereignty; sovereign power; “lord rights”). The same syllable can also mean main, principal, or chief, as in 주목적 (a leading motive; a main purpose), 주력 부대 (main force units), and 주장 (the captain [of a team]; “main commander”). The last syllable 교 (敎) means teaching, religion, or church, as in 교사 (a teacher; a schoolteacher), 교과서 (a textbook; “teaching type book”), 불교 (Buddhism; “Buddhist religion”), 무교 (having no religion; without religion; irreligious), and 기독교 (Christianity; the Christian religion). Thus the word 천주교 literally means “religion of the Lord of the heavens,” and the word refers to the Roman Catholic Church or Catholicism.

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 대륙 (大陸)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean word means a continent. As in words like 대학교 (university; “big school”) and 대회 (a conference; “big meeting”), and 대법원 (the Supreme Court), the first syllable 대 (大) means big, large, or great, and the second syllable 륙/육 (陸) means land, as in words like 육군 (army; “land military”), 육로 (a land route), 착륙 (landing [from the air]; touchdown [of aircraft]; “touching the land”), and 상륙 (disembarkation; going ashore [from a ship]; “up [to the] land”). Thus the word 대륙 literally means “big land” or “great land,” and the word refers to any of the six or seven great areas of land on the globe. The book asks you to guess the meaning of 육군 대장, 대로, 육해공, 육지, 대식가 and 육교 (the book glosses 교 [橋]: bridge; my answers):

rows: landing (from the air); touchdown; “touching the land”
an Army general; a four-star general
an overpass; a pedestrian bridge; “land bridge”

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 전문직 (專門職)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean word is made up of the two words 전문 and 직(업). The word 전문 (專門) means specialty, special subject, or specialized, as in 전문가 (an expert; “specialized professional”), 전문기술 (expertise; “specialized skill”), 전문의 (a medical specialist; “specialized doctor”), and 전문대학 (a junior college; “specialized college”). It is interesting to note that the literal meaning of the word 전문 is “exclusive door” or “only gate,” and the literal meaning has evolved to mean specialty, special subject, or specialized. The word 직(업) means job, position, or occupation, as in 농업 (agriculture; farming industry; “agricultural job”) and 어업 (fishery; “fishing job”). Thus the literal meaning of the word 전문직 is “specialty job” or “specialized job,” and the word refers to a professional job that requires specialized skills. The book asks you to guess the meaning of 전공, 부전공, 버스전용, 대문, 정문, 후문, 사무직, 노동직 and 직장 (my answers):

rows: a major; a field of specialization
a front gate; the main entrance
a back gate; a rear entrance
an office job; a clerical position
a labor job; a manual job

explanations.title: Topic A: Going to a nursing home to volunteer (양로원에 자원봉사 하러 가요)
explanations.body: Two neighbors are talking about volunteer activities they will participate in over the coming weekend. (The English is mine; the book gives none; the book’s “아…” is written 아, and its footnote numbers are dropped. The book’s footnotes: 아니에요 or 뭘요 is a common response to a compliment; this type of expression conveys the recipient’s humble attitude. (생활이) 어려운 이웃, which literally means “neighbors whose living is difficult,” refers to needy people.)

examples.text: 민준: 유나 씨, 이번 주말에 뭐 할 거예요?
examples.translation: minjun: yuna ssi, ibeon jumare mwo hal geoyeyo? — Yuna, what are you going to do this weekend?

examples.text: 유나: 저는 이번 토요일에 양로원으로 자원봉사 하러 가요.
examples.translation: yuna: jeoneun ibeon toyoire yangnowoneuro jawonbongsa hareo gayo. — This Saturday I am going to a nursing home to do volunteer work.

examples.text: 민준: 그래요? 좋은 일 하러 가시네요. 혼자 가세요?
examples.translation: minjun: geuraeyo? joeun il hareo gasineyo. honja gaseyo? — Really? You are going to do a good deed. Are you going alone?

examples.text: 유나: 아니요. 제가 다니는 교회의 봉사 단체 회원들과 함께 갈 거예요.
examples.translation: yuna: aniyo. jega danineun gyohoeui bongsa danche hoewondeulgwa hamkke gal geoyeyo. — No. I will go with the members of the volunteer group of the church I attend.

examples.text: 민준: 봉사활동 하러 자주 가세요?
examples.translation: minjun: bongsahwaldong hareo jaju gaseyo? — Do you go to do volunteer work often?

examples.text: 유나: 매주 토요일마다 가요. 보통 양로원과 고아원을 격주로 방문해요. 또 명절이나 성탄절 때는 장애인 복지시설에도 봉사하러 가구요.
examples.translation: yuna: maeju toyoilmada gayo. botong yangnowongwa goawoneul gyeokjuro bangmunhaeyo. tto myeongjeorina seongtanjeol ttaeneun jangaein bokjisiseoredo bongsahareo gaguyo. — I go every Saturday. I usually visit a nursing home and an orphanage every other week. Also, on holidays or at Christmas, I go to do volunteer work at welfare facilities for the disabled too.

examples.text: 민준: 아, 정말 좋은 일을 많이 하시네요.
examples.translation: minjun: a, jeongmal joeun ireul mani hasineyo. — Oh, you really do a lot of good things.

examples.text: 유나: 아니에요. 참, 민준 씨는 주말에 뭐 특별한 계획 있으세요?
examples.translation: yuna: anieyo. cham, minjun ssineun jumare mwo teukbyeolhan gyehoek isseuseyo? — Not at all. By the way, Minjun, do you have any special plans for the weekend?

examples.text: 민준: 이번 주 일요일이 석가탄신일이잖아요. 그때 우리 절에서 어려운 이웃을 위한 자선 행사를 해요. 저도 가서 도와드리려고요.
examples.translation: minjun: ibeon ju iryoiri seokgatansinirijanayo. geuttae uri jeoreseo eoryeoun iuseul wihan jaseon haengsareul haeyo. jeodo gaseo dowadeuriryeogoyo. — This Sunday is Buddha’s birthday, you know. At that time, our temple holds a charity event for needy neighbors. I am going to help there too.

examples.text: 유나: 아, 네. 의미 있는 행사네요. 요즘 어려운 이웃들을 돕는 종교단체행사가 많은 것 같아요.
examples.translation: yuna: a, ne. uimi inneun haengsaneyo. yojeum eoryeoun iutdeureul domneun jonggyodanchehaengsaga maneun geot gatayo. — Oh, yes. It is a meaningful event. These days there seem to be many religious group events that help needy neighbors.

examples.text: 민준: 그래요. 아주 바람직한 일이에요.
examples.translation: minjun: geuraeyo. aju baramjikan irieyo. — Yes. It is a very desirable thing.

explanations.body: The book shows a pie chart of religions in Korea with the labels 개신교, 천주교, 불교, 무교 (종교 없음) and 기타 종교 (the chart is a picture and is left out; the numbers are in the article below).

explanations.title: 한국에서는: Shamanism in Korea
explanations.body: In traditional Korean society, shamanism had its roots in various indigenous beliefs that widely influenced people’s lives. Koreans in the past would frequently visit shamans, called 무당 (巫堂), who acted as an intermediary between the gods and humans, to gain good fortune, cure illness, etc. The shaman would then hold a ritual called 굿 to pray to the gods. As Korean society modernized, this practice diminished and was ultimately regarded as superstition. Recently, however, songs and dances that are part of 굿 have been recognized as important assets of traditional Korean culture.

examples.translation: choegeun tonggyereul bomyeon jonggyoga inneun hangugin jungeseo sasibo peosenteuga gaesingyo sinjarago hamnida. — According to recent statistics, they say 45 percent of Koreans who have a religion are Protestants.

examples.text: 불교 신자는 전체 종교 인구의 삼십오 퍼센트 정도 됩니다.

lessons.subtitle: 연말 봉사활동 · 따뜻한 겨울 캠페인 · 빨간 밥차 · 과외수업 · 종교계 · 나라별 종교

explanations.title: Activity 3 (Reading): a news article
explanations.body: Read the news article and complete the tasks that follow (the book glosses ~계: a community, a world, a circle). The article is the book’s with the numbers spelled out; the English is mine.

examples.text: 연말에 종교계에서 이웃을 위해 다양한 봉사활동을 계획하고 있다.
examples.translation: yeonmare jonggyogyeeseo iuseul wihae dayanghan bongsahwaldongeul gyehoekago itda. — At the end of the year, religious communities are planning various volunteer activities for their neighbors.

examples.text: 개신교는 십이월 한 달간 따뜻한 겨울 캠페인을 벌인다.
examples.translation: gaesingyoneun sibiwol han dalgan ttatteutan gyeoul kaempeineul beorinda. — Protestants hold the “Warm Winter” campaign for the month of December.

examples.text: 난방비가 없는 오천오백여 가정에 삼만 원씩 지원할 계획이다.
examples.translation: nanbangbiga eomneun ocheonobaegyeo gajeonge samman wonssik jiwonhal gyehoegida. — They plan to support more than 5,500 households without heating money with 30,000 won each.

examples.text: 이를 위해 오억 원 규모의 모금 운동을 하고 있다.
examples.translation: ireul wihae oeok won gyumoui mogeum undongeul hago itda. — For this, they are running a fundraising drive on the scale of 500 million won.

examples.text: 서울 천주교 사회복지회는 집 없는 사람들을 위해 무료급식 빨간 밥차 두 대를 운영한다.
examples.translation: seoul cheonjugyo sahoebokjihoeneun jip eomneun saramdeureul wihae muryogeupsik ppalgan bapcha du daereul unyeonghanda. — The Seoul Catholic Social Welfare Association operates two “Red Rice Cars” of free meal service for homeless people.

examples.text: 빨간 밥차는 한 시간에 삼백 인분의 식사를 준비할 수 있으며, 일주일에 다섯 번씩 서울역 등에서 급식 활동을 한다.
examples.translation: ppalgan bapchaneun han sigane sambaek inbunui siksareul junbihal su isseumyeo, iljuire daseot beonssik seoullyeok deungeseo geupsik hwaldongeul handa. — A Red Rice Car can prepare 300 servings of meals in an hour, and does meal service activities at Seoul Station and elsewhere five times a week.

examples.text: 불교계는 겨울방학 동안 종로구에 사는 육백여 명의 고아에게 과외수업을 해 주기로 했다.
examples.translation: bulgyogyeneun gyeoulbanghak dongan jongnogue saneun yukbaegyeo myeongui goaege gwaoesueobeul hae jugiro haetda. — The Buddhist community decided to give tutoring classes during the winter vacation to more than 600 orphans living in Jongno-gu.

examples.text: 학원에 다닐 수 없는 아이들한테 국어, 영어, 수학 등의 공부를 무료로 가르칠 예정이다.
examples.translation: hagwone danil su eomneun aideulhante gugeo, yeongeo, suhak deungui gongbureul muryoro gareuchil yejeongida. — They plan to teach children who cannot attend private academies subjects such as Korean, English and math for free.

explanations.title: The answers (mine)
explanations.body: 1. The book gives three possible titles and asks you to check the right one: “Volunteer Work Offered by Various Religious Groups During the Winter Season” (my answer: the first). 2. The table:

rows: The “Warm Winter” campaign in December: 30,000 won each to more than 5,500 households without heating money; a fundraising drive of 500 million won
Two “Red Rice Cars” for free meals for homeless people: 300 servings an hour, five times a week at Seoul Station and elsewhere
Free tutoring (Korean, English, math) for more than 600 orphans in Jongno-gu during the winter vacation

explanations.title: Activity 4 (Research): religions of each country
explanations.body: The teacher gives you a country to research; you use the links (Wikipedia, Naver, Yahoo, Google) to find the percent of followers of each religion (개신교, 천주교, 불교, 이슬람교, 기타) and fill in the table, make a pie chart or bar graph in the class notebook (MS Teams), present your results, and then organize two classmates’ presentations in a table (country 1, country 2). This is an internet and group activity and is left out.

explanations.title: Activities left out
explanations.body: Activity 1 (SMART Board) and Activity 2 (listening to three conversations between two friends talking about religious volunteer work at different welfare facilities and filling in religion, welfare facility and activities planned) are audio and computer activities.

explanations.title: Topic B: How is life in Korea? (한국생활이 어떠세요?)
explanations.body: A magazine reporter is interviewing a woman from Thailand who immigrated to Korea 10 years ago. (The English is mine; the book gives none; the book’s “!” is dropped. The book’s footnote: 서투르다 belongs to the 르 irregular verbs [부르다, 빠르다, 누르다, etc.]. However, since 서투르다 can contract into 서툴다, both 서투른 and 서툰 are accepted as attributive forms.)

examples.text: 기자: 터몬토 씨, 한국생활이 어떠세요?
examples.translation: gija: teomonto ssi, hanguksaenghwari eotteoseyo? — Ms. Termonto, how is life in Korea?

examples.text: 터몬토: 좋아요. 처음에는 좀 힘들었지만, 지금은 많이 적응됐어요.
examples.translation: teomonto: joayo. cheoeumeneun jom himdeureotjiman, jigeumeun mani jeogeungdwaesseoyo. — It’s good. It was a little hard at first, but now I have adapted a lot.

examples.text: 기자: 그러세요? 처음에 어떤 점이 힘드셨어요?
examples.translation: gija: geureoseyo? cheoeume eotteon jeomi himdeusyeosseoyo? — Is that so? What was hard for you at first?

examples.text: 터몬토: 언어와 문화가 달라서 고생했어요. 풍습도 다르고 말이 안 통해서 실수도 많이 했고요.
examples.translation: teomonto: eoneowa munhwaga dallaseo gosaenghaesseoyo. pungseupdo dareugo mari an tonghaeseo silsudo mani haetgoyo. — The language and culture were different, so I had a hard time. The customs were different too, and we could not understand each other, so I made many mistakes.

examples.text: 기자: 근데 지금은 한국어를 유창하게 아주 잘하시는데요.
examples.translation: gija: geunde jigeumeun hangugeoreul yuchanghage aju jalhasineundeyo. — But now you speak Korean fluently and very well.

examples.text: 터몬토: 아니에요. 아직도 발음이나 문법은 어려워요. 집에서는 대화하는 도중에 식구들이 서투른 표현을 고쳐 줘요.
examples.translation: teomonto: anieyo. ajikdo bareumina munbeobeun eoryeowoyo. jibeseoneun daehwahaneun dojunge sikgudeuri seotureun pyohyeoneul gocheo jwoyo. — Not at all. Pronunciation and grammar are still difficult. At home, in the middle of conversation, my family corrects my clumsy expressions.

examples.text: 기자: 그렇군요. 이웃 사람들은 잘 해주세요?
examples.translation: gija: geureokunyo. iut saramdeureun jal haejuseyo? — I see. Do your neighbors treat you well?

examples.text: 터몬토: 네. 모두 따뜻하게 대해 주세요. 그래서 이제는 한국이 고향 같아요.
examples.translation: teomonto: ne. modu ttatteutage daehae juseyo. geuraeseo ijeneun hangugi gohyang gatayo. — Yes. Everyone treats me warmly. So now Korea feels like my hometown.

examples.text: 기자: 자녀들 언어교육은 어떻게 하세요?
examples.translation: gija: janyeodeul eoneogyoyugeun eotteoke haseyo? — How do you do your children’s language education?

examples.text: 터몬토: 남들은 애들이 한국 말만 해도 된다고 생각해요. 하지만, 저는 아이들이 한국 말도 잘하고 태국 말도 잘하면 좋겠어요. 그래서 애들하고는 태국 말로 의사소통을 해요.
examples.translation: teomonto: namdeureun aedeuri hanguk malman haedo doendago saenggakaeyo. hajiman, jeoneun aideuri hanguk maldo jalhago taeguk maldo jalhamyeon jokesseoyo. geuraeseo aedeulhagoneun taeguk mallo uisasotongeul haeyo. — Other people think it is fine for the children to speak only Korean. But I would like my children to speak both Korean and Thai well. So I communicate with the kids in Thai.

explanations.title: Core words and phrases of Topic B
explanations.body: The meanings are the book’s (from the Core Vocabulary of the chapter). The book also lists –(으)ㄴ/는데(요) and ~ (도)중에/(–는/던) (도)중에 (see the grammar).

rows: (母國語) mother tongue; native language; “mother country language”
(流暢) to be fluent; to be eloquent
(意思疎通) communication (to communicate/to be communicated) (~하다/되다)
(依存) reliance; dependence (to depend upon; to rely on) (~하다)
(通) to understand each other; “flow freely (both ways)”
to be unskillful; to be clumsy

explanations.title: Follow-up 2 (Reading): foreign students in Daejeon
explanations.body: The following newspaper article discusses the changing foreign student population in the Daejeon area; the book asks (1) what change is being reported and (2) to translate the underlined sentence (the book glosses 국적: nationality; 생김새: [physical] appearance). The article is the book’s with the numbers spelled out; the English is mine (I translate every sentence).

examples.text: 늘어나는 외국인 유학생 국적도 다양화
examples.translation: neureonaneun oegugin yuhaksaeng gukjeokdo dayanghwa — The increasing number of foreign students; their nationalities are diversifying too

examples.text: 대전지역에 다양한 국적의 외국인 유학생들이 늘어나고 있다.
examples.translation: daejeonjiyeoge dayanghan gukjeogui oegugin yuhaksaengdeuri neureonago itda. — Foreign students of various nationalities are increasing in the Daejeon area.

examples.text: 이 영향으로 대학가를 중심으로 다문화 바람이 불고 있다.
examples.translation: i yeonghyangeuro daehakgareul jungsimeuro damunhwa barami bulgo itda. — As a result, a multicultural wind is blowing, centered on the university neighborhoods.

examples.text: 예전에는 중국, 일본, 베트남 등 아시아 지역 유학생이 대부분이었다.
examples.translation: yejeoneneun jungguk, ilbon, beteunam deung asia jiyeok yuhaksaengi daebubunieotda. — In the past, most were students from Asian regions such as China, Japan and Vietnam.

examples.text: 그런데 최근에는 다양한 국적의 유학생들을 볼 수 있다.
examples.translation: geureonde choegeuneneun dayanghan gukjeogui yuhaksaengdeureul bol su itda. — But recently, students of various nationalities can be seen.

examples.text: 그 변화는 캠퍼스에 보이는 학생들의 피부색과 생김새만 봐도 금방 알 수 있다.
examples.translation: geu byeonhwaneun kaempeoseue boineun haksaengdeurui pibusaekgwa saenggimsaeman bwado geumbang al su itda. — You can tell that change right away just by looking at the skin colors and appearances of the students seen on campus.

examples.text: 배재대학교는 대전지역에서 두 번째로 외국인 유학생이 많은 학교이다.
examples.translation: baejaedaehakgyoneun daejeonjiyeogeseo du beonjjaero oegugin yuhaksaengi maneun hakgyoida. — Pai Chai University is the school with the second most foreign students in the Daejeon area.

examples.text: 배재대에는 사십육 개국 구백여 명의 외국인 유학생이 등록해 있다.
examples.translation: baejaedaeeneun sasimnyuk gaeguk gubaegyeo myeongui oegugin yuhaksaengi deungnokae itda. — More than 900 foreign students from 46 countries are registered at Pai Chai.

examples.text: 북미, 아시아, 유럽 국가의 유학생뿐만 아니라 아프리카, 중남미 국가의 유학생도 많이 있다.
examples.translation: bungmi, asia, yureop gukgaui yuhaksaengppunman anira apeurika, jungnammi gukgaui yuhaksaengdo mani itda. — There are many students not only from North American, Asian and European countries but also from African and Central and South American countries.

explanations.title: The answer to question 1 (mine)
explanations.body: The change reported: the number of foreign students in the Daejeon area is increasing, and their nationalities are becoming diverse (in the past most were Asian students from China, Japan and Vietnam; now there are students from North America, Europe, Africa and Central and South America too).

explanations.title: Useful links
explanations.body: The book lists two links: 안산시 외국인 주민센터 (Ansan City Foreigner Residents Center) and 한국외국인노동자지원센터 (the Korea Foreign Workers Support Center).

explanations.title: Activities left out
explanations.body: The presentation steps of Topic B (SMART Board and pair role-reading) and Follow-up 1 (listening to three voice mails in which a Korean friend leaves a message for a foreigner seeking information at a visitors’ center, and filling in the nationality, occupation, problem mentioned and question asked) are audio and computer activities.

lessons.title: 540. Ch 43 · Grammar A: ~ (도)중에 and –는/던 (도)중에 (in the middle of doing something)
lessons.subtitle: ~ 중에 · ~ 도중에 · –는 도중에 · –던 도중에 · 회의 중에 전기가 나갔어요 · ~ 중이다

explanations.title: Recall ~ 중이다
explanations.body: Recall the verbal phrase ~ 중이다 or –는 중이다, as in 지금 요리 중입니다 (I am cooking right now) and 숙제하는 중입니다 (I am doing my homework). This phrase literally means “to be in the middle of doing (something)” because the Sino-Korean syllable 중 (中) means middle. Thus, the whole phrase is used to express an action in progress.

examples.text: 지금 요리 중입니다.
examples.translation: jigeum yori jungimnida. — I am cooking right now.

examples.text: 숙제하는 중입니다.
examples.translation: sukjehaneun jungimnida. — I am doing my homework.

explanations.title: ~ (도)중에 and –는/던 (도)중에
explanations.body: 중 in the phrase ~ (도)중에 or –는 (도)중에 is the same Sino-Korean character with 중 in the phrase ~중이다 or –는 중이다. Thus, the phrase literally means “in the middle of doing (something)”; it can be translated as in the middle of, while, or during. For example (the English is the book’s; the book writes 도 in parentheses, as it is optional):

examples.text: 요리하는 중에 전화를 받았어요.
examples.translation: yorihaneun junge jeonhwareul badasseoyo. — I got a phone call while cooking.

examples.text: 식사 도중에 전화를 받았어요.
examples.translation: siksa dojunge jeonhwareul badasseoyo. — I got a phone call while eating.

examples.text: 수업 도중에 전화를 받았어요.
examples.translation: sueop dojunge jeonhwareul badasseoyo. — I got a phone call in (the middle of) class.

explanations.title: The past tense
explanations.body: –는 (도)중에 can be used for the past tense. However, –던 (도)중에 is specifically used for the past tense. For example (the English is the book’s):

examples.text: 요리하던 도중에 전화를 받았어요.
examples.translation: yorihadeon dojunge jeonhwareul badasseoyo. — I got a phone call while cooking.

explanations.title: The patterns
explanations.body: noun + (도)중에; action verb stem + 는 (도)중에. More examples (the English is the book’s):

examples.text: 회의 중에 전기가 나갔어요.
examples.translation: hoeui junge jeongiga nagasseoyo. — In the middle of the meeting, the power went out.

examples.text: 김 일병은 수업을 하던 도중에 화장실에 갔습니다.
examples.translation: gim ilbyeongeun sueobeul hadeon dojunge hwajangsire gatseumnida. — In the middle of class, PFC Kim left to go to the bathroom.

examples.text: 김 일병은 수업을 하는 도중에 화장실에 갔습니다.
examples.translation: gim ilbyeongeun sueobeul haneun dojunge hwajangsire gatseumnida. — In the middle of class, PFC Kim left to go to the bathroom.

explanations.title: Follow-up 1 (Speaking): the model
explanations.body: Student A picks a card and conjugates the phrase aloud, using –는/던 (도)중에 (결혼식을 하다 → 결혼식을 하던 도중에 or 결혼식을 하는 도중에). Student B creates a sentence that includes Student A’s phrase. The book’s model sentences (the English is mine):

examples.text: 결혼식을 하던 도중에 전기가 나갔어요.
examples.translation: gyeolhonsigeul hadeon dojunge jeongiga nagasseoyo. — The power went out in the middle of the wedding.

examples.text: 결혼식을 하는 중에 불이 났어요.
examples.translation: gyeolhonsigeul haneun junge buri nasseoyo. — A fire broke out in the middle of the wedding.

examples.text: 결혼식을 하던 중에 친구가 쓰러졌어요.
examples.translation: gyeolhonsigeul hadeon junge chinguga sseureojeosseoyo. — A friend collapsed in the middle of the wedding.

explanations.title: More sentences (mine)
explanations.body: Sample sentences of my own (the English is mine):

examples.translation: unjeonhaneun dojunge joreumi wasseoyo. — I got sleepy while driving.

examples.translation: gongbuhadeon dojunge chinguga chajawasseoyo. — A friend came to see me while I was studying.

examples.translation: hoeui dojunge hyudaeponi ullyeosseoyo. — My cell phone rang in the middle of the meeting.

examples.text: 식사하던 중에 지진이 났어요.
examples.translation: siksahadeon junge jijini nasseoyo. — An earthquake occurred while we were eating.

lessons.title: 541. Ch 43 · Grammar B: the sentence ending –(으)ㄴ/는데(요)
lessons.subtitle: -(으)ㄴ/는데(요) · 놀람 · 해결 요구 · 더 알고 싶음 · 비가 많이 오는데요 · 어디에 사는데요

explanations.title: Three implicit meanings
explanations.body:
The sentence ending –(으)ㄴ/는데(요) is another variation of the informal verb ending –아/어요; this ending is often used to convey one of the following implicit meanings:

1. “I am surprised.” (비가 많이 오는데요: It is raining a lot! 한국말이 쉬운데요: Korean is easy [to learn]!)

2. “Something has to be done.” (천장에서 물이 새는데요: The ceiling is leaking [and something has to be done about it]. 여보, 아기가 우는데: Honey, the baby is crying [and I want you to do something about it].)

3. “I’d like to know more about what you said.” (A: 우리 가족이 미국에 살아요. My family lives in the U.S. B: 그래요? 미국 어디에 사는데요? Really? Where in the U.S. do they live?)

Keep in mind that the first two uses work only in a statement. The third use only works in a wh- question.

examples.text: 비가 많이 오는데요.
examples.translation: biga mani oneundeyo. — It is raining a lot!

examples.text: 한국말이 쉬운데요.
examples.translation: hangungmari swiundeyo. — Korean is easy (to learn)!

examples.text: 천장에서 물이 새는데요.
examples.translation: cheonjangeseo muri saeneundeyo. — The ceiling is leaking (and something has to be done about it).

examples.text: 여보, 아기가 우는데.
examples.translation: yeobo, agiga uneunde. — Honey, the baby is crying (and I want you to do something about it).

examples.text: 우리 가족이 미국에 살아요.
examples.translation: uri gajogi miguge sarayo. — My family lives in the U.S.

examples.text: 그래요? 미국 어디에 사는데요?
examples.translation: geuraeyo? miguk eodie saneundeyo? — Really? Where in the U.S. do they live?

explanations.title: Follow-up 3 (Writing): change the endings to –(으)ㄴ/는데(요)
explanations.body: Change the endings of the following sentences into the –(으)ㄴ/는데(요) form; the first one is done for you (멋있는데요). The sentences are the book’s with the time spelled out; the answers and the English are mine.

Your wife cooks really well! (I am surprised)
There aren’t this many people on weekdays! (I am surprised)
When did you go to Oregon? (I’d like to know more)

explanations.title: Follow-up 5 (Speaking): one minute of talking
explanations.body: Sit in a circle; the first student chooses a topic from the list (내가 좋아하는 식당, 재미있었던 여행, 내가 다니던 고등학교, 군대에 입대하기 전에 한 일, 가장 친한 친구, 좋아하는 취미) and talks about it in Korean, using –(으)ㄴ/는데(요) as often as you can; each student has one minute. examples.text: 거기 온천도 있다고 하는데요.
examples.translation: geogi oncheondo itdago haneundeyo. — I hear there are hot springs there too.

examples.translation: jeoneun ajikdo mot ga bwasseoyo. — I still haven’t been able to go.

examples.translation: seonsaengnimdo bikseoe ga boseyo. — Teacher, you should go to Big Sur too.

examples.text: 얼마나 멋있는데요.

lessons.title: 542. Ch 43 · Activities B: two foreigners living in Korea
lessons.subtitle: 한국 생활에 적응하고 있어요 · 한미나 · 이용기 · 외국인의 어려움 · 이웃과 친해지기

explanations.title: Activity 3 (Listening, reading and speaking): adjusting to life in Korea
explanations.body: As a group, you will provide advice for a foreigner living in Korea. In step a, two foreigners describe the difficulties and concerns they face while living in Korea (Group A reads Foreigner A, Group B reads Foreigner B) and fill in a table in English (Korean name; occupation; difficulties and concerns). The passages are the book’s with the numbers spelled out; the English is mine.

examples.text: 제 한국 이름은 한미나에요.
examples.translation: je hanguk ireumeun hanminaeyo. — My Korean name is Han Mina.

examples.text: 저는 태국에서 왔어요.
examples.translation: jeoneun taegugeseo wasseoyo. — I came from Thailand.

examples.text: 오 년 전에 태국에서 한국인 남편을 만나 한국에 왔어요.
examples.translation: o nyeon jeone taegugeseo hangugin nampyeoneul manna hanguge wasseoyo. — Five years ago I met a Korean husband in Thailand and came to Korea.

examples.text: 지금은 주부예요.
examples.translation: jigeumeun jubuyeyo. — Now I am a housewife.

examples.text: 요즘 일자리를 찾고 있지만 쉽지 않아요.
examples.translation: yojeum iljarireul chatgo itjiman swipji anayo. — These days I am looking for a job, but it is not easy.

examples.text: 한국에 와서 한국말을 열심히 공부했어요.
examples.translation: hanguge waseo hangungmareul yeolsimhi gongbuhaesseoyo. — After coming to Korea, I studied Korean hard.

examples.text: 그렇지만, 한국말이 여전히 서툴러요.
examples.translation: geureochiman, hangungmari yeojeonhi seotulleoyo. — However, my Korean is still clumsy.

examples.text: 그리고 이웃과 친해지기도 쉽지 않아요.
examples.translation: geurigo iutgwa chinhaejigido swipji anayo. — And it is not easy to become close with the neighbors either.

examples.text: 가장 큰 걱정은 아이들의 교육이에요.
examples.translation: gajang keun geokjeongeun aideurui gyoyugieyo. — My biggest worry is my children’s education.

examples.text: 제 한국이름은 이용기입니다.
examples.translation: je hangugireumeun iyonggiimnida. — My Korean name is Lee Yonggi.

examples.text: 영국에서 왔습니다.
examples.translation: yeonggugeseo watseumnida. — I came from England.

examples.text: 한국에 온 지 삼 년 됐습니다.
examples.translation: hanguge on ji sam nyeon dwaetseumnida. — It has been three years since I came to Korea.

examples.text: 지금 영어학원 강사입니다.
examples.translation: jigeum yeongeohagwon gangsaimnida. — I am now an English academy instructor.

examples.text: 한국인 친구를 사귀고 싶지만, 기회가 없습니다.
examples.translation: hangugin chingureul sagwigo sipjiman, gihoega eopseumnida. — I want to make Korean friends, but there is no opportunity.

examples.text: 한국말 실력이 좋아졌지만, 여전히 회화는 어렵습니다.
examples.translation: hangungmal sillyeogi joajeotjiman, yeojeonhi hoehwaneun eoryeopseumnida. — My Korean ability has improved, but conversation is still difficult.

examples.text: 지금도 식당에 가면 한국말로 주문하기가 어려워요.
examples.translation: jigeumdo sikdange gamyeon hangungmallo jumunhagiga eoryeowoyo. — Even now, when I go to a restaurant, it is hard to order in Korean.

examples.text: 그리고 문화가 너무 달라서 이웃과 친해지기가 쉽지 않습니다.
examples.translation: geurigo munhwaga neomu dallaseo iutgwa chinhaejigiga swipji anseumnida. — And the culture is so different that it is not easy to become close with the neighbors.

examples.text: 어떻게 하면 이웃과 친해질 수 있을까요?
examples.translation: eotteoke hamyeon iutgwa chinhaejil su isseulkkayo? — How can I become close with my neighbors?

rows: Thailand (came five years ago after meeting her Korean husband)
Hard to find a job; Korean is still clumsy; hard to become close with neighbors; the biggest worry is the children’s education
No chance to make Korean friends; conversation and ordering in Korean are still hard; cultural differences make it hard to befriend neighbors (How can I become close with neighbors?)

explanations.title: Steps b and c
explanations.body: In step b, six tips on how foreigners can successfully adjust to life in Korea are on audio (summarized in English in a table; the group discusses which tips fit the foreigner). In step c, the group writes a list of advice tips, using the tips and its own ideas, and presents the advice and the passage summary to the class in Korean. These are audio and group activities and are left out.

explanations.title: Activities left out
explanations.body: Activity 1 (SMART Board) and Activity 2 (listening to four statements in which middle school students talk about a family member who is originally from a foreign country, writing the name of the continent for each country on the map [Germany, Mexico, China, Thailand] in Korean, and noting the relationship and the person’s speaking proficiency) are audio, map and computer activities.
